questions.text: Paella, a rice dish cooked in a wide, shallow pan, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Paella originated in the Valencia region, and its name is the Valencian word for frying pan.

questions.text: Hummus is a dip made mainly from which legume?
questions.fun_fact: In Arabic, hummus simply means 'chickpeas'; the full name of the dish means 'chickpeas with tahini'.

questions.text: The meringue dessert pavlova is named after a famous what?
questions.fun_fact: Australia and New Zealand both claim to have invented it, in honor of Anna Pavlova's tours in the 1920s.

questions.text: Pesto alla genovese comes from which Italian region?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Genoese verb pestâ, 'to pound', after the mortar and pestle used to make it.

questions.text: Ceviche, raw fish cured in citrus juice, is considered the national dish of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Citric acid in the lemon or lime juice alters the fish's proteins, turning the flesh firm and opaque as if cooked.

questions.text: Which French chef created the dessert peach Melba?
questions.fun_fact: It was first served at the Savoy Hotel in London in 1892 or 1893, to honor soprano Nellie Melba.

questions.text: Tempura was introduced to Japan in the 16th century by visitors from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Portugal still has a similar dish, peixinhos da horta ('garden fishes'): green beans dipped in batter and fried.

questions.text: Bobotie, spiced minced meat baked with an egg topping, is a traditional dish of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was adopted by the Cape Malay community and is usually served with 'yellow rice', cooked with turmeric.

questions.text: The word 'kindergarten' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: Educator Friedrich Fröbel coined it in 1840 for his play-based school; it means 'children's garden'.

questions.text: What does the Latin phrase 'carpe diem' mean?
questions.fun_fact: The phrase comes from a poem in the Roman poet Horace's 'Odes', published in 23 BC.

questions.text: The word 'sauna' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: The oldest known saunas in Finland were pits dug into a slope, used mainly as dwellings in winter.

questions.text: The word 'robot' was introduced in a 1920 play by which Czech writer?
questions.fun_fact: Čapek credited his brother Josef with the word, from the Czech 'robota', meaning forced labor.

questions.text: The word 'algebra' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: It comes from 'al-jabr', originally a term for bonesetting, which took on a mathematical meaning in the 9th century.

questions.text: The word 'safari' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: Swahili borrowed it from the Arabic word 'safar', meaning journey.

questions.text: Who created the constructed language Esperanto, published in 1887?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from Zamenhof's pen name, Doktoro Esperanto, meaning 'one who hopes'.

questions.text: The word 'muscle' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Greek has the same link: its word mys means both 'mouse' and 'muscle'.

questions.text: Who wrote the novel 'Don Quixote'?
questions.fun_fact: Published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615, it is often called the first modern novel.

questions.text: Who wrote the 1813 novel 'Pride and Prejudice'?
questions.fun_fact: Austen's original title for the novel was 'First Impressions'.

questions.text: Which Colombian author wrote 'One Hundred Years of Solitude'?
questions.fun_fact: The novel follows seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo.

questions.text: Which Nigerian author wrote the 1958 novel 'Things Fall Apart'?
questions.fun_fact: Its hero, Okonkwo, is a wrestling champion and leader in the fictional Igbo clan of Umuofia.

questions.text: Which Indian poet won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913?
questions.fun_fact: He was also a prolific composer; his roughly 2,230 songs are known as Rabindra Sangeet.

questions.text: The 11th-century Japanese classic 'The Tale of Genji' was written by whom?
questions.fun_fact: Murasaki Shikibu was a lady-in-waiting at the Heian imperial court; her real name is unknown.

questions.text: Which poet wrote 'The Lusiads', Portugal's national epic?
questions.fun_fact: Published in 1572, it celebrates Vasco da Gama's sea voyage from Portugal to India.

questions.text: Which Egyptian novelist wrote the 'Cairo Trilogy'?
questions.fun_fact: The trilogy's three novels, Palace Walk, Palace of Desire and Sugar Street, are named after streets in Cairo.

questions.text: Which artist painted 'The Scream'?
questions.fun_fact: Munch created several versions of it, in paint, in pastel and as a lithograph print.

questions.text: The painter Frida Kahlo came from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Her family home, La Casa Azul ('the Blue House'), is now the Frida Kahlo Museum.

questions.text: Which Dutch artist painted 'Girl with a Pearl Earring'?
questions.fun_fact: It is a 'tronie', a Dutch study of a head rather than a portrait, and the girl's identity is uncertain.

questions.text: Which Japanese artist created the woodblock print 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa'?
questions.fun_fact: It belongs to his series 'Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji', and Fuji appears small in the background.

questions.text: The Impressionist movement took its name from a painting by which artist?
questions.fun_fact: The painting, 'Impression, Sunrise' (1872), shows the port of Le Havre in France.

questions.text: Which painter created 'Las Meninas' in 1656?
questions.fun_fact: Velázquez painted himself into the scene, at work on a large canvas just behind the young princess.

questions.text: Who painted 'The Arnolfini Portrait' in 1434?
questions.fun_fact: Its convex mirror is painted larger than any such mirror that could actually be made at the time.

questions.text: Which artist painted 'A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte'?
questions.fun_fact: Seurat built the large canvas from countless tiny dots of color, a technique known as pointillism.

questions.text: The Lego toy company was founded in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Danish phrase 'leg godt', meaning 'play well'.

questions.text: The furniture company IKEA was founded in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The name combines founder Ingvar Kamprad's initials with Elmtaryd and Agunnaryd, his family farm and home village.

questions.text: The car brand Volvo takes its name from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Its logo, a circle with an arrow, is the old alchemical symbol for iron.

questions.text: When Nintendo was founded in 1889, what did it make?
questions.fun_fact: Its first cards were hanafuda, Japanese 'flower cards' with a different plant for each month of the year.

questions.text: The car maker Škoda comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: It began in 1895 as Laurin & Klement, a bicycle workshop in the town of Mladá Boleslav.

questions.text: When Nokia was founded in Finland in 1865, what did it operate?
questions.fun_fact: The company takes its name from the town of Nokia, where it opened a second mill in 1868.

questions.text: Before making cars, the Toyoda family business was best known for making what?
questions.fun_fact: The brand became Toyota partly because it takes eight strokes to write in katakana, and eight is a lucky number.

questions.text: The French luxury house Hermès began in 1837 as a maker of what?
questions.fun_fact: Its logo shows a horse-drawn carriage, a duc, with a groom standing beside it.

questions.text: Johannes Gutenberg is famous for developing which invention around 1440?
questions.fun_fact: Movable type had been invented centuries earlier in China, by the artisan Bi Sheng in the 11th century.

questions.text: The 'lead' in a pencil is actually made mainly of which material?
questions.fun_fact: A huge graphite deposit found at Borrowdale, England, in the 16th century fueled early pencil making.

questions.text: Which everyday item did Hungarian-born inventor László Bíró patent in 1938?
questions.fun_fact: In Britain and several other countries, a ballpoint pen is still commonly called a 'biro'.

questions.text: Swiss engineer George de Mestral was inspired to invent Velcro by what?
questions.fun_fact: The name Velcro blends the French words 'velours' (velvet) and 'crochet' (hook).

questions.text: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web while working at which organization?
questions.fun_fact: Berners-Lee also wrote the first web browser, called WorldWideWeb, in 1990.

questions.text: Paper money was first used in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Early notes, called jiaozi, were issued by merchants in Sichuan before the government took over in 1023.

questions.text: Which Dutch scientist invented the pendulum clock in 1656?
questions.fun_fact: Pendulum clocks remained the world's most accurate timekeepers until the 1930s.

questions.text: Bubble wrap was invented in 1957 as a failed attempt to make what?
questions.fun_fact: One of its first big uses came in 1960, protecting new IBM 1401 computers shipped to customers.

questions.text: Which mammals are the only ones capable of true powered flight?
questions.fun_fact: Bats are the second-largest order of mammals after rodents, making up about a fifth of all mammal species.

questions.text: What is a baby kangaroo called?
questions.fun_fact: A newborn joey is only about the size of a lima bean when it crawls into its mother's pouch.

questions.text: Which of these mammals lays eggs?
questions.fun_fact: Male platypuses have a venomous spur on each hind leg.

questions.text: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.fun_fact: Its blood is blue because it uses copper-rich hemocyanin to carry oxygen.

questions.text: What color is a polar bear's skin under its fur?
questions.fun_fact: Its fur is not actually white: the outer guard hairs are transparent and scatter light.

questions.text: The axolotl, sometimes called the Mexican walking fish, is actually a type of what?
questions.fun_fact: Axolotls can regrow lost limbs and gills, and even parts of their eyes and brain.

questions.text: Which animals are the closest living relatives of the hippopotamus?
questions.fun_fact: Hippos secrete a reddish fluid, nicknamed 'blood sweat', that acts as a natural sunscreen.

questions.text: Which plant produces the largest individual flowers in the world?
questions.fun_fact: It has no leaves, stems or roots of its own and lives as a parasite on a tropical vine.

questions.text: In Greek myth, who flew too close to the sun on wings made of feathers and wax?
questions.fun_fact: His father, Daedalus, who made the wings, also built the Labyrinth for King Minos of Crete.

questions.text: Which goddess was the patron of the ancient city of Athens?
questions.fun_fact: In myth she won the city by offering an olive tree, beating Poseidon's gift of a saltwater spring.

questions.text: In Roman legend, the twins Romulus and Remus were nursed by which animal?
questions.fun_fact: The twins were said to be nursed in a cave called the Lupercal, at the foot of Rome's Palatine Hill.

questions.text: In Norse mythology, what is the name of Thor's hammer?
questions.fun_fact: Small Mjölnir pendants were widely worn across Viking Age Scandinavia.

questions.text: Which Egyptian god is usually shown with the head of a falcon?
questions.fun_fact: The 'Eye of Horus' was a widely used ancient Egyptian symbol of protection.

questions.text: Which Aztec deity was known as the 'Feathered Serpent'?
questions.fun_fact: The resplendent quetzal, the bird whose name forms part of his, is Guatemala's national bird.

questions.text: Gilgamesh, hero of an ancient Mesopotamian epic, was king of which city?
questions.fun_fact: The most complete version of the epic survives on clay tablets from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh.

questions.text: In Polynesian myth, which demigod fished up islands from the sea and slowed the sun?
questions.fun_fact: In Māori tradition, New Zealand's North Island is Te Ika-a-Māui, 'the fish of Māui'.

questions.text: The teddy bear is named after which US president?
questions.fun_fact: Around the same time, in 1902, German toymaker Richard Steiff also designed a stuffed bear.

questions.text: Matryoshka nesting dolls are a traditional craft of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The first Russian set, carved in the 1890s, had eight dolls, the outermost a mother holding a rooster.

questions.text: The Rubik's Cube was invented in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first called it the 'Magic Cube' when he made it in 1974.

questions.text: Chaturanga, the ancient game widely seen as the ancestor of chess, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its name refers to the four divisions of an ancient army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots.

questions.text: The video game Tetris was created in 1984 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its name blends 'tetra', as every piece has four squares, with tennis, its creator's favorite sport.

questions.text: How many tiles are in a standard double-six set of dominoes?
questions.fun_fact: The earliest known mentions of dominoes come from Song dynasty China.

questions.text: Which board game is played on a board split by a 'river', with pieces including elephants and cannons?
questions.fun_fact: In xiangqi, the elephants may not cross the river into the opponent's half of the board.

questions.text: The name 'Frisbee' comes from a company that made what?
questions.fun_fact: Wham-O first marketed the plastic disc as the Pluto Platter, then renamed it after hearing students call it a 'Frisbee'.

questions.text: Machu Picchu in Peru was built by which civilization?
questions.fun_fact: Built in the 15th century, it is believed to have served as an estate for the emperor Pachacuti.

questions.text: The Petronas Twin Towers stand in which city?
questions.fun_fact: From 1998 to 2004 they were the tallest buildings in the world.

questions.text: Which Danish architect designed the Sydney Opera House?
questions.fun_fact: Utzon won the design competition in 1957, but the building did not open until 1973.

questions.text: The Eiffel Tower was built for the World's Fair held in Paris in which year?
questions.fun_fact: It was due to be taken down after 20 years, but was saved partly by its usefulness for radio telegraphy.

questions.text: Which architect designed Park Güell in Barcelona?
questions.fun_fact: It was planned as a luxury housing estate, but only two homes were ever built, neither by Gaudí.

questions.text: Which architect designed the National Congress building in Brasília?
questions.fun_fact: In 1988 Niemeyer won the Pritzker Architecture Prize, often called architecture's highest honor.

questions.text: The Colosseum in Rome was built under emperors of which dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: Its name is believed to come from a colossal bronze statue of Nero that once stood beside it.

questions.text: The rock-cut city of Petra, in modern Jordan, was the capital of which ancient people's kingdom?
questions.fun_fact: Petra is nicknamed the 'Rose City' after the color of the sandstone it is carved from.

questions.text: How many days are in a leap year?
questions.fun_fact: Century years are leap years only if divisible by 400, so 2000 was a leap year but 1900 was not.

questions.text: How long is a fortnight?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from Old English for 'fourteen nights', as the Anglo-Saxons counted time by nights.

questions.text: The name of which month comes from the Latin word for 'eight'?
questions.fun_fact: It was the eighth month of the early Roman calendar, which began the year in March.

questions.text: Exactly how many centimeters are in one inch?
questions.fun_fact: The word inch comes from the Latin 'uncia', meaning one-twelfth, as a foot has 12 inches.

questions.text: The Celsius temperature scale is named after an astronomer from which country?
questions.fun_fact: His original 1742 scale was upside down: 0 was the boiling point of water and 100 the freezing point.

questions.text: How many meters are in one international nautical mile?
questions.fun_fact: It was originally based on one minute of arc of latitude measured along a meridian.

questions.text: Which country's calendar has 12 months of 30 days plus a short 13th month?
questions.fun_fact: The Ethiopian new year usually falls on 11 September in the Gregorian calendar.

questions.text: The old unit of length called the furlong originally described the length of what?
questions.fun_fact: There are eight furlongs in a mile, so one furlong is about 201 meters.

questions.text: In the NATO phonetic alphabet, which word represents the letter H?
questions.fun_fact: Its code words were chosen after hundreds of thousands of comprehension tests involving 31 nationalities.

questions.text: What is the name of the symbol '&'?
questions.fun_fact: It began as a ligature of the letters e and t, spelling the Latin word 'et', meaning 'and'.

questions.text: Which number does the Roman numeral M represent?
questions.fun_fact: Roman numerals had no symbol for zero; medieval scholars wrote the word nulla, or just N, instead.

questions.text: In Morse code, which letter is sent as a single dot?
questions.fun_fact: E got the shortest code because it is the most common letter in English.

questions.text: How many dot positions make up a standard braille cell?
questions.fun_fact: It grew out of Charles Barbier's raised-dot code, later nicknamed 'night writing' when considered for soldiers' use in the dark.

questions.text: The interrobang (‽) combines which two punctuation marks?
questions.fun_fact: Martin K. Speckter proposed it in 1962; 'bang' is printers' slang for the exclamation mark.

questions.text: In Italian, the @ symbol is called 'chiocciola', which means what?
questions.fun_fact: In Dutch the same symbol is called 'apenstaart', meaning 'monkey's tail'.

questions.text: What does the pilcrow symbol (¶) traditionally mark?
questions.fun_fact: Scribes left gaps for pilcrows to be painted in later; when they were skipped, the gap became the indent.

questions.text: Money gifts at Chinese New Year are traditionally given in envelopes of which color?
questions.fun_fact: In Cantonese they are called lai see, and they are also given at weddings and birthdays.

questions.text: Which color is the national color of the Netherlands?
questions.fun_fact: The color honors the royal House of Orange-Nassau, named after the Principality of Orange in France.

questions.text: The pigment ultramarine was originally made by grinding which stone?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'beyond the sea', as the stone was shipped to Europe from mines in Afghanistan.

questions.text: On a screen, which color is produced by mixing red and green light?
questions.fun_fact: Most screens build every color they show from just three colors of light: red, green and blue.

questions.text: The dye indigo takes its name from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Denim jeans traditionally get their blue color from indigo dye.

questions.text: Vermilion is a bright shade of which color?
questions.fun_fact: It was traditionally made by grinding cinnabar, a mineral form of mercury sulfide.

questions.text: The ancient dye Tyrian purple was made from which source?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Tyre, in ancient Phoenicia, and making it took tens of thousands of snails.

questions.text: La Tomatina, a festival where crowds throw tomatoes at each other, is held in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It takes place in the town of Buñol, near Valencia, on the last Wednesday of August.

questions.text: The haka is a traditional ceremonial dance of which people?
questions.fun_fact: The famous 'Ka Mate' haka, popularized worldwide by the All Blacks, is attributed to Ngāti Toa leader Te Rauparaha.

questions.text: Which dish is the centerpiece of a traditional Scottish Burns supper?
questions.fun_fact: Burns's poem 'Address to a Haggis' is recited before the haggis is cut open.

questions.text: Mooncakes are traditionally eaten during which Chinese festival?
questions.fun_fact: Many mooncakes hide one or more salted egg yolks in the center to symbolize the full moon.

questions.text: The tango dance originated in the Río de la Plata region of Argentina and which other country?
questions.fun_fact: Tango was born in the region's poor port districts, blending styles such as the milonga and the habanera.

questions.text: Kente, a brightly colored cloth woven in narrow strips, is most associated with which country?
questions.fun_fact: According to Asante tradition, kente originated in the village of Bonwire, in the Ashanti Region.

questions.text: Up Helly Aa, a fire festival ending with the burning of a Viking-style galley, is held in which islands?
questions.fun_fact: The main festival in Lerwick is held on the last Tuesday of January.

questions.text: Which king of Macedon built an empire stretching from Greece to northwestern India by the age of 30?
questions.fun_fact: As a boy, Alexander was tutored by the philosopher Aristotle until the age of 16.

questions.text: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.fun_fact: Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface more than six and a half hours after Apollo 11's lunar module touched down.

questions.text: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.fun_fact: The Mona Lisa is painted in oil on a poplar wood panel rather than on canvas.

questions.text: In which year did Christopher Columbus first sail across the Atlantic?
questions.fun_fact: Columbus's three ships on that first voyage were the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María.

questions.text: The Parthenon stands on the Acropolis of which city?
questions.fun_fact: The Parthenon was completed in 438 BC, although work on its decoration continued until 432 BC.

questions.text: Who became the first human in space, in April 1961?
questions.fun_fact: Gagarin's Vostok 1 flight completed one orbit of Earth in about 108 minutes.

questions.text: Which scientist invented the World Wide Web in 1989?
questions.fun_fact: Berners-Lee wrote his proposal for the Web while working at CERN, near Geneva.

questions.text: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
questions.fun_fact: The statue's internal iron framework was designed by Gustave Eiffel, the engineer behind the Eiffel Tower.

questions.text: Genghis Khan founded which empire?
questions.fun_fact: At its height, the Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history.

questions.text: Which physicist developed the theories of special and general relativity?
questions.fun_fact: Einstein's 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for explaining the photoelectric effect, not for relativity.

questions.text: Who wrote 'On the Origin of Species', published in 1859?
questions.fun_fact: Darwin developed many of his ideas after a five-year voyage around the world aboard HMS Beagle.

questions.text: Which British monarch reigned from 1837 to 1901?
questions.fun_fact: Victoria became queen at the age of 18, and the Victorian era is named after her.

questions.text: Which pharaoh's largely intact tomb did Howard Carter discover in 1922?
questions.fun_fact: Carter's excavation in the Valley of the Kings was funded by the English aristocrat Lord Carnarvon.

questions.text: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
questions.fun_fact: The marathon made its debut at the 1896 Games and was won by the Greek runner Spyridon Louis.

questions.text: What was the capital city of the Byzantine Empire?
questions.fun_fact: Emperor Constantine I dedicated Constantinople as his new capital in AD 330, on the site of ancient Byzantium.

questions.text: Who developed a movable-type printing press in Mainz in the mid-1400s?
questions.fun_fact: Gutenberg's innovations included adjustable molds for casting type and the use of oil-based ink for printing books.

questions.text: The Maya city of Chichén Itzá is in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: Chichén Itzá was named one of the New 7 Wonders of the World in a 2007 global poll.

questions.text: Which South American country is named after Simón Bolívar?
questions.fun_fact: Bolívar was born in Caracas, Venezuela, in 1783 and became known as 'El Libertador'.

questions.text: From which country did Brazil declare independence in 1822?
questions.fun_fact: After independence, Brazil became an empire, with Pedro I as its first emperor.

questions.text: In which year was the Bastille stormed in Paris?
questions.fun_fact: France's national day, known in English as Bastille Day, is celebrated every year on 14 July.

questions.text: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
questions.fun_fact: Historian Arnold Toynbee's 1881 lectures helped popularize the term 'Industrial Revolution'.

questions.text: Which machine did Scottish engineer James Watt famously improve?
questions.fun_fact: The watt, the SI unit of power, is named after him.

questions.text: In 1610, Galileo described four moons orbiting which planet?
questions.fun_fact: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto are still known as the Galilean moons in his honor.

questions.text: Which country launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, in 1957?
questions.fun_fact: Sputnik 1 was a polished metal sphere about 58 cm across with four external radio antennas.

questions.text: Which company launched the Walkman portable cassette player in 1979?
questions.fun_fact: The first Walkman model, the TPS-L2, went on sale in Japan in July 1979.

questions.text: The Americas are named after which Italian explorer?
questions.fun_fact: The name 'America' was first applied to the New World on a 1507 map by the German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller.

questions.text: Claude Monet was a founder of which art movement?
questions.fun_fact: The movement took its name from Monet's 1872 painting 'Impression, Sunrise'.

questions.text: Which artist painted 'The Persistence of Memory', with its melting clocks?
questions.fun_fact: Despite its fame, the 1931 painting is small, measuring only about 24 by 33 cm.

questions.text: Which French ruler was exiled to the Mediterranean island of Elba in 1814?
questions.fun_fact: Napoleon escaped from Elba only ten months later and marched on Paris to reclaim power.

questions.text: Which network of trade routes linked China with the West from the 2nd century BC to the 15th century?
questions.fun_fact: The name was popularized in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.

questions.text: In which year did India gain independence from British rule?
questions.fun_fact: India's independence took effect at midnight on 15 August, the date now celebrated as Independence Day.

questions.text: By what name was Thailand known before 1939?
questions.fun_fact: Bangkok became the Siamese capital in 1782 under King Rama I.

questions.text: Which Ford car model was introduced in 1908?
questions.fun_fact: Ford introduced a moving assembly line in 1913, greatly speeding up Model T production.

questions.text: Mexico City stands on the site of which Aztec capital?
questions.fun_fact: Tenochtitlan, traditionally founded in 1325, was built on an island in Lake Texcoco.

questions.text: Who was the first Roman emperor?
questions.fun_fact: The month of August is named in honor of Augustus.

questions.text: Which state unified China in 221 BC?
questions.fun_fact: The Qin standardized coins, weights, measures and the written script across China.

questions.text: Ferdinand Magellan's 1519 expedition sailed in the service of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Magellan named the Pacific 'Mar Pacífico', meaning peaceful sea, because its waters seemed calm.

questions.text: Who painted 'The Birth of Venus' in the 1480s?
questions.fun_fact: The painting shows the goddess Venus arriving at the shore standing on a giant scallop shell.

questions.text: Hammurabi, famous for his code of laws, was king of which ancient city?
questions.fun_fact: His law code is the longest legal text to have survived from the ancient Near East.

questions.text: Which Norse explorer reached a land called Vinland around the year 1000?
questions.fun_fact: A Norse site found at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada, proves Vikings reached North America.

questions.text: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World stood in Alexandria?
questions.fun_fact: Its name, Pharos, became the root of the word for lighthouse in languages such as French (phare).

questions.text: The Rosetta Stone was key to deciphering which writing system?
questions.fun_fact: The stone carries the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphic, Demotic and ancient Greek.

questions.text: Cuneiform, one of the earliest writing systems, developed in which region?
questions.fun_fact: Cuneiform was written by pressing a cut reed stylus into tablets of wet clay.

questions.text: Which ancient civilization built the city of Mohenjo-daro?
questions.fun_fact: Built around 2500 BC, Mohenjo-daro had a planned street grid and an advanced drainage system.

questions.text: Emperor Ashoka belonged to which Indian dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: The State Emblem of India is an adaptation of the Lion Capital of Ashoka, found at Sarnath.

questions.text: Who founded the Mughal Empire in 1526?
questions.fun_fact: Babur wrote his memoirs, the Baburnama, in Chagatai, a Turkic language.

questions.text: Mansa Musa ruled which West African empire?
questions.fun_fact: Mansa Musa expanded his empire to include the trading cities of Gao and Timbuktu.

questions.text: The ancient city of Carthage lies in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: Carthage was founded by Phoenician settlers from the city of Tyre, in modern Lebanon.

questions.text: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas divided newly claimed lands between Spain and which country?
questions.fun_fact: The treaty's dividing line ran 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands.

questions.text: In which year was the double-helix structure of DNA first published?
questions.fun_fact: James Watson and Francis Crick's paper describing the double helix appeared in the journal Nature.

questions.text: In which year was Magna Carta first sealed by King John?
questions.fun_fact: King John agreed to the charter at Runnymede, beside the River Thames near Windsor.

questions.text: Which was the last imperial dynasty of China?
questions.fun_fact: The last Qing emperor, Puyi, abdicated in 1912 when he was just six years old.

questions.text: The historic Kingdom of Benin, famed for the Benin Bronzes, was in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: Despite their name, most of the Benin Bronzes are actually made of brass.

questions.text: Which era of Japanese history began in 1868?
questions.fun_fact: Japan's first railway opened in 1872 during the Meiji era, linking Tokyo and Yokohama.

questions.text: Angkor was the capital of which Southeast Asian empire?
questions.fun_fact: The ruins of Angkor lie in modern Cambodia, near the city of Siem Reap.

questions.text: Which Ottoman sultan was known in Europe as 'the Magnificent'?
questions.fun_fact: In Turkey he is known as Kanuni, meaning 'the Lawgiver'.

questions.text: Who founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire?
questions.fun_fact: Cyrus built his capital, Pasargadae, in modern Iran, with palaces set in vast formal gardens.

questions.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for which pharaoh?
questions.fun_fact: When completed it stood about 146.6 m tall; the loss of its smooth limestone casing has since lowered it.

questions.text: Which city was the capital of the Inca Empire?
questions.fun_fact: Cusco sits high in Peru's Andes, at an altitude of about 3,400 m.

questions.text: Which Mesoamerican civilization carved giant stone heads?
questions.fun_fact: The heads were carved from volcanic basalt boulders from the Tuxtla Mountains of Veracruz, Mexico.

questions.text: In which year did the Panama Canal open?
questions.fun_fact: Locks lift ships about 26 m above sea level to cross Gatun Lake in the middle of the canal.

questions.text: Which Portuguese navigator reached India by sea in 1498?
questions.fun_fact: Da Gama landed near Calicut, now Kozhikode, on India's southwest coast.

questions.text: Which navigator charted the east coast of Australia in 1770?
questions.fun_fact: Cook made this voyage aboard HMS Endeavour.

questions.text: Which Caribbean nation declared independence from France in 1804?
questions.fun_fact: The Haitian Revolution made Haiti the first sovereign state in the Caribbean.

questions.text: Which astronomer published 'On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres' in 1543?
questions.fun_fact: Copernicus was born in 1473 in Toruń, in what is now Poland.

questions.text: Which Russian chemist published a periodic table of the elements in 1869?
questions.fun_fact: Mendeleev was born in 1834 in Siberia, near the town of Tobolsk.

questions.text: Which mathematician proposed the 'imitation game' test of machine intelligence in 1950?
questions.fun_fact: Turing set out the idea in his paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', published in the journal Mind.

questions.text: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module?
questions.fun_fact: Michael Collins orbited the Moon alone in the command module Columbia while the lunar module was on the surface.

questions.text: The Venetian traveler Marco Polo spent years in the service of which Mongol ruler?
questions.fun_fact: Kublai Khan's summer capital, Shangdu, is also known as Xanadu.

questions.text: The ruins of ancient Troy lie in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: Archaeologists have identified nine layers at the site, each a city built on the ruins of the one before.

questions.text: Which city became the seat of Japan's imperial court in 794 and remained so for over 1,000 years?
questions.fun_fact: The city was laid out on a grid modeled on Chang'an, the ancient capital of China.

questions.text: Which banking family was a major patron of the arts in Renaissance Florence?
questions.fun_fact: The Medici family's art acquisitions form the core of the Uffizi museum in Florence.

questions.text: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in December 1911?
questions.fun_fact: Amundsen's team relied on sled dogs to haul their supplies across the ice.

questions.text: The medieval traveler Ibn Battuta was born in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: He spent nearly three decades traveling, and his journeys are recorded in a book known as the Rihla.

questions.text: Admiral Zheng He led great treasure voyages for which Chinese dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: His fleets reached as far as the east coast of Africa in the early 15th century.

questions.text: The House of Wisdom, a great medieval center of learning, was in which city?
questions.fun_fact: Scholars there translated many Greek works of science and philosophy into Arabic.

questions.text: Which people carved the moai statues of Easter Island?
questions.fun_fact: Most moai were carved from volcanic tuff at the Rano Raraku quarry on the island.

questions.text: Which Athenian is credited with democratic reforms around 508 BC?
questions.fun_fact: His reforms reorganized the citizens of Athens into ten new tribes.

questions.text: Which king commissioned the Domesday Book, completed in 1086?
questions.fun_fact: The survey names a total of 13,418 places across England.

questions.text: Bi Sheng invented movable type printing around 1040 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Bi Sheng's system used fired clay pieces, one for each Chinese character.

questions.text: Which ancient African kingdom built the pyramids of Meroë?
questions.fun_fact: Kushite kings also ruled Egypt as its 25th Dynasty in the 8th and 7th centuries BC.

questions.text: Which woman ruled ancient Egypt as pharaoh in the 15th century BC?
questions.fun_fact: Hatshepsut was often depicted in official art wearing a pharaoh's false beard.

questions.text: What were the knotted cords the Inca used for keeping records called?
questions.fun_fact: Quipus could record numbers using knots in a base-10 positional system.

questions.text: In which year did the Suez Canal open?
questions.fun_fact: Unlike the Panama Canal, the Suez Canal has no locks, so seawater flows freely through it.

questions.text: In which year was the Treaty of Waitangi signed in New Zealand?
questions.fun_fact: The first signing, on 6 February, is marked every year by Waitangi Day, New Zealand's national day.

questions.text: Who invented the spinning jenny in the 1760s?
questions.fun_fact: The spinning jenny let a single worker operate eight or more spools at once.

questions.text: In which year was Isaac Newton's 'Principia' first published?
questions.fun_fact: The astronomer Edmond Halley encouraged the work and gave financial help for its publication.

questions.text: Ada Lovelace wrote famous notes on which machine designed by Charles Babbage?
questions.fun_fact: Ada Lovelace was the only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron.

questions.text: Which space shuttle carried the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit in 1990?
questions.fun_fact: A flaw in Hubble's main mirror was corrected by astronauts on a servicing mission in 1993.

questions.text: In which year were the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 space probes launched?
questions.fun_fact: Each Voyager carries a Golden Record with sounds and images chosen to represent life on Earth.

questions.text: Which artist painted the fresco 'The School of Athens'?
questions.fun_fact: The philosophers Plato and Aristotle stand together at the center of the fresco.

questions.text: The ancient city of Aksum, known for its giant carved stone stelae, is in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: The Kingdom of Aksum minted its own coins in gold, silver and bronze.

questions.text: Which Korean king introduced the Hangul alphabet in the 15th century?
questions.fun_fact: The alphabet was promulgated in 1446 in a document called the Hunminjeongeum.

questions.text: Which clan's shoguns ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868?
questions.fun_fact: Their seat of power, Edo, was renamed Tokyo in 1868.

questions.text: In which year was the Republic of Turkey proclaimed?
questions.fun_fact: Ankara, rather than Istanbul, was chosen as the capital of the new republic.

questions.text: Which Spanish conquistador founded the city of Santiago, Chile, in 1541?
questions.fun_fact: He named it Santiago del Nuevo Extremo, partly after his home region of Extremadura in Spain.

questions.text: In which year is the Western Roman Empire traditionally said to have fallen?
questions.fun_fact: That year the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer.

questions.text: Eratosthenes of Cyrene is famous for estimating what?
questions.fun_fact: He compared the Sun's noon angle at Syene and at Alexandria to make his calculation.

questions.text: The word 'algorithm' comes from the name of which medieval scholar?
questions.fun_fact: The word 'algebra' comes from 'al-jabr', a term in the title of one of his books.

questions.text: The medieval Hanseatic League of trading towns was centered on which sea?
questions.fun_fact: Many Hanseatic towns adopted 'Lübeck law', named after the league's most prominent member city.

questions.text: Which city became the first capital of the unified Kingdom of Italy in 1861?
questions.fun_fact: The capital moved to Florence in 1865 and finally to Rome in 1871.

questions.text: In 1513, Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed which isthmus to see the Pacific Ocean?
questions.fun_fact: Balboa called the ocean the 'Mar del Sur', or South Sea, because it lay south of the isthmus.

questions.text: In which city did the Lumière brothers hold their public film screening of 28 December 1895?
questions.fun_fact: Their Cinématographe worked as a camera, a film printer and a projector all in one.

questions.text: The Bauhaus school of design was founded in 1919 in which German city?
questions.fun_fact: The school was founded by the architect Walter Gropius.

questions.text: The Majapahit Empire was based on which island?
questions.fun_fact: The Majapahit Empire flourished from 1293 until around 1527.

questions.text: Which king united the Hawaiian Islands into one kingdom in 1810?
questions.fun_fact: Hawaii's King Kamehameha I Day holiday was first proclaimed in 1871 by his grandson, Kamehameha V.

questions.text: Independence leader José de San Martín was born in which present-day country?
questions.fun_fact: San Martín was given the title 'Protector of Peru' in 1821.

questions.text: In which year did the Mexican Revolution begin?
questions.fun_fact: It began with a call to revolt issued by Francisco Madero in his Plan of San Luis Potosí.

questions.text: In which year was the Dutch East India Company (VOC) founded?
questions.fun_fact: The VOC founded Batavia, now Jakarta, as its Asian headquarters in 1619.

questions.text: The medieval Swahili trading city of Kilwa Kisiwani is in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: For about 500 years, from around 1100 to 1600, Kilwa minted its own coins.

questions.text: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
questions.fun_fact: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be beaten into a sheet about one square meter in area.

questions.text: Which is the lightest chemical element?
questions.fun_fact: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, making up roughly three quarters of all normal matter by mass.

questions.text: Sodium chloride is better known by which everyday name?
questions.fun_fact: As a natural mineral, sodium chloride is called halite, or rock salt.

questions.text: Rust is an oxide of which metal?
questions.fun_fact: Aluminum oxidizes too, but its thin oxide layer seals the surface and protects the metal beneath from further corrosion.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.fun_fact: At Earth's surface, an object with a mass of about 102 grams weighs roughly one newton.

questions.text: Which scientist formulated the three laws of motion that underpin classical mechanics?
questions.fun_fact: Newton wrote the Principia in Latin; its full title means 'Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy'.

questions.text: Which physicist is famous for the equation E = mc²?
questions.fun_fact: His 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics honored his explanation of the photoelectric effect, not his theories of relativity.

questions.text: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.fun_fact: Mars is home to Olympus Mons, a giant volcano about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.

questions.text: Which is the largest planet in the Solar System?
questions.fun_fact: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets in the Solar System combined.

questions.text: Which planet orbits closest to the Sun?
questions.fun_fact: A year on Mercury, one full orbit of the Sun, lasts only about 88 Earth days.

questions.text: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our Solar System?
questions.fun_fact: The Solar System takes about 240 million years to complete one orbit around the center of the Milky Way.

questions.text: What does a light-year measure?
questions.fun_fact: One light-year is about 9.46 trillion kilometers, the distance light travels in a vacuum in one Julian year.

questions.text: In which year did astronauts first walk on the Moon?
questions.fun_fact: The Apollo 11 crew brought back about 21.5 kilograms of lunar rock and soil.

questions.text: What is a space rock that survives its fall through Earth's atmosphere and reaches the ground called?
questions.fun_fact: Meteorites that are seen falling and then recovered are called 'falls'; all others are known as 'finds'.

questions.text: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make sugars by photosynthesis?
questions.fun_fact: Most of a tree's dry mass ultimately comes from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.

questions.text: Which cell structure is often called the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.fun_fact: Mitochondria carry their own small set of DNA, which in most animals is inherited only from the mother.

questions.text: What is the process called in which a caterpillar transforms into a butterfly?
questions.fun_fact: Inside the chrysalis, much of the caterpillar's body breaks down and is rebuilt into adult structures.

questions.text: What is the scientific name for modern humans?
questions.fun_fact: The name was coined by Carl Linnaeus in 1758 and is Latin for 'wise man'.

questions.text: Which pigment gives plants their green color?
questions.fun_fact: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light strongly but absorbs green light poorly, so leaves look green.

questions.text: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.fun_fact: Each heartbeat starts in the sinoatrial node, a cluster of cells in the right atrium that acts as a natural pacemaker.

questions.text: What is the longest bone in the human body?
questions.fun_fact: The femur is also the strongest bone in the body, and it is the only bone in the thigh.

questions.text: Which type of blood cell carries oxygen around the body?
questions.fun_fact: Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus and circulate for about 100–120 days before being recycled.

questions.text: What is molten rock called while it is still beneath Earth's surface?
questions.fun_fact: When it erupts as lava, its temperature is almost always between about 700 °C and 1,400 °C.

questions.text: Which instrument is used to measure atmospheric pressure?
questions.fun_fact: Standard atmospheric pressure at sea level is defined as exactly 101.325 kilopascals.

questions.text: The Ring of Fire, a belt of volcanoes and earthquakes, runs around the edges of which ocean?
questions.fun_fact: This horseshoe-shaped belt is about 40,000 kilometers long.

questions.text: What is the scientific study of prehistoric life, mainly through fossils, called?
questions.fun_fact: Paleontologists also study trace fossils, such as preserved footprints, burrows and coprolites, or fossilized dung.

questions.text: In computing, what does CPU stand for?
questions.fun_fact: The Intel 4004 microprocessor, released in 1971, contained about 2,300 transistors.

questions.text: In modern computing, how many bits make up one byte?
questions.fun_fact: The term byte was coined by IBM engineer Werner Buchholz in 1956, during design work on the Stretch computer.

questions.text: What is the value of pi rounded to two decimal places?
questions.fun_fact: Pi is irrational: its decimal digits never end and never settle into a repeating pattern.

questions.text: In flat (Euclidean) geometry, what do the interior angles of a triangle add up to?
questions.fun_fact: On a curved surface such as a sphere, the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180°.

questions.text: What is the name of a polygon with eight sides?
questions.fun_fact: Each interior angle of a regular octagon measures exactly 135°.

questions.text: Which theorem states that, in a right triangle, a² + b² = c²?
questions.fun_fact: Babylonian mathematicians were using this relationship more than 1,000 years before Pythagoras was born.

questions.text: Which organs do fish use to take in oxygen from water?
questions.fun_fact: Fish gills use countercurrent exchange: blood in the gill filaments flows in the opposite direction to the water.

questions.text: Which element has the chemical symbol Na?
questions.fun_fact: The symbol comes from natrium, a Latin name linked to natron, a natural salt used in ancient Egypt.

questions.text: Diamond and graphite are two forms of which element?
questions.fun_fact: At everyday temperature and pressure, graphite is the more stable form, though diamond turns into it extremely slowly.

questions.text: Which element is named after the Greek word for the Sun?
questions.fun_fact: Helium was detected in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, decades before it was first isolated on Earth in 1895.

questions.text: Which chemist used gaps in his periodic table to predict undiscovered elements such as gallium and germanium?
questions.fun_fact: Element 101, mendelevium, is named in his honor.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of frequency?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Heinrich Hertz, who was the first to conclusively prove that electromagnetic waves exist.

questions.text: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
questions.fun_fact: Since 1983, the meter has been defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

questions.text: Which British physicist is credited with discovering the electron in 1897?
questions.fun_fact: His son, George Paget Thomson, later shared a Nobel Prize for showing that electrons also behave like waves.

questions.text: Which German physicist discovered X-rays in 1895?
questions.fun_fact: He received the first Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded in 1901.

questions.text: Which color of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.fun_fact: Just beyond red lies infrared, discovered by William Herschel in 1800 when he measured temperatures past the red end of a spectrum.

questions.text: What is the change in pitch of a siren as it passes you called?
questions.fun_fact: Christian Doppler described the effect in 1842; astronomers use it to measure how fast stars move toward or away from us.

questions.text: Which planet has the hottest surface?
questions.fun_fact: Venus rotates so slowly that one rotation takes about 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day year.

questions.text: Titan, a moon with a thick nitrogen-rich atmosphere, orbits which planet?
questions.fun_fact: Titan has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane on its surface.

questions.text: Which planet is tilted so far over, at about 98°, that it effectively spins on its side?
questions.fun_fact: William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781, making it the first planet found with a telescope.

questions.text: Which is the closest known star to the Sun?
questions.fun_fact: Proxima Centauri is a small red dwarf, far too faint to be seen with the naked eye.

questions.text: Which astronomer showed that planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits?
questions.fun_fact: Kepler based his laws on the precise observations of Tycho Brahe, whose assistant he became in 1600.

questions.text: What was the name of the first artificial satellite, launched in 1957?
questions.fun_fact: Sputnik 1 was a polished metal sphere 58 centimeters across with four long radio antennas.

questions.text: Which marsupial has the northernmost native range in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Opossums have 50 teeth, more than any other North American land mammal.

questions.text: Which plant tissue carries water from the roots up to the leaves?
questions.fun_fact: Its partner tissue, phloem, carries sugars made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

questions.text: In animals, which type of cell division produces sperm and egg cells?
questions.fun_fact: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so human sperm and egg cells each carry 23 chromosomes instead of 46.

questions.text: Which scientist's experiments with pea plants laid the foundations of genetics?
questions.fun_fact: His results, published in 1866, were largely overlooked until they were rediscovered around 1900.

questions.text: In the main ranks of biological classification, which rank sits directly above genus?
questions.fun_fact: Lions and tigers share the genus Panthera, which belongs to the cat family, Felidae.

questions.text: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.fun_fact: Together with the malleus and incus, it passes sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear.

questions.text: Which organ produces the hormone insulin?
questions.fun_fact: Insulin is made by beta cells grouped in tiny clusters called the islets of Langerhans.

questions.text: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
questions.fun_fact: Enamel is about 96% mineral, mostly a crystalline calcium phosphate called hydroxyapatite.

questions.text: Which part of the brain plays the main role in coordinating movement and balance?
questions.fun_fact: Although it makes up only about 10% of the brain's volume, the cerebellum holds more than half of its neurons.

questions.text: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.fun_fact: In adults, the pulmonary arteries are the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood.

questions.text: What name is given to the supercontinent that joined almost all of Earth's land about 250 million years ago?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from Ancient Greek words meaning 'all' and 'Earth'.

questions.text: In which layer of the atmosphere does nearly all weather happen?
questions.fun_fact: Air in the troposphere gets colder with height, by about 6.5 °C per kilometer on average.

questions.text: Which layer of Earth is made mostly of liquid iron and nickel?
questions.fun_fact: Swirling motion in this liquid metal generates Earth's magnetic field.

questions.text: Which towering cloud type produces thunderstorms?
questions.fun_fact: The top of a cumulonimbus can spread out against the tropopause into a flat shape known as an anvil.

questions.text: Which mineral marks the softest point, 1, on the Mohs hardness scale?
questions.fun_fact: German geologist Friedrich Mohs devised the scale in 1812, with diamond at the top as 10.

questions.text: Which number system, widely used in computing, has a base of 16?
questions.fun_fact: Web colors in HTML and CSS are often written as six hex digits, such as #FF00FF for magenta.

questions.text: Whose 1948 paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' founded the field of information theory?
questions.fun_fact: In his 1937 master's thesis, he showed that Boolean algebra could be used to design electrical switching circuits.

questions.text: Which programming language did Guido van Rossum create?
questions.fun_fact: The language is named after the British comedy group Monty Python, not the snake.

questions.text: Which binary number is equal to 10 in the decimal system?
questions.fun_fact: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz published an influential study of binary arithmetic in 1703.

questions.text: In electronics, what does LED stand for?
questions.fun_fact: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics went to three Japanese-born scientists for inventing efficient blue LEDs.

questions.text: What is 2 to the power of 10?
questions.fun_fact: This is why the binary prefix kibi, as in kibibyte, means exactly 1,024.

questions.text: What is the name of the sequence 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, in which each number is the sum of the two before it?
questions.fun_fact: Fibonacci brought it to Western Europe in Liber Abaci (1202), but Indian mathematicians had described it centuries earlier.

questions.text: Which ancient Greek mathematician wrote the geometry treatise 'Elements'?
questions.fun_fact: Written around 300 BC, Elements is divided into 13 books covering geometry and number theory.

questions.text: What is the name of the number 10 to the power of 100?
questions.fun_fact: The name was coined by nine-year-old Milton Sirotta, nephew of the American mathematician Edward Kasner.

questions.text: Who won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics and the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry?
questions.fun_fact: Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie also won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry, in 1935.

questions.text: Which New Zealand-born physicist proposed in 1911 that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus?
questions.fun_fact: The gold foil experiments behind his model were carried out by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden.

questions.text: Which Austrian physicist devised a famous thought experiment about a cat in a sealed box?
questions.fun_fact: He proposed it in 1935 to highlight what he saw as a problem with the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.

questions.text: Which Swedish chemist invented dynamite and left his fortune to fund a set of famous prizes?
questions.fun_fact: The synthetic element nobelium, number 102, is named in his honor.

questions.text: Which element has the chemical symbol W?
questions.fun_fact: The symbol comes from its other name, wolfram, and tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,422 °C.

questions.text: Which element is a reddish-brown liquid at room temperature?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Greek bromos, meaning 'stench', because of its sharp smell.

questions.text: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
questions.fun_fact: Fluorine is so reactive that it even forms compounds with the noble gases krypton, xenon and radon.

questions.text: Which element makes up the largest share of Earth's crust by mass?
questions.fun_fact: Silicon comes second, and together the two elements make up roughly three quarters of the crust's mass.

questions.text: Which SI unit is used to measure magnetic flux density?
questions.fun_fact: The unit was adopted in 1960 and is named after the inventor and engineer Nikola Tesla.

questions.text: Which physicist discovered the neutron in 1932?
questions.fun_fact: The discovery earned him the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.text: Which French physicist discovered radioactivity in 1896 while studying uranium salts?
questions.fun_fact: The SI unit of radioactivity, the becquerel, is named after him.

questions.text: Which law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases?
questions.fun_fact: The zeroth law got its odd name because it was stated after the other three but seen as more fundamental.

questions.text: Which physicist's 1928 equation for the electron led him to predict the existence of antimatter?
questions.fun_fact: The positron, the electron's antiparticle, was discovered in 1932 by Carl Anderson.

questions.text: Which planet was found in 1846 after mathematicians predicted its position from irregularities in Uranus's orbit?
questions.fun_fact: Galileo observed Neptune in 1612 and 1613 but took it for a fixed star.

questions.text: What is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter?
questions.fun_fact: When Giuseppe Piazzi discovered Ceres in 1801, it was initially classified as a planet.

questions.text: The platypus and the echidnas belong to which group of mammals?
questions.fun_fact: Male platypuses have venomous spurs on their hind legs, a rare trait among mammals.

questions.text: Which molecule serves as the main energy currency inside cells?
questions.fun_fact: An average adult recycles around 50 kilograms of ATP every day.

questions.text: What term describes animals that are mainly active at dawn and dusk?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Latin crepusculum, meaning 'twilight'.

questions.text: Which African animal is the giraffe's closest living relative?
questions.fun_fact: The okapi lives in the wild only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and was first scientifically described in 1901.

questions.text: Which bone in the neck is unusual because it does not form a joint with any other bone?
questions.fun_fact: It anchors muscles of the tongue, and its name comes from Greek for 'shaped like the letter upsilon'.

questions.text: Which light-sensitive cells in the retina are responsible for color vision?
questions.fun_fact: Most people have three types of cones, most sensitive to short, medium and long wavelengths of light.

questions.text: Nephrons are the tiny filtering units of which organ?
questions.fun_fact: A healthy adult kidney contains about 1 million to 1.5 million nephrons.

questions.text: What is the name of the boundary between Earth's crust and mantle?
questions.fun_fact: Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovičić identified it in 1909 by studying earthquake waves.

questions.text: Marble is a metamorphic rock that typically forms from which sedimentary rock?
questions.fun_fact: The white marble of India's Taj Mahal was quarried at Makrana in Rajasthan.

questions.text: Which gemstone is a red variety of the mineral corundum?
questions.fun_fact: Gem-quality corundum of almost any other color is called sapphire; the red of ruby comes from chromium.

questions.text: What type of volcano has broad, gentle slopes built from fluid lava flows, like Mauna Loa in Hawaii?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from its profile, which resembles a warrior's shield lying on the ground.

questions.text: Which Dutch computer scientist devised a famous algorithm for finding the shortest path between nodes in a graph?
questions.fun_fact: He said he designed it in about 20 minutes, without pencil and paper, while sitting at a café in Amsterdam.

questions.text: Which early electronic computer was built at the University of Pennsylvania and unveiled in 1946?
questions.fun_fact: It contained more than 17,000 vacuum tubes and weighed about 27 metric tons.

questions.text: Which programming language did Dennis Ritchie create at Bell Labs in the early 1970s?
questions.fun_fact: In 1973 the Unix kernel was largely rewritten in it, one of the first operating system kernels not written in assembly.

questions.text: Moore's law describes the regular doubling of what?
questions.fun_fact: Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, first described the trend in 1965.

questions.text: Which mathematician proved Fermat's Last Theorem, with the proof published in 1995?
questions.fun_fact: Pierre de Fermat claimed around 1637 that he had a proof too large to fit in the margin of his book.

questions.text: What is the value of 0! (zero factorial)?
questions.fun_fact: It reflects the idea that there is exactly one way to arrange zero objects.

questions.text: The identity e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 is named after which mathematician?
questions.fun_fact: It links five fundamental constants: 0, 1, e, i and pi.

questions.text: What is the smallest perfect number, one equal to the sum of its proper divisors?
questions.fun_fact: Euclid showed that 2^(p−1) × (2^p − 1) is a perfect number whenever 2^p − 1 is prime.

questions.text: Which Indian physicist won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the scattering of light?
questions.fun_fact: India celebrates National Science Day every 28 February to mark his 1928 discovery of the Raman effect.

questions.text: Which French chemist gave oxygen and hydrogen their names?
questions.fun_fact: His wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, translated English scientific papers for him and drew his laboratory instruments.

questions.text: The 1952 X-ray diffraction image known as Photo 51 shows which molecule?
questions.fun_fact: It was taken by PhD student Raymond Gosling, working under Rosalind Franklin at King's College London.

questions.text: Which Southeast Asian river reverses its direction of flow during the rainy season?
questions.fun_fact: When the flow reverses, Tonle Sap Lake swells from about 2,500–3,000 km² to as much as 16,000 km².

questions.text: In which country is Petra, the ancient city carved into rose-red rock?
questions.fun_fact: Petra became the capital of the Nabataean Kingdom in the 2nd century BC.

questions.text: The White Nile and the Blue Nile meet in which city?
questions.fun_fact: The Blue Nile flows out of Lake Tana in the highlands of Ethiopia.

questions.text: Which of these countries is crossed by the Tropic of Capricorn?
questions.fun_fact: The Tropic of Capricorn marks the southernmost latitude where the Sun can be directly overhead at noon.

questions.text: On which island is Manila, the capital of the Philippines?
