questions.text: What is the two-part system of naming species, such as Panthera leo, called?
questions.fun_fact: The first part names the genus and is capitalized; the second part is always written in lowercase.

questions.text: Which part of a plant mainly takes in water and minerals from the soil?
questions.fun_fact: Tiny root hairs greatly increase a root's surface area for soaking up water.

questions.text: Which Dutch scientist was the first to describe bacteria, calling them 'animalcules'?
questions.fun_fact: He built his own single-lens microscopes; the surviving ones magnify up to 275 times.

questions.text: The titan arum, or 'corpse flower', grows wild only on which Indonesian island?
questions.fun_fact: It was first brought to flower in cultivation at Kew Gardens, London, in 1889.

questions.text: Robert Hooke coined the biological term 'cell' after looking at thin slices of what?
questions.fun_fact: His 1665 book Micrographia has a fold-out engraving of a louse that opens to four times the size of the book.

questions.text: What powdery substance do bees carry between flowers, helping plants make seeds?
questions.fun_fact: Pollen grains have tough outer walls that can survive in rocks and sediments for millions of years.

questions.text: Which gas, given off by ripening fruit such as bananas, acts as a plant hormone that speeds ripening?
questions.fun_fact: This is why one overripe apple can make the fruit stored next to it ripen faster.

questions.text: Animals that have a backbone are known as what?
questions.fun_fact: The vast majority of animal species, most of them insects, have no backbone at all.

questions.text: Humans' two closest living relatives are the chimpanzee and which other ape?
questions.fun_fact: Bonobos live in the wild only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River.

questions.text: Which codon is the usual 'start' signal for making a protein?
questions.fun_fact: AUG also codes for the amino acid methionine, so most new proteins begin with it.

questions.text: What is the scientific study of birds called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Greek 'ornis', meaning bird.

questions.text: Mushrooms belong to which kingdom of living things?
questions.fun_fact: A mushroom is only the fruiting body; most of a fungus is a hidden network of threads called mycelium.

questions.text: The tallest known living trees on Earth belong to which species?
questions.fun_fact: Coast redwoods grow wild only along the foggy Pacific coast of California and southern Oregon.

questions.text: Barbara McClintock discovered 'jumping genes' while studying which crop plant?
questions.fun_fact: She received the 1983 Nobel Prize, decades after making her discovery in the 1940s.

questions.text: The Venus flytrap grows wild only in which country?
questions.fun_fact: A trap usually snaps shut only if its trigger hairs are touched twice within about 20 seconds.

questions.text: What word describes a species with no living members left anywhere?
questions.fun_fact: Scientists estimate that more than 99% of all species that ever lived on Earth have died out.

questions.text: Which type of RNA carries amino acids to the ribosome as proteins are built?
questions.fun_fact: Each one has a three-base anticodon that matches a codon on the messenger RNA.

questions.text: How many legs does a spider have?
questions.fun_fact: Most spiders also have eight eyes, arranged in four pairs.

questions.text: Plants such as pines, whose seeds are not enclosed in a fruit, are known as what?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from Greek words meaning 'naked seed'.

questions.text: Which Danish scientist coined the word 'gene' in 1909?
questions.fun_fact: He also coined the terms 'genotype' and 'phenotype'.

questions.text: What is the growth of a plant toward a light source called?
questions.fun_fact: The hormone auxin makes cells on the shaded side grow longer, so the stem bends toward the light.

questions.text: Trees that shed all their leaves each year, usually in autumn, are called what?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Latin 'decidere', meaning 'to fall off'.

questions.text: A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and which kind of partner?
questions.fun_fact: Lichens can grow on bare rock and are often among the first living things to colonize it.

questions.text: Bat wings and human arms share a basic bone layout from a common ancestor. What are such structures called?
questions.fun_fact: Analogous structures, like insect and bird wings, do a similar job but evolved separately.

questions.text: What are the tiny pores, mostly on the undersides of leaves, that let gases in and out called?
questions.fun_fact: Each pore is opened and closed by a pair of guard cells.

questions.text: Insects, spiders and crabs have a hard skeleton on the outside of their bodies. What is it called?
questions.fun_fact: An exoskeleton cannot grow, so to get bigger these animals must shed it and form a new one, a process called molting.

questions.text: Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould proposed which theory of evolution in 1972?
questions.fun_fact: Gould also wrote 300 monthly essays for Natural History magazine.

questions.text: What is a section of DNA that carries the instructions for making a particular protein called?
questions.fun_fact: Humans have only about 20,000 protein-coding genes, roughly as many as a tiny roundworm.

questions.text: What is the term for the complete set of genetic material in an organism?
questions.fun_fact: The Human Genome Project, declared complete in 2003, read about 3 billion DNA base pairs.

questions.text: Which 1871 book by Charles Darwin applied his theory of evolution to humans?
options: The Power of Movement in Plants
questions.fun_fact: In it, Darwin suggested that humans most likely first evolved in Africa.

questions.text: In which country was Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, created?
questions.fun_fact: She was born in 1996 at the Roslin Institute, near Edinburgh.

questions.text: On which ship did Charles Darwin sail around the world between 1831 and 1836?
questions.fun_fact: Darwin spent most of the five-year voyage on land, exploring while the ship surveyed the coasts.

questions.text: How many DNA or RNA bases make up one codon?
questions.fun_fact: Four bases in groups of three give 64 combinations, more than enough to code for 20 amino acids.

questions.text: The Wallace Line, dividing Asian and Australian wildlife, passes between Bali and which island?
questions.fun_fact: Bali and Lombok are only about 35 km apart, yet their wildlife differs strikingly.

questions.text: A trait that shows only when an organism inherits two copies of its allele is called what?
questions.fun_fact: Gregor Mendel introduced the notation of capital letters for dominant alleles and lowercase letters for recessive ones.

questions.text: The finches that helped inspire Darwin's ideas on evolution come from which islands?
questions.fun_fact: Despite their name, Darwin's finches are not true finches; they are now classed as tanagers.

questions.text: A harmless hoverfly that looks like a wasp is an example of which kind of mimicry?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after English naturalist Henry Walter Bates, who studied butterflies in the Amazon.

questions.text: Mammals whose young usually develop in a pouch, such as kangaroos and koalas, are called what?
questions.fun_fact: Most living marsupials are found in Australasia, and most of the rest live in the Americas.

questions.text: What term describes an organism's observable traits, such as height or flower color?
questions.fun_fact: A flamingo's pink color is part of its phenotype that comes from its diet, not its genes.

questions.text: Jellyfish sting using special explosive cells called what?
questions.fun_fact: Corals and sea anemones, which belong to the same phylum, have them too.

questions.text: Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for which gene-editing tool?
questions.fun_fact: CRISPR is adapted from a natural defense system that bacteria use against viruses.

questions.text: What is it called when an animal's colors or patterns help it blend into its surroundings?
questions.fun_fact: The word probably comes from 'camoufler', Parisian slang meaning 'to disguise'.

questions.text: Thomas Hunt Morgan showed that genes sit on chromosomes by studying which animal?
questions.fun_fact: His lab at Columbia University was nicknamed the 'Fly Room'.

questions.text: What is the ribbon of tiny teeth that snails use to scrape up food called?
questions.fun_fact: It works like a rasp, scraping food such as algae off hard surfaces like rocks.

questions.text: What does PCR, the polymerase chain reaction invented by Kary Mullis in 1983, do to DNA?
questions.fun_fact: Mullis shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the invention.

questions.text: What are male honeybees called?
questions.fun_fact: Drones have no stinger, and they do not collect nectar or pollen.

questions.text: A relationship in which one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed is called what?
questions.fun_fact: Birds that feed on insects stirred up by grazing animals are a classic example.

questions.text: Ivan Pavlov's famous studies of conditioned reflexes were carried out mainly on which animals?
questions.fun_fact: Pavlov won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his earlier research on digestion.

questions.text: Who coined the phrase 'survival of the fittest' in 1864?
questions.fun_fact: Darwin later adopted the phrase in the fifth edition of On the Origin of Species.

questions.text: Which German zoologist coined the word 'ecology' in 1866?
questions.fun_fact: His book 'Art Forms in Nature', with over 100 detailed drawings of animals and sea creatures, influenced Art Nouveau.

questions.text: Which French naturalist proposed that traits acquired during life could be passed on to offspring?
questions.fun_fact: His imagined example: giraffes that stretched their necks for high leaves would pass longer necks on.

questions.text: What is a tropical grassland with scattered trees, like much of East Africa, called?
questions.fun_fact: Savannas cover roughly a fifth of Earth's land surface.

questions.text: Sharks and dolphins evolved similar streamlined shapes independently. What is this called?
questions.fun_fact: Camera-like eyes also evolved separately in vertebrates and in octopuses and squid.

questions.text: What is it called when excess nutrients, such as farm fertilizer, make algae overgrow in a lake?
questions.fun_fact: When the algae die and rot, bacteria use up the oxygen in the water, creating 'dead zones'.

questions.text: What word describes body parts that have lost most or all of their original function through evolution?
questions.fun_fact: The tiny, hidden wings of the flightless kiwi are often given as an example.

questions.text: What is a predator at the top of a food chain, with no natural predators of its own, called?
questions.fun_fact: Orcas are apex predators that have been seen hunting even great white sharks.

questions.text: Which American microbiologist identified the Archaea as a separate branch of life in 1977?
questions.fun_fact: He identified them by comparing ribosomal RNA, a method that reshaped microbiology.

questions.text: Which thin layer surrounds every cell and controls what enters and leaves it?
questions.fun_fact: It is built mainly from a double layer of fat-like molecules called phospholipids.

questions.text: Which insect became mostly dark in polluted areas of Britain during the Industrial Revolution?
questions.fun_fact: As air pollution fell in the late 20th century, the pale form became common again.

questions.text: Gram staining, which sorts bacteria into two big groups, is named after a scientist from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Gram-positive bacteria stain purple because their thick cell walls hold on to the violet dye.

questions.text: Starfish, sea urchins and sea cucumbers belong to which group of animals?
questions.fun_fact: The name means 'spiny skin' in Greek.

questions.text: What is the jelly-like substance that fills a cell around the nucleus called?
questions.fun_fact: The fluid part of the cytoplasm, called the cytosol, is mostly water.

questions.text: Mammals get their name from which feature that they all share?
questions.fun_fact: Even the egg-laying platypus feeds its young on milk, which seeps from patches on its skin.

questions.text: Diatoms, single-celled algae, build their glassy cell walls from what?
questions.fun_fact: Diatoms generate an estimated 20 to 50 percent of the oxygen produced on Earth each year.

questions.text: Which Austrian scientist showed that newly hatched geese bond with the first moving thing they see?
questions.fun_fact: Goslings he raised imprinted on him and followed him around as if he were their parent.

questions.text: What is the movement of water through a membrane, from a weaker to a stronger solution, called?
questions.fun_fact: Osmosis is why a raisin left in a glass of water plumps up again.

questions.text: Thermus aquaticus, source of the Taq enzyme used in PCR, was first found in which US national park?
questions.fun_fact: Its name is Latin for 'hot water'.

questions.text: What are the proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living things called?
questions.fun_fact: Biological washing powders use enzymes to break down food and grass stains.

questions.text: Ants lay trails for their nestmates to follow using which chemical signals?
questions.fun_fact: The word 'pheromone' was coined in 1959 from Greek words meaning 'to carry' and 'stimulating'.

questions.text: Which German scientist extended cell theory to animals in 1839, after Matthias Schleiden's work on plants?
questions.fun_fact: Schwann cells, which wrap many nerve fibers in an insulating sheath, are named after him.

questions.text: What is a relationship between two species in which both of them benefit called?
questions.fun_fact: Bees and flowers are a classic example: the bees get food and the plants get pollinated.

questions.text: Proteins are built from long chains of which smaller molecules?
questions.fun_fact: Living things use about 20 standard amino acids to build all of their proteins.

questions.text: A species with an outsized effect on its ecosystem, like the sea otter, is known as what?
questions.fun_fact: Ecologist Robert Paine introduced the idea in 1969 after removing starfish from rocky shores in Washington State.

questions.text: In 2006, Shinya Yamanaka found a way to turn ordinary adult cells back into what?
questions.fun_fact: He shared the 2012 Nobel Prize with John Gurdon, who had cloned frogs in 1958.

questions.text: Cane toads were brought to Australia in 1935 to protect which crop from beetles?
questions.fun_fact: Cane toads are native to South America and mainland Central America.

questions.text: Humans, apes and monkeys belong to which order of mammals?
questions.fun_fact: Lemurs, lorises and tarsiers are primates too.

questions.text: Which American biologist, a leading expert on ants, founded the field of sociobiology?
questions.fun_fact: He also developed the theory of island biogeography with Robert MacArthur in 1967.

questions.text: Which British scientist began studying wild chimpanzees at Gombe Stream, Tanzania, in 1960?
questions.fun_fact: She discovered that chimpanzees make and use tools, such as stripped twigs to fish for termites.

questions.text: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in which swellings on the roots of peas and beans?
questions.fun_fact: That is why farmers grow legumes such as clover to enrich their soil.

questions.text: Which pupil and successor of Aristotle is often called the 'father of botany'?
questions.fun_fact: He was born at Eresos, on the Greek island of Lesbos.

questions.text: According to endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria are descended from what kind of free-living organisms?
questions.fun_fact: American biologist Lynn Margulis championed the theory from the late 1960s.

questions.text: What is the scientific study of plants called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Ancient Greek 'botanē', meaning pasture or grass.

questions.text: What are viruses that infect bacteria called?
questions.fun_fact: The name means 'bacteria eater' in Greek.

questions.text: Maria Sibylla Merian's famous 1705 book illustrated the insects of which South American land?
questions.fun_fact: She sailed there in 1699, aged 52, with her younger daughter Dorothea Maria.

questions.text: Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments helped disprove which old idea?
questions.fun_fact: Broth in his flasks stayed free of microbes because dust was trapped in the curved neck.

questions.text: What is the inactive winter state of animals such as hedgehogs and dormice called?
questions.fun_fact: A hibernating animal's body temperature, heart rate and breathing drop far below normal.

questions.text: Darwin predicted a moth with a very long tongue after studying a star-shaped orchid from which island?
questions.fun_fact: A moth with a matching tongue was found in Madagascar in 1903, confirming his prediction.

questions.text: Acorns are the nuts of which tree?
questions.fun_fact: Oaks produce huge crops of acorns in some years, known as mast years.

questions.text: Amoebas move and catch food by pushing out temporary arm-like bulges called what?
questions.fun_fact: The word means 'false feet' in Greek.

questions.text: Which cycle in photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide into sugar?
questions.fun_fact: Melvin Calvin won the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for mapping it.

questions.text: Seals, sea lions and walruses form which group, whose name means 'fin-footed'?
questions.fun_fact: Their closest living relatives are the musteloids: weasels, raccoons, skunks and red pandas.

questions.text: What word describes the variety of all life in a particular area or on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: The short form 'biodiversity', from 'biological diversity', was coined in 1986.

questions.text: Which American scientist studied mountain gorillas in Rwanda for nearly 20 years?
questions.fun_fact: Her 1983 book Gorillas in the Mist was made into a film in 1988.

questions.text: Which Indian scientist invented the crescograph, a device for measuring plant growth?
questions.fun_fact: He was also a pioneer of radio and microwave research in the 1890s.

questions.text: Svante Pääbo won a 2022 Nobel Prize for sequencing the genome of which extinct human relative?
questions.fun_fact: His work showed that most people outside Africa carry a small share of Neanderthal DNA.

questions.text: What are organisms like fungi and bacteria that break down dead plants and animals called?
questions.fun_fact: By breaking down dead matter, decomposers return nutrients such as nitrogen to the soil for plants to reuse.

questions.text: Hundreds of species of which fish family evolved rapidly in African lakes such as Lake Malawi?
questions.fun_fact: Many cichlids are mouthbrooders, carrying their eggs and young in their mouths.

questions.text: The theory of universal grammar is usually credited to which linguist?
questions.fun_fact: It holds that humans are born with built-in limits on what a possible human grammar can be.

questions.text: Which of these is an official language of South Africa?
questions.fun_fact: Zulu is the most common first language among South Africans.

questions.text: In Welsh, which of these letters counts as a vowel?
questions.fun_fact: The circumflex on Welsh vowels is nicknamed 'to bach', meaning 'little roof'.

questions.text: Besides French, which language is official in Haiti?
questions.fun_fact: Its vocabulary comes largely from 18th-century French, but its grammar resembles that of West African languages.

questions.text: The Hebrew word 'shalom' means what?
questions.fun_fact: It is also used as a greeting, meaning both hello and goodbye.

questions.text: Hittite, the oldest attested Indo-European language, was spoken in what is now which country?
questions.fun_fact: Czech scholar Bedřich Hrozný showed in 1915 that Hittite was Indo-European.

questions.text: Shakespeare wrote in which stage of the English language?
questions.fun_fact: This stage ran from the late 15th century to the late 17th century.

questions.text: 'Hygge', a word for cozy contentment, is most associated with which country?
questions.fun_fact: Collins English Dictionary named 'hygge' a runner-up for its 2016 word of the year.

questions.text: Ferdinand de Saussure, a founder of modern linguistics, came from which country?
questions.fun_fact: His famous Course in General Linguistics was compiled by his students from their lecture notes.

questions.text: Besides 'hello' and 'goodbye', the Hawaiian word 'aloha' also means what?
questions.fun_fact: Related words with similar meanings are found in all Polynesian languages.

questions.text: The Hawaiian name 'ukulele' is roughly translated as what?
questions.fun_fact: One theory links the name to the quick movement of the player's fingers.

questions.text: English is written in which alphabet?
questions.fun_fact: The Latin script is used to write more than 3,000 languages.

questions.text: The word 'hammock' comes, via Spanish, from the language of which Indigenous people?
questions.fun_fact: Hammocks were developed by native peoples of the Americas; sailors later slept in them to save space aboard ships.

questions.text: In which language are all nouns written with a capital letter?
questions.fun_fact: The polite word for 'you', Sie, is also always capitalized.

questions.text: Which language of India has the most native speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Despite a common belief, India's constitution gives no language the status of national language.

questions.text: Which constructed language, first published in 1879, won a big following before Esperanto?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'world speak', and its grammar drew largely on German.

questions.text: Which of these Scandinavian languages has the most native speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Swedish is also a co-official language of Finland.

questions.text: What is the last letter of the Greek alphabet?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'big O', to set it apart from omicron, whose name means 'small O'.

questions.text: In his preface to Pygmalion, Shaw linked the phonetician Henry Sweet to which character?
questions.fun_fact: A society for the history of linguistic ideas, founded in 1984, is named after Sweet.

questions.text: Which of these is a Celtic language?
questions.fun_fact: It is the only Celtic language still in use on the European mainland.

questions.text: Tok Pisin, an English-based creole, is an official language of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the English words 'talk' and 'pidgin'.

questions.text: Which country has the most native English speakers?
questions.fun_fact: English takes its name from the Angles, a Germanic people who settled in Britain.

questions.text: Roughly how many native speakers does Estonian have?
questions.fun_fact: Estonian nouns have no grammatical gender but are declined in 14 cases.

questions.text: Which of these African languages is famous for its click sounds?
questions.fun_fact: One count found that about 10% of basic Xhosa vocabulary items contain a click.

questions.text: The Dothraki language was developed for which TV series?
questions.fun_fact: Linguist David J. Peterson built it from the handful of Dothraki words in George R. R. Martin's novels.

questions.text: Which of these languages is the closest living relative of Lithuanian?
questions.fun_fact: Lithuanian is famously conservative, keeping grammar features otherwise found only in ancient languages like Sanskrit.

questions.text: Which country has Dutch, French and German as its official languages?
questions.fun_fact: German is the least common of the three, spoken natively by under 1% of the population.

questions.text: The Japanese loanword 'origami' names the art of doing what with paper?
questions.fun_fact: Designs that also use cuts are often called kirigami.

questions.text: The word 'magazine' comes from an Arabic word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: It reached English by way of Italian 'magazzino' and French 'magasin'.

questions.text: The word 'ombudsman' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: It is rooted in Old Norse, and its old meaning is roughly 'a representative'.

questions.text: Which country has the most native Arabic speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to Egyptian films and music, Egyptian Arabic is understood across most of the Arab world.

questions.text: Which of these languages has the most native speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Mandarin is tonal: said with different tones, the syllable 'ma' can mean 'mother' or 'horse'.

questions.text: Which European language is routinely written in both Cyrillic and Latin letters?
questions.fun_fact: In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić reformed it on the principle 'Write as you speak.'

questions.text: The word 'mosquito' means what in Spanish and Portuguese?
questions.fun_fact: It is formed from 'mosca', meaning fly, plus the diminutive ending '-ito'.

questions.text: What do German speakers call their own language?
questions.fun_fact: 'Hochdeutsch', or High German, is named after the mountainous south of Germany, where its dialects arose.

questions.text: Unlike American Sign Language, British Sign Language fingerspells using what?
questions.fun_fact: Auslan and New Zealand Sign Language use the same two-handed alphabet.

questions.text: Which country has the most native Spanish speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Spanish grew out of the Vulgar Latin dialects of the Iberian Peninsula.

questions.text: What is the official language of Liechtenstein?
questions.fun_fact: In the local Alemannic dialect, the country's own name is 'Liachtaschta'.

questions.text: Roughly how many native speakers does Faroese have?
questions.fun_fact: Its closest living relative is Icelandic; the two look alike in writing but are hard to follow when spoken.

questions.text: The constructed language Toki Pona is known for what?
questions.fun_fact: Its word 'toki' comes, via Tok Pisin, from the English word 'talk'.

questions.text: What is the German letter ß called?
questions.fun_fact: A capital form, ẞ, was officially adopted in German spelling in 2017.

questions.text: The constructed language Klingon was created for which science fiction franchise?
questions.fun_fact: Linguist Marc Okrand turned it into a full language for the third Star Trek film, released in 1984.

questions.text: Navajo belongs to which language family?
questions.fun_fact: It is the most widely spoken Native American language north of the US–Mexico border.

questions.text: Roughly how many people speak English as their first language?
questions.fun_fact: Counting second-language speakers too, English is used by well over a billion people.

questions.text: French, Spanish and Italian all developed from which language?
questions.fun_fact: They descend from Vulgar Latin, the everyday spoken Latin of the Roman world.

questions.text: Roughly how many native speakers does Maltese have?
questions.fun_fact: About half of its vocabulary comes from Italian and Sicilian.

questions.text: The term 'cul-de-sac' comes from French, where it originally meant what?
questions.fun_fact: English first used the term in anatomy, from 1738, before applying it to streets.

questions.text: Arabic is an official language of which of these countries?
questions.fun_fact: The everyday Moroccan Arabic spoken there is known as Darija.

questions.text: Which of these African languages has the most native speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Every Yoruba syllable carries one of three tones: high, mid or low.

questions.text: 'Kia ora' is a greeting in which language?
questions.fun_fact: It translates literally as 'have life' or 'be healthy'.

questions.text: Yiddish developed mainly from which language?
questions.fun_fact: Yiddish is written in the Hebrew alphabet.

questions.text: In Spanish-speaking countries, what is a siesta?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Latin 'sexta hora', the sixth hour counted from dawn.

questions.text: Which US island once had so many deaf residents that it developed its own sign language?
questions.fun_fact: It is thought to be one of the sign languages that merged to form American Sign Language.

questions.text: What do linguists call the reconstructed common ancestor of English, Hindi and Russian?
questions.fun_fact: No written record of it exists; it was rebuilt by comparing the languages descended from it.

questions.text: Which language starts written questions with an upside-down question mark (¿)?
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Spanish Academy recommended the upside-down question mark in 1754.

questions.text: Georgian is the most widely spoken language of which small family?
questions.fun_fact: Georgian counts in twenties: its number system is based on 20, not 10.

questions.text: The Russian title 'tsar' ultimately comes from which Roman name?
questions.fun_fact: It reached the Slavic languages through the Gothic word 'kaisar'.

questions.text: The word 'fjord' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: Norway's Sognefjord reaches about 1,300 m below sea level.

questions.text: In Greek, the question mark looks like which English punctuation mark?
questions.fun_fact: The Greek question mark appeared in the 8th century, around the same time as the Latin one.

questions.text: Which writing system was used by the Bronze Age Harappan civilization?
questions.fun_fact: Its inscriptions are very short, averaging only about five signs each.

questions.text: What is the national language of Pakistan?
questions.fun_fact: Urdu is also one of the official languages of India.

questions.text: Na'vi is the constructed language of the alien people in which 2009 film?
questions.fun_fact: It was created by Paul Frommer, a business school professor with a doctorate in linguistics.

questions.text: Which of these languages is spoken natively by the most people?
questions.fun_fact: Bengali is the official language of Bangladesh and is also official in India's state of West Bengal.

questions.text: What is the official language of Iran?
questions.fun_fact: Persian, Azeri and Kurdish are consistently reported as the three most spoken languages in Iran.

questions.text: Besides English, which language is official at the federal level in Canada?
questions.fun_fact: The province of Quebec is officially unilingual, with French as its only official language.

questions.text: Papiamento is the most widely spoken language on which islands?
questions.fun_fact: It is a creole based largely on the Portuguese of the 15th and 16th centuries.

questions.text: Roughly how many native speakers does Korean have?
questions.fun_fact: South Koreans call the language Hangugeo, while North Koreans call it Chosŏnŏ.

questions.text: Newspeak is the invented language of which novel?
questions.fun_fact: George Orwell set out its rules in an appendix to the novel, 'The Principles of Newspeak'.

questions.text: The undeciphered rongorongo script comes from which island?
questions.fun_fact: About two dozen wooden objects carrying the script survive, and none remain on the island.

questions.text: Roughly how many people speak Finnish?
questions.fun_fact: Finnish is one of the few languages of Europe that are not Indo-European.

questions.text: Which of these European languages has the most native speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Portuguese is the most widely spoken language in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.text: The word 'graffiti' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: Its root goes back to the Greek 'graphein', meaning 'to write'.

questions.text: Captain Cook brought the word 'taboo' into English in 1777 after a visit to which islands?
questions.fun_fact: Related forms include Māori 'tapu' and Hawaiian 'kapu'.

questions.text: Modern Vietnamese is written in which script?
questions.fun_fact: Its diacritics mark the language's tones, as in à, á, ả, ã and ạ.

questions.text: Cockney rhyming slang is traditionally associated with which city?
questions.fun_fact: In it, 'apples and pears' means stairs, so 'going up the apples' means going upstairs.

questions.text: Catalan is the only official language of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Catalan also has semi-official status in Alghero, a town on the Italian island of Sardinia.

questions.text: Indonesian, the national language of Indonesia, is a standardized form of which language?
questions.fun_fact: It was proclaimed the unifying language at the Youth Pledge of 28 October 1928.

questions.text: Japanese kanji characters were originally adopted from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The word 'kanji' itself literally means 'Han characters'.

questions.text: What is the small dot over a lowercase i or j called?
questions.fun_fact: In Turkish, dotted i and dotless ı are two different letters with different sounds.

questions.text: Which of these places officially uses Traditional Chinese characters?
questions.fun_fact: Hong Kong and Macau also use traditional characters.

questions.text: In 1973, which language became the sixth official language of the United Nations?
questions.fun_fact: Two years earlier, in 1971, the UN had switched from Traditional to Simplified Chinese characters.

questions.text: Which Slavic language has the most native speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian together form the East Slavic branch of the family.

questions.text: The Behistun inscription, key to deciphering cuneiform, is carved on a cliff in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It gives the same text in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian.

questions.text: Arabic and Hebrew both belong to which group of languages?
questions.fun_fact: Semitic words grow from consonant roots: k-t-b is linked to writing in both Arabic and Hebrew.

questions.text: Which author invented the Elvish languages Quenya and Sindarin?
questions.fun_fact: A philologist by profession, he built his Elvish tongues with the same comparative method used to trace real language families.

questions.text: Spanish is the main official language of which African country?
questions.fun_fact: French and, since 2010, Portuguese are also official languages there.

questions.text: Which scholar announced the decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822?
questions.fun_fact: On grasping the breakthrough, he reportedly ran to his brother shouting 'Je tiens mon affaire!'

questions.text: After the Norman Conquest of 1066, which language did England's new ruling class speak?
questions.fun_fact: Anglo-French stayed in heavy use in English law reports and charters until the early 15th century.

questions.text: How many letters are in the modern Russian alphabet?
questions.fun_fact: They are 20 consonants, 10 vowels, the semivowel й and two signs that have no sound of their own.

questions.text: Which of these Asian languages has the most native speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Japan is the only country where Japanese is the national language.

questions.text: Which of these languages is most closely related to Finnish?
questions.fun_fact: The two are related, yet speakers of standard Finnish and Estonian cannot easily understand each other.

questions.text: Which country has the most Portuguese speakers?
questions.fun_fact: Brazil is the only country in the Americas where Portuguese is the official language.

questions.text: Vietnamese belongs to which language family?
questions.fun_fact: It has several times more speakers than the rest of its language family combined.

questions.text: Under Ireland's constitution, which is the country's first official language?
questions.fun_fact: Irish is also one of the official languages of the European Union.

questions.text: Which Romance language has the most native speakers?
questions.fun_fact: 'Romance' comes from the Latin adverb 'romanice', 'in Roman', meaning in the everyday Latin vernacular.

questions.text: The ʻokina in written Hawaiian marks which sound?
questions.fun_fact: Unlike most letters, it has no separate uppercase and lowercase forms.

questions.text: Quechua was the main language of which empire?
questions.fun_fact: Quechua had already spread across the Andes long before the Incas came to power.

questions.text: Which of these West African countries has French as its official language?
questions.fun_fact: Wolof is the most widely spoken language there, used by about 80% of people.

questions.text: Which of these Central Asian languages is a Turkic language?
questions.fun_fact: Uzbek and Uyghur are sister languages in the Karluk branch of the Turkic family.

questions.text: Which language became an official language of New Zealand in 1987?
questions.fun_fact: Its Latin-alphabet spelling was standardized in the 19th century by Northern Māori working with English clergy.

questions.text: The word 'wiki', as in Wikipedia, is Hawaiian for what?
questions.fun_fact: Ward Cunningham picked it after riding the Wiki Wiki Shuttle bus at Honolulu's airport.

questions.text: What is the wavy mark over the n in the Spanish word 'España' called?
questions.fun_fact: In Portuguese the same mark shows a nasal vowel, as in 'mão', meaning 'hand'.

questions.text: Silbo Gomero, a whistled form of Spanish, is used on an island in which archipelago?
questions.fun_fact: In 2009 UNESCO added it to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.text: Not counting the light 'neutral' tone, how many tones does Standard Mandarin have?
questions.fun_fact: Compared with other varieties of Chinese, Standard Mandarin has fewer tones.

questions.text: How many letters are there in the modern English alphabet?
questions.fun_fact: W began as a doubled u (or v), which is why English calls it 'double U'.

questions.text: Tolkien's Elvish language Quenya was inspired mainly by which real language?
questions.fun_fact: Welsh was the main inspiration for Sindarin, Tolkien's other major Elvish language.

questions.text: Gallaudet University, a university for deaf students, is in which city?
questions.fun_fact: The football huddle began there, to stop opponents from reading the team's signed plays.

questions.text: What is a person who speaks many languages called?
questions.fun_fact: Many polyglots know five or six languages, but far fewer people master more than that.

questions.text: Burmese belongs to which language family?
questions.fun_fact: It is the most widely spoken language of its family outside the Chinese languages.

questions.text: Roughly how many native speakers does Icelandic have?
questions.fun_fact: Written Icelandic has changed so little that modern readers can follow sagas written 800 years ago.

questions.text: Which element has the chemical symbol Pb?
questions.fun_fact: Pb comes from the Latin plumbum; the word plumber shares that root because Roman water pipes were made of lead.

questions.text: What is the chemical symbol for silver?
questions.fun_fact: Ag comes from argentum, the Latin word for silver, which also gave Argentina its name.

questions.text: Which English chemist's 1865 'law of octaves' compared the elements to the notes of a musical scale?
questions.fun_fact: His idea was ridiculed at first, but the Royal Society awarded him its Davy Medal for the work in 1887.

questions.text: What is the joining of many small molecules into long chains, as in the making of plastics, called?
questions.fun_fact: Nature makes polymers too: starch, silk, natural rubber and DNA are all long chains of repeating units.

questions.text: What is the change from a gas into a liquid, as when steam forms droplets on a cold window, called?
questions.fun_fact: Dew is condensation: water vapor in the air turns liquid on surfaces that have cooled overnight.

questions.text: Which process, developed by a Belgian chemist in the 1860s, makes sodium carbonate from salt and limestone?
questions.fun_fact: Ernest Solvay's fortune paid for the famous Solvay Conferences on physics, first held in 1911.

questions.text: Which element was once commonly called quicksilver?
questions.fun_fact: Its symbol, Hg, comes from hydrargyrum, a Latinized Greek word meaning 'water-silver'.

questions.text: Which element has the chemical symbol Cu?
questions.fun_fact: Cu comes from the Latin cuprum, a name linked to Cyprus, a major source of the metal in Roman times.

questions.text: In a flame test, which metal gives an intense yellow-orange color?
questions.fun_fact: The same yellow-orange glow is why sodium-vapor streetlights give off such orange-tinted light.

questions.text: Which Swedish chemist introduced the system of one- and two-letter chemical symbols, such as Na and Cl?
questions.fun_fact: He is also credited with coining the chemical terms catalysis, polymer and isomer.

questions.text: What are the vertical columns of the periodic table called?
questions.fun_fact: Elements in the same group tend to behave alike because they have the same number of outer electrons.

questions.text: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container?
questions.fun_fact: Surface tension, a property of liquids, lets insects such as water striders walk on water.

questions.text: What is an alloy of mercury with another metal called?
questions.fun_fact: Gold miners once used mercury to gather fine specks of gold as an amalgam, then heated it to drive the mercury off.

questions.text: Glow sticks give off light through which process?
questions.fun_fact: Putting a glow stick in the freezer slows the reaction, so it glows more dimly but lasts longer.

questions.text: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
questions.fun_fact: Iron is the most common element in Earth as a whole by mass, because so much of it sits in the planet's core.

questions.text: The Swedish village of Ytterby gave its name to how many chemical elements?
questions.fun_fact: Yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium were all found in minerals from a quarry near the village.

questions.text: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine belong to which group of elements?
questions.fun_fact: The name halogen means 'salt-former' in Greek, because they react with metals to make salts.

questions.text: Which acid gives vinegar its sour taste?
questions.fun_fact: The name acetic comes from acetum, the Latin word for vinegar.

questions.text: Galvanized steel is coated with a thin layer of which metal to protect it from rust?
questions.fun_fact: The zinc corrodes first, so it keeps protecting the steel even where the coating is scratched.

questions.text: Which form of carbon, a ball of 60 atoms shaped like a soccer ball, was discovered in 1985?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after architect Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes it resembles.

questions.text: Lithium, sodium and potassium belong to which group of the periodic table?
questions.fun_fact: They react so readily with air and water that they are usually stored under oil.

questions.text: What do chemists call a pure substance made of only one type of atom?
questions.fun_fact: Of all the known elements, 94 occur naturally on Earth; the rest have only been made in laboratories.

questions.text: Which element is named after the Austrian-Swedish physicist Lise Meitner?
questions.fun_fact: It is element 109, first made in 1982 at the GSI laboratory in Darmstadt, Germany.

questions.text: Bronze is an alloy of copper and which other metal?
questions.fun_fact: Adding tin makes bronze much harder than pure copper, which made it ideal for tools and weapons.

questions.text: Which acid is found in large amounts in lemons and limes?
questions.fun_fact: Most commercial citric acid is made by a mold, Aspergillus niger, that is fed on sugar.

questions.text: James Dewar, inventor of the vacuum flask, was the first to liquefy which gas, in 1898?
questions.fun_fact: He never patented his flask, and two German glassblowers later sold it under the brand name Thermos.

questions.text: Which element's name comes from the Greek word for 'violet', after the color of its vapor?
questions.fun_fact: French chemist Bernard Courtois discovered it in 1811 in the ash of burned seaweed.

questions.text: What does an element's atomic number count?
questions.fun_fact: Change the number of protons and you change the element: every atom with 79 protons is gold.

questions.text: Stainless steel resists rust mainly because it contains which element?
questions.fun_fact: The chromium forms a thin, invisible oxide layer that quickly repairs itself if scratched.

questions.text: Which element was discovered in Mexico in 1801 by the mineralogist Andrés Manuel del Río?
questions.fun_fact: It was later named after Vanadís, a Norse goddess, because of its many colorful compounds.

questions.text: Which element's name comes from the Greek word for 'pale green', the color of its gas?
questions.fun_fact: Humphry Davy showed in 1810 that it is an element, and he gave it its name.

questions.text: On the pH scale, what is a solution with a pH of exactly 7 called?
questions.fun_fact: Pure water at 25 °C has a pH of 7, while lemon juice is around 2.

questions.text: Which Irish-born scientist wrote the 1661 book 'The Sceptical Chymist'?
questions.fun_fact: He is also known for Boyle's law: at a fixed temperature, a gas's pressure rises as its volume shrinks.

questions.text: Pyrite, known as fool's gold, is a compound of iron and which element?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Greek word for fire, because it gives off sparks when struck against steel.

questions.text: Which group of elements, including neon and argon, is famous for being very unreactive?
questions.fun_fact: Their full outer shells of electrons make them very reluctant to form chemical compounds.

questions.text: The element hafnium is named after the Latin name of which city?
questions.fun_fact: Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy found it in that city, Niels Bohr's hometown, using X-ray spectroscopy.

questions.text: Which is the lightest of all metals?
questions.fun_fact: Lithium is so light that it floats on water, and even on some light oils.

questions.text: Blue litmus paper turns which color when dipped in an acid?
questions.fun_fact: Litmus is a natural dye extracted from lichens.

questions.text: Isotopes of the same element differ in their number of which particle?
questions.fun_fact: The word isotope means 'same place', because isotopes share one spot in the periodic table.

questions.text: In 1828, Friedrich Wöhler made which organic compound from inorganic chemicals?
questions.fun_fact: His experiment is often cited as the starting point of modern organic chemistry.

questions.text: Which metal can melt in your hand, with a melting point of about 30 °C?
questions.fun_fact: A classic prank uses spoons made of it, which melt away when stirred into a hot drink.

questions.text: Which noble gas glows reddish-orange in classic advertising signs?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from neos, the Greek word for 'new'.

questions.text: Which Scottish chemist, working with colleagues, discovered argon, neon, krypton and xenon in the 1890s?
questions.fun_fact: He won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; his argon partner, Lord Rayleigh, won the Physics prize the same year.

questions.text: Which isotope is used to date ancient wood, bone and other once-living material?
questions.fun_fact: Its half-life is about 5,730 years, so the method works for remains up to about 50,000 years old.

questions.text: What is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up called?
questions.fun_fact: Car catalytic converters use platinum, palladium and rhodium to clean up exhaust gases.

questions.text: Which American chemist won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for research into the nature of the chemical bond?
questions.fun_fact: He is the only person to have won two Nobel Prizes that he did not share with anyone.

questions.text: Which gas has the chemical formula NH3?
questions.fun_fact: Most of the ammonia made in the world is turned into fertilizers for farming.

questions.text: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.fun_fact: Lightning splits nitrogen molecules, letting the element join with oxygen and reach the soil in rain.

questions.text: What type of chemical bond forms when two atoms share a pair of electrons?
questions.fun_fact: In table salt the bonds are ionic instead: each sodium atom gives an electron to a chlorine atom.

questions.text: Which compound gives black pepper its pungent bite?
questions.fun_fact: Black, white and green peppercorns all come from the same climbing vine, Piper nigrum.

questions.text: Limestone is made mostly of which compound?
questions.fun_fact: Much limestone formed from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures that piled up on ancient seabeds.

questions.text: What is the chemical reaction called when a fuel burns in oxygen?
questions.fun_fact: A candle flame looks yellow because of tiny particles of hot, glowing soot.

questions.text: Which British chemist won the 1964 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for finding the structures of molecules such as vitamin B12?
questions.fun_fact: She was the third woman to win the chemistry prize, after Marie Curie and Irène Joliot-Curie.

questions.text: Avogadro's number, about 6.022 × 10²³, is the number of particles in one what?
questions.fun_fact: Chemists celebrate Mole Day every October 23, from 6:02 in the morning to 6:02 in the evening.

questions.text: Organic chemistry is the study of compounds built around which element?
questions.fun_fact: Carbon can form four bonds and long chains, which lets it build millions of different compounds.

questions.text: Teflon's non-stick polymer was discovered by accident at DuPont in 1938 by which chemist?
questions.fun_fact: He found that a cylinder of gas which seemed empty had turned into a waxy white solid inside.

questions.text: What is the common name for sodium hydroxide?
questions.fun_fact: It is a key ingredient in many oven and drain cleaners, and in traditional soap making.

questions.text: Yeast fermentation turns sugar into carbon dioxide and which alcohol?
questions.fun_fact: The gas bubbles make bread dough rise, and the alcohol mostly evaporates during baking.

questions.text: In 2004, scientists in Manchester isolated graphene with the help of which everyday item?
questions.fun_fact: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work.

questions.text: Which English scientist identified hydrogen as a distinct substance in 1766, calling it 'inflammable air'?
questions.fun_fact: He was famously shy, and he also measured the density of the Earth in a celebrated 1798 experiment.

questions.text: Which compound is the main flavor molecule of vanilla?
questions.fun_fact: Most vanillin used in food is made artificially, from petrochemicals or from lignin in wood pulp.

questions.text: Which element is the main material used to make computer chips?
questions.fun_fact: Silicon Valley in California takes its nickname from the silicon chips made by its early tech firms.

questions.text: What is the direct change from a gas into a solid, as when frost forms, called?
questions.fun_fact: Snowflakes grow the same way, as water vapor in clouds turns straight into ice crystals.

questions.text: What is the cone-shaped laboratory flask with a flat bottom and a narrow neck called?
questions.fun_fact: German chemist Emil Erlenmeyer created it in 1860.

questions.text: Passing electricity through water splits it into hydrogen and which other gas?
questions.fun_fact: Twice as much hydrogen as oxygen is given off, matching the two-to-one ratio in the water molecule.

questions.text: Which Egyptian-born chemist won the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying reactions on a femtosecond time scale?

questions.text: Which synthetic fiber did Wallace Carothers' team at DuPont create in 1935?

questions.text: What is the chemical formula for water?
questions.fun_fact: Ice floats because water is one of very few substances that is less dense as a solid than as a liquid.

questions.text: Which long glass tube with a tap at the bottom is used to add exact amounts of liquid during a titration?
questions.fun_fact: A titration finds the unknown concentration of a solution, often using an indicator that changes color.

questions.text: What is the one temperature and pressure at which a substance can exist as solid, liquid and gas together?
questions.fun_fact: Water's is at 0.01 °C and a pressure of about 611 pascals, far below normal air pressure.

questions.text: What is the change from a solid straight into a gas, as dry ice does, called?

questions.text: What is a metal made by mixing two or more metals, such as brass, called?
questions.fun_fact: Sterling silver is an alloy too: 92.5% silver, usually mixed with copper.

questions.text: Japanese chemist Hideki Shirakawa shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for plastics that can do what?
questions.fun_fact: The discovery began with a lab mix-up in which about a thousand times too much catalyst was used.

questions.text: A Liebig condenser is mainly used in which laboratory process?
questions.fun_fact: Although it is named after Justus von Liebig, he made it popular rather than inventing it.

questions.text: Which liquid is often called the 'universal solvent'?
questions.fun_fact: It dissolves so many substances that seawater carries about 3.5% dissolved salts by weight.

questions.text: Which acid did 17th-century naturalists first obtain by distilling ants?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from formica, the Latin word for ant, and it is also found in the stings of nettles.

questions.text: Which state of matter, a gas of charged particles, makes up lightning and the Sun?
questions.fun_fact: Neon signs glow because electricity turns the gas inside them into a plasma.

questions.text: Which particle in an atom's nucleus has a positive electric charge?
questions.fun_fact: A proton is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron.

questions.text: Which technique separates the different dyes in ink as a solvent carries them up a strip of paper?
questions.fun_fact: Botanist Mikhail Tsvet developed it in the early 1900s to separate plant pigments, and he coined its name.

questions.text: Mexican chemist Mario Molina shared the 1995 Nobel Prize for showing which chemicals damage the ozone layer?
questions.fun_fact: He shared the prize with Sherwood Rowland and Paul Crutzen.

questions.text: Which acid is used in the lead-acid batteries of cars?
questions.fun_fact: Medieval alchemists called it 'oil of vitriol'.

questions.text: Which gas gives fizzy drinks their bubbles?
questions.fun_fact: Dissolved in water, the gas forms carbonic acid, which gives sparkling water its slightly sour bite.

questions.text: Which acid gives cola drinks part of their sharp, tangy taste?
questions.fun_fact: It is also used to remove rust, because it turns iron oxide into iron phosphate.

questions.text: Which English chemist, who proposed a modern atomic theory around 1803, also studied his own color blindness?
questions.fun_fact: Color blindness used to be called Daltonism in his honor.

questions.text: Which German chemist gave his name to the gas burner found in school laboratories?
questions.fun_fact: He and Gustav Kirchhoff discovered cesium and rubidium by studying the light given off by heated elements.

questions.text: Which German alchemist discovered phosphorus in 1669 by boiling down large amounts of urine?
questions.fun_fact: The name phosphorus means 'light-bearer' in Greek, because the white form glows in the dark.

questions.text: Which word describes a chemical reaction that gives out heat?
questions.fun_fact: Instant cold packs use the opposite kind of process: dissolving certain salts in water absorbs heat.

questions.text: What is the chemical name for baking soda?
questions.fun_fact: When heated or mixed with an acid it gives off carbon dioxide, and the bubbles make cakes rise.

questions.text: Which chemist first isolated sodium and potassium in 1807, using electricity?
questions.fun_fact: In 1815 he also invented a safety lamp for coal miners.

questions.text: Which Danish chemist introduced the pH scale in 1909?
questions.fun_fact: He worked at the Carlsberg Laboratory, the research lab founded by the Copenhagen brewery.

questions.text: Which reaction between amino acids and sugars browns bread crusts, seared steak and roasted coffee?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912.

questions.text: Which laboratory machine separates substances of different density by spinning samples very fast?
questions.fun_fact: Dairies use the same idea in cream separators, which spin milk to pull the cream away.

questions.text: Which group of plant pigments makes red cabbage juice change color with pH, so it can be used as an indicator?
questions.fun_fact: Their name comes from the Greek words for 'flower' and 'dark blue'.

questions.text: What color was the synthetic dye that 18-year-old William Perkin discovered by accident in 1856?
questions.fun_fact: It was first sold as aniline purple and renamed in 1859 after the French name for the mallow flower.

questions.text: What is the chemical name for ordinary table sugar?
questions.fun_fact: Each of its molecules is made of one glucose unit and one fructose unit joined together.

questions.text: Aqua regia, which can dissolve gold, is a mixture of hydrochloric acid and which other acid?
questions.fun_fact: In 1940 George de Hevesy dissolved two gold Nobel medals in it in Copenhagen to keep them from being seized.

questions.text: Which industrial process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen?
questions.fun_fact: German chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed it, and both later won Nobel Prizes in Chemistry.

questions.text: Alchemists searched for which legendary substance, said to turn ordinary metals into gold?
questions.fun_fact: Isaac Newton wrote or copied out about a million words on alchemy.

questions.text: Which drink did English chemist Joseph Priestley invent a way of making in 1767?
questions.fun_fact: He first made it by hanging a bowl of water above a vat of fermenting beer at a brewery in Leeds.

questions.text: Which light-producing compound makes fireflies glow when an enzyme oxidizes it?
questions.fun_fact: Besides the enzyme, the firefly's light-making reaction also needs oxygen and ATP.

questions.text: Which process, patented by Charles Goodyear in 1844, toughens rubber by heating it with sulfur?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Vulcan, the Roman deity of fire and metalworking.

questions.text: Which compound in mint gives a cooling feeling in the mouth?
questions.fun_fact: It triggers TRPM8, the same nerve receptor that senses real cold.

questions.text: In chemistry, what is the loss of electrons by an atom or ion called?
questions.fun_fact: Students remember it with 'OIL RIG': Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

questions.text: Bananas are slightly radioactive because they contain which element?
questions.fun_fact: The tiny dose from one banana is sometimes used as an informal unit, the banana equivalent dose.

questions.text: When sugar dissolves in tea, what is the sugar called?
questions.fun_fact: Hot water can dissolve far more sugar than cold water, which is how syrups and candies are made.

questions.text: Which compound gives beetroot its earthy taste and freshly dug soil its earthy smell?
questions.fun_fact: Human noses are extremely sensitive to it and can detect it at concentrations as low as about 5 parts per trillion.

questions.text: Which compound did the German chemist August Kekulé say a dream of a snake biting its tail helped him picture as a ring?
questions.fun_fact: Michael Faraday first isolated it in 1825, from an oily residue left by the making of gas for lighting.

questions.text: Which gas gives rotten eggs their smell?
questions.fun_fact: Hot springs and volcanoes release it too, giving places like Rotorua in New Zealand their sulfur smell.

questions.text: Which metal atom sits at the center of a chlorophyll molecule?
questions.fun_fact: Heme, which carries oxygen in our blood, has a similar ring structure but with iron at its center.

questions.text: What is the reaction of fats with a strong alkali, used to make soap, called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from sapo, the Latin word for soap.

questions.text: The name Volkswagen means what in English?
questions.fun_fact: The company was founded in 1937 to build an affordable car for ordinary Germans, which became the Beetle.

questions.text: Before building sports cars, Ferruccio Lamborghini made his fortune building what?
questions.fun_fact: He set up his tractor company in 1948, long before his first production car, the 350 GT, appeared in 1964.

questions.text: Ferrari's prancing horse emblem was first painted on the plane of which Italian World War I pilot?
questions.fun_fact: In 1923 Baracca's parents met Enzo Ferrari, and his mother suggested he use the horse on his cars for good luck.

questions.text: Car maker Hyundai comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Hyundai means 'modernity' in Korean.

questions.text: Before making cars, Swedish company Saab was known for building what?
questions.fun_fact: Saab was short for Svenska Aeroplan Aktiebolaget, meaning 'Swedish Aeroplane Company'.

questions.text: Kia began in 1944 as a maker of steel tubing and parts for what?
questions.fun_fact: In 1951 it built South Korea's first domestic bicycle, the Samchuly.

questions.text: Which of these car makers comes from Sweden?
questions.fun_fact: Volvo's first series-built car, the ÖV4, left the factory in Gothenburg in April 1927.

questions.text: In the name FIAT, what does the letter 'T' stand for?
questions.fun_fact: FIAT stands for Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino, and the company was founded in 1899.

questions.text: Chinese company Geely started out in 1986 making parts for what?
questions.fun_fact: Geely moved into motorcycles in 1994 and began making cars in 1997.

questions.text: Which car maker introduced the Mustang in 1964?
questions.fun_fact: It created a new class of affordable sporty cars, nicknamed 'pony cars' after the Mustang.

questions.text: What does the 'B' in BMW stand for?
questions.fun_fact: BMW started out making aircraft engines during World War I, before it built motorcycles and cars.

questions.text: Mercedes cars take their name from the daughter of which businessman?
questions.fun_fact: Jellinek raced Daimler cars under the pseudonym 'Monsieur Mercedes' and later added the name to his own.

questions.text: Which country is home to the car makers Ferrari, Lamborghini and Maserati?
questions.fun_fact: All three have their roots in the northern Italian region of Emilia-Romagna.

questions.text: Peugeot's lion emblem, dating from 1858, first stood for the qualities of which Peugeot product?

questions.text: The name Audi is a Latin translation of which founder's surname?
questions.fun_fact: In German 'horch!' means 'listen!', and so does 'audi!' in Latin.

questions.text: Which Japanese maker launched the Corolla in 1966?
questions.fun_fact: Corolla is Latin for 'small crown', following Toyota's earlier Crown and Corona models.

questions.text: Which Japanese maker won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1991?

questions.text: Hongqi, China's oldest passenger car brand, launched in 1958, has a name meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: The first Hongqi model was the CA72, introduced on 1 August 1958.

questions.text: Before it built cars, Honda was best known for making what?
questions.fun_fact: Honda was incorporated in 1948, and its first production car, a small pickup truck, followed in 1963.

questions.text: The name Mitsubishi refers to which shapes in the company's logo?
questions.fun_fact: The company began in 1870 as a shipping firm founded by Iwasaki Yatarō.

questions.text: Ettore Bugatti, founder of the Bugatti car company, was born in which city?
questions.fun_fact: He set up his car factory in 1909 in Molsheim, Alsace, which was then part of Germany.

questions.text: Car maker Renault was founded in 1899 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was started by three brothers: Louis, Marcel and Fernand Renault.

questions.text: The Maruti 800, launched in India in 1983, was based on a model from which Japanese maker?
questions.fun_fact: Maruti Suzuki built it in Gurgaon from 1983 to 2014, and its three-cylinder engine displaced 796 cc.

questions.text: Louis Chevrolet, co-founder of the Chevrolet car company, was born in which country?
questions.fun_fact: He was a racing driver too, and his brother Gaston won the 1920 Indianapolis 500.

questions.text: The Tata Nano, unveiled in 2008 as a very low-cost car, was made in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Tata aimed to sell it for one lakh rupees, or 100,000 rupees, which was about US$2,000 at the time.

questions.text: Chinese company BYD began in 1995 as a maker of what?
questions.fun_fact: It was founded by Wang Chuanfu and later grew into a major maker of electric cars.

questions.text: Supercar maker Horacio Pagani was born in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Before founding his own company in 1992, he ran Lamborghini's composites department.

questions.text: The former car brand Holden came from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The company began in 1856 in Adelaide as a saddlery business.

questions.text: Scuderia Ferrari was founded in 1929 to race cars made by which company?
questions.fun_fact: By 1947 Ferrari had begun building racing cars of its own.

questions.text: Which Italian car maker uses a black prancing horse as its badge?
questions.fun_fact: The horse sits on a canary-yellow background, the color of Enzo Ferrari's home city of Modena.

questions.text: Which animal appears on the Lamborghini badge?
questions.fun_fact: Founder Ferruccio Lamborghini was born under the star sign Taurus, the bull.

questions.text: Which German car maker's round badge is divided into blue and white quarters?
questions.fun_fact: Its blue and white quarters recall the flag and coat of arms of Bavaria.

questions.text: Which car maker's badge shows four interlinked rings?
questions.fun_fact: The rings stand for four firms that merged in 1932 to form Auto Union.

questions.text: Which car maker's badge is a three-pointed star in a circle?
questions.fun_fact: The three points stand for Daimler engines used on land, on water and in the air.

questions.text: Besides a red cross, what creature appears on the Alfa Romeo badge?
questions.fun_fact: Both emblems come from Milan: the red cross of the city and the serpent of the Visconti family.

questions.text: What is the name of the winged figure on the hood of Rolls-Royce cars?
questions.fun_fact: Sculptor Charles Sykes created it, and it has decorated Rolls-Royce cars since 1911.

questions.text: Maserati's trident badge was inspired by the statue of Neptune in which city?
questions.fun_fact: It was designed by Mario Maserati, the only brother who chose an artistic career over racing.

questions.text: Luxury car maker Rolls-Royce was founded in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its founders, Charles Rolls and Henry Royce, first met at the Midland Hotel in Manchester in May 1904.

questions.text: Which engineer's team developed the original Volkswagen Beetle in the 1930s?
questions.fun_fact: More than 21.5 million original Beetles were built, in factories around the world.

questions.text: Which car was nicknamed the 'Tin Lizzie'?
questions.fun_fact: Production ran until 1927, by which time more than 15 million had been built.

questions.text: What does '2CV' in the name of the Citroën 2CV refer to?
questions.fun_fact: Its design brief called for a cheap, rugged car that could carry 50 kg of farm goods to market at 50 km/h.

questions.text: The name of the 1955 Citroën DS sounds like the French word for what?
questions.fun_fact: Its hydropneumatic suspension leveled itself automatically, and the driver could raise or lower the car.

questions.text: The 1936 Fiat 500 was nicknamed 'Topolino'. What does that mean in Italian?
questions.fun_fact: Topolino is also the Italian name for Mickey Mouse.

questions.text: Which engineer designed the Fiat Nuova 500 of 1957?
questions.fun_fact: His team had also created the rear-engined Fiat 600 of 1955.

questions.text: The East German Trabant's body panels were made of what?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'companion' or 'satellite', a nod to the Soviet Sputnik.

questions.text: The Soviet VAZ-2101 'Zhiguli', sold abroad as a Lada, was based on which Italian car?
questions.fun_fact: Its nickname 'Kopeyka' comes from the smallest Soviet coin.

questions.text: Romania's Dacia 1300, first built in 1969, was based on which car?
questions.fun_fact: Dacia is named after the ancient region that covered much of modern Romania.

questions.text: The Hindustan Ambassador, made in India until 2014, was based on which British car?
questions.fun_fact: Hindustan Motors built it at its Uttarpara plant in West Bengal, using tooling transferred from Morris.

questions.text: What was the name of Hyundai's first own car, launched in 1975?
questions.fun_fact: The Pony was South Korea's first mass-produced car, and its hatchback body was styled in Italy by Italdesign.

questions.text: The streamlined Tatra 77 of 1934 was built in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its rear-mounted, air-cooled V8 sat behind a body shaped with help from Zeppelin engineer Paul Jaray.

questions.text: Which British four-wheel-drive vehicle was launched in 1948?
questions.fun_fact: Its body was made of aluminum alloy because steel was in short supply after World War II.

questions.text: Ferrari's F40, launched in 1987, was named to mark what?
questions.fun_fact: It was the last Ferrari personally approved by Enzo Ferrari.

questions.text: The Porsche 911 was first shown in 1963 as the '901'. Which maker objected to that name?
questions.fun_fact: Peugeot claimed the rights in France to car names made of three digits with a zero in the middle.

questions.text: Which Japanese sports car appeared as an open-top car in the 1967 James Bond film 'You Only Live Twice'?
questions.fun_fact: Toyota never sold a convertible 2000GT; two open-top cars were built just for the film.

questions.text: Which Italian designer styled the first Volkswagen Golf of 1974?
questions.fun_fact: In North America the first Golf was sold as the Volkswagen Rabbit.

questions.text: Which designer, working at Bertone, styled the Lamborghini Countach?
questions.fun_fact: The name Countach comes from an exclamation of amazement in the Piedmontese dialect.

questions.text: The 1938 Buick Y-Job, often called the first concept car, was designed by whom?
questions.fun_fact: Earl drove the Y-Job himself for years before replacing it with a newer show car.

questions.text: The tailfins of the 1948 Cadillac were inspired by which aircraft?
questions.fun_fact: A GM designer got the idea after seeing the P-38's twin tail rudders at an air base.

questions.text: The Mercedes-Benz 300 SL of 1954 is famous for which kind of doors?
questions.fun_fact: Its lightweight steel tubular frame gave the coupé an unusually high sill, making it tricky to climb in and out.

questions.text: Where did the driver sit in the 1992 McLaren F1 road car?
questions.fun_fact: Its engine bay was lined with gold foil to reflect heat.

questions.text: The first Chevrolet Corvette of 1953 had a body made of what?
questions.fun_fact: Only 300 Corvettes were built in 1953, all painted Polo White.

questions.text: What are Japan's 'kei' cars, a class created by law in 1949, defined by?
questions.fun_fact: Under the first kei rules of 1949, engines were limited to just 150 cc, or 100 cc for two-strokes.

questions.text: In cars, what does ABS stand for?
questions.fun_fact: By stopping the wheels from locking, ABS lets a driver keep steering while braking hard.

questions.text: The Toyota Prius, launched in Japan in 1997, was a pioneering example of what kind of car?
questions.fun_fact: It won the Car of the Year Japan award in 1997 and went on sale around the world in 2000.

questions.text: What does SUV stand for?
questions.fun_fact: SUVs combine a passenger car body with features of off-road vehicles, such as high ground clearance.

questions.text: In motoring, what does 'EV' stand for?
questions.fun_fact: Electric power was popular on early cars because it was quieter and easier to operate than gasoline engines.

questions.text: What does a car's tachometer, or rev counter, show?
questions.fun_fact: It counts engine revolutions per minute, and a red zone marks the engine's maximum safe speed.

questions.text: What does a car's odometer measure?
questions.fun_fact: The Roman architect Vitruvius described an early odometer in the 1st century BC.

questions.text: What does a car's catalytic converter reduce?
questions.fun_fact: Converters use precious metals such as platinum, palladium and rhodium as catalysts.

questions.text: What spins the turbine of a car's turbocharger?
questions.fun_fact: A supercharger does a similar job but is driven mechanically by the engine itself.

questions.text: How is the fuel ignited in a diesel engine?
questions.fun_fact: Diesel engines have no spark plugs, though some designs use glow plugs to help them start.

questions.text: The four-stroke engine cycle is often named after which German engineer?
questions.fun_fact: Otto's first working four-stroke engine was a stationary engine that ran on coal gas and air.

questions.text: In a Wankel rotary engine, what shape is the spinning rotor?
questions.fun_fact: Felix Wankel's first working rotary engine ran in 1957 at the German firm NSU.

questions.text: Citroën's 1934 'Traction Avant' was named after which feature?
questions.fun_fact: It was also one of the first mass-produced cars with a unibody instead of a separate chassis.

questions.text: In 1953, which maker won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with cars using pioneering disc brakes?
questions.fun_fact: C-Types also won Le Mans in 1951, at their first attempt, and in 1953 they finished first, second and fourth.

questions.text: In 1912, which maker first fitted Charles Kettering's electric self-starter to its cars?
questions.fun_fact: Before electric starters, engines had to be started with a hand crank at the front of the car.

questions.text: Dutch maker DAF's Variomatic, first sold on its small DAF 600, was what kind of car transmission?
questions.fun_fact: Each rear wheel was driven by its own belt, so the car needed no differential.

questions.text: The Audi Quattro, which changed rallying from 1981, was famous for what?
questions.fun_fact: Michèle Mouton won the 1981 Rallye Sanremo in a Quattro and finished second in the 1982 drivers' world championship.

questions.text: In 1899, 'La Jamais Contente' became the first road vehicle to pass 100 km/h. What powered it?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'The Never Contented', and it was driven by Belgian Camille Jenatzy.

questions.text: In 1997, Thrust SSC became the first car to do what?
questions.fun_fact: It was powered by two jet engines of the kind used in the Phantom fighter plane.

questions.text: In Disney's 'The Love Bug' (1968), what kind of car is Herbie?
questions.fun_fact: Herbie wears the racing number 53 on his hood and doors.

questions.text: Which small British car does Mr. Bean drive in the TV series?
questions.fun_fact: He locks it with a padlock and bolt on the door, and sometimes takes the steering wheel with him.

questions.text: Which car did James Bond drive in the 1964 film 'Goldfinger'?
questions.fun_fact: Its film gadgets included a smoke screen, a rear bullet shield and revolving number plates.

questions.text: In the original 1982 TV series 'Knight Rider', the talking car KITT was a modified version of which car?
questions.fun_fact: KITT stands for Knight Industries Two Thousand.

questions.text: In car names such as the Ford GT40, what does 'GT' stand for?
questions.fun_fact: Grand tourers are built for fast, comfortable long-distance driving; the Ferrari 250 GT is a classic example.

questions.text: Which US city is nicknamed 'Motor City'?
questions.fun_fact: The city was founded in 1701 by French explorer Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac, whose name was later given to a car brand.

questions.text: What is Italy's traditional national color in motor racing?
questions.fun_fact: Before sponsor liveries, racing cars wore national colors, such as green for Britain and blue for France.

questions.text: In motor racing, what does the black-and-white checkered flag signal?
questions.fun_fact: In US racing a waved white flag marks the last lap, but in Formula One it warns of a slow-moving vehicle on track.

questions.text: In motor racing, what does a waved yellow flag tell drivers?
questions.fun_fact: A red flag stops the session when conditions are too dangerous to continue.

questions.text: How long does the famous endurance race at Le Mans, France, last?
questions.fun_fact: Each car is shared by several drivers, who take turns through the day and night.

questions.text: In Formula One, what is the first starting place at the front of the grid called?
questions.fun_fact: The term comes from horse racing, where the best starting place was next to the pole on the inside rail.

questions.text: Which Grand Prix, first held in 1929, runs through the streets of Monte Carlo?
questions.fun_fact: The first race was won by William Grover-Williams, driving a Bugatti.

questions.text: What drink is traditionally given to the winner of the Indianapolis 500?
questions.fun_fact: It goes back to Louis Meyer, who asked for buttermilk after winning the race in 1933.

questions.text: Which driver won the Monaco Grand Prix six times, including five in a row from 1989 to 1993?
questions.fun_fact: Senna won his three world titles in 1988, 1990 and 1991, all with McLaren.

questions.text: Which Argentine driver won five Formula One world titles in the 1950s?
questions.fun_fact: He won his titles with four different makers: Alfa Romeo, Maserati, Mercedes-Benz and Ferrari.

questions.text: Which French Formula One driver was nicknamed 'The Professor'?
questions.fun_fact: He won four world titles, in 1985, 1986, 1989 and 1993.

questions.text: Which Australian won the 1966 Formula One world title in a car bearing his own name?
questions.fun_fact: Brabham won three world titles in all: 1959, 1960 and 1966.

questions.text: The McLaren racing team was founded in 1963 by a driver from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Bruce McLaren had won the Monaco Grand Prix in 1962, driving for Cooper.

questions.text: Who became Brazil's first Formula One world champion, in 1972?
questions.fun_fact: He later won the Indianapolis 500 twice, in 1989 and 1993.

questions.text: Which Scottish driver won the 1965 Indianapolis 500 in a Lotus?
questions.fun_fact: He was the first non-American to win the race in 49 years.

questions.text: Which car won the 24 Hours of Le Mans four years in a row, from 1966 to 1969?
questions.fun_fact: The '40' in its name was its height in inches, about 1.02 m.

questions.text: In which year was the first 24 Hours of Le Mans held?
questions.fun_fact: The race is usually held in June, but in 1968 it was moved to September.

questions.text: Which driver won the 1964 Monte Carlo Rally in a Mini Cooper S?
