questions.fun_fact: Hopkirk came from Northern Ireland, and his winning Mini carried the number 37.

questions.text: Which wedge-shaped Lancia won the World Rally Championship in 1974, 1975 and 1976?
questions.fun_fact: It was powered by a V6 engine from the Ferrari Dino.

questions.text: The first Dakar Rally, in 1978–1979, started in which European city?
questions.fun_fact: The event moved to South America in 2009 and to Saudi Arabia in 2020.

questions.text: Italy's Mille Miglia road race was named after a distance of about 1,000 what?
questions.fun_fact: It ran as a loop from Brescia to Rome and back, from 1927 to 1957.

questions.text: Porsche's 'Carrera' name comes from a 1950s road race held in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The race ran from 1950 to 1954 along the newly built Mexican section of the Pan-American Highway.

questions.text: NASCAR was founded in 1948 in which Florida city?
questions.fun_fact: Before NASCAR, Daytona's hard-packed beach was a favorite place for land speed record attempts.

questions.text: The Kyalami circuit hosted which country's Formula One Grand Prix?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Zulu words 'Khaya lami', meaning 'my home'.

questions.text: German Grand Prix cars of the 1930s from Mercedes-Benz and Auto Union were nicknamed what?
questions.fun_fact: German cars had traditionally raced in white, Germany's national racing color at the time.

questions.text: Which planet is best known for its spectacular system of rings?
questions.fun_fact: Saturn's rings are made almost entirely of water ice, yet in places they are only about 10 m thick.

questions.text: Which famous comet can be seen from Earth about once every 74 to 79 years?
questions.fun_fact: Edmond Halley predicted that it would return in 1758, and it was duly spotted on Christmas Day that year.

questions.text: Which planet is often called Earth's 'twin' because of its similar size and mass?
questions.fun_fact: Seen from Earth, Venus shines brighter than any star or any other planet.

questions.text: What is the powerful, brilliant explosion of a star called?
questions.fun_fact: The supernova of 1054, which created the Crab Nebula, was recorded by Chinese astronomers.

questions.text: Who became the first woman to travel into space, in June 1963?
questions.fun_fact: Her call sign aboard Vostok 6 was Chaika, Russian for 'seagull'.

questions.text: Which NASA rover landed on Mars in February 2021, carrying the Ingenuity helicopter?
questions.fun_fact: In April 2021, Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.

questions.text: Which spacecraft became the first to enter interstellar space, in 2012?
questions.fun_fact: In 1990 it took the 'Pale Blue Dot' photo, which shows Earth from about 6 billion km away.

questions.text: What is the brightest star in Earth's night sky?
questions.fun_fact: Sirius is a binary star: its faint companion, Sirius B, is a white dwarf.

questions.text: Which country's Chandrayaan-3 mission landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023?
questions.fun_fact: Its lander was named Vikram, after Vikram Sarabhai, who is regarded as the father of India's space program.

questions.text: Who performed the first ever spacewalk, in March 1965?
questions.fun_fact: Leonov's spacesuit swelled in the vacuum of space, so he let out some of its air to squeeze back into the airlock.

questions.text: Which rocket launched the James Webb Space Telescope in December 2021?
questions.fun_fact: Webb operates near the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million km from Earth.

questions.text: In which year was 51 Pegasi b, the first exoplanet found orbiting a Sun-like star, announced?
questions.fun_fact: Its discoverers, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.text: Kimchi is a traditional fermented side dish from which cuisine?
questions.fun_fact: UNESCO lists kimjang, the Korean tradition of making and sharing kimchi, as intangible cultural heritage.

questions.text: Couscous, tiny steamed granules of semolina, is a staple dish of which region?
questions.fun_fact: In 2020, UNESCO added couscous to its heritage list after a joint bid by Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia.

questions.text: Chocolate is made from the beans of which plant?
questions.fun_fact: The Aztecs valued cacao beans so highly that they used them as a form of currency.

questions.text: Tiramisu is a classic dessert from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Italian 'tirami su', meaning 'pick me up' or 'cheer me up'.

questions.text: Roquefort cheese is made from which animal's milk?
questions.fun_fact: Only cheese aged in the natural Combalou caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon in France may be sold as Roquefort.

questions.text: Rooibos, a caffeine-free herbal tea, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The name rooibos means 'red bush' in Afrikaans.

questions.text: Which Andean crop did the Incas nickname the 'mother of all grains'?
questions.fun_fact: Botanically, quinoa is not a cereal grass but a pseudocereal, related to spinach.

questions.text: Vegemite, the dark yeast-extract spread, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Vegemite was created in Melbourne in 1922 from leftover brewer's yeast extract.

questions.text: Which spice comes from the dried stigmas of a crocus flower?
questions.fun_fact: It takes roughly 150,000 hand-picked crocus flowers to produce one kilogram of saffron.

questions.text: Which part of the clove tree is dried to make the spice cloves?
questions.fun_fact: Clove trees are native to the Maluku Islands of Indonesia, once famous as the Spice Islands.

questions.text: Injera, the spongy, sour flatbread of Ethiopia, is traditionally made from which grain?
questions.fun_fact: Injera serves as both plate and cutlery: diners tear off pieces of it to scoop up stews.

questions.text: Halloumi cheese traditionally comes from which Mediterranean island?
questions.fun_fact: Halloumi has a high melting point, so it can be grilled or fried without melting.

questions.text: What is the fastest land animal?
questions.fun_fact: Cheetahs purr when content, much like house cats but far louder.

questions.text: What is the largest living animal?
questions.fun_fact: Blue whales feed almost entirely on krill, tiny shrimp-like crustaceans.

questions.text: What is a group of lions called?
questions.fun_fact: Lionesses in a pride usually hunt together, while resident males rarely join group hunts.

questions.text: What makes up about 99% of a giant panda's diet?
questions.fun_fact: An average giant panda eats 9 to 14 kg of bamboo every day.

questions.text: What does a camel store in its hump?
questions.fun_fact: A dromedary camel has one hump, while a Bactrian camel has two.

questions.text: Which bird is the fastest animal on Earth when diving for prey?
questions.fun_fact: Peregrine falcons have adapted to city life, often nesting on tall buildings and bridges.

questions.text: What is the largest living reptile?
questions.fun_fact: Its range stretches from India's east coast across Southeast Asia to northern Australia.

questions.text: Which bird can turn its head about 270 degrees?
questions.fun_fact: Owls cannot move their eyes in their sockets, so they turn their whole head to look around.

questions.text: Lemurs are native to which island?
questions.fun_fact: The aye-aye, a lemur, uses its long, thin middle finger to pull food out of tiny holes.

questions.text: What is a group of flamingos called?
questions.fun_fact: Flamingos get their pink color from pigments called carotenoids in the food they eat.

questions.text: Which ape's name comes from Malay words meaning 'person of the forest'?
questions.fun_fact: Orangutans build an elaborate sleeping nest of branches and leaves in the trees each night.

questions.text: The axolotl is native to lakes near which city?
questions.fun_fact: Axolotls keep their gilled, juvenile form as adults, a trait known as neoteny.

questions.text: Which company released the Game Boy handheld console in 1989?
questions.fun_fact: Its design team was led by Gunpei Yokoi and Satoru Okada.

questions.text: Which famous doll did Ruth Handler create, launching it in 1959?
questions.fun_fact: The doll was named after Handler's daughter, Barbara.

questions.text: American engineer Percy Spencer is credited with inventing which kitchen appliance?
questions.fun_fact: The first commercial model, sold in 1947, stood about 1.8 m tall and weighed about 340 kg.

questions.text: Papyrus, an early writing material, was first made in which ancient land?
questions.fun_fact: The English word 'paper' comes from the word 'papyrus'.

questions.text: Which company developed the Post-it Note?
questions.fun_fact: Its reusable, low-tack glue was found by accident in 1968, when chemist Spencer Silver was trying to make a super-strong adhesive.

questions.text: In which country was the QR code invented in 1994?
questions.fun_fact: QR codes were first used to track car parts during manufacturing, and QR stands for 'Quick Response'.

questions.text: Which brothers built the balloon used in the first free flight carrying people, in Paris in 1783?
questions.fun_fact: Before any people flew, a sheep, a duck and a rooster rode one of their balloons at Versailles in 1783.

questions.text: Elisha Otis is famous for inventing a safety device for which machine?
questions.fun_fact: Otis demonstrated his safety device to the public at New York's Crystal Palace in 1854.

questions.text: The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by René Laennec, a doctor from which country?
questions.fun_fact: His first stethoscope was a simple wooden tube that he listened through with one ear.

questions.text: Which Hollywood actress co-patented a frequency-hopping radio system in 1942?
questions.fun_fact: She devised it with composer George Antheil, who had synchronized player pianos using matching piano rolls.

questions.text: Which company introduced the compact audio cassette in 1963?
questions.fun_fact: A team led by engineer Lou Ottens created it, and Philips later licensed the format to other makers free of charge.

questions.text: Kevlar was invented in 1965 by chemist Stephanie Kwolek at which company?
questions.fun_fact: Weight for weight, Kevlar fiber is about five times stronger than steel.

questions.text: Which swimmer won eight gold medals at a single Olympic Games, in 2008?
questions.fun_fact: That broke Mark Spitz's record of seven gold medals at a single Games.

questions.text: Which sprinter won the Olympic 100 m title in 2008, 2012 and 2016?
questions.fun_fact: He also won the 200 m at all three of those Games.

questions.text: At which ancient Greek site is the Olympic flame traditionally lit?
questions.fun_fact: The flame is kindled from the Sun's rays, focused by a parabolic mirror.

questions.text: The 'Bird's Nest' stadium was built as the main venue for which Olympic Games?
questions.fun_fact: It also staged the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2022 Winter Olympics.

questions.text: In 2012, which city became the first to host the modern Olympics three times?
questions.fun_fact: Its two earlier Games were held in 1908 and 1948.

questions.text: Which city hosted the first Olympic Games held in Asia, in 1964?
questions.fun_fact: Japan's first Shinkansen bullet train line opened just days before those Games began.

questions.text: Waldi the dachshund, the first official Olympic mascot, was created for which Games?
questions.fun_fact: A skiing figure called Schuss had appeared at the 1968 Grenoble Winter Games, but only as an unofficial mascot.

questions.text: Which runner won the 5,000 m, 10,000 m and marathon at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics?
questions.fun_fact: The Helsinki race was the first marathon he had ever run.

questions.text: In which event did Bob Beamon make his famous 8.90 m leap at the 1968 Olympics?
questions.fun_fact: It beat the previous world record by 55 cm and stood as the world record for nearly 23 years.

questions.text: Syd, one of the mascots of the Sydney 2000 Olympics, was which animal?
questions.fun_fact: Syd's fellow mascots were Olly the kookaburra and Millie the echidna.

questions.text: Which Soviet gymnast won 18 Olympic medals between 1956 and 1964?
questions.fun_fact: Her total stood as the Olympic record for the most medals for 48 years.

questions.text: In which year did women first compete at the modern Olympic Games?
questions.fun_fact: British tennis player Charlotte Cooper became the first individual female Olympic champion at those Games.

questions.text: What is the capital of the United States?
questions.fun_fact: The city is not part of any state; D.C. stands for District of Columbia.

questions.text: What is the capital of Germany?
questions.fun_fact: Berlin is also one of Germany's states, and it is completely surrounded by the state of Brandenburg.

questions.text: What is the capital of Thailand?
questions.fun_fact: Thais usually call the city Krung Thep, a name often translated as 'City of Angels'.

questions.text: What is the capital of Peru?
questions.fun_fact: Francisco Pizarro founded the city in 1535 as the 'City of Kings'.

questions.text: What is the capital of Turkey?
questions.fun_fact: The Angora cat, goat and rabbit are named after Angora, the city's historical name.

questions.text: What is the capital of Nigeria?
questions.fun_fact: Abuja, a planned city built mainly in the 1980s, replaced Lagos as Nigeria's capital in 1991.

questions.text: What is the capital of New Zealand?
questions.fun_fact: Wellington replaced Auckland as the capital in 1865, chosen for its central location and good harbor.

questions.text: What is the capital of Vietnam?
questions.fun_fact: In 1010 the city was named Thăng Long, meaning 'ascending dragon'.

questions.text: What is the capital of Ecuador?
questions.fun_fact: Its historic center was among the first sites added to UNESCO's World Heritage List, in 1978.

questions.text: What is the capital of Slovenia?
questions.fun_fact: The city's symbol is a dragon, which appears on its coat of arms and on its famous Dragon Bridge.

questions.text: What is the capital of Bhutan?
questions.fun_fact: Thimphu sits more than 2,200 m above sea level, making it one of the world's highest capitals.

questions.text: What is the capital of Namibia?
questions.fun_fact: Windhoek lies close to the geographic center of Namibia, on the Khomas Highland plateau.

questions.text: The humerus is the long bone of which part of the body?
questions.fun_fact: The 'funny bone' is really the ulnar nerve near the elbow end of the humerus; the nickname may be a pun on 'humorous'.

questions.text: Which part of the eye gives it its color?
questions.fun_fact: The pupil is not a structure at all but a hole in the center of the iris that lets light reach the retina.

questions.text: Which tough bands of tissue attach muscles to bones?
questions.fun_fact: The Achilles tendon, which links the calf muscles to the heel bone, is the thickest tendon in the human body.

questions.text: What is the anatomical name for the kneecap?
questions.fun_fact: The patella is the body's largest sesamoid bone, meaning it is embedded within a tendon.

questions.text: What are the tiny air sacs in the lungs, where gas exchange happens, called?
questions.fun_fact: Alveoli are lined with surfactant, a fluid that lowers surface tension; without it, they would collapse.

questions.text: Which iron-containing protein carries oxygen in red blood cells?
questions.fun_fact: A single hemoglobin molecule can bind and carry up to four oxygen molecules.

questions.text: Which organ produces bile, a fluid that helps the body digest fats?
questions.fun_fact: An adult's liver makes about 400 to 800 mL of bile a day, which is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder.

questions.text: Which sheet of muscle separates the chest from the abdomen and is the main muscle of breathing?
questions.fun_fact: The esophagus reaches the stomach through an opening in the diaphragm called the esophageal hiatus.

questions.text: In which organ are most nutrients from food absorbed, through tiny finger-like villi?
questions.fun_fact: In a living person it is typically 3 to 5 m long, and it has three sections: the duodenum, the jejunum and the ileum.

questions.text: Which thick band of nerve fibers connects the brain's left and right hemispheres?
questions.fun_fact: Corpus callosum is Latin for 'tough body'.

questions.text: The pineal gland produces which hormone, linked to the body's sleep-wake cycle?
questions.fun_fact: The pineal gland takes its name from its shape, which resembles a pine cone.

questions.text: Which cranial nerve carries the sense of smell to the brain?
questions.fun_fact: It is the shortest of the 12 cranial nerves and, like the optic nerve, does not emerge from the brainstem.

questions.text: Who ruled as king of the gods on Mount Olympus in Greek mythology?
questions.fun_fact: His mother Rhea hid the newborn Zeus on Crete so that his father Cronus could not swallow him.

questions.text: Who is the mischievous trickster among the Norse gods?
questions.fun_fact: With the giantess Angrboða, he fathered Hel, the wolf Fenrir and the world serpent Jörmungandr.

questions.text: Who was the ancient Egyptian deity of the sun?
questions.fun_fact: Egyptians imagined Ra crossing the sky by day in a boat, then sailing through the underworld at night.

questions.text: Which twin brothers feature in the legend of the founding of Rome?
questions.fun_fact: In Rome's famous Capitoline Wolf bronze, the suckling twins beneath the wolf were added in the late 15th century.

questions.text: Which Titan stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity?
questions.fun_fact: His brother Epimetheus, whose name means 'afterthought', ignored his warning and accepted Pandora from the gods.

questions.text: What is the name of the immense ash tree at the center of the Norse cosmos?
questions.fun_fact: A squirrel named Ratatoskr runs up and down it, carrying messages between an eagle at the top and the dragon Níðhöggr below.

questions.text: Which Japanese folk hero was born from a giant peach?
questions.fun_fact: On his quest to the demons' island, he wins over a dog, a monkey and a pheasant by sharing his millet dumplings.

questions.text: In Greek myth, which king was condemned to push a boulder up a hill forever, only for it to roll back down?
questions.fun_fact: His punishment gave English the adjective 'Sisyphean' for a task that is both laborious and futile.

questions.text: Which figure of Greek myth was punished by standing in water that receded whenever he tried to drink?
questions.fun_fact: His endless torment, with fruit always just out of reach, gave English the word 'tantalize'.

questions.text: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, which wild man becomes Gilgamesh's closest companion?
questions.fun_fact: In the epic, the goddess Aruru creates the hairy Enkidu in the wild, where he grazes and drinks alongside the animals.

questions.text: Which Egyptian deity, often shown with the head of an ibis, was linked with writing and wisdom?
questions.fun_fact: The Greeks identified Thoth with their own Hermes, and he was also often depicted as a baboon.

questions.text: What is the name of Odin's eight-legged horse in Norse mythology?
questions.fun_fact: Odin also kept two ravens, Huginn and Muninn, who flew across the world each day to bring him information.

questions.text: In which museum does Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa hang?
questions.fun_fact: For a brief period, the Mona Lisa hung in Napoleon's bedroom in the Tuileries Palace in Paris.

questions.text: Which artist painted The Starry Night?
questions.fun_fact: The village in the painting is imaginary; it could not be seen from the window whose view Van Gogh painted.

questions.text: Who painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling frescoes between 1508 and 1512?
questions.fun_fact: Contrary to a popular myth, he painted it standing up on freestanding scaffolding, not lying on his back.

questions.text: Which American pop artist created the series Campbell's Soup Cans?
questions.fun_fact: The original series has 32 canvases, each showing a different variety of Campbell's soup.

questions.text: Which Latin American artist is famous for depicting people and figures in large, exaggerated volume?
questions.fun_fact: His style is known as 'Boterismo'; he donated many works to museums in Bogotá and his hometown, Medellín.

questions.text: Which American artist painted American Gothic in 1930?
questions.fun_fact: The models were Wood's sister Nan and the family's dentist; Wood meant them as a farmer and his grown-up daughter.

questions.text: Which Austrian painter created The Kiss, famous for its use of gold leaf?
questions.fun_fact: Besides gold leaf, Klimt added silver and platinum to the oil-on-canvas painting.

questions.text: Which Mexican painter created Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird?
questions.fun_fact: The dead hummingbird hanging from her necklace is seen in Mexican folklore as a charm for luck in love.

questions.text: Which French sculptor created The Thinker?
questions.fun_fact: The figure was first called The Poet and was designed for Rodin's monumental doorway The Gates of Hell.

questions.text: Velázquez's Las Meninas hangs in which Madrid museum?
questions.fun_fact: In 1957 Picasso painted 58 reinterpretations of it, now in the Museu Picasso in Barcelona.

questions.text: Which Japanese artist created the woodblock print series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo?
questions.fun_fact: Van Gogh painted copies of two of its prints: Plum Park in Kameido and Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge.

questions.text: Which sculptor carved the marble Apollo and Daphne in Rome's Galleria Borghese?
questions.fun_fact: It captures the moment the nymph Daphne escapes Apollo by turning into a laurel tree.

questions.text: The word 'dinosaur' comes from Greek words meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Megalosaurus, named in 1824, was the first dinosaur genus to be validly named, years before the word 'dinosaur' existed.

questions.text: Which dinosaur had large upright plates along its back and spikes on its tail?
questions.fun_fact: Its tail spikes are nicknamed the 'thagomizer', a joke word from a 1982 Far Side cartoon.

questions.text: Which group of living animals is descended from dinosaurs?
questions.fun_fact: Birds are theropods, the same group of dinosaurs that includes Tyrannosaurus rex.

questions.text: The prehistoric giant known as megalodon was what kind of animal?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'big tooth'. Like all sharks, its skeleton was cartilage rather than bone, so most fossils are poorly preserved.

questions.text: Which period was the first of the three that make up the Mesozoic Era?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after a sequence of three distinct rock layers found across southern Germany.

questions.text: Flying reptiles such as Pteranodon belonged to which group?
questions.fun_fact: Pterosaurs were not dinosaurs, but they were the earliest vertebrates known to have evolved powered flight.

questions.text: In which desert was the first Velociraptor fossil found, in 1923?
questions.fun_fact: The famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossil, found in 1971, shows a Velociraptor locked in combat with a Protoceratops.

questions.text: In which country were the first Archaeopteryx fossils discovered?
questions.fun_fact: The first complete specimen was announced in 1861, just two years after Darwin published On the Origin of Species.

questions.text: What does the dinosaur name Triceratops mean?
questions.fun_fact: American paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh named it in 1889; it lived in what is now western North America.

questions.text: The name of the Cretaceous period comes from the Latin word for which rock?
questions.fun_fact: The White Cliffs of Dover are Cretaceous chalk, made largely from coccoliths, the tiny skeletons of ancient algae.

questions.text: Sinosauropteryx, a small feathered dinosaur described in 1996, was found in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first dinosaur outside birds and their closest relatives to be found with evidence of feathers.

questions.text: Fossil hunter Mary Anning made her famous finds around which English seaside town?
questions.fun_fact: Her discoveries included the first correctly identified ichthyosaur skeleton, found when she was 12.

questions.text: How many arms does an octopus have?
questions.fun_fact: Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are found in the nerve cords of its arms.

questions.text: What is the regular rise and fall of sea level, caused mainly by the Moon's gravity, called?
questions.fun_fact: The Sun raises tides too, but its tide-generating force is only about 46% as strong as the Moon's.

questions.text: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of which animal?
questions.fun_fact: A mucus coating keeps clownfish from being stung, possibly by mimicking the anemone's own mucus.

questions.text: Which coral reef system off Queensland, Australia, is the largest in the world?
questions.fun_fact: The reef was built by billions of tiny animals called coral polyps.

questions.text: In which sea creature does the male carry the eggs in a pouch until the young are born?
questions.fun_fact: Seahorses are bony fish; their genus name, Hippocampus, comes from Ancient Greek words for 'horse' and 'sea monster'.

questions.text: The 1872–1876 voyage of HMS Challenger laid the foundation of which science?
questions.fun_fact: In March 1875 its crew recorded a depth of 8,184 m at a spot in the Pacific now known as the Challenger Deep.

questions.text: Which marine mammal often floats on its back and uses rocks to crack open shellfish?
questions.fun_fact: Instead of relying on blubber, sea otters stay warm with the densest fur of any animal.

questions.text: The narwhal's long spiral tusk is actually an enlarged what?
questions.fun_fact: In medieval times, narwhal tusks were believed to be the horns of the legendary unicorn.

questions.text: Which North Atlantic sea has no land boundaries and is defined by ocean currents?
questions.fun_fact: Portuguese sailors named it after the sargassum seaweed that floats in its waters.

questions.text: In 1960, which vessel carried Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh to the bottom of the Mariana Trench?
questions.fun_fact: The descent took nearly five hours, yet the two men spent only about 20 minutes on the ocean floor.

questions.text: Which ocean zone, where no sunlight reaches, is nicknamed the 'midnight zone'?
questions.fun_fact: Without sunlight there is no photosynthesis, so no plants or phytoplankton can grow there.

questions.text: Which of these land animals is most closely related to the manatee?
questions.fun_fact: Manatees belong to the order Sirenia, named after the sirens of Greek mythology.

questions.text: Which of these words is a palindrome?
questions.fun_fact: James Joyce coined the palindrome 'tattarrattat' in Ulysses (1922) for the sound of a knock on a door.

questions.text: The word 'karaoke' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: It means 'empty orchestra', from kara ('empty') and a shortened form of ōkesutora ('orchestra').

questions.text: What is a word formed from initials and said as a word, like NASA, called?
questions.fun_fact: The word 'laser' began as an acronym for 'light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation'.

questions.text: What is a word that imitates a sound, such as 'buzz' or 'sizzle', called?
questions.fun_fact: The term comes from Ancient Greek for 'name-making'; in Japanese, a dog's bark is 'wan-wan'.

questions.text: Which author coined the words 'chortle' and 'galumphing' in his poem Jabberwocky?
questions.fun_fact: In the same book, Humpty Dumpty explains that 'slithy' packs two meanings, 'lithe and slimy', into one word.

questions.text: The Devanagari script is used to write which of these languages?
questions.fun_fact: Its letters hang from a horizontal line that runs along their tops, called the shirorekha.

questions.text: Who compiled A Dictionary of the English Language, published in 1755?
questions.fun_fact: Johnson defined 'lexicographer' as 'a writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge'.

questions.text: The word 'galaxy' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: In Greek myth, the Milky Way formed from milk spilled by the goddess Hera while she was nursing the infant Heracles.

questions.text: Hungarian belongs to which language family?
questions.fun_fact: Its closest relatives are Mansi and Khanty, two languages spoken in western Siberia.

questions.text: What is a sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet at least once called?
questions.fun_fact: The best-known English example, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog', is often used to display typefaces.

questions.text: Swahili, widely spoken in East Africa, belongs to which group of languages?
questions.fun_fact: The name Swahili comes from an Arabic word meaning 'coasts'.

questions.text: The English words 'avocado' and 'tomato' come from which language of the Aztecs?
questions.fun_fact: Coyote and chili also come from Nahuatl; many of these words reached English by way of Spanish.

questions.text: What is the tallest living land animal?
questions.fun_fact: Giraffes are also the largest ruminants: like cows, they chew the cud.

questions.text: What is the largest living bird?
questions.fun_fact: Its eyes, about 50 mm across, are the largest of any land vertebrate.

questions.text: Which is the largest living land animal?
questions.fun_fact: It lives in sub-Saharan Africa, and its large ears help it shed body heat.

questions.text: Which is the largest living primate?
questions.fun_fact: Gorillas build nests of branches and leaves, often about an hour before dusk, to sleep in at night.

questions.text: What is a group of wolves usually called?
questions.fun_fact: Wolves usually travel in family groups made up of a mated pair and their offspring.

questions.text: What is a group of geese on the ground called?
questions.fun_fact: Geese in flight are called a skein, a team or a wedge.

questions.text: What is a male duck called?
questions.fun_fact: In mallards and several related ducks, it is the female that makes the classic loud quack.

questions.text: Many bats find their way and hunt in the dark using what?
questions.fun_fact: Toothed whales such as dolphins also hunt by echolocation.

questions.text: Spiders belong to which class of animals?
questions.fun_fact: Unlike insects, spiders have bodies made of two main parts: the cephalothorax and the abdomen.

questions.text: How many legs does an adult insect have?
questions.fun_fact: An insect's body has three parts, the head, thorax and abdomen, and all six legs attach to the thorax.

questions.text: Koalas feed almost entirely on the leaves of which tree?
questions.fun_fact: Their low-energy diet means koalas are largely inactive and sleep up to 20 hours a day.

questions.text: The giant panda belongs to which family of animals?
questions.fun_fact: Its classification was long debated, until molecular studies in 1985 showed it is a true bear.

questions.text: The domestic dog was domesticated from which wild animal?
questions.fun_fact: The dog was the first species to be domesticated, over 14,000 years ago, before the development of farming.

questions.text: A mule is the offspring of a female horse and a male what?
questions.fun_fact: Mules are almost always infertile, because horses and donkeys have different numbers of chromosomes.

questions.text: The Siamese cat breed comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its dark 'points' come from a heat-sensitive enzyme that only works in the cooler parts of the body.

questions.text: How many compartments does a cow's stomach have?
questions.fun_fact: The four parts are the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum; only the abomasum is a 'true stomach'.

questions.text: On which continent are there no native snakes?
questions.fun_fact: Several large islands, including Ireland, Iceland and New Zealand, have no native land snakes either.

questions.text: Which animal makes up most of the 'Great Migration' across the Serengeti and Maasai Mara?
questions.fun_fact: Zebras often travel with them, eating the taller grass and exposing the greener shoots that wildebeest prefer.

questions.text: The dodo, a flightless bird, lived only on which island?
questions.fun_fact: The dodo was a relative of pigeons and doves; its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon.

questions.text: Piranhas live in the rivers of which continent?
questions.fun_fact: Despite their fierce reputation, piranhas also eat plant material such as seeds and fruit.

questions.text: Commercial silk comes mainly from the cocoons of which insect?
questions.fun_fact: Domestic silk moths have lost the ability to fly; their closest wild relative is Bombyx mandarina.

questions.text: Which bird is famous for laying its eggs in other birds' nests?
questions.fun_fact: A cuckoo chick often pushes its host's own eggs out of the nest soon after hatching.

questions.text: The 'flying fox' is actually a type of what?
questions.fun_fact: The name 'flying fox' has been used for these large fruit bats since at least 1759.

questions.text: Which monkey is famous for bathing in hot springs in Japan?
questions.fun_fact: Also known as the snow monkey, it is the northernmost-living non-human primate.

questions.text: A tadpole is the larval stage of which kind of animal?
questions.fun_fact: As tadpoles turn into frogs, their back legs grow first, then the front legs, and they develop lungs.

questions.text: Which mammal builds dams across streams using branches and mud?
questions.fun_fact: A beaver's front teeth are orange because their enamel contains iron compounds.

questions.text: Which is the smallest living bird?
questions.fun_fact: It lives only in Cuba, and males weigh around 2 grams.

questions.text: Which is the largest living species of deer?
questions.fun_fact: It is the tallest land animal in North America and the second-largest by weight, after the American bison.

questions.text: The spectacled bear is the only living bear species native to which continent?
questions.fun_fact: Also called the Andean bear, it eats mostly plants, such as cacti and bromeliads.

questions.text: Which is the heaviest living snake?
questions.fun_fact: It is slightly shorter than the reticulated python, the longest snake, but far bulkier.

questions.text: Which is the longest venomous snake?
questions.fun_fact: The king cobra is an apex predator that mainly hunts other snakes.

questions.text: Pregnancy in which animal typically lasts between one and a half and two years?
questions.fun_fact: Elephants are strong swimmers and can swim for up to six hours without touching the bottom.

questions.text: Which bird makes the longest yearly migration of any animal, flying from pole to pole and back?
questions.fun_fact: Its journey means it sees two summers a year and more daylight than any other creature on the planet.

questions.text: What is a group of owls called?
questions.fun_fact: There are over 200 species of owls, most of them solitary, nocturnal birds of prey.

questions.text: What is a huge, swirling flock of starlings called?
questions.fun_fact: A 2008 study showed that each starling in a flock typically interacts with at most seven of its nearest neighbors.

questions.text: What is a group of kangaroos called?
questions.fun_fact: At slow speeds, a kangaroo uses its tail as a fifth limb, forming a tripod with its forelimbs.

questions.text: What is a young swan called?
questions.fun_fact: Adult male swans are called cobs and females are called pens.

questions.text: What is a female fox called?
questions.fun_fact: Red foxes live across the entire Northern Hemisphere and were introduced into Australia.

questions.text: Which Australian bird is famous for mimicking sounds such as camera shutters and chainsaws?
questions.fun_fact: It can imitate the calls of about twenty other bird species as well as human-made sounds.

questions.text: Microscopic tardigrades are often nicknamed what?
questions.fun_fact: Tardigrades are among the most resilient animals known and have even survived exposure to outer space.

questions.text: A woodlouse, found under stones and logs, is what kind of animal?
questions.fun_fact: Woodlice lose water quickly through their cuticle, so they live in damp, dark places.

questions.text: The Komodo dragon lives in the wild only in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Female Komodo dragons at two English zoos have produced eggs without a male, through parthenogenesis.

questions.text: The tailless Manx cat breed comes from which island?
questions.fun_fact: Many Manx cats have a small stub of a tail, but the breed is best known for being entirely tailless.

questions.text: The kākāpō of New Zealand is the world's only flightless species of which kind of bird?
questions.fun_fact: It is also the world's heaviest parrot, and it is active mainly at night.

questions.text: Which is the largest cat native to the Americas?
questions.fun_fact: It is the third-largest cat species in the world, after the tiger and the lion.

questions.text: A badger's underground home is called what?
questions.fun_fact: Badger setts can be very complex, and they are passed down from generation to generation.

questions.text: Eastern monarch butterflies spend the winter in forests of which country?
questions.fun_fact: No single butterfly makes the whole round trip: two to three generations complete the journey north.

questions.text: Fireflies are actually which type of insect?
questions.fun_fact: Fireflies make a 'cold light', which contains no infrared or ultraviolet frequencies.

questions.text: Some periodical cicadas of North America emerge every 13 years. Others emerge every how many years?
questions.fun_fact: Both 13 and 17 are prime numbers, which may help the cicadas avoid predators with shorter life cycles.

questions.text: Leafcutter ants use the leaves they cut to grow what?
questions.fun_fact: The central mound of a leafcutter nest can grow to more than 30 m across.

questions.text: The basenji, a dog breed known for not barking, originated on which continent?
questions.fun_fact: Instead of barking, it makes an unusual yodel-like sound because of its unusually shaped larynx.

questions.text: The Andean condor is a type of what?
questions.fun_fact: With a wingspan of up to 3.3 m, it is one of the largest flying birds and soars for hours on rising air.

questions.text: How does the African secretarybird usually kill its prey?
options: By spearing it with its bill
By digging it out of burrows
questions.fun_fact: Unlike most birds of prey, it is largely terrestrial and hunts on foot.

questions.text: Which is the largest living frog?
questions.fun_fact: Goliath frogs live along fast-flowing rivers in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea.

questions.text: Many geckos can climb smooth walls thanks to millions of tiny what on their toes?
questions.fun_fact: These hairs, called setae, cling to surfaces through van der Waals forces between molecules.

questions.text: The domestic cat descends from which wild cat?
questions.fun_fact: Genetic and archaeological studies show that cat domestication began in the Near East around 7500 BC.

questions.text: The domestic chicken descends mainly from which wild bird?
questions.fun_fact: Red junglefowl still live wild across South and Southeast Asia.

questions.text: The Dalmatian dog breed is named after a region of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Dalmatian puppies are born with plain white coats; their first spots usually appear within 10 days.

questions.text: Which Australian marsupial is famous for producing cube-shaped droppings?
questions.fun_fact: In 2019, research into how wombats make cube-shaped feces won an Ig Nobel Prize.

questions.text: Reindeer are unique among deer because which of them can grow antlers?
questions.fun_fact: In North America, wild reindeer are known as caribou.

questions.text: Which mammal lives in underground colonies with a single breeding queen, much like ants or bees?
questions.fun_fact: Its queens age more slowly than the non-breeding members of the colony.

questions.text: Some common swifts can stay in continuous flight, without landing, for up to about how long?
questions.fun_fact: Swifts never settle on the ground by choice, where they would be vulnerable to accidents and predators.

questions.text: What is a young hare called?
questions.fun_fact: Hares are generally larger than rabbits, with longer ears and bigger eyes.

questions.text: What is a female donkey called?
questions.fun_fact: A male donkey is called a jack, and a young donkey is called a foal.

questions.text: Snakes flick their tongues to carry scent particles to which organ in the roof of the mouth?
questions.fun_fact: The same organ is found in many mammals, including cats, dogs and cattle.

questions.text: Despite its name, the electric eel is not a true eel. What kind of fish is it?
questions.fun_fact: It can stun its prey with electric shocks of up to 860 volts.

questions.text: Which African bird is famous for leading people to wild bees' nests?
questions.fun_fact: Honey-hunters in Mozambique summon it with a special call, and the bird eats the wax left behind.

questions.text: Hyenas look like dogs, but they belong to the branch of carnivores that includes which animals?
questions.fun_fact: In spotted hyenas it is the females that are larger and dominate the males.

questions.text: Rabbits and hares are not rodents. Which order of mammals do they belong to?
questions.fun_fact: Lagomorphs have four upper incisors, including a small pair of 'peg teeth', while rodents have two.

questions.text: Caecilians look like worms or snakes, but what kind of animal are they?
questions.fun_fact: In some species, the young feed on their mother's skin, a behavior called maternal dermatophagy.

questions.text: Bats belong to which order, whose name means 'hand wing'?
questions.fun_fact: Bats are the second-largest order of mammals after rodents, making up about 20% of all mammal species.

questions.text: Which animal is the only living member of the mammal order Tubulidentata?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from Afrikaans and means 'earth pig'.

questions.text: The tuatara, last survivor of an ancient order of reptiles, lives only in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Like some lizards, the tuatara has a 'third eye', called the parietal eye, on top of its head.

questions.text: The alpaca was domesticated from which wild South American animal?
questions.fun_fact: The alpaca was long assumed to descend from the llama, despite its many similarities to the vicuña.

questions.text: Przewalski's horse is native to the steppes of which country, where it was reintroduced in the 1990s?
questions.fun_fact: It is also known as the takhi, or the Mongolian wild horse.

questions.text: The Philippine eagle is also known by which nickname?
questions.fun_fact: It is the national bird of the Philippines and one of the largest eagles in the world.

questions.text: Which bird is the only one with a bill longer than its body, not counting the tail?
questions.fun_fact: It lives in the Andes and feeds on flowers with very long tubes, such as passionflowers.

questions.text: The extinct quagga of South Africa was a subspecies of which animal?
questions.fun_fact: It had brown and white stripes mainly on the front part of its body.

questions.text: The golden poison frog, one of the most poisonous animals, is native to which country?
questions.fun_fact: Indigenous hunters in Colombia have used its poison to tip their hunting darts.

questions.text: Bagheera kiplingi, a jumping spider named after a Jungle Book character, is unusual for what?
questions.fun_fact: It feeds on Beltian bodies, protein-rich nubs that acacias grow at their leaf tips to feed the ants guarding them.

questions.text: Gibbons travel through trees by swinging from their arms. What is this called?
questions.fun_fact: Gibbons can cover up to 15 m in a single swing and reach speeds of about 55 km/h.

questions.text: The gelada of the Ethiopian Highlands is unusual among primates because it eats mainly what?
questions.fun_fact: It is also called the 'bleeding-heart monkey' for the bright red patch of bare skin on its chest.

questions.text: Young hoatzins of South America have claws on which part of their bodies?
questions.fun_fact: Hoatzins digest leaves by fermenting them in an enlarged crop, which gives the bird a manure-like smell.

questions.text: Some nocturnal African dung beetles find their way using what?
questions.fun_fact: The species Scarabaeus satyrus is one of the few invertebrates known to orient itself by the Milky Way.

questions.text: The turkey was first domesticated in which region?
questions.fun_fact: Its English name likely comes from confusion with the guineafowl, which reached England through Turkey.

questions.text: Which scientist shared a 1973 Nobel Prize partly for decoding the honeybee's waggle dance?
questions.fun_fact: The angle of the waggle run relative to vertical tells other bees the direction of food relative to the Sun.

questions.text: The springbok's habit of making repeated high leaps into the air is called what?
questions.fun_fact: The springbok is South Africa's national animal and gives its name to the country's rugby team.

questions.text: Which is the largest living carnivorous marsupial?
questions.fun_fact: For its size, it has one of the strongest bites of any living predatory land mammal.

questions.text: Esther Mahlangu is famous for painting in the bold geometric style of which South African people?
questions.fun_fact: In 1991 she painted a BMW 525i art car in Ndebele patterns.

questions.text: Which French Post-Impressionist painter moved to Tahiti and painted its people?
questions.fun_fact: He first sailed to Tahiti in 1891.

questions.text: Piet Mondrian was a leading member of which Dutch art movement?
questions.fun_fact: De Stijl means 'The Style' in Dutch.

questions.text: Marc Chagall was born near which city, now in Belarus?
questions.fun_fact: He later painted part of the ceiling of the Paris Opéra.

questions.text: Joaquín Sorolla, famed for sunlit beach scenes, was born in which Spanish city?
questions.fun_fact: His former house and studio in Madrid is now the Sorolla Museum.

questions.text: What are the small pieces of glass, stone or tile used to make a mosaic called?
questions.fun_fact: Ancient Roman mosaic makers often used tesserae of natural stone in different colors.

questions.text: The famous painted bust of Queen Nefertiti was found in 1912 at which ancient Egyptian site?
questions.fun_fact: It is thought to be the work of the sculptor Thutmose; its left eye, unlike the right, has no inlay.

questions.text: Which 16th-century artist wrote The Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects?
questions.fun_fact: Vasari is often called the first art historian.

questions.text: Nam June Paik is regarded as the founder of which art form?
questions.fun_fact: Paik was born in Seoul in 1932 and later worked in Germany and the United States.

questions.text: South African artist William Kentridge is known for animated films made from what?
questions.fun_fact: He films each drawing, then erases and redraws parts of it, leaving faint traces of earlier frames.

questions.text: Painting onto fresh, wet lime plaster is known as what?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Italian 'affresco', meaning 'fresh'.

questions.text: Which Berlin building did Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrap in fabric in 1995?
questions.fun_fact: About 100,000 square meters of silvery fabric covered the building for two weeks.

questions.text: The Group of Seven painters are celebrated for their landscapes of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The group held its first exhibition in Toronto in 1920.

questions.text: Leonardo da Vinci's drawing Vitruvian Man is named after an ancient Roman what?
questions.fun_fact: The fragile drawing is kept in Venice and is only rarely put on public display.

questions.text: Frans Hals's The Laughing Cavalier hangs in which London museum?
questions.fun_fact: Despite its title, the man in the portrait is not actually laughing.

questions.text: What did Marcel Duchamp call ordinary manufactured objects that he presented as art?
questions.fun_fact: The most famous, Fountain (1917), is a porcelain urinal signed with the made-up name 'R. Mutt'.

questions.text: In encaustic painting, pigments are mixed with what?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Greek word for 'burning in'.

questions.text: Which English artist painted The Hay Wain (1821)?
questions.fun_fact: The cottage on the left was home to Willy Lott, a tenant farmer, and still stands at Flatford in Suffolk.

questions.text: Andy Warhol was a leading artist of which movement?
questions.fun_fact: His New York studio was known as the Factory.

questions.text: The prehistoric Lascaux cave paintings are in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The cave was discovered in 1940 by a teenager, Marcel Ravidat, and three friends.

questions.text: Chicago's mirrored sculpture Cloud Gate is popularly nicknamed what?
questions.fun_fact: It was designed by Anish Kapoor and is made of 168 stainless steel plates welded together.

questions.text: Which artist painted a famous series of still lifes of sunflowers in a vase?
questions.fun_fact: He painted them in Arles to decorate the room of his friend Paul Gauguin.

questions.text: Serbian artist Marina Abramović is best known for which kind of art?
questions.fun_fact: In 2010 she sat silently at MoMA for more than 700 hours in 'The Artist Is Present'.

questions.text: Which American artist is famous for 'drip paintings' made by pouring paint onto canvas laid on the floor?
questions.fun_fact: His wife, Lee Krasner, was also an important Abstract Expressionist painter.

questions.text: Claude Monet painted the water lily pond in his garden at which French village?
questions.fun_fact: Monet designed the garden himself, including the Japanese-style footbridge over the pond.

questions.text: Batik, a way of dyeing cloth using wax, is especially associated with which country?
questions.fun_fact: UNESCO added Indonesian batik to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2009.

questions.text: Chinese painter Xu Beihong was especially famous for ink paintings of which animal?
questions.fun_fact: He studied art in Paris and later headed China's Central Academy of Fine Arts.

questions.text: Sculptor Constantin Brâncuși, creator of Bird in Space, was born in which country?
questions.fun_fact: In 1903 he walked much of the way from Bucharest to Western Europe, passing through Vienna and Munich.

questions.text: What is missing from the ancient Greek statue known as the Venus de Milo?
questions.fun_fact: It was discovered in 1820 on the Aegean island of Milos.

questions.text: Since 1992, Picasso's Guernica has hung in which Madrid museum?
questions.fun_fact: The huge canvas is about 3.5 m tall and 7.8 m wide.

questions.text: Alphonse Mucha became famous for his Art Nouveau posters of which actress?
questions.fun_fact: His first poster for her, made for the play Gismonda, appeared in Paris in 1895.

questions.text: The Lion-man, one of the oldest known figurative sculptures, was carved from what?
questions.fun_fact: It was found in 1939 in the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in southern Germany.

questions.text: Tingatinga, a colorful style of painting animals, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The style is named after Edward Saidi Tingatinga, who began painting in Dar es Salaam in the 1960s.

questions.text: The painter known as El Greco was born on which island?
questions.fun_fact: His real name was Domenikos Theotokopoulos; 'El Greco' means 'the Greek'.

questions.text: Which French sculptor designed the Statue of Liberty?
questions.fun_fact: Bartholdi also made the Lion of Belfort, a huge lion built from red sandstone blocks below Belfort's castle in France.

questions.text: Ben Enwonwu's 1974 portrait Tutu, of a Nigerian princess, has been nicknamed the African what?
questions.fun_fact: The painting was rediscovered in a London flat in 2017, decades after it went missing.

questions.text: The Japanese art form ukiyo-e takes its name from words meaning 'pictures of the' what?
questions.fun_fact: Ukiyo-e prints strongly influenced European artists such as Van Gogh and Monet.

questions.text: The State Hermitage Museum is in which city?
questions.fun_fact: It was founded in 1764 by Empress Catherine the Great.

questions.text: Which American sculptor is credited with inventing the mobile?
questions.fun_fact: The name 'mobile' was suggested by his friend Marcel Duchamp in 1931.

questions.text: Antony Gormley's steel sculpture Angel of the North stands near which English town?
questions.fun_fact: Its wings span 54 m, much wider than the sculpture's 20 m height.

questions.text: Vermeer's painting The Milkmaid belongs to which Amsterdam museum?
questions.fun_fact: The museum acquired it in 1908 as part of the famous Six collection, with the Dutch government's backing.

questions.text: Which Spanish city is home to a Guggenheim Museum designed by Frank Gehry?
questions.fun_fact: Its curving walls are clad in thin sheets of titanium.

questions.text: Wassily Kandinsky, a pioneer of abstract art, was born in which country?
questions.fun_fact: He trained as a lawyer and economist before deciding at 30 to study painting.

questions.text: Which Song dynasty painter is credited with the scroll Along the River During the Qingming Festival?
questions.fun_fact: The scroll is over 5 m long and shows more than 800 people.

questions.text: Fernando Amorsolo, famed for sunlit rural scenes, became the first National Artist of which country?
questions.fun_fact: He was nicknamed the 'Grand Old Man of Philippine Art'.

questions.text: The Dada movement began in 1916 at the Cabaret Voltaire in which city?
questions.fun_fact: One story says the name was picked by sticking a knife into a dictionary at random.

questions.text: Edgar Degas is especially famous for paintings and sculptures of what?
questions.fun_fact: More than half of Degas's works show dancers.

questions.text: Which 18th-century Italian painter is best known for detailed views of Venice?
questions.fun_fact: Many of his paintings were bought by wealthy British travelers on the Grand Tour.

questions.text: Whistler's Mother belongs to which Paris museum?
questions.fun_fact: Its full title is Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1.

questions.text: Kazimir Malevich's painting Black Square is the key work of which movement?
questions.fun_fact: Malevich first showed it in 1915, hung high across a room's corner.

questions.text: The jeweled Fabergé eggs were made for the imperial family of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The first of them, the Hen Egg of 1885, opens to reveal a golden yolk holding a gold hen.

questions.text: Van Gogh's The Starry Night has been in which New York museum's collection since 1941?
questions.fun_fact: Although it shows a night sky, Van Gogh painted it during the day in his ground-floor studio.

questions.text: Which ancient Greek sculptor created the Discobolus, or Discus Thrower?
questions.fun_fact: The original bronze is lost; the statue is known from Roman copies.

questions.text: Which French artist developed Cubism together with Pablo Picasso?
questions.fun_fact: The term 'Cubism' grew out of a critic's remark that Braque's landscapes were made of little cubes.

questions.text: Which French artist is famous for his posters of the Moulin Rouge cabaret?
questions.fun_fact: When the cabaret opened in 1889, he was commissioned to produce a series of its posters.

questions.text: Kamāl ud-Dīn Behzād of Herat was a celebrated master of which art?
questions.fun_fact: He headed the royal workshops of the Safavid court in Tabriz.

questions.text: Azulejos, painted tin-glazed ceramic tiles, are a famous art form of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Lisbon has a National Museum of Azulejos devoted to them.

questions.text: Which German Romantic painted Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (around 1818)?
questions.fun_fact: The painting belongs to the Hamburger Kunsthalle in Hamburg.

questions.text: Amrita Sher-Gil, a pioneer of modern Indian art, was born in 1913 in which city?
questions.fun_fact: At 16 she sailed to Europe with her mother to train as a painter in Paris.

questions.text: Francisco Goya's 'Black Paintings' were originally painted directly onto what?
questions.fun_fact: They were later transferred to canvas and are now in the Prado Museum in Madrid.

questions.text: What is a painting made of three hinged panels called?
questions.fun_fact: Hieronymus Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights is one of the best-known triptychs.

questions.text: Which ingredient traditionally binds the pigment in egg tempera paint?
questions.fun_fact: Tempera was the main painting medium in Europe until oil paint took over in the 15th and 16th centuries.

questions.text: Which Italian poet launched Futurism with a manifesto in 1909?
questions.fun_fact: The manifesto was first published on the front page of the French newspaper Le Figaro.

questions.text: Michelangelo's statue of David is carved from what material?
questions.fun_fact: It is carved from Carrara marble and stands 5.17 m tall.

questions.text: Kintsugi is the Japanese art of mending broken pottery with lacquer mixed with what?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'golden joinery'.

questions.text: Ikebana is the Japanese art of arranging what?
questions.fun_fact: The name combines the Japanese words ikeru, 'to be living', and hana, 'flower'.

questions.text: Georgia O'Keeffe is especially known for large, close-up paintings of what?
questions.fun_fact: She spent much of her later life painting the desert landscapes of New Mexico.

questions.text: The Terracotta Army was discovered in 1974 near which Chinese city?
questions.fun_fact: It was found by farmers digging a well about 1.5 km east of the First Emperor's tomb mound.

questions.text: Ghanaian artist El Anatsui is known for shimmering wall hangings made largely from what?
questions.fun_fact: He won the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at the 2015 Venice Biennale.

questions.text: Albrecht Dürer's famous woodcut of 1515 shows which animal?
questions.fun_fact: Dürer never saw the animal; he worked from a written description and a sketch by someone else.

questions.text: Which Japanese artist is famous for her polka dots and pumpkin sculptures?
questions.fun_fact: Her Infinity Mirror Rooms use mirrors to make small spaces seem to go on forever.

questions.text: Tarsila do Amaral's 1928 painting Abaporu inspired which Brazilian art movement?
questions.fun_fact: Abaporu means 'the man who eats people' in the Tupi language.

questions.text: Which Dutch artist made the print Relativity, with its impossible staircases?
questions.fun_fact: Relativity is a lithograph, first printed in 1953.

questions.text: Salvador Dalí was a leading figure of which art movement?
questions.fun_fact: Dalí designed the logo of the Chupa Chups lollipop company in 1969.

questions.text: Henri Matisse was a leader of which movement, named after French for 'wild beasts'?
questions.fun_fact: In his last years Matisse made large works from paper cut-outs painted with gouache.

questions.text: Which French architect designed the Louvre Abu Dhabi, opened in 2017?
questions.fun_fact: Its vast dome lets sunlight filter through in a pattern its designer called a 'rain of light'.

questions.text: In René Magritte's painting The Son of Man, what hides the man's face?
questions.fun_fact: Magritte painted it in 1964 as a self-portrait.

questions.text: Which Paris museum displays Monet's huge Water Lilies murals in two oval rooms?
questions.fun_fact: The museum stands in the Tuileries Garden, next to the Place de la Concorde.

questions.text: Cape Town's Zeitz MOCAA art museum was built inside a former what?
questions.fun_fact: Its architects carved its atrium out of the silo's concrete tubes.

questions.text: Which French painter created The Horse Fair (1852–55), now in New York's Metropolitan Museum?
questions.fun_fact: To study animals at horse markets, she obtained a police permit to wear trousers.

questions.text: Which Mexican muralist was married to Frida Kahlo?
questions.fun_fact: Rivera and Kahlo married in 1929, divorced in 1939 and married each other again in 1940.

questions.text: Which artist went through a 'Blue Period' between 1901 and 1904?
questions.fun_fact: It was followed by his Rose Period, with warmer pinks and oranges.

questions.text: Artemisia Gentileschi was the first woman admitted to which Florence art academy?
questions.fun_fact: Her father, Orazio Gentileschi, was also a painter and introduced her to painting in his workshop.

questions.text: Which Ottoman painter created The Tortoise Trainer (1906)?
questions.fun_fact: The painting sold for US$3.5 million in 2004.

questions.text: The hei-tiki, a carved neck pendant traditionally made of pounamu (greenstone), comes from which culture?
questions.fun_fact: The South Island's official Māori name, Te Waipounamu, means 'the waters of greenstone'.

questions.text: The Aztec Sun Stone is displayed in which city's National Museum of Anthropology?
questions.fun_fact: The basalt disk is about 3.6 m across and was rediscovered in 1790 in the city's main square.

questions.text: Albert Namatjira, famed for his watercolors of the Australian outback, belonged to which people?
questions.fun_fact: In 1957 he was granted full citizenship rights, freeing him from restrictions then placed on Aboriginal people.

questions.text: The Musée d'Orsay in Paris occupies a former what?
questions.fun_fact: The Gare d'Orsay was built for the 1900 Paris Exposition and became a museum in 1986.

questions.text: Which bone is commonly known as the collarbone?
questions.fun_fact: It is the only long bone in the body that lies horizontally, linking the shoulder blade to the breastbone.

questions.text: Which bone is commonly called the shinbone?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the Latin word for a flute, and it is the second-largest bone in the body after the femur.

questions.text: What is the anatomical name for the lower jawbone?
questions.fun_fact: It is the largest and strongest bone of the face, and the only movable bone of the skull apart from the ear bones.

questions.text: Most people have how many pairs of ribs?
questions.fun_fact: The lowest two pairs are called floating ribs because they are not attached to the breastbone at the front.

questions.text: In adults, where are most of the body's blood cells made?
questions.fun_fact: In adults, the red marrow that makes blood cells is found mainly in the pelvis, sternum, skull, ribs and vertebrae.

questions.text: What is the common name for the trachea?
questions.fun_fact: It is held open by 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of cartilage, which are joined to each other by ligaments.

questions.text: Which muscle at the back of the upper arm straightens the elbow?
questions.fun_fact: Its name is Latin for 'three-headed', after its three parts: the long, lateral and medial heads.

questions.text: Which large muscle gives the buttocks most of their shape?
questions.fun_fact: It is the largest of the three gluteal muscles and the main muscle that extends, or straightens, the hip.

questions.text: What are the body's smallest blood vessels called?
questions.fun_fact: Their walls are only one cell thick, letting oxygen and nutrients pass through to the surrounding tissue.

questions.text: Which tiny cell fragments in the blood help it to clot?
questions.fun_fact: Platelets have no nucleus; they break off from huge cells in the bone marrow called megakaryocytes.

questions.text: What is the scientific name for a nerve cell?
questions.fun_fact: The German anatomist Heinrich Wilhelm Waldeyer introduced the term 'neuron' in 1891.

questions.text: Which part of a human cell holds most of its DNA?
questions.fun_fact: It is wrapped in a double membrane, the nuclear envelope, which is pierced by pores that let molecules in and out.

questions.text: What is the common name for the tympanic membrane?
questions.fun_fact: It separates the outer ear from the middle ear and passes sound vibrations on to the tiny middle-ear bones.

questions.text: What happens to your pupils when you step into bright light?
questions.fun_fact: Shine a light into just one eye and the other pupil shrinks too, a response called the consensual light reflex.

questions.text: Which muscular tube carries food from the throat to the stomach?
questions.fun_fact: About 25 cm long in adults, it moves food along with waves of muscle contraction called peristalsis.

questions.text: Which hollow organ stores urine before it leaves the body?
questions.fun_fact: Urine reaches it from the kidneys through two narrow tubes called the ureters.

questions.text: What is the outermost layer of the skin called?
questions.fun_fact: The epidermis has no blood supply of its own and gets its oxygen almost entirely by diffusion from the air.

questions.text: Which bones surround and protect the spinal cord?
questions.fun_fact: In adults the spinal cord is shorter than the spine, ending around the first or second lumbar vertebra.

questions.text: How many teeth make up a full adult set, including wisdom teeth?
questions.fun_fact: Wisdom teeth are the third molars, the rearmost teeth in each quarter of the mouth; the set of 20 baby teeth has none.

questions.text: Which fluid in the mouth begins the digestion of starch?
questions.fun_fact: Its enzyme amylase turns starch into sugar, which is why rice or potatoes can taste sweet as you chew them.

questions.text: What type of joint is the hip?
questions.fun_fact: The base of the thumb has a saddle joint, where a concave and a convex bone surface fit together.

questions.text: Which smooth, flexible tissue covers the ends of bones where they meet in joints?
questions.fun_fact: Most cartilage has no blood vessels or nerves; its cells get their nutrients by diffusion instead.

questions.text: Which flat, chisel-shaped teeth at the front of the mouth are used for biting?
questions.fun_fact: Adults have eight incisors, four in the upper jaw and four in the lower jaw.

questions.text: Which body system is made up of the brain, spinal cord and nerves?
questions.fun_fact: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system; all the other nerves make up the peripheral nervous system.

questions.text: What is the roof of the mouth called?
questions.fun_fact: It has two parts: the bony hard palate at the front and the fleshy soft palate, or velum, at the back.

questions.text: Hair grows out of tiny pockets in the skin called what?
questions.fun_fact: Together with its oil-producing sebaceous gland and a tiny muscle, each follicle forms a pilosebaceous unit.

questions.text: How many vertebrae are in the human neck?
questions.fun_fact: Almost all mammals have seven neck vertebrae, giraffes included; manatees and sloths are the known exceptions.

questions.text: Which forearm bone is on the same side as the thumb?
questions.fun_fact: Joints between the radius and the ulna let the forearm rotate, so you can turn your palm up or down.

questions.text: What are the bones of the fingers and toes called?
questions.fun_fact: Each hand has 14 of them: three in each finger and two in the thumb.

questions.text: What is the anatomical name for the tailbone?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Greek word for cuckoo, because its shape was thought to resemble a cuckoo's beak.

questions.text: What are the soft spots on a newborn baby's skull called?
questions.fun_fact: They let the skull flex during birth and give the brain room to grow; the largest usually closes by about 18 months.

questions.text: The first vertebra of the neck, which holds up the skull, is named after which Titan?
questions.fun_fact: Together with the axis below it, the atlas allows the head a wider range of motion than other vertebrae permit.

questions.text: Which group of four muscles at the front of the thigh straightens the knee?
questions.fun_fact: One of its four parts, the rectus femoris, also crosses the hip joint and helps to flex it.

questions.text: What is the main job of the masseter muscle?
questions.fun_fact: It runs from the cheekbone to the lower jaw and is especially powerful in plant-eating mammals.

questions.text: Which triangular muscle forms the rounded shape of the shoulder?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the Greek letter delta, because its shape resembles a triangle.

questions.text: What is the largest artery in the human body?
questions.fun_fact: It rises from the left ventricle, arches over the heart and then runs down through the chest and abdomen.

questions.text: What are the heart's two upper chambers called?
questions.fun_fact: Atrium is Latin for 'entry hall'; the atria receive the blood returning to the heart.

questions.text: What is the light amber-colored liquid part of blood called?
questions.fun_fact: It makes up about 55% of blood's volume and is mostly water, with dissolved proteins, salts and sugars.

questions.text: Which organ in the upper left of the abdomen filters blood and removes old red blood cells?
questions.fun_fact: Its red pulp also stores monocytes, white blood cells that can be sent out to help heal injured tissue.

questions.text: Which strong acid does the stomach lining produce to help digest food?
questions.fun_fact: A thick layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from being digested by its own acid.

questions.text: Which flap of cartilage closes over the windpipe when you swallow?
questions.fun_fact: It is made of elastic cartilage covered with a mucous membrane, and sits behind the tongue at the entrance to the larynx.

questions.text: Which glands sit on top of the kidneys?
questions.fun_fact: Each has an outer cortex, which makes steroid hormones such as cortisol, and an inner medulla, which makes adrenaline.

questions.text: Which small gland at the base of the brain releases growth hormone?
questions.fun_fact: About the size of a kidney bean, it sits in a small hollow of the skull's sphenoid bone.

questions.text: Which pigment is the main cause of differences in human skin color?
questions.fun_fact: It is made by cells called melanocytes, and exposure to UV light triggers more of it, darkening the skin.

questions.text: Which tough protein are hair and nails mainly made of?
questions.fun_fact: The same protein forms animal horns, hooves, claws and feathers.

questions.text: Which snail-shaped part of the inner ear turns sound vibrations into nerve signals?
questions.fun_fact: In humans it makes about two and three-quarter turns around a central bony core called the modiolus.

questions.text: Which three fluid-filled loops in the inner ear help you keep your balance?
questions.fun_fact: They are aligned with three axes, pitch, roll and yaw, so together they sense head rotation in any direction.

questions.text: Which light-sensitive cells in the retina work best in dim light?
questions.fun_fact: Rods are so sensitive that they can respond to a single photon of light.

questions.text: The eye's blind spot is where which structure leaves the eyeball?
questions.fun_fact: We rarely notice it because the brain fills the gap using surrounding detail and information from the other eye.

questions.text: Which basic taste was identified and named by Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908?
questions.fun_fact: He linked it to glutamic acid, and from 1909 MSG was sold in Japan as the first umami seasoning, under the brand name Ajinomoto.

questions.text: What is the tiny junction across which one nerve cell passes a signal to another?
questions.fun_fact: The word was introduced in 1897 by the English neurophysiologist Charles Sherrington.

questions.text: Which tiny structures inside cells build proteins?
questions.fun_fact: They read the instructions carried by messenger RNA and link amino acids together in the order it specifies.

questions.text: Which kind of cell division makes two identical cells for growth and repair in the body?
questions.fun_fact: The term comes from the Greek mitos, 'warp thread', after the thread-like chromosomes seen as cells divide.

questions.text: In DNA, which base pairs with adenine?
questions.fun_fact: In RNA, thymine is replaced by a similar base called uracil.

questions.text: What is the largest part of the human brain?
questions.fun_fact: Its wrinkled outer layer, the cerebral cortex, is folded so that a large surface area fits inside the skull.

questions.text: Which paired brain structure, deep in the temporal lobes, plays a key role in processing fear?
questions.fun_fact: It was first identified and named by the anatomist Karl Friedrich Burdach in 1822.

questions.text: Which nerve, the longest and widest single nerve in the body, runs down the back of the leg?
questions.fun_fact: It runs down the back of the thigh and splits into the tibial and common fibular nerves near the back of the knee.

questions.text: Which part of the nervous system triggers the 'fight-or-flight' response?
questions.fun_fact: Its counterpart, the parasympathetic system, handles calmer 'rest and digest' functions.

questions.text: Which English physician described the circulation of the blood in 1628?
questions.fun_fact: He set out his findings in a short book known as De Motu Cordis, published in Frankfurt.

questions.text: On the tongue, taste buds sit mainly in small bumps called what?
questions.fun_fact: Filiform papillae cover most of the top of the tongue, but they are the one kind with no taste buds.

questions.text: How many lobes does the right lung have?
questions.fun_fact: The left lung has only two lobes and a notch in its border, the cardiac notch, that makes room for the heart.

questions.text: What is the anatomical name for the heel bone?
questions.fun_fact: It is the largest of the tarsal bones and the largest bone in the foot.

questions.text: How many carpal bones make up the human wrist?
questions.fun_fact: One of them, the scaphoid, takes its name from the Greek word for 'boat' because of its shape.

questions.text: Which cells build new bone tissue?
questions.fun_fact: Osteoblasts that become buried in the bone matrix they produce are known as osteocytes.

questions.text: The ilium, ischium and pubis fuse together to form which bone?
questions.fun_fact: They are separate at birth and fuse by the end of puberty, meeting at the acetabulum, the hip joint's socket.

questions.text: The sartorius, the longest muscle in the body, is named after the Latin word for which worker?
questions.fun_fact: Tailors once sat cross-legged to work, a pose that uses all four of the muscle's actions: three at the hip and one at the knee.

questions.text: The Golgi apparatus, which packages proteins in cells, is named after a scientist from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Camillo Golgi identified it in 1898, but the structure was only named after him in the 1910s.

questions.text: Muscles contract when filaments of actin slide past filaments of which protein?
questions.fun_fact: This 'sliding filament' model was proposed in 1954 by two research teams working independently.

questions.text: Which heart valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle?
questions.fun_fact: The first heart sound, the 'lub' of 'lub-dub', is made as this valve and the mitral valve close.

questions.text: T cells, a type of white blood cell, mature in which organ?
questions.fun_fact: It is most active before adolescence; from the early teens its tissue is gradually replaced by fat.

questions.text: Which Austrian scientist discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901?
questions.fun_fact: He received the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery.

questions.text: Which anatomist published the landmark illustrated book 'De humani corporis fabrica' in 1543?
questions.fun_fact: Born in Brussels, Vesalius taught anatomy at the University of Padua and based the book on his own dissections.

questions.text: Which Spanish scientist showed that the nervous system is made up of separate cells, the neurons?
questions.fun_fact: He was the first Spaniard to win a scientific Nobel Prize, sharing the 1906 award with Camillo Golgi.

questions.text: Which tube connects the middle ear to the back of the nose and throat?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the 16th-century Italian anatomist Bartolomeo Eustachi; swallowing opens it to equalize pressure.

questions.text: What is the small central pit of the retina, which gives the sharpest vision, called?
questions.fun_fact: At its very center, the foveola, there are only cones and virtually no rods.

questions.text: Which part of the eye provides about two-thirds of its focusing power?
questions.fun_fact: Medical terms for the cornea often begin with 'kerat-', from the Greek word for horn.

questions.text: Which glands produce tears?
questions.fun_fact: Tears drain through tiny openings at the inner corners of the eyelids into the nose, which is why crying can make your nose run.

questions.text: What is the sense of the position and movement of your own body called?
questions.fun_fact: It relies on sensors called proprioceptors, found in muscles, tendons and joints.

questions.text: Which fatty layer wraps around many nerve fibers and speeds up their signals?
questions.fun_fact: Signals leap between small gaps in the sheath called nodes of Ranvier.

questions.text: In what form does the liver store glucose?
questions.fun_fact: An adult liver weighing about 1.5 kg can store roughly 100 to 120 grams of it.

questions.text: Which small region of the brain acts as the body's thermostat?
questions.fun_fact: It also helps control hunger, thirst, sleep and the body's daily circadian rhythms.

questions.text: Broca's area, named after a French physician, is mainly involved in what?
questions.fun_fact: Paul Broca reported it in 1861; it lies in the frontal lobe of the dominant hemisphere, usually the left.

questions.text: The dura mater, the tough outer membrane around the brain, has a Latin name meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: The name is a loan translation of an Arabic phrase meaning 'thick mother of the brain'.

questions.text: The vagus nerve's name comes from the Latin word for what?
questions.fun_fact: The same Latin root gives English the words vagrant, vagabond and vague.

questions.text: Tiny muscles called arrector pili cause which effect in the skin?
questions.fun_fact: In furry animals the raised hairs trap a layer of insulating air, or make the animal look bigger.

questions.text: The urge to breathe is driven mainly by the level of which gas in the blood?
questions.fun_fact: Sensors on the surface of the medulla oblongata, in the brainstem, detect it through the rise in acidity it causes.

questions.text: Which element does the thyroid gland need to make its hormones?
questions.fun_fact: The thyroid is shaped like a butterfly and sits at the front of the neck, below the larynx.

questions.text: What shape is a typical human red blood cell?
questions.fun_fact: They are flexible enough to deform as they squeeze through the body's narrowest capillaries.

questions.text: What is the capital of Argentina?
questions.fun_fact: The city is an autonomous district: it is neither part of Buenos Aires Province nor that province's capital.

questions.text: What is the capital of Spain?
