questions.fun_fact: Madrid's Prado Museum building was originally planned as a natural science museum.

questions.text: What is the capital of Russia?
questions.fun_fact: The city's name is thought to come from the Moskva River, on whose banks it stands.

questions.text: What is the capital of India?
questions.fun_fact: Designed by British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker, the new capital was inaugurated in 1931.

questions.text: Lisbon is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Lisbon is the second-oldest capital city in Europe, after Athens.

questions.text: What is the capital of Ireland?
questions.fun_fact: The name Dublin comes from Irish words meaning 'black pool'.

questions.text: What is the capital of Norway?
questions.fun_fact: Frogner Park in Oslo displays a large collection of sculptures by Gustav Vigeland.

questions.text: What is the capital of Sweden?
questions.fun_fact: The city stretches across 14 islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea.

questions.text: What is the capital of South Korea?
questions.fun_fact: Gyeongbokgung, the main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, was completed in 1395.

questions.text: What is the capital of Cuba?
questions.fun_fact: Old Havana was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

questions.text: What is the capital of Colombia?
questions.fun_fact: The city sits on a high Andean plateau, at an average altitude of about 2,640 m.

questions.text: What is the capital of Poland?
questions.fun_fact: The city's symbol is a mermaid, which appears on Warsaw's coat of arms.

questions.text: What is the capital of the Czech Republic?
questions.fun_fact: The city's Old Town Square is home to the famous Prague astronomical clock.

questions.text: What is the capital of Saudi Arabia?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'gardens' in Arabic, after the date orchards that once surrounded it.

questions.text: What is the capital of Venezuela?
questions.fun_fact: A steep mountain range about 2,200 m high, Cerro El Ávila, separates the city from the Caribbean Sea.

questions.text: The Little Mermaid statue, unveiled in 1913, is a landmark of which capital city?
questions.fun_fact: The bronze statue by Edvard Eriksen is based on a fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen.

questions.text: What is the capital of Finland?
questions.fun_fact: The sea fortress of Suomenlinna, on islands off the city, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991.

questions.text: What is the capital of Belgium?
questions.fun_fact: The city's 102 m-tall Atomium was built for the 1958 World's Fair, Expo 58.

questions.text: What is the capital of Syria?
questions.fun_fact: Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

questions.text: What is the capital of Ukraine?
questions.fun_fact: The city straddles both banks of the Dnieper River.

questions.text: What is the capital of Chile?
questions.fun_fact: The city lies in a valley between the Andes to the east and the Chilean Coastal Range to the west.

questions.text: What is the capital of Jamaica?
questions.fun_fact: The city faces a natural harbor sheltered by the Palisadoes, a long, narrow sand spit.

questions.text: What is the capital of Italy?
questions.fun_fact: Vatican City, an independent country, lies entirely within Rome's city boundaries.

questions.text: What is the capital of Afghanistan?
questions.fun_fact: The city lies in a narrow valley of the Hindu Kush, about 1,790 m above sea level.

questions.text: What is the capital of France?
questions.fun_fact: The city is divided into 20 arrondissements, numbered in a clockwise spiral.

questions.text: Vienna is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The Wiener Riesenrad, a Ferris wheel in the Prater park, stands almost 65 m tall.

questions.text: What is the capital of the United Arab Emirates?
questions.fun_fact: The city's core sits on an island less than 250 m from the mainland, linked to it by bridges.

questions.text: What is the capital of Pakistan?
questions.fun_fact: It is a planned city, built in the 1960s along the foot of the Margalla Hills.

questions.text: Which capital city's name means 'northern capital'?
questions.fun_fact: The name was adopted in 1403, during the Ming dynasty, to set it apart from Nanjing, the 'southern capital'.

questions.text: What is the capital of Ghana?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from an Akan word for 'ants', after the many anthills in the surrounding countryside.

questions.text: Which African capital's name means 'new flower' in Amharic?
questions.fun_fact: Emperor Menelik II founded the city in 1886.

questions.text: What is the capital of Senegal?
questions.fun_fact: Standing on the Cap-Vert peninsula, it is the westernmost city on the African mainland.

questions.text: Kathmandu is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its Durbar Square, the old royal palace complex, is one of seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site.

questions.text: Ulaanbaatar is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The city's name means 'Red Hero'.

questions.text: Which city is the capital of Georgia, the country in the Caucasus?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from an Old Georgian word for 'warm', after the area's sulfur hot springs.

questions.text: Yerevan is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The city traces its history to the fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BC.

questions.text: What is the capital of Latvia?
questions.fun_fact: Its historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, famed for its Art Nouveau buildings.

questions.text: Sarajevo is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The city hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics.

questions.text: Montevideo is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The 'Monte' in its name refers to the Cerro de Montevideo, a hill across the bay.

questions.text: What is the capital of Paraguay?
questions.fun_fact: Founded in 1537, it is one of South America's oldest cities and is nicknamed the 'Mother of Cities'.

questions.text: What is the capital of Costa Rica?
questions.fun_fact: San José became the capital of Costa Rica in 1823.

questions.text: Doha is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Doha hosted the 2006 Asian Games.

questions.text: Phnom Penh is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The city is named partly after Lady Penh, its traditional founder.

questions.text: Valletta is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Jean de Valette, who laid the city's foundation stone in 1566.

questions.text: Which river flows through Rome?
questions.fun_fact: It rises on Mount Fumaiolo in the Apennines and meets the sea at Ostia.

questions.text: Which river flows through the center of Dublin?
questions.fun_fact: James Joyce personified the river as Anna Livia Plurabelle in Finnegans Wake.

questions.text: On which river does Baghdad stand?
questions.fun_fact: The Sumerian name of the river can be read as 'the swift river'.

questions.text: Which river flows through Bangkok?
questions.fun_fact: European visitors once called it the Menam, from the Thai word for 'river'.

questions.text: Which city did Peter the Great make Russia's capital in 1712?
questions.fun_fact: It stayed the capital until 1918, apart from a short spell between 1728 and 1730.

questions.text: Which city was the capital of Poland until 1596?
questions.fun_fact: That year King Sigismund of the House of Vasa moved the royal court to Warsaw.

questions.text: Which city was the capital of Finland until 1812?
questions.fun_fact: Turku is Finland's oldest city.

questions.text: Which city was the capital of West Germany from 1949 to 1990?
questions.fun_fact: The composer Ludwig van Beethoven was born in the city in 1770.

questions.text: Which city served as Pakistan's capital from 1947 to 1959?
questions.fun_fact: Karachi is the capital of the province of Sindh.

questions.text: Which city was the capital of British India until 1911?
questions.fun_fact: Its official name was Calcutta until 2001.

questions.text: Which city was the capital of the United States immediately before Washington, D.C.?
questions.fun_fact: The city was founded in 1682 by William Penn.

questions.text: Japan's capital moved in 710 to Heijō-kyō, on the site of which modern city?
questions.fun_fact: Heijō-kyō remained the capital until 784, apart from a five-year break in the 740s.

questions.text: Kampala is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from a local phrase meaning 'hill of the impala'.

questions.text: What is the capital of Papua New Guinea?
questions.fun_fact: In Tok Pisin, the city is called Pot Mosbi.

questions.text: What is the capital of Cameroon?
questions.fun_fact: France chose Yaoundé as the capital of its Cameroon colony in 1922, even though Douala was the more important town.

questions.text: What is the capital of Algeria?
questions.fun_fact: Its whitewashed buildings earned it the nickname 'Algiers the White'.

questions.text: Bratislava is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It is the only national capital that borders two other sovereign states, Austria and Hungary.

questions.text: Buda, Pest and which third town merged in 1873 to form Budapest?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'Old Buda'.

questions.text: Which river flows through Madrid?
questions.fun_fact: It rises in the Sierra de Guadarrama and drains into the Jarama, a tributary of the Tagus.

questions.text: Which city was Brazil's first capital, from 1549 to 1763?
questions.fun_fact: It was founded in 1549 by Tomé de Sousa, Brazil's first governor-general.

questions.text: Which city was Australia's seat of government from 1901 to 1927?
questions.fun_fact: The first federal parliament met in the city's Royal Exhibition Building on 9 May 1901.

questions.text: Which city was the official capital of the Philippines from 1948 to 1976?
questions.fun_fact: The city was established in 1939 and planned as a center for government institutions.

questions.text: From 1808 to 1821, which city was the seat of the Portuguese royal court?
questions.fun_fact: The court fled there to escape Napoleon's invasion of Portugal.

questions.text: In which year did Philip II move the Spanish royal court to Madrid?
questions.fun_fact: Madrid's population grew from about 18,000 in 1561 to 80,000 by 1598.

questions.text: In which year did Athens become the capital of modern Greece?
questions.fun_fact: It replaced Nafplio, which had been the provisional capital since 1829.

questions.text: Under which name was Oslo known from 1624 until 1925?
questions.fun_fact: From 1877 the government spelled the name Kristiania.

questions.text: Until 1982, Zimbabwe's capital Harare was known by what name?
questions.fun_fact: It was founded in 1890 as Fort Salisbury, named after the British statesman Lord Salisbury.

questions.text: Until 1966, Kinshasa was known by what name?
questions.fun_fact: The new name was chosen as a tribute to Nshasa, a village that once stood in the area.

questions.text: Ouagadougou is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: In 1919 the French colonial administration made it the capital of the Upper Volta territory.

questions.text: What is the capital of Mauritania?
questions.fun_fact: It was a small fishing town until 1958, when construction began to turn it into the new nation's capital.

questions.text: Which Central Asian capital's name means 'Monday', after a weekly market held there?
questions.fun_fact: From 1929 to 1961 the city was called Stalinabad.

questions.text: Honiara is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The city lies on the northwestern coast of the island of Guadalcanal.

questions.text: Apia is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The home that writer Robert Louis Stevenson built at nearby Vailima is now a museum.

questions.text: Paramaribo is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its historic inner city has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2002.

questions.text: What is the capital of Botswana?
questions.fun_fact: The city is named after Chief Gaborone of the Tlokwa people.

questions.text: Which city did Lilongwe replace as the capital of Malawi in 1975?
questions.fun_fact: Zomba had earlier been the capital of the British Nyasaland Protectorate.

questions.text: Asmara is the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: In 2017 it became the first modernist city to be listed in its entirety as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.text: Which is the highest capital city in Europe, at about 1,023 m above sea level?
questions.fun_fact: The city stands where two mountain streams meet to form the Gran Valira river.

questions.text: Which city was the Ottoman capital before the conquest of Constantinople in 1453?
questions.fun_fact: The Roman emperor Hadrian refounded the city as Hadrianopolis, later known in English as Adrianople.

questions.text: Which city was the imperial capital of Vietnam under the Nguyễn dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: The city was called Phú Xuân when it first became a provincial capital, in 1687.

questions.text: Which city was founded in 1351 and served as the Siamese capital until 1767?
questions.fun_fact: By around 1700 its population may have reached a million, making it one of the largest cities in the world.

questions.text: Which city served as Lithuania's temporary capital between the two world wars?
questions.fun_fact: Kaunas stands where Lithuania's two largest rivers, the Nemunas and the Neris, meet.

questions.text: Which capital city was known in Greco-Roman times as Philadelphia?
questions.fun_fact: The city's Roman Theater was built in the second century AD.

questions.text: Belgrade lies where the Danube is joined by which river?
questions.fun_fact: Farther upstream, the Sava also flows through Zagreb, the capital of Croatia.

questions.text: What does 'rex' mean in the name Tyrannosaurus rex?
questions.fun_fact: The full name means 'tyrant lizard king'; Henry Fairfield Osborn gave it in 1905.

questions.text: Which geological era is often called the 'Age of Reptiles'?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'middle life', and it lasted from about 252 to 66 million years ago.

questions.text: Which period of the Mesozoic Era came between the Triassic and the Cretaceous?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the Jura Mountains, on the border of France and Switzerland, where its limestone was studied.

questions.text: What did Ankylosaurus have at the end of its tail?
questions.fun_fact: Its body was protected by bony plates called osteoderms set into the skin.

questions.text: What is the name for fossilized tree resin that sometimes holds trapped insects?
questions.fun_fact: Spiders, frogs, flowers, feathers and even hair have all been found preserved inside pieces of amber.

questions.text: Which large dinosaur had a tall sail along its back?
questions.fun_fact: Its first fossils were found in Egypt in 1912 and described by the German paleontologist Ernst Stromer in 1915.

questions.text: Pachycephalosaurus is known for its thick, domed what?
questions.fun_fact: It was one of the last non-bird dinosaurs, living in western North America just before the mass extinction.

questions.text: Huge, long-necked, four-legged plant-eaters like Brachiosaurus belong to which dinosaur group?
questions.fun_fact: Brachiosaurus means 'arm lizard', a reference to its proportionately long front limbs.

questions.text: Which group of marine reptiles had dolphin-like bodies?
questions.fun_fact: They breathed air, bore live young, and many had a layer of blubber for insulation.

questions.text: The extinct 'Irish elk' was actually a giant species of what?
questions.fun_fact: It ranged across northern Eurasia from Ireland to Siberia, and was not closely related to either animal now called an elk.

questions.text: The armored Ice Age mammal Glyptodon was a giant relative of which living animal?
questions.fun_fact: Charles Darwin collected glyptodont fossils in South America during the voyage of HMS Beagle.

questions.text: Smilodon, with its huge upper canine teeth, was what kind of animal?
questions.fun_fact: Despite the popular name 'saber-toothed tiger', it was not closely related to tigers.

questions.text: In which period did the first dinosaurs appear?
questions.fun_fact: Eoraptor, one of the earliest known dinosaurs, lived about 231 to 228 million years ago in what is now Argentina.

questions.text: The Chicxulub crater, linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs, is in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was found in the late 1970s by geophysicists who were searching the Yucatán Peninsula for oil.

questions.text: Dinosaur Provincial Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site rich in dinosaur fossils, is in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It lies in the badlands of Alberta and was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1979.

questions.text: Which dinosaurs are commonly called 'duck-billed dinosaurs'?
questions.fun_fact: Their teeth were stacked into 'dental batteries' that formed effective grinding surfaces.

questions.text: Which of these prehistoric reptiles was a dinosaur?
questions.fun_fact: Parasaurolophus means 'beside crested lizard', a reference to its crested relative Saurolophus.

questions.text: Megatherium was an elephant-sized giant ground what?
questions.fun_fact: It lived in South America and could rear up on its hind legs to reach high branches.

questions.text: Dunkleosteus, a giant predator of Devonian seas, was what kind of animal?
questions.fun_fact: It was a placoderm, one of an extinct group of armored fish whose name means 'plate-skinned'.

questions.text: Which era followed the Mesozoic and is often called the 'Age of Mammals'?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Greek for 'new life'.

questions.text: Which group of beaked, often horned and frilled dinosaurs includes Triceratops?
questions.fun_fact: Ceratopsians had a unique toothless bone at the tip of the upper jaw, called the rostral bone.

questions.text: About how long ago did the non-bird dinosaurs die out?
questions.fun_fact: Homo sapiens emerged only around 300,000 years ago, so no person ever saw a living non-bird dinosaur.

questions.text: The prefix 'paleo-', as in paleontology, comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: The French word paléontologie was introduced for the study of ancient life in 1822.

questions.text: What were pterosaur wings mainly made of?
questions.fun_fact: The wing membrane was strengthened by closely spaced fibers called actinofibrils.

questions.text: Which of these dinosaurs was a plant-eater?
questions.fun_fact: Its skull could reach almost a third of the length of its whole body.

questions.text: Which of these reptile groups survived the extinction that ended the age of dinosaurs?
questions.fun_fact: Sea turtles also survived, but every pterosaur, plesiosaur and mosasaur died out.

questions.text: Which living animal is the woolly mammoth's closest relative?
questions.fun_fact: A small population survived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, until about 4,000 years ago.

questions.text: Dimetrodon, a sail-backed animal often mistaken for a dinosaur, was more closely related to which group?
questions.fun_fact: It lived in the Permian period, tens of millions of years before the first dinosaurs appeared.

questions.text: Trilobites, common fossils from ancient seas, belonged to which animal group?
questions.fun_fact: They first appeared in the Cambrian and died out at the end of the Permian, after some 270 million years.

questions.text: Ammonites, fossils with coiled shells, belonged to which group of sea animals that includes squid?
questions.fun_fact: Pliny the Elder called their fossils 'horns of Ammon', after the Egyptian deity often shown with ram's horns.

questions.text: The famous 3.2-million-year-old hominin skeleton known as 'Lucy' was found in which country?
questions.fun_fact: She was named after the Beatles song 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds', played loudly at the expedition camp.

questions.text: The marine reptile Mosasaurus is named after which river, near where it was first found?
questions.fun_fact: Its skull, found near Maastricht in the Netherlands, was seized by French troops in 1794 and taken to Paris.

questions.text: Which marine reptiles had four flippers and, often, very long necks?
questions.fun_fact: Elasmosaurus, a plesiosaur, had more than 70 vertebrae in its neck.

questions.text: In 2007, small bumps called quill knobs on a Velociraptor forearm bone showed it had what?
questions.fun_fact: In living birds, quill knobs mark where the ligaments of the wing feathers anchor to the bone.

questions.text: How many clawed fingers did Tyrannosaurus rex have on each hand?
questions.fun_fact: Its forelimbs were short but unusually powerful for their size.

questions.text: Which dinosaur lived closer in time to modern humans than to Stegosaurus?
questions.fun_fact: Stegosaurus lived roughly 155 to 145 million years ago, while Tyrannosaurus lived about 68 to 66 million years ago.

questions.text: In 1938, a coelacanth, a fish known only from fossils, was caught off which country?
questions.fun_fact: Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted it in a fisherman's catch; its genus, Latimeria, honors her.

questions.text: Which British anatomist coined the name 'Dinosauria' in 1842?
questions.fun_fact: Owen later drove the founding of London's Natural History Museum, which opened in 1881.

questions.text: The 'Bone Wars' were a bitter rivalry between Othniel Charles Marsh and which paleontologist?
questions.fun_fact: Their rivalry led to 142 new species of dinosaurs being discovered and described.

questions.text: In 1878, dozens of Iguanodon skeletons were found in a coal mine in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Miners struck the first skeleton 322 m underground at Bernissart; many now stand in a Brussels museum.

questions.text: Oviraptor's name means 'egg thief', but later finds showed it was actually doing what?
questions.fun_fact: It was named in 1924, when its skeleton was found on a nest thought to belong to Protoceratops.

questions.text: Carnotaurus, a meat-eater with two horns above its eyes, was found in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'meat-eating bull'; it was named in 1985 by the Argentine paleontologist José Bonaparte.

questions.text: Microraptor, a small dinosaur from China, is famous for having long flight feathers on what?
questions.fun_fact: Melanosomes preserved in one fossil suggest its feathers were a glossy, iridescent black, like a starling's.

questions.text: Which steel magnate gave casts of a Diplodocus skeleton to museums around the world?
questions.fun_fact: The original skeleton, nicknamed 'Dippy', is in Pittsburgh's Carnegie Museum of Natural History.

questions.text: What does the name of the dinosaur Maiasaura mean?
questions.fun_fact: Jack Horner and Robert Makela named it in 1979 after finding nests, eggs and young at a site in Montana.

questions.text: Therizinosaurus, a plant-eating theropod from Mongolia, is famous for what?
questions.fun_fact: Its first remains, found in 1948, were at first thought to come from a large turtle-like reptile.

questions.text: The Deccan Traps, vast lava flows from the end of the Cretaceous, are in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Their eruptions spanned the end of the Cretaceous, around the time of the mass extinction of the dinosaurs.

questions.text: Cryolophosaurus, a crested meat-eating dinosaur, was discovered on which continent?
questions.fun_fact: Its tall, furrowed head crest resembled a pompadour hairstyle, earning it the nickname 'Elvisaurus'.

questions.text: What does the name of the flying reptile Pteranodon mean?
questions.fun_fact: Othniel Charles Marsh named it in 1876; unlike many earlier pterosaurs, it had a beak with no teeth.

questions.text: Dinosaurs are traditionally split into two main groups based on the structure of which body part?
questions.fun_fact: Oddly, birds descend from theropod dinosaurs, not from the 'bird-hipped' ornithischians.

questions.text: How did dinosaurs hold their legs, unlike most other reptiles?
questions.fun_fact: Pterosaurs, plesiosaurs and Dimetrodon are often mistaken for dinosaurs, but none of them had this upright leg posture.

questions.text: Which mass extinction, the most severe known, is nicknamed the 'Great Dying'?
questions.fun_fact: It happened about 252 million years ago and marks the boundary between the Paleozoic and Mesozoic eras.

questions.text: The Permian period is named after a region in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Scottish geologist Roderick Murchison named it in 1841 after the region around the city of Perm.

questions.text: Which geological period is often called the 'Age of Fishes'?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Devon, in England, where its rocks were first studied.

questions.text: Which geological period's name means 'coal-bearing'?
questions.fun_fact: Its vast forests and swamps eventually became the coal beds that give the period its name.

questions.text: What name is given to the rapid appearance of most major animal groups over 500 million years ago?
questions.fun_fact: American paleontologist Charles Walcott studied many of its strange animals in Canada's Burgess Shale.

questions.text: When Pangaea broke apart, what was the southern supercontinent called?
questions.fun_fact: Eduard Suess named it after a region of India whose name means 'forest of the Gonds'.

questions.text: What are fossils of short-lived, widespread species, used to date rock layers, called?
questions.fun_fact: Surveyor William Smith helped establish the method long before Darwin explained the evolution behind it.

questions.text: Which epoch, ending about 11,700 years ago, was marked by repeated glaciations?
questions.fun_fact: Its name, meaning 'most new', was coined by the geologist Charles Lyell in 1839.

questions.text: Fossils of the reptile Mesosaurus in both South America and Africa supported which idea?
questions.fun_fact: Alfred Wegener used mesosaur finds on both sides of the Atlantic as evidence for his theory.

questions.text: The dinosaur Baryonyx, found in England in 1983, was named for what feature?
questions.fun_fact: Amateur fossil collector William Walker found it in the Smokejack Clay Pit in Surrey.

questions.text: Which living animals are the closest relatives of crocodiles?
questions.fun_fact: Birds and crocodilians are the only living archosaurs, a name meaning 'ruling lizards'.

questions.text: Tiktaalik, a 'fishapod' fossil discovered in 2004, was found in which part of Canada?
questions.fun_fact: Its name, suggested by Inuit elders, is an Inuktitut word meaning 'large freshwater fish'.

questions.text: The Ordovician and Silurian periods are named after ancient peoples of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Roderick Murchison named the Silurian in 1835, and Charles Lapworth named the Ordovician in 1879.

questions.text: The Ediacaran period is named after hills in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Ratified in 2004, it was the first new geological period to be declared in 120 years.

questions.text: Which English doctor named Iguanodon, the second dinosaur genus to be named, in 1825?
questions.fun_fact: He placed what he thought was a horn on its nose; better skeletons later showed it was a thumb spike.

questions.text: Which French naturalist is credited with making extinction an accepted scientific idea?
questions.fun_fact: He also named the giant ground sloth Megatherium and the flying reptile Pterodactylus.

questions.text: In 1980, which father-and-son team proposed that an asteroid impact ended the age of dinosaurs?
questions.fun_fact: Their evidence was a clay layer rich in iridium; Luis had won the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.text: John Ostrom's 1969 study of which 'terrible claw' dinosaur sparked the Dinosaur Renaissance?
questions.fun_fact: Its name refers to the large, sickle-shaped claw on the second toe of each hind foot.

questions.text: A pterosaur's wing was supported mainly by a hugely lengthened what?
questions.fun_fact: The wing membrane stretched from the ankles all the way to the tip of that finger.

questions.text: What are the stones swallowed by some dinosaurs and living birds to help grind food called?
questions.fun_fact: Among living animals, crocodiles, plant-eating birds, seals and sea lions all carry such stones.

questions.text: Leaellynasaura, a small dinosaur that lived inside the Antarctic Circle, was found in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was named after Leaellyn Rich, daughter of the paleontologists Tom Rich and Patricia Vickers-Rich.

questions.text: The Tendaguru fossil beds, source of the sauropod Giraffatitan, are in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Expeditions from Berlin's Museum für Naturkunde dug there from 1907 to 1913.

questions.text: Franz Nopcsa argued that dinosaurs from Hațeg, in which modern country, were dwarfed island species?
questions.fun_fact: Isolated on an island, species such as the sauropod Magyarosaurus grew far smaller than their relatives.

questions.text: The Brazilian dinosaur Irritator was named for researchers' annoyance that its skull had been what?
questions.fun_fact: Fossil traders had hidden much of the skull under plaster to make it look more complete and valuable.

questions.text: The Cambrian predator Anomalocaris has a name meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Joseph Whiteaves named it in 1892, mistaking its grasping front appendages for the abdomens of shrimp-like crustaceans.

questions.text: Futabasaurus, a plesiosaur first found by a high school student, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: In the anime film Doraemon: Nobita's Dinosaur, Nobita hatches and raises a Futabasaurus.

questions.text: Titanoboa, a giant snake from soon after the dinosaurs died out, was found in a coal mine in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its fossils were found alongside turtles and crocodilians from about 60 to 58 million years ago.

questions.text: Stromatolites, among the oldest known fossils, are layered mounds built mainly by what?
questions.fun_fact: Living stromatolites grow in Shark Bay, Western Australia.

questions.text: The extinction that ended the non-bird dinosaurs marks the boundary between the Cretaceous and which period?
questions.fun_fact: It was formerly called the K–T boundary, after the Tertiary period.

questions.text: What name is given to the vast ocean that surrounded the supercontinent Pangaea?
questions.fun_fact: The Pacific Plate began forming about 190 million years ago at a triple junction in the middle of it.

questions.text: In 1998, the skull of which Triassic dinosaur flew into space aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavour?
questions.fun_fact: It was the second dinosaur in space, after a piece of Maiasaura flew on an earlier shuttle mission.

questions.text: Mei long, a small dinosaur found in China, was fossilized in which bird-like position?
questions.fun_fact: The rock around it suggests it was buried instantly in volcanic ash while resting.

questions.text: Suchomimus, a fish-eating dinosaur found in Niger, has a name meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Its species name refers to the Ténéré Desert in Niger, where its fossils were discovered.

questions.text: Which tusked synapsid became extremely common at the start of the Triassic?
questions.fun_fact: Its fossils have been found in Antarctica, India, China, Mongolia, Russia and South Africa.

questions.text: Basilosaurus, named as a 'king lizard' in 1834, turned out to be what kind of animal?
questions.fun_fact: Richard Owen proposed renaming it Zeuglodon in 1839, but the original name stuck.

questions.text: How many eyes did the Cambrian animal Opabinia have?
questions.fun_fact: When Harry Whittington first presented his analysis of it, the audience laughed at how strange it looked.

questions.text: Which artist made the life-size Crystal Palace Dinosaurs sculptures unveiled in London in 1854?
questions.fun_fact: Hawkins marked the launch with a dinner on New Year's Eve 1853, held inside the mold of an Iguanodon.

questions.text: Sushi is traditionally prepared with which vinegared ingredient?
questions.fun_fact: Modern nigiri sushi is credited to Hanaya Yohei, who is said to have created it in Edo, now Tokyo, around 1824.

questions.text: Guacamole is made mainly from which fruit?
questions.fun_fact: It is traditionally made by mashing avocados and salt in a molcajete, a Mexican stone mortar and pestle.

questions.text: Feta, a white cheese cured in brine, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: In the EU, feta must be made in parts of Greece from sheep's milk, or sheep's milk with up to 30% goat's milk.

questions.text: Gouda cheese is named after a city in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Gouda is now a generic name: similar cheeses called Gouda are made all over the world.

questions.text: Pho, a noodle soup served with fresh herbs, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The modern dish emerged between 1900 and 1907 in northern Vietnam, in Nam Định province southeast of Hanoi.

questions.text: Goulash is a traditional meat stew from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its Hungarian name, gulyás, means 'cattle herder': the stew grew out of meals cooked by herdsmen.

questions.text: Borscht, the sour soup of Eastern Europe, usually gets its red color from which vegetable?
questions.fun_fact: Not all borscht is red: there are sorrel-based green borscht and rye-based white borscht too.

questions.text: Which drink is made from the leaves of the plant Camellia sinensis?
questions.fun_fact: White, green, oolong and black teas are all made from the leaves of this same species.

questions.text: Marzipan is a sweet paste made mainly from sugar and which ground nut?
questions.fun_fact: Lübeck in northern Germany is famous for its marzipan, and Lübecker Marzipan is protected by EU law.

questions.text: Which spice gives many curries their bright yellow color?
questions.fun_fact: Turmeric comes from the dried rhizome of a plant in the ginger family.

questions.text: Sauerkraut is made by fermenting which vegetable?
questions.fun_fact: Its name is German for 'sour cabbage', and its tang comes from lactic acid made by bacteria.

questions.text: Prunes are the dried form of which fruit?
questions.fun_fact: In 2001, US plum growers were allowed to start calling prunes 'dried plums'.

questions.text: Small savory dishes called tapas are a tradition of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The word tapas comes from the Spanish verb tapar, meaning 'to cover'.

questions.text: Which Swiss dish involves dipping bread into a shared pot of melted cheese?
questions.fun_fact: The Swiss Cheese Union promoted fondue as a national dish in the 1930s to boost cheese consumption.

questions.text: Tofu is made by curdling the milk of which bean?
questions.fun_fact: Chinese legend credits its invention to Liu An, a Han dynasty prince who lived in the 2nd century BC.

questions.text: Which Southeast Asian fruit, called the 'king of fruits', is famous for its strong smell?
questions.fun_fact: Its odor can linger for days, so some hotels and public transport services in Singapore and Bangkok ban the fruit.

questions.text: Botanically, the peanut is not a true nut. What is it?
questions.fun_fact: Peanut flowers bloom above ground, then a stalk called a peg grows down into the soil, where the pods develop.

questions.text: Pastel de nata, a custard tart, is a classic pastry from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The famous Pastéis de Belém bakery in Lisbon has been selling these tarts since 1837.

questions.text: Which French dessert's name means 'burnt cream'?
questions.fun_fact: Its top is made by sprinkling sugar on the custard and caramelizing it with a torch or a hot iron called a salamander.

questions.text: Baba ghanoush, a smoky Levantine dip, is made mainly from which roasted vegetable?
questions.fun_fact: The eggplant is traditionally roasted over an open flame before peeling, which gives the dip its smoky taste.

questions.text: Pizza Margherita is traditionally associated with which Italian city?
questions.fun_fact: Its red tomato, white mozzarella and green basil echo the colors of the Italian flag.

questions.text: What is the main sugar found in milk?
questions.fun_fact: Lactose is made of two simpler sugars, glucose and galactose, joined together.

questions.text: Matcha, whisked in the Japanese tea ceremony, is a fine powder of which type of tea?
questions.fun_fact: Japanese labeling rules require matcha tea leaves to be shaded for two to three weeks before harvest.

questions.text: Where was bubble tea, a drink with chewy tapioca pearls, invented in the 1980s?
questions.fun_fact: Tea shops in both Taichung and Tainan claim to have invented the drink.

questions.text: What is the Japanese dish of thinly sliced raw fish served without rice called?
questions.fun_fact: Sashimi is often served on a bed of shredded daikon radish, with soy sauce and wasabi.

questions.text: Tzatziki is a Greek dip of yogurt, garlic and which grated vegetable?
questions.fun_fact: The word tzatziki reached English in the mid-20th century from Greek, which borrowed it from the Turkish name cacık.

questions.text: The kiwifruit is native to which country?
questions.fun_fact: Once called the Chinese gooseberry, it was renamed 'kiwifruit' in 1959 by the New Zealand exporter Turners & Growers.

questions.text: The potato was first domesticated in which mountain region?
questions.fun_fact: Genetic studies trace the cultivated potato to farmers around Lake Titicaca, about 7,000 to 10,000 years ago.

questions.text: Naan is often baked by pressing the dough against the inner wall of which kind of clay oven?
questions.fun_fact: The inner walls of a tandoor can reach temperatures of up to 480 °C.

questions.text: Dim sum is most closely associated with which regional Chinese cuisine?
questions.fun_fact: Dim sum is traditionally enjoyed with tea at a meal called yum cha, Cantonese for 'drink tea'.

questions.text: Baklava is made from layers of which paper-thin pastry?
questions.fun_fact: In 2013, Gaziantep baklava became the first Turkish product to gain protected status in the European Union.

questions.text: Poutine, fries topped with cheese curds and gravy, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: It emerged in the Centre-du-Québec region in the late 1950s, and several restaurants there claim to have invented it.

questions.text: Lamingtons are squares of sponge cake coated in chocolate and what?
questions.fun_fact: They are believed to be named after Lord Lamington, governor of Queensland from 1896 to 1901, or his wife.

questions.text: Japanese soba noodles are made mainly from which flour?
questions.fun_fact: The word soba itself means 'buckwheat'; many soba noodles also contain some wheat flour.

questions.text: The North African dish tagine is named after what?
options: The clay pot it is cooked in
questions.fun_fact: The pot's cone-shaped lid returns condensed steam to the food, so the dish needs very little water.

questions.text: Vanilla comes from the seed pods of which kind of plant?
questions.fun_fact: In 1841, Edmond Albius, a 12-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion, found a quick way to pollinate vanilla flowers by hand.

questions.text: Which compound gives chili peppers their hot, spicy taste?
questions.fun_fact: The heat of a chili pepper is often measured on the Scoville scale.

questions.text: Cinnamon is made from which part of a tree?
questions.fun_fact: As the thin strips of bark dry, they curl naturally into rolls called quills.

questions.text: Pumpernickel, a dark German bread, is made mainly from which grain?
questions.fun_fact: Westphalian pumpernickel is baked for 16 to 24 hours at a low temperature in a steam-filled oven.

questions.text: In 2022, UNESCO added the craft and culture of which French bread to its heritage list?
questions.fun_fact: A 1993 French decree sets strict rules for the 'traditional' baguette, including a ban on using premade dough.

questions.text: Arepas, cornmeal cakes, are a staple food of Venezuela and which other country?
questions.fun_fact: The arepa is a pre-Columbian dish from the area that is now Colombia, Panama and Venezuela.

questions.text: Cheddar cheese is named after a village in which English county?
questions.fun_fact: Caves in nearby Cheddar Gorge offered the ideal humidity and steady temperature for maturing the cheese.

questions.text: Which Dutch cheese is traditionally sold with a coat of red paraffin wax?
questions.fun_fact: In Spain and some former Spanish colonies, such as the Philippines, Edam is known as queso de bola, 'ball cheese'.

questions.text: Coffea arabica, the main coffee plant, is native to the highlands of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Yemen and southern Ethiopia were probably the first regions where coffee beans were cultivated.

questions.text: Brunost, a caramel-colored 'brown cheese', is a specialty of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its brown color and sweet taste come from milk sugars that caramelize as the whey is boiled down.

questions.text: Feijoada, a stew of black beans with pork and beef, is a classic dish of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was first documented in Recife, and is typically served with rice, collard greens, sliced oranges and farofa.

questions.text: True caviar is the salt-cured roe of which fish?
questions.fun_fact: Traditionally, the name was reserved for roe of wild sturgeon from the Caspian Sea and Black Sea.

questions.text: Gravlax is raw salmon cured with salt, sugar and which herb?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from a word for 'dig': medieval fishermen salted salmon and buried it in the sand above the tide line.

questions.text: Khachapuri, a bread filled with cheese, is a national dish of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The Adjarian version is shaped like a boat, with cheese, butter and an egg yolk in the middle.

questions.text: To be sold as Wiener Schnitzel in Austria, the breaded cutlet must be made from which meat?
questions.fun_fact: A pork version may be sold as 'Schnitzel Wiener Art', meaning Viennese-style schnitzel.

questions.text: Adobo, meat braised in vinegar, soy sauce and garlic, is a signature dish of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Spanish colonists gave it a Spanish name, but the vinegar-braising method is indigenous to the Philippines.

questions.text: The Sachertorte, a chocolate cake layered with apricot jam, comes from which city?
questions.fun_fact: By one account, Franz Sacher created it in 1832 for Prince Metternich, when he was a teenage apprentice.

questions.text: Which herb is the main ingredient of the Levantine salad tabbouleh?
questions.fun_fact: Lebanon has celebrated a National Tabbouleh Day on the first Saturday of July since 2001.

questions.text: A hāngī is a traditional Māori way of cooking food in what?
options: A pit oven in the ground
questions.fun_fact: Logs burn for 3 to 4 hours to heat the rocks to 600–700 °C; the food is then covered with wet cloths and earth.

questions.text: Macadamia nuts come from trees native to which country?
questions.fun_fact: It is the only widely grown food plant native to Australia, yet it was first farmed on a large scale in Hawaii.

questions.text: Earl Grey tea is flavored with oil from which citrus fruit?
questions.fun_fact: The blend is thought to be named after Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey, who led the British government in the 1830s.

questions.text: Kopi luwak coffee is made from beans that have passed through which animal's gut?
questions.fun_fact: It is produced mainly on the Indonesian islands of Sumatra, Java, Bali and Sulawesi.

questions.text: Pilsner lager is named after a city in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The first pale lager of this style was brewed in Plzeň in 1842 by the Bavarian brewer Josef Groll.

questions.text: Nachos were first made in 1943 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: They are named after their creator, Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya, who improvised them for guests in Piedras Negras.

questions.text: The Michelin Guide, famous for its restaurant stars, was first published by a company making what?
questions.fun_fact: France had fewer than 3,000 cars in 1900, so the guide was meant to boost demand for cars, and for tires.

questions.text: Garum, a fermented fish sauce, was a favorite condiment of which civilization?
questions.fun_fact: Garum appears in many recipes in the Roman cookbook Apicius, and the philosopher Seneca condemned it as an expensive craze.

questions.text: Katsuobushi, the dried fish flakes used in Japanese dashi, is made from which fish?
questions.fun_fact: Smoked, fermented and sun-dried, the fish fillet ends up as hard as a piece of wood.

questions.text: Valencian horchata, a sweet milky drink, is made from which tubers?
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico and Central America, horchata is usually made from rice instead.

questions.text: Yerba mate is traditionally sipped through a metal straw called what?
questions.fun_fact: The lower end of a metal bombilla is perforated and works as a filter to keep the leaves out of your mouth.

questions.text: Pu'er tea is named after a town in which Chinese province?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the old tea-trading town of Pu'er, now Ning'er Town in Yunnan.

questions.text: Turkish coffee is traditionally brewed in a small long-handled pot called what?
questions.fun_fact: The same pot is called a džezva in Serbo-Croatian and a dzsezva in Hungarian.

questions.text: Lapsang souchong tea gets its smoky flavor from being dried over fires of which wood?
questions.fun_fact: The tea comes from the Wuyi Mountains in China's Fujian province.

questions.text: Port wine is made from grapes grown in which river valley?
questions.fun_fact: The Douro region was demarcated in 1756, making it one of the oldest protected wine regions in the world.

questions.text: Which spice comes from the same fruit as nutmeg?
questions.fun_fact: Nutmeg is the seed, while mace is the dried red lacy covering, or aril, that wraps around it.

questions.text: Harissa, a chili paste added to UNESCO's heritage list in 2022, is especially associated with which country?
questions.fun_fact: Harissa is usually made from roasted red peppers, hot chilies, garlic and spices such as caraway and coriander.

questions.text: Stollen, a fruit bread dusted with icing sugar, is most famously associated with which German city?
questions.fun_fact: In 1730, Augustus the Strong had Dresden's bakers make a giant 1.7-tonne stollen for about 24,000 guests.

questions.text: Under its protected status, Stilton cheese may be made in only three English counties. Which is one of them?
questions.fun_fact: It takes its name from the village of Stilton, now in Cambridgeshire, where the cheese was originally sold.

questions.text: Thieboudienne, fish cooked with rice and vegetables, is the national dish of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The popular West African dish jollof rice is thought to have originated from thieboudienne.

questions.text: Bunny chow, a hollowed-out loaf of bread filled with curry, comes from which South African city?
questions.fun_fact: It originated among Durban's large Indian community and is often called simply a 'bunny'.

questions.text: Mansaf, lamb cooked in a sauce of dried yogurt and served on rice, is the national dish of which country?
questions.fun_fact: The hard, dried yogurt used to make its sauce is called jameed.

questions.text: South Indian dosa is made from a fermented batter of rice and which legume?
questions.fun_fact: In Malaysia and Singapore, the dosa is known as thosai.

questions.text: Cullen skink, a thick Scottish soup, is made mainly with which fish?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Cullen, a town in Moray on the northeast coast of Scotland, where it is a local specialty.

questions.text: The Caesar salad was created in 1924 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Caesar Cardini, an Italian immigrant restaurateur whose restaurant in Tijuana first served it.

questions.text: Beef carpaccio is named after Vittore Carpaccio. Who was he?
questions.fun_fact: Giuseppe Cipriani created the dish at Harry's Bar in Venice in 1950, naming it after the painter's red and white tones.

questions.text: Fresh wasabi paste is made by grating which part of the wasabi plant?
questions.fun_fact: Wasabi belongs to the same plant family as horseradish and mustard, and its heat hits the nose more than the tongue.

questions.text: Dijon mustard is named after a city in which French region?
questions.fun_fact: Its modern recipe dates from 1856, when Jean Naigeon of Dijon swapped vinegar for verjuice, the sour juice of unripe grapes.

questions.text: Two Mexican states claim to be the birthplace of mole sauce. One is Puebla. What is the other?
questions.fun_fact: The classic mole poblano has an average of 20 ingredients, while Oaxacan moles can have more than 30.

questions.text: The North African spice blend ras el hanout has a name meaning what in Arabic?
questions.fun_fact: The name implies a mix of the best spices a seller has to offer, usually more than a dozen of them.

questions.text: Genmaicha is Japanese green tea mixed with which roasted ingredient?
questions.fun_fact: It is nicknamed 'popcorn tea' because some rice grains pop while roasting.

questions.text: Sichuan pepper, which makes the mouth tingle, comes from a plant in which family?
questions.fun_fact: Its tingling numbness, called 'má' in Chinese, is paired with chili heat in Sichuan's famous 'málà' flavor.

questions.text: Ratatouille, the stewed vegetable dish, originated in which region of France?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Occitan 'ratatolha', related to the French verb 'touiller', meaning to stir.

questions.text: The prized white truffle of Alba comes mainly from which Italian region?
questions.fun_fact: A 1.31 kg white truffle found near Buje, Croatia, in 1999 entered the Guinness Book of Records.

questions.text: Koshari, a street food of pasta, rice and lentils, is the national dish of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It is topped with chickpeas, a garlicky tomato sauce, garlic vinegar and crispy fried onions.

questions.text: Which Hungarian-born physicist won the 1971 Nobel Prize in Physics for inventing holography?
questions.fun_fact: He came up with the idea in 1947 while trying to improve electron microscopes.

questions.text: Which company launched the iPhone in 2007?
questions.fun_fact: Apple announced it on January 9, 2007, and it went on sale in the US that June.

questions.text: Bluetooth wireless technology was first developed at which Swedish company?
questions.fun_fact: Its name honors Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century king of Denmark.

questions.text: In 1934 Ford launched a coupé utility, or 'ute', designed by Lewis Bandt, in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Bandt had been the first designer at Ford's factory in Geelong, Victoria.

questions.text: Who took the oldest surviving camera photograph, View from the Window at Le Gras?
questions.fun_fact: Its exposure is thought to have lasted at least eight hours, perhaps several days.

questions.text: Wootz, a prized high-carbon steel of the ancient world, originated in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Wootz ingots were traded far and wide and used to forge famous Damascus steel.

questions.text: The first working transistor was built in 1947 at which research lab?
questions.fun_fact: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

questions.text: The compact disc was developed jointly by Philips and which Japanese company?
questions.fun_fact: The first CD players and discs went on sale in Japan in 1982.

questions.text: Which company released the Astron, the first quartz wristwatch sold to the public, in 1969?
questions.fun_fact: Seiko had earlier launched Japan's first automatic wristwatch, in 1956.

questions.text: Which locomotive, built by George and Robert Stephenson, won the Rainhill Trials in 1829?
questions.fun_fact: Rocket's top speed was about 48 km/h (30 mph).

questions.text: The ancient Greek Antikythera mechanism is often described as the oldest known example of what?
questions.fun_fact: It could predict eclipses and the positions of the Sun and Moon decades in advance.

questions.text: Nikola Tesla was born in 1856 in a village in which present-day country?
questions.fun_fact: Before going his own way, Tesla briefly worked for Thomas Edison in New York.

questions.text: The board game snakes and ladders originated in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The game reached Britain in the 1890s and later became known in the US as Chutes and Ladders.

questions.text: Which English agriculturist developed a horse-drawn seed drill in 1701?
questions.fun_fact: His name inspired the name of the progressive rock band Jethro Tull.

questions.text: The MP3 audio format was largely developed at which German research organization?
questions.fun_fact: Engineer Karlheinz Brandenburg fine-tuned it by listening again and again to Suzanne Vega's song 'Tom's Diner'.

questions.text: The Tetra Pak carton was developed in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The first cartons, launched in 1952, were shaped like a tetrahedron, which gave the company its name.

questions.text: Fazlur Rahman Khan, pioneer of 'tube' structures for skyscrapers, was born in which present-day country?
questions.fun_fact: He was the structural engineer of Chicago's Sears Tower, now called the Willis Tower.

questions.text: The world's first traffic light, a gas-lit signal, was installed in 1868 in which city?
questions.fun_fact: It was designed by railway engineer John Peake Knight and used semaphore arms by day.

questions.text: Ondol, a traditional system of heating under the floor, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Ondol carries smoke and heat from a fire through channels beneath thick stone floors.

questions.text: Which inventor created the phonograph in 1877?
questions.fun_fact: Edison's first phonograph recorded sound on a sheet of tinfoil wrapped around a grooved cylinder.

questions.text: In which country was the cheese slicer invented, in 1925?
questions.fun_fact: Its inventor, the carpenter Thor Bjørklund, based it on a carpenter's plane.

questions.text: The Ferris wheel made its debut at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in which US city?
questions.fun_fact: Each of its 36 cars could carry as many as 60 people.

questions.text: Akira Yoshino shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing which device?
questions.fun_fact: He shared the prize with John B. Goodenough and M. Stanley Whittingham.

questions.text: Eli Whitney's cotton gin, patented in 1794, separated cotton fibers from what?
questions.fun_fact: The word 'gin' in its name is short for 'engine'.

questions.text: Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, who developed the mercury-in-glass thermometer, was born in which city, now in Poland?
questions.fun_fact: Fahrenheit spent most of his working life in the Dutch Republic and died in The Hague.

questions.text: Louis Braille, who created a reading system for blind people, came from which country?
questions.fun_fact: He first presented his system to his fellow students in 1825, when he was 15.

questions.text: The IMAX film format was developed in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The first permanent IMAX theater opened in Toronto in 1971.

questions.text: Bill Hamilton, who developed the modern jet boat in the 1950s, came from which country?
questions.fun_fact: His jet boats were designed to run up shallow, fast-flowing rivers that propellers could not handle.

questions.text: George Eastman founded which company, famous for its cameras and film?
questions.fun_fact: His first Kodak camera, sold in 1888, came loaded with enough roll film for 100 pictures.

questions.text: The Kreepy Krauly, an automatic swimming pool cleaner, was invented in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its inventor, hydraulics engineer Ferdinand Chauvier, had moved there from the Belgian Congo.

questions.text: The mobile phone money service M-Pesa was launched in 2007 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: 'Pesa' is the Swahili word for money.

questions.text: Who made the first descent with a frameless parachute, over Paris in 1797?
questions.fun_fact: His wife, Jeanne Geneviève, also flew balloons and made parachute jumps.

questions.text: Which Song dynasty polymath built a famous water-powered astronomical clock tower in Kaifeng in the 11th century?
questions.fun_fact: The tower's mechanism used the first known endless chain drive to transmit power.

questions.text: The VHS videotape format was developed by which Japanese company?
questions.fun_fact: VHS beat Sony's rival Betamax format in a long battle for the home video market.

questions.text: The 'running machine' Karl Drais invented in 1817, a forerunner of the bicycle, had no what?
questions.fun_fact: Riders pushed it along with their feet; it was also nicknamed the dandy horse.

questions.text: How did the phonautograph, patented by Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville in 1857, record sound?
options: As lines traced on blackened paper
questions.fun_fact: In 2008, researchers played back one of his recordings, made in 1860, for the first time.

questions.text: The Etch A Sketch drawing toy was invented by André Cassagnes in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its screen is coated on the inside with aluminum powder, which a stylus scrapes away.

questions.text: Engineer Nils Bohlin developed the three-point seat belt in 1959 for which car maker?
questions.fun_fact: Volvo made the patent available for other car makers to use free of charge.

questions.text: Czech chemist Otto Wichterle is famous for inventing soft what?
questions.fun_fact: He made some early lenses at home using a children's construction set.

questions.text: Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, was invented by a chemist born in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its inventor, Leo Baekeland, had earlier sold his Velox photographic paper to George Eastman.

questions.text: Jikji, the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, was printed in 1377 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its only surviving volume is kept at the National Library of France in Paris.

questions.text: The Jacuzzi whirlpool bath is named after brothers who emigrated to the US from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The company was founded in Berkeley, California, in 1915 by seven Jacuzzi brothers.

questions.text: The 'macadam' type of road surface is named after an engineer from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Tarmac, short for 'tar macadam', came later, when tar was added to bind the stones.

questions.text: Which Joseon-era court inventor built a famous self-striking water clock in the 15th century?
questions.fun_fact: Although he was born a nobi, of the lowest social class, King Sejong gave him a post at the royal court.

questions.text: The first product scanned with a UPC barcode, in 1974, was a pack of what?
questions.fun_fact: The historic scan took place at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio.

questions.text: What did Margaret Knight's 1871 patented machine make?
questions.fun_fact: She won a court case against a man who claimed her invention, using her detailed drawings as proof.

questions.text: Gunpowder was invented in the 9th century in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Early Chinese texts called it huoyao, which means 'fire medicine'.

questions.text: How many wheels did Karl Benz's Patent-Motorwagen of 1885 have?
questions.fun_fact: In August 1888 Bertha Benz drove one from Mannheim to Pforzheim with two of her sons.

questions.text: Richard Trevithick's Penydarren steam locomotive made its historic run in 1804 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: On its first run it hauled 10 tons of iron, five wagons and about 70 men.

questions.text: Augustin-Jean Fresnel designed his famous lens for use in what?
questions.fun_fact: The first lighthouse Fresnel lens was lit at Cordouan, in France, in 1823.

questions.text: Edwin Land's company Polaroid became famous for which kind of camera?
questions.fun_fact: Land said the idea came when his young daughter asked why she could not see a photo right away.

questions.text: Josephine Cochrane is famous for inventing which kitchen machine?
questions.fun_fact: She showed her machine at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

questions.text: Which Polish pharmacist invented the modern kerosene lamp in 1853?
questions.fun_fact: He also built one of the world's first modern oil refineries, in 1856.

questions.text: Theodore Maiman built the first working laser in 1960 using a crystal of which gem?
questions.fun_fact: He built it at Hughes Research Laboratories in Malibu, California.

questions.text: Blaise Pascal built his mechanical calculator to help with his father's work in which field?
questions.fun_fact: After building about 50 prototypes, Pascal presented the machine to the public in 1645.

questions.text: Nicolas Appert, the 'father of canning', first sealed food in what containers?
questions.fun_fact: In 1810 the French government paid him 12,000 francs on condition that he publish his method.

questions.text: John Harrison's marine chronometers solved the problem of finding what at sea?
questions.fun_fact: His first longcase clock, built in 1713 when he was 20, was made entirely of wood.

questions.text: Chinampas, used by the Aztecs for farming, were what?
questions.fun_fact: Farmers built them in shallow lake beds from layers of mud, plants and stakes.

questions.text: Which English inventor patented the cat's eye road reflector in 1934?
questions.fun_fact: When a car drives over a cat's eye, the reflector is pushed into its rubber housing and wiped clean.

questions.text: Which musical instrument did Benjamin Franklin invent in 1761?
questions.fun_fact: Mozart and Beethoven both composed music for it.

questions.text: The board game Trivial Pursuit was created in 1979 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its creators, Montreal journalists Chris Haney and Scott Abbott, came up with the game on December 15, 1979.

questions.text: Which designer created the original Mini car, launched in 1959?
questions.fun_fact: To save space, its engine was mounted sideways and drove the front wheels.

questions.text: Which Spanish engineer invented the autogyro, first flown in 1923?
questions.fun_fact: Its rotor is not driven by the engine but spins freely as air flows through it.

questions.text: Rigid airships known as zeppelins are named after a count from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The first zeppelin, LZ 1, made its maiden flight over Lake Constance in 1900.

questions.text: James Dyson is best known for designing which appliance?
questions.fun_fact: He says he built 5,127 prototypes before getting his design right.

questions.text: The 18th-century automaton known as the Mechanical Turk appeared to play which game?
questions.fun_fact: It was really operated by a skilled chess player hidden inside its cabinet.

questions.text: Which Italian physicist invented the electric battery in 1800?
questions.fun_fact: The volt, the unit of electric potential, is named in his honor.

questions.text: King Camp Gillette made his fortune selling which grooming product?
questions.fun_fact: His key idea was a cheap, thin steel blade that people threw away once it was dull.

questions.text: Google Maps began as a program developed at Where 2 Technologies, a start-up based in which city?
questions.fun_fact: Its founders included the Danish brothers Lars and Jens Rasmussen; Google bought the company in 2004.

questions.text: Ancient Persians used the domed yakhchāl to store what?
questions.fun_fact: Some yakhchāls also had shady walls and pools where water froze overnight in winter.

questions.text: Linus Torvalds created the Linux kernel in 1991 while a student in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Torvalds also created Git, a widely used system for tracking changes to code.

questions.text: Margarine was invented in 1869 in response to a challenge set by which French ruler?
questions.fun_fact: Its inventor, Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès, first called it oleomargarine, partly from the Greek margarite, 'pearl'.

questions.text: Instant noodles were invented in 1958 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Their inventor, Momofuku Ando, went on to create Cup Noodles in 1971.

questions.text: NASA engineer Lonnie Johnson invented which water toy?
questions.fun_fact: Johnson is also credited with toys in the Nerf Blaster line.

questions.text: Barcode co-inventor Norman Joseph Woodland drew his first design in beach sand, inspired by which code?
questions.fun_fact: He and Bernard Silver were granted a US patent for the barcode in 1952.

questions.text: Tailor Jacob Davis and Levi Strauss patented which famous garment in 1873?
questions.fun_fact: They strengthened the weak points of the work trousers with copper rivets.

questions.text: Frank Zamboni invented a machine for resurfacing what?
questions.fun_fact: Zamboni and his brother built and ran their own ice rink in Paramount, California, which opened in 1940.

questions.text: Ancient Mesoamericans made rubber by mixing latex with the juice of which plant?
questions.fun_fact: The Mesoamerican ballgame, played with solid rubber balls, dates back to at least 1650 BC.

questions.text: Which inventor of ancient Alexandria built the hydraulis, a water-powered pipe organ?
questions.fun_fact: Ctesibius is often called the father of pneumatics.

questions.text: The Slinky toy, first sold in 1945, is essentially a long what?
questions.fun_fact: It was invented by naval engineer Richard James together with his wife, Betty.

questions.text: Cai Lun, a Han dynasty court official, is traditionally credited with inventing what?
questions.fun_fact: Earlier forms of paper existed in China as far back as the 3rd century BC.

questions.text: What powered the spinning aeolipile described by Hero of Alexandria?
questions.fun_fact: It is considered the first recorded steam engine, though it was never a practical source of power.

questions.text: Norwegian engineer Erik Rotheim is credited with inventing which everyday item in the 1920s?
questions.fun_fact: Norway honored the invention with a postage stamp in 1998.

questions.text: Rudolf Diesel, inventor of the diesel engine, was born in 1858 in which city?
questions.fun_fact: His parents were Bavarian immigrants living in Paris.

questions.text: The oldest known physical water clock, from around 1400 BC, was found in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was used at Karnak; an official's tomb inscription from the 16th century BC is the oldest written record of a water clock.

questions.text: Which engineer wrote The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, completed in 1206?
questions.fun_fact: His elephant clock used a slowly sinking bowl hidden inside the elephant to mark each half hour.

questions.text: The software behind Skype, launched in 2003, was written by developers from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Skype was founded by Niklas Zennström of Sweden and Janus Friis of Denmark.

questions.text: Which Han dynasty polymath built a seismoscope to detect distant earthquakes in 132 AD?
questions.fun_fact: His device was said to drop a bronze ball from a dragon's mouth into the mouth of a toad below.

questions.text: Which Greek deity ruled the sea and carried a trident?
questions.fun_fact: His title 'Earth-Shaker' already appears on Bronze Age Linear B tablets from Knossos and Pylos.

questions.text: What is the name of the winged horse of Greek myth?
questions.fun_fact: A strike of his hoof was said to have opened the Hippocrene spring on Mount Helicon, sacred to the Muses.

questions.text: Which Greek hero performed twelve labors?
questions.fun_fact: He carried out the labors in the service of King Eurystheus of Mycenae.

questions.text: Who led the Argonauts on the quest for the Golden Fleece?
questions.fun_fact: The Argonauts took their name from their ship, the Argo.

questions.text: Which Greek hero beheaded the Gorgon Medusa?
questions.fun_fact: On his way home he rescued the princess Andromeda from a sea monster and later married her.

questions.text: Who was the Greek goddess of love and beauty?
questions.fun_fact: In Hesiod's account she was born from sea foam, and both Cythera and Cyprus claimed to be her birthplace.

questions.text: What was the name of the three-headed dog that guarded the Greek underworld?
questions.fun_fact: He was said to be the offspring of the monsters Typhon and Echidna.

questions.text: Which Greek hero took ten years to return home after the Trojan War?
questions.fun_fact: He was king of Ithaca, where his wife and son waited for him.

questions.text: The Greeks hid soldiers inside a giant wooden horse to capture which city?
questions.fun_fact: In Virgil's Aeneid, a Greek named Sinon tricks the Trojans into bringing the horse inside their walls.

questions.text: Which king of Greek myth turned everything he touched into gold?
questions.fun_fact: He washed the golden touch away in the river Pactolus, whose sands were then said to sparkle with gold.

questions.text: Which Greek deity, wearing winged sandals, served as messenger of the gods?
questions.fun_fact: He was also the protector of travelers, merchants and even thieves.

questions.text: Which Greek goddess of the hunt was the twin sister of Apollo?
questions.fun_fact: Ancient sources disagree on where she and her twin were born, naming either Delos or Ortygia.

questions.text: Which Greek deity was the blacksmith of Mount Olympus?
questions.fun_fact: His epithet Aitnaios reflected the belief that his workshop lay beneath Mount Etna.

questions.text: Which winged Roman deity of love shot arrows to make people fall in love?
questions.fun_fact: His Greek counterpart was Eros, and he was usually called the son of Venus.

questions.text: Which Norse deity is the all-father and chief of the Æsir?
questions.fun_fact: He is often accompanied by two ravens and by two wolves, Geri and Freki.

questions.text: What is the name of Odin's great hall, where warriors slain in battle feast?
questions.fun_fact: Its rafters were said to be spear shafts, and its roof was thatched with shields.

questions.text: In Norse myth, which female figures chose which warriors would fall in battle?
questions.fun_fact: Their Old Norse name, valkyrja, means 'chooser of the slain'.

questions.text: What is the name of the destruction of the world in Norse myth?
questions.fun_fact: It is preceded by Fimbulwinter, three winters in a row with no summer in between.

questions.text: Which Egyptian deity had the head of a jackal?
questions.fun_fact: Anubis was linked with embalming and was the protector of tombs.

questions.text: What is the name of King Arthur's legendary sword?
questions.fun_fact: In some versions of the legend, Arthur receives it from the Lady of the Lake.

questions.text: Which wizard was King Arthur's mentor and adviser?
questions.fun_fact: In some tales he is finally trapped by the enchantress Nimue, the Lady of the Lake.

questions.text: What is the name of King Arthur's castle and court?
questions.fun_fact: Camelot first appears in Lancelot, a 12th-century French poem by Chrétien de Troyes.

questions.text: In Irish folklore, which small bearded fairy hides a pot of gold?
questions.fun_fact: Leprechauns are traditionally said to work as shoemakers.

questions.text: Which mythical bird is reborn from its own ashes?
questions.fun_fact: The Roman historian Tacitus wrote that it reappeared after a cycle of either 500 or 1,461 years.

questions.text: What is the name of a creature that is half human and half horse?
questions.fun_fact: In Greek myth the centaurs fought the Lapiths at the wedding of the Lapith king Pirithous.

questions.text: Which legendary creature has a lion's body and an eagle's head and wings?
questions.fun_fact: Griffins were often said to guard treasure and gold.

questions.text: Which goddess sprang fully armed from the head of Zeus?
questions.fun_fact: Zeus had swallowed her mother, the Titaness Metis, while she was pregnant.

questions.text: Which musician went to the underworld to bring back his wife Eurydice?
questions.fun_fact: He lost her for good when he looked back at her before they reached the upper world.

questions.text: Who answered the riddle of the Sphinx at Thebes?
questions.fun_fact: The answer was a human, who crawls on all fours as a baby and walks with a stick in old age.

questions.text: Which sorceress turned Odysseus's crew into pigs?
questions.fun_fact: She lived on the island of Aeaea, where Odysseus stayed with her for a year.

questions.text: Which Athenian hero slew the Minotaur in the Labyrinth?
questions.fun_fact: His father, King Aegeus, is said to have given his name to the Aegean Sea.

questions.text: Eating pomegranate seeds bound which goddess to the underworld for part of each year?
questions.fun_fact: Her yearly return to her mother, Demeter, was said to bring the spring.

questions.text: Which princess did Zeus carry off to Crete in the form of a white bull?
questions.fun_fact: She became the first queen of Crete and the mother of King Minos.

questions.text: Which Trojan princess could foresee the future but was cursed never to be believed?
questions.fun_fact: Her gift of prophecy came from Apollo, who added the curse when she rejected him.

questions.text: Which bird was sacred to the goddess Hera?
questions.fun_fact: In Hellenistic art, her chariot was pulled by peacocks.

questions.text: What was the Roman name of the goddess Artemis?
questions.fun_fact: One of her most famous sanctuaries stood beside Lake Nemi, south of Rome.

questions.text: Which Trojan hero fled burning Troy and became a forefather of the Romans?
questions.fun_fact: He escaped carrying his elderly father, Anchises, on his back.

questions.text: Which Roman poet wrote the Metamorphoses?
questions.fun_fact: In AD 8 Emperor Augustus banished him to Tomis, on the Black Sea coast.

questions.text: Which Norse deity lost a hand to the wolf Fenrir?
questions.fun_fact: He placed his hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge of good faith while the gods bound Fenrir.

questions.text: Which animals pull the chariot of the Norse deity Thor?
questions.fun_fact: Thor could eat his two goats and bring them back to life the next morning with his hammer.

questions.text: Which plant was the only thing that could harm the Norse deity Baldr?
questions.fun_fact: Loki tricked the blind Höðr into throwing mistletoe at Baldr.

questions.text: Who was the wife of Odin in Norse myth?
questions.fun_fact: She was said to know the fate of all beings, though she never revealed it.

questions.text: Which monster does Beowulf fight first in the Old English poem?
questions.fun_fact: Grendel raids Heorot, the great hall of the Danish king Hrothgar.

questions.text: Which Egyptian deity ruled the underworld and judged the dead?
questions.fun_fact: He was often shown with green skin, a symbol of rebirth.

questions.text: Which Egyptian goddess was usually shown as a cat or with a cat's head?
questions.fun_fact: Her main cult center was the city of Bubastis in the Nile Delta.

questions.text: Which Egyptian deity was shown with the head of a crocodile?
questions.fun_fact: His cult centers included Kom Ombo and Crocodilopolis, in the Faiyum region.

questions.text: In Egyptian myth, the heart was weighed against the feather of which goddess?
questions.fun_fact: Maat personified truth, justice and the order of the universe.

questions.text: Which Babylonian deity defeated the sea goddess Tiamat in the Enuma Elish?
questions.fun_fact: He split her body in two to make the sky and the earth.

questions.text: Inanna, the Sumerian goddess of love and war, was known to the Akkadians by what name?
questions.fun_fact: She was associated with the planet Venus.

questions.text: Which Irish hero earned his name after slaying a smith's fierce guard dog?
questions.fun_fact: He offered to take the dog's place until a new one was raised, and his name means 'Culann's Hound'.

questions.text: Which Irish hero gained wisdom by tasting the Salmon of Knowledge?
questions.fun_fact: He burned his thumb while cooking the fish, and sucking it gave him the salmon's wisdom.

questions.text: Which creatures of Scottish and Irish folklore shed seal skins to take human form?
questions.fun_fact: In many tales a selkie wife returns to the sea as soon as she finds her hidden skin.

questions.text: To which island was King Arthur taken after his last battle?
questions.fun_fact: Its name is generally thought to come from the Welsh word for 'apple tree'.

questions.text: Who was the Aztec deity of rain?
questions.fun_fact: One of the two shrines on top of the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan was dedicated to him.

questions.text: Who was the Inca deity of the sun?
questions.fun_fact: His great festival was Inti Raymi, the 'Sun Festival'.

questions.text: Which witch of Slavic folklore lives in a hut that stands on chicken legs?
questions.fun_fact: She is often said to fly in a mortar, steering it with a pestle.

questions.text: Who was the Slavic deity of thunder and lightning?
questions.fun_fact: The oak tree was sacred to him.

questions.text: Who compiled the Finnish national epic, the Kalevala?
questions.fun_fact: A district doctor by profession, he gathered folk poems on field trips through Finland and Karelia.

questions.text: In Japanese folklore, what kind of animal is a kitsune?
questions.fun_fact: Kitsune were said to grow extra tails as they aged, up to a total of nine.

questions.text: Which water creature of Japanese folklore keeps a dish of water on its head?
questions.fun_fact: Kappa are said to love cucumbers.

questions.text: Anansi, the trickster of Akan folklore, usually takes the form of what animal?
questions.fun_fact: In the Americas his tales gave rise to characters such as Aunt Nancy.

questions.text: Which giant man of bronze guarded the island of Crete?
questions.fun_fact: He ran around the island three times a day, and his single vein was sealed with a bronze nail.

questions.text: Which three sisters of Greek myth shared a single eye and a single tooth?
questions.fun_fact: Their name means 'old women', and they were also called the Grey Sisters.

questions.text: Which dragon guarded the golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides?
questions.fun_fact: Some accounts gave him a hundred heads.

questions.text: Which goddess of discord threw a golden apple marked 'to the fairest' among the goddesses?
questions.fun_fact: The quarrel it caused led to the Judgement of Paris and, in the end, the Trojan War.

questions.text: Which son of the sun deity Helios lost control of his father's chariot?
questions.fun_fact: His grieving sisters were turned into poplar trees, and their tears became amber.

questions.text: Which of the three Fates cut the thread of life?
questions.fun_fact: Clotho spun the thread and Lachesis measured it out.

questions.text: Which Roman deity protected boundary stones?
questions.fun_fact: A stone of Terminus stood inside the Temple of Jupiter on Rome's Capitoline Hill.

questions.text: Which queen of Carthage fell in love with Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid?
questions.fun_fact: She cut an oxhide into thin strips to encircle a hill, later named Byrsa, meaning 'hide'.

questions.text: Odin gave up an eye to drink from the well of which wise figure?
