questions.fun_fact: Odin later kept Mímir's head, preserved with herbs, and consulted it for advice.

questions.text: Which fire giant will lead the forces of Muspelheim at Ragnarök?
questions.fun_fact: He carries a sword that shines brighter than the sun.

questions.text: Which Icelandic writer composed the Prose Edda?
questions.fun_fact: Written around 1220, it served partly as a handbook for poets.

questions.text: Which Norse goddess kept the apples that kept the gods young?
questions.fun_fact: She is the wife of Bragi, the deity of poetry.

questions.text: Njörðr was sent to the Æsir as a hostage by which group of deities?
questions.fun_fact: In return, the Æsir sent Hœnir to them, and the exchange sealed the peace.

questions.text: Which Egyptian deity of the rising sun was shown as a scarab beetle?
questions.fun_fact: Egyptians likened the sun's daily journey to a scarab rolling its ball of dung.

questions.text: Which ram-headed Egyptian deity shaped humans on a potter's wheel?
questions.fun_fact: He was linked with the source of the Nile and had a major temple on Elephantine island.

questions.text: Which Egyptian sky goddess arched her body over the earth?
questions.fun_fact: She was said to swallow the sun each evening and give birth to it again each morning.

questions.text: How many deities made up the Ennead of Heliopolis?
questions.fun_fact: The group was headed by the creator deity Atum.

questions.text: Which Mesopotamian goddess ruled the underworld?
questions.fun_fact: In the myth of Inanna's descent to the underworld, she is Inanna's older sister.

questions.text: Which monstrous guardian of the Cedar Forest did Gilgamesh and Enkidu face?
questions.fun_fact: Humbaba was appointed guardian of the forest by the deity Enlil.

questions.text: Which Sumerian deity of fresh water and wisdom was called Ea by the Akkadians?
questions.fun_fact: He was said to live in the Abzu, a freshwater ocean beneath the earth.

questions.text: Which Irish deity owned a cauldron that never ran empty?
questions.fun_fact: His magic harp leapt from the wall and flew to him when he called it by its two names.

questions.text: In the Táin Bó Cúailnge, Queen Medb's army raids Ulster to seize what?
questions.fun_fact: Medb wanted the Brown Bull of Cooley so her wealth would match her husband's.

questions.text: Whose 12th-century History of the Kings of Britain made King Arthur famous across Europe?
questions.fun_fact: He wrote the book in Latin, under the title Historia Regum Britanniae.

questions.text: What was the name of the Aztec underworld?
questions.fun_fact: Souls were said to need four years to pass through its nine levels.

questions.text: Which Inca creator deity was said to have risen from Lake Titicaca?
questions.fun_fact: In one myth he emerged during a time of darkness to bring forth light.

questions.text: In the Kalevala, which magical object does the smith Ilmarinen forge?
questions.fun_fact: It ends up in the northern land of Pohjola, from which the epic's heroes try to steal it.

questions.text: In Russian tales, Koschei the Deathless keeps his death hidden inside what?
questions.fun_fact: The needle is in an egg, the egg in a duck, and the duck in a hare.

questions.text: What is a baby whale called?
questions.fun_fact: In some whale species, mothers nurse their calves for one to two years.

questions.text: What is the opening on top of a whale's head that it breathes through called?
questions.fun_fact: Baleen whales have two blowholes side by side, while toothed whales such as dolphins have just one.

questions.text: Which is the smallest of the world's oceans?
questions.fun_fact: It is also the shallowest and the coldest of the world's oceans.

questions.text: Which is the second-largest ocean on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: The Atlantic covers about 17% of Earth's surface.

questions.text: What is a large chunk of freshwater ice that has broken off a glacier and floats in the sea called?
questions.fun_fact: Smaller pieces of floating glacier ice are called 'growlers' or 'bergy bits'.

questions.text: What are the tiny organisms that drift in the sea, unable to swim against the flow of water, called?
questions.fun_fact: Their name comes from the Greek planktos, meaning 'drifter' or 'wanderer'.

questions.text: Which sea creature, usually with five arms, can regrow arms it has lost?
questions.fun_fact: In some species a single severed arm can regrow into a whole new animal.

questions.text: Which flightless seabirds use their flipper-like wings to 'fly' underwater?
questions.fun_fact: Penguins spend about half of their lives on land and the other half in the sea.

questions.text: Which whale is famous for the long, complex songs sung by its males?
questions.fun_fact: Its long flippers are each around a third of its body length.

questions.text: Which shark has a flattened, T-shaped head with an eye at each end?
questions.fun_fact: The wide head, called a cephalofoil, may help the shark sense prey and maneuver.

questions.text: What is a group of fish swimming together in the same direction in a coordinated way called?
questions.fun_fact: About a quarter of all fish species shoal for their entire lives.

questions.text: Which sea animals swim by pulsing a bell-shaped body and have no true brain?
questions.fun_fact: Instead of a brain, they have a loose network of nerves called a nerve net.

questions.text: Which shellfish is best known for producing pearls?
questions.fun_fact: A pearl is made of calcium carbonate, laid down in thin concentric layers.

questions.text: Which fish defends itself by gulping water to inflate its body into a ball?
questions.fun_fact: Many pufferfish also contain tetrodotoxin, which makes them a dangerous meal for predators.

questions.text: Which is the largest kind of seal, named for the male's trunk-like nose?
questions.fun_fact: Adult males can weigh up to 4,000 kg.

questions.text: Which Arctic marine mammal has long tusks and a thick mustache of stiff whiskers?
questions.fun_fact: Walruses sometimes use their tusks to hang on at breathing holes in the sea ice.

questions.text: Which fish famously swims from the sea back up the river where it hatched in order to spawn?
questions.fun_fact: Their homing ability is thought to depend on remembering the smell of their home stream.

questions.text: Which is the tallest and heaviest of all living penguin species?
questions.fun_fact: The male incubates the single egg for just over two months while the female returns to the sea to feed.

questions.text: Which deep-sea fish lures prey with a glowing growth dangling from its head?
questions.fun_fact: In deep-sea anglerfish, the lure glows thanks to bacteria living inside it.

questions.text: What is the production of light by living things, such as many deep-sea animals, called?
questions.fun_fact: Bioluminescence has evolved independently at least 94 times.

questions.text: Which large seabird scoops up fish in a stretchy throat pouch beneath its bill?
questions.fun_fact: Before the breeding season, a pelican's bill, pouch and bare facial skin turn bright colors.

questions.text: Which salt-tolerant trees grow along tropical coasts with their roots in seawater?
questions.fun_fact: The red mangrove props itself above the water on stilt-like roots.

questions.text: Which crab protects its soft body by living inside empty snail shells?
questions.fun_fact: There are over 800 species of hermit crab, and most must find bigger shells as they grow.

questions.text: Which deep-sea octopus is named after a Disney elephant because of its ear-like fins?
questions.fun_fact: Unlike most octopuses, it swims mainly by flapping its fins rather than by jet propulsion.

questions.text: Roughly what share of Earth's surface is covered by the ocean?
questions.fun_fact: The ocean holds about 97% of all the water on Earth.

questions.text: Seawater's saltiness comes mainly from which two dissolved ions?
questions.fun_fact: On average, each liter of seawater holds about 35 grams of dissolved salts.

questions.text: The orca, or killer whale, is the largest member of which family?
questions.fun_fact: Orcas live in family groups called pods, and some pods pass down their own hunting techniques and calls.

questions.text: Which warm, swift stream of Atlantic water runs up the US East Coast and then across toward Europe?
questions.fun_fact: Benjamin Franklin had an early chart of it printed in 1769 to help mail ships cross faster.

questions.text: Which cold, nutrient-rich flow of seawater runs north along the west coast of South America?
questions.fun_fact: It supports one of the world's richest fisheries, yielding roughly a fifth of the global marine fish catch.

questions.text: What name is given to the periodic warming of surface waters in the tropical Pacific Ocean?
questions.fun_fact: Its cool counterpart is La Niña, and the cycle repeats irregularly about every two to seven years.

questions.text: Which is the largest living species of turtle?
questions.fun_fact: It feeds mainly on jellyfish and other soft, jelly-like animals.

questions.text: What is the second-largest living fish, after the whale shark?
questions.fun_fact: Despite its size, it is a harmless filter feeder that strains plankton through its huge mouth.

questions.text: Baleen plates, which some whales use to filter food, are made of which material?
questions.fun_fact: Baleen was once called 'whalebone', a misnomer since it contains no bone.

questions.text: Which animal has the largest brain on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Its clicks can reach 236 decibels underwater, the loudest sound made by any animal.

questions.text: The marine iguana, the only lizard that forages in the sea, lives only on which islands?
questions.fun_fact: It feeds almost entirely on algae, which large males dive underwater to graze.

questions.text: Which seabird has the greatest known wingspan of any living bird?
questions.fun_fact: Some individuals circle the Southern Ocean three times in a single year, covering more than 120,000 km.

questions.text: The mesopelagic zone, roughly 200 to 1,000 m deep, is nicknamed what?
questions.fun_fact: Only faint light reaches it, yet it makes up about 20% of the ocean's volume.

questions.text: The hadal zone, the deepest part of the ocean found in trenches, is named after which figure from Greek myth?
questions.fun_fact: Hadal habitats cover less than 0.25% of the seafloor, yet trenches span over 40% of the ocean's depth range.

questions.text: Food webs around deep-sea hydrothermal vents are powered by which process instead of photosynthesis?
questions.fun_fact: Giant tube worms at the vents have no digestive system and rely on bacteria living inside them.

questions.text: In 2012, which film director piloted the Deepsea Challenger to the bottom of the Challenger Deep?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first solo dive to the Challenger Deep, and the first to spend hours exploring the bottom.

questions.text: Coral bleaching happens when stressed corals lose which partners living in their tissues?
questions.fun_fact: These algae, called zooxanthellae, feed the coral with nutrients made by photosynthesis.

questions.text: What is a ring-shaped coral reef or island that encircles a lagoon called?
questions.fun_fact: Charles Darwin explained atolls as reefs left behind after volcanic islands slowly sank beneath the sea.

questions.text: Ningaloo Reef, famous for its gatherings of whale sharks, lies off which Australian state?
questions.fun_fact: At about 260 km long, it is Australia's largest fringing coral reef.

questions.text: The Raja Ampat islands, famed for their rich coral reefs, belong to which country?
questions.fun_fact: The name means 'Four Kings'; its four main islands are Misool, Salawati, Batanta and Waigeo.

questions.text: Which small reef fish runs 'cleaning stations' where it eats parasites off larger fish?
questions.fun_fact: The bluestreak cleaner wrasse may even pass the mirror test, a classic test of self-recognition.

questions.text: Which shelled cephalopod, often called a living fossil, has a coiled shell divided into chambers?
questions.fun_fact: Nautiluses are the only living members of the ancient subclass Nautiloidea.

questions.text: Kelp, which forms dense underwater forests, is a type of what?
questions.fun_fact: Some giant kelp can grow as much as half a meter in a single day.

questions.text: Sand dollars are flattened, burrowing members of which group of animals?
questions.fun_fact: In New Zealand they are known as sea cookies or snapper biscuits.

questions.text: Barnacles, which cling to rocks and ship hulls, are most closely related to which animals?
questions.fun_fact: In folklore, barnacle geese were once believed to hatch from goose barnacles.

questions.text: Which crab has the largest leg span of any arthropod, at up to about 3.7 m?
questions.fun_fact: Its Japanese name, taka-ashi-gani, means 'tall-legged crab'.

questions.text: Despite their name, horseshoe crabs are more closely related to which animals?
questions.fun_fact: Horseshoe crabs have changed little since they first appeared about 250 million years ago.

questions.text: Which white Arctic whale is nicknamed the 'sea canary' for its high-pitched calls?

questions.text: Hector's dolphin is the only cetacean found exclusively around which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its rare North Island subspecies is known as the Māui dolphin.

questions.text: In 1947, Thor Heyerdahl's balsa raft Kon-Tiki set sail across the Pacific from which country?

questions.text: Which French explorer co-invented the Aqua-Lung diving regulator with engineer Émile Gagnan?
questions.fun_fact: His 1956 documentary The Silent World won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival.

questions.text: Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance was trapped by pack ice and sank in which sea in 1915?
questions.fun_fact: Its wreck was found in 2022, about 3,000 m down and remarkably well preserved.

questions.text: The 'haline' in the ocean's thermohaline circulation refers to what?
questions.fun_fact: Climate scientist Wallace Broecker coined its nickname, the 'global conveyor belt'.

questions.text: Which is the only penguin species that lives naturally north of the equator?
questions.fun_fact: Most Galápagos penguins live on Fernandina Island and the west coast of Isabela Island, where cool currents bring food.

questions.text: Which large, filter-feeding rays have horn-shaped fins on their heads and can span up to 7 m?
questions.fun_fact: They have one of the highest brain-to-body ratios of all fish.

questions.text: The vaquita, a tiny porpoise, is endemic to which body of water?
questions.fun_fact: Its name is Spanish for 'little cow'.

questions.text: Which crustacean is known for smashing its prey with a powerful, club-like appendage?
questions.fun_fact: Other mantis shrimp species are 'spearers' that impale prey with spiny appendages instead.

questions.text: Although it resembles a jellyfish, the Portuguese man o' war is actually what?

questions.text: The 'immortal jellyfish', Turritopsis dohrnii, can do what when stressed or old?
questions.fun_fact: It does this by transdifferentiation, turning its existing cells into new types of cells.

questions.text: The mimic octopus, famous for impersonating other sea animals, was discovered in 1998 off which island?
questions.fun_fact: It was first found on the muddy bottom of a river mouth in Indonesia.

questions.text: Which Arctic shark is estimated to live for centuries, reaching maturity at around 150 years old?
questions.fun_fact: In Iceland its fermented meat is eaten as the pungent delicacy kæstur hákarl.

questions.text: Sharks use jelly-filled pores called ampullae of Lorenzini to detect what?
questions.fun_fact: Most bony fishes and land vertebrates have lost these sense organs.

questions.text: The green sea turtle is named for the color of its what?
questions.fun_fact: It is the only sea turtle that is mainly herbivorous as an adult, grazing on seagrass.

questions.text: Which giant relative of the dugong, described by Europeans in 1741, had vanished within 27 years?
questions.fun_fact: Some adults may have weighed 8–10 tonnes; the animals fed mainly on kelp around the Commander Islands in the Bering Sea.

questions.text: In 1977, scientists in which submersible first observed life thriving around deep-sea hydrothermal vents?
questions.fun_fact: The vents they explored lie on the Galápagos Rift in the eastern Pacific.

questions.text: Naturalist William Beebe and engineer Otis Barton set depth records in the 1930s in which diving vessel?
questions.fun_fact: Their deepest dive, off Bermuda in 1934, reached 923 m.

questions.text: Which American cartographer co-created the first scientific map of the Atlantic Ocean floor in the 1950s?
questions.fun_fact: Her work revealed the Mid-Atlantic Ridge in detail and helped win acceptance for plate tectonics.

questions.text: Which American oceanographer, nicknamed 'Her Deepness', was the first chief scientist of NOAA?
questions.fun_fact: In 1979 she walked untethered on the seafloor off Oahu in a JIM suit, at a depth of 381 m.

questions.text: In 1976, the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaii to where, using only traditional navigation?
questions.fun_fact: The double-hulled canoe navigates without instruments, using traditional Polynesian wayfinding.

questions.text: Who made the first solo voyage around the world under sail, from 1895 to 1898?
questions.fun_fact: His boat was the Spray, and his book Sailing Alone Around the World became an international best-seller.

questions.text: Which ship carried Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld's expedition through the Northeast Passage in 1878–1879?
questions.fun_fact: It was also the first voyage to sail all the way around Eurasia.

questions.text: What is the daily mass movement of ocean animals up toward the surface at night and back down by day called?
questions.fun_fact: Measured by biomass, it is the largest synchronous migration on Earth.

questions.text: Which Arctic baleen whale is thought to be able to live for more than 200 years?
questions.fun_fact: It has the largest mouth of any animal, almost a third of its body length.

questions.text: Sea sponges belong to which animal phylum, whose name means 'pore bearer'?
questions.fun_fact: Sponges have no complex nervous, digestive or circulatory systems; water flowing through them does those jobs.

questions.text: Which underwater ridge crosses the Arctic Ocean from the New Siberian Islands to Ellesmere Island?
questions.fun_fact: Unusually, this undersea ridge is made of continental crust rather than oceanic crust.

questions.text: Calypso Deep, the deepest point of the Mediterranean Sea, lies off the coast of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It plunges to about 5,200 m in the Hellenic Trench, southwest of Pylos.

questions.text: Which Swedish oceanographer explained why wind-driven sea ice drifts at an angle to the wind?
questions.fun_fact: He published his theory of the 'Ekman spiral' in 1905, after drift was noticed during the Fram expedition.

questions.text: Which warm Pacific flow runs north past Japan, its name meaning 'black stream'?
questions.fun_fact: Like the Gulf Stream in the Atlantic, it carries warm tropical water toward the pole.

questions.text: The 'West Wind Drift' is another name for which great flow of seawater?
questions.fun_fact: It circles Antarctica from west to east and carries more water than any other ocean flow.

questions.text: The Tubbataha Reefs, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the Sulu Sea, belong to which country?
questions.fun_fact: The reefs serve as nesting grounds for hawksbill and green sea turtles.

questions.text: Which pigment-containing cells, controlled by muscles, let octopuses change color in an instant?
questions.fun_fact: Charles Darwin described the cuttlefish's remarkable color changes in The Voyage of the Beagle.

questions.text: Which 1951 best-seller about the ocean was written by marine biologist Rachel Carson?
options: The Old Man and the Sea
questions.fun_fact: It won the 1952 US National Book Award for Nonfiction.

questions.text: What are the weakest tides, when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles to each other, called?
questions.fun_fact: The strongest tides, at new and full moon, are called spring tides, which has nothing to do with the season.

questions.text: The Puerto Rico Trench contains the deepest part of which ocean?
questions.fun_fact: It lies on the boundary between the North Atlantic and the Caribbean Sea, just north of Puerto Rico.

questions.text: Which boxing legend lit the Olympic cauldron at the 1996 Atlanta Games?
questions.fun_fact: Ali had won Olympic light heavyweight gold at Rome 1960, competing under his birth name, Cassius Clay.

questions.text: By tradition, which nation's team enters first in the parade at an Olympic opening ceremony?
questions.fun_fact: The host nation's team traditionally enters the stadium last.

questions.text: What did winners at the ancient Olympic Games receive as their prize?
questions.fun_fact: At Athens 2004, medal winners also received olive wreaths in honor of the ancient tradition.

questions.text: Which of these colors does NOT appear in the five Olympic rings?
questions.fun_fact: Coubertin said the ring colors, with the white background, could reproduce the flag of every country of his day.

questions.text: Misha, the mascot of the 1980 Moscow Olympics, was which animal?
questions.fun_fact: Drawn by illustrator Victor Chizhikov, Misha was the first sporting mascot to become a big merchandising success.

questions.text: Bing Dwen Dwen, the mascot of the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics, is which animal?
questions.fun_fact: The mascot wears a 'suit of ice', and 'bing' means ice in Chinese.

questions.text: The Paris 2024 Olympic medals each contain a piece of iron from which landmark?
questions.fun_fact: The medals were designed by the Paris jewelry house Chaumet and struck by the Monnaie de Paris.

questions.text: In which sport did Britain's Steve Redgrave win gold at five consecutive Olympics?
questions.fun_fact: His golds came from 1984 to 2000, the last of them in the coxless four.

questions.text: Which Italian city hosted the 2006 Winter Olympics?
questions.fun_fact: Cross-country skier Stefania Belmondo, a 10-time Olympic medalist, lit the cauldron.

questions.text: Eddie 'the Eagle' Edwards became famous at the 1988 Calgary Olympics in which sport?
questions.fun_fact: He finished last in both of his events, yet held the British record in his sport from 1988 to 2001.

questions.text: The 1980 'Miracle on Ice' was a famous Olympic upset in which sport?
questions.fun_fact: A US team made up mostly of amateurs beat the Soviet Union, the four-time defending champions, 4–3.

questions.text: Jamaica made a famous Winter Olympic debut at Calgary 1988 in which sport?
questions.fun_fact: The team's story inspired the 1993 Disney film Cool Runnings.

questions.text: Skateboarding, surfing and sport climbing all made their Olympic debut at which Games?
questions.fun_fact: Baseball and softball also returned there, for the first time since 2008.

questions.text: The 2014 Winter Olympics were held in Sochi, in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its Olympic Park was built on the Black Sea coast, while the snow events were held in the nearby mountains.

questions.text: Pierre de Coubertin, who revived the Olympic Games, came from which country?
questions.fun_fact: He won an Olympic gold medal himself, for literature, in the 1912 art competitions.

questions.text: At the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, athletes paraded by boat along which river?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first Summer Olympics opening ceremony to be held outside a stadium.

questions.text: India won six consecutive Olympic golds, from 1928 to 1956, in which team sport?
questions.fun_fact: India added two more Olympic hockey titles, in 1964 and 1980.

questions.text: Snowboarding made its Olympic debut in 1998 in which Japanese city?
questions.fun_fact: Women's ice hockey was also introduced at those Games.

questions.text: Which US city hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics?
questions.fun_fact: A women's bobsleigh event was held there for the first time.

questions.text: Which Canadian city hosted the 2010 Winter Olympics?

questions.text: Hodori, the mascot of the 1988 Seoul Olympics, was which animal?

questions.text: Which race combining swimming, cycling and running made its Olympic debut at Sydney 2000?
questions.fun_fact: The first Olympic triathlons were staged at the Sydney Opera House.

questions.text: Which British runner won both the 5,000 m and the 10,000 m at London 2012 and again at Rio 2016?
questions.fun_fact: Only Finland's Lasse Virén, in 1972 and 1976, had won both titles at successive Games before him.

questions.text: The 1994 Winter Olympics were held in Lillehammer, in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Because of a calendar change, they came just two years after the previous Winter Games.

questions.text: Which of these sports was on the program of the first modern Olympics, in 1896?
questions.fun_fact: Olympic fencers compete with three weapons: the foil, the épée and the saber.

questions.text: Which Canadian city hosted the 1976 Summer Olympics?
questions.fun_fact: Canada won no gold medals there, the first time a Summer Games host had failed to win one.

questions.text: Which city hosted the 1900 Olympics as part of a World's Fair?

questions.text: At which Games were gold, silver and bronze medals first awarded for the top three places?
questions.fun_fact: They were also the first Olympic Games held outside Europe.

questions.text: The athletes' Olympic oath was first taken at which Games?
questions.fun_fact: Belgian fencer Victor Boin swore it on behalf of all the athletes.

questions.text: At which Summer Games was a symbolic Olympic flame lit for the first time?

questions.text: The Olympic torch relay was first held for which Summer Games?

questions.text: Which city hosted the 1960 Games now recognized as the first Paralympics?

questions.text: How was the Olympic cauldron lit at the Barcelona 1992 opening ceremony?

questions.text: Which film director staged the London 2012 Olympic opening ceremony?

questions.text: Women's boxing made its Olympic debut at which Games?

questions.text: The first Refugee Olympic Team competed at which Games?

questions.text: What form did the Paris 2024 Olympic cauldron take?

questions.fun_fact: He also took silver in the high jump and bronze in the long jump at those Games.

questions.text: Which Italian runner was disqualified from the 1908 Olympic marathon after officials helped him finish?

questions.text: Which force keeps the planets in their orbits around the Sun?

questions.text: Phobos and Deimos are the moons of which planet?

questions.text: Which US agency, founded in 1958, runs the country's civilian space program?

questions.text: On which planet is the Great Red Spot, a giant, long-lasting storm?

questions.text: A 'shooting star' is the popular name for what?
questions.fun_fact: Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through streams of debris, often left behind by comets.

questions.text: Which world, long counted as the ninth planet, was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006?
questions.fun_fact: The name Pluto was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old schoolgirl from Oxford, England.

questions.text: Which planet is often called the 'Morning Star' or the 'Evening Star'?

questions.text: What occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and blocks the Sun's light?

questions.text: What was the name of NASA's reusable crewed spacecraft, flown from 1981 to 2011?

questions.text: What are the rocky bodies orbiting the Sun, mostly in a belt between Mars and Jupiter, called?

questions.text: What is a region of space whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape?
questions.fun_fact: The boundary beyond which nothing can return from a black hole is called its event horizon.

questions.text: Which planet is named after the Roman deity of the sea?

questions.text: Which NASA program landed astronauts on the Moon between 1969 and 1972?

questions.text: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?

questions.text: What is a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun called?

questions.text: What is the scientific name for the northern lights?

questions.text: Which 1970 Moon mission was aborted after an oxygen tank failed, yet brought its crew home safely?

questions.text: Which star, lying almost directly above Earth's North Pole, is known as the North Star?

questions.text: Which theory says the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense early state?

questions.text: What is a vast cloud of gas and dust in space, often a birthplace of stars, called?

questions.text: What are the darker, cooler patches that appear on the Sun's surface called?

questions.text: Which is the smallest planet in the Solar System?

questions.text: ISRO is the national space agency of which country?

questions.text: Who was the second person to walk on the Moon, shortly after Neil Armstrong?

questions.text: What is a space traveler from the Soviet Union or Russia traditionally called?

questions.text: Jupiter and Saturn are often described as what kind of planets?

questions.text: The Big Dipper, also called the Plough, is part of which constellation?

questions.text: How many constellations does the International Astronomical Union officially recognize?

questions.text: Which astronaut famously hit golf balls on the Moon during Apollo 14?
questions.fun_fact: Ten years earlier, in 1961, Shepard had become the first American to travel into space.

questions.text: Which mission carried the first humans to orbit the Moon, in December 1968?

questions.text: What is the nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way?

questions.text: Which American astronomer showed in the 1920s that many 'spiral nebulae' are galaxies far beyond our own?

questions.text: On which planet is Valles Marineris, one of the largest canyon systems in the Solar System?
questions.fun_fact: It stretches more than 4,000 km across Mars and plunges up to about 7 km deep.

questions.text: Which astronomer urged NASA to have Voyager 1 photograph Earth from afar, creating the 'Pale Blue Dot'?
questions.fun_fact: In the 1990 photo, taken from over 6 billion km away, Earth appears smaller than a single pixel.

questions.text: Which way does a comet's tail generally point?
questions.fun_fact: The tail is pushed outward by sunlight and the solar wind; a comet may have a dust tail, an ion tail, both or neither.

questions.text: The Kármán line, often used to mark where space begins, lies about how high above sea level?
questions.fun_fact: Some scientists argue that space should instead be said to begin at about 80 km.

questions.text: What is the faint radiation that fills the universe, left over from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang?
questions.fun_fact: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered it by accident in 1964 with a horn-shaped radio antenna.

questions.text: The 'Pillars of Creation', made famous by a 1995 Hubble photo, lie in which nebula?
questions.fun_fact: The James Webb Space Telescope photographed the pillars again in infrared light in 2022.

questions.text: What is the vast, hypothesized shell of icy bodies thought to surround the Solar System far beyond Pluto?
questions.fun_fact: Dutch astronomer Jan Oort proposed it in 1950 to explain where long-period comets come from.

questions.text: In 1986, Voyager 2 became the first spacecraft to fly past which planet?
questions.fun_fact: Three years later, in 1989, Voyager 2 also made the first flyby of Neptune.

questions.text: Which is the largest moon in the Solar System?
questions.fun_fact: Ganymede is larger than the planet Mercury and may hide an ocean beneath its icy crust.

questions.text: Which outer layer of the Sun appears as a pearly white halo during a total solar eclipse?
questions.fun_fact: During a total eclipse, the corona and reddish solar prominences can be seen with the naked eye.

questions.text: Who launched the world's first liquid-fueled rocket, in Massachusetts in 1926?
questions.fun_fact: Goddard and his team went on to launch 34 rockets between 1926 and 1941.

questions.text: Mauna Kea, a summit crowded with major astronomical observatories, is in which US state?
questions.fun_fact: It hosts telescopes run by many countries, including the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope.

questions.text: Which NASA probe made the first flyby of Pluto, in July 2015?
questions.fun_fact: At its closest, it swept past Pluto at a distance of about 12,500 km.

questions.text: Which spacecraft orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, studying its rings and moons?
questions.fun_fact: It carried ESA's Huygens probe, which landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005.

questions.text: In 1970, Venera 7 became the first spacecraft to send back data from the surface of which planet?
questions.fun_fact: It probably bounced onto its side, so only very weak signals reached Earth, for about 23 minutes.

questions.text: Which country's Hope probe entered orbit around Mars in February 2021?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first mission to Mars by an Arab country.

questions.text: Who became the first American woman in space, in 1983?
questions.fun_fact: At 32, she was also the youngest American astronaut to have flown in space at that time.

questions.text: What is the name of China's space station, which means 'Heavenly Palace'?
questions.fun_fact: Its core module, Tianhe, was launched on 29 April 2021.

questions.text: In which country is the Baikonur Cosmodrome, the launch site of Sputnik 1?

questions.text: In 2019, which country made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon?
questions.fun_fact: Its lander touched down on 3 January 2019, carrying the rover Yutu-2.

questions.text: Betelgeuse and Rigel are the two brightest stars of which constellation?

questions.text: Which star cluster in Taurus is also known as the Seven Sisters?

questions.text: What type of star is the Sun informally called?

questions.text: The James Webb Space Telescope mainly observes in which kind of light?

questions.text: Which NASA space telescope, launched in 2009, found thousands of exoplanets by watching stars dim?

questions.text: What mainly causes Earth's seasons?

questions.text: Who built the first practical reflecting telescope, in 1668?
questions.fun_fact: Mirrors avoid chromatic aberration, the colored fringes that the lenses of early telescopes produced.

questions.text: In which country is ALMA, the giant radio telescope array on the Chajnantor plateau?

questions.text: Which ESA mission put the first lander, Philae, on a comet in 2014?

questions.text: What was the name of the first space station, launched by the Soviet Union in 1971?

questions.text: In 2003, which spacecraft carried China's first astronaut into orbit?

questions.text: Japan's Hayabusa2 probe brought back samples from which asteroid in 2020?

questions.text: In 1966, which Soviet probe made the first soft landing on the Moon?

questions.text: Which British astronomer coined the term 'Big Bang' in a 1949 radio broadcast?
questions.fun_fact: Hoyle himself rejected the theory, favoring a 'steady state' universe with no beginning.

questions.text: Who discovered the first pulsar in 1967, while a graduate student at Cambridge?

questions.text: Which Indian-American astrophysicist gives his name to the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf?
questions.fun_fact: NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, launched in 1999, is named in his honor.

questions.text: The 15th-century astronomer Ulugh Beg built a great observatory in which city?

questions.text: India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after which ancient Indian astronomer?

questions.text: Which ancient Greek astronomer proposed the first known Sun-centered model of the universe?

questions.text: Who discovered the link between the pulsation period and brightness of Cepheid variable stars?

questions.text: Which red supergiant is the brightest star in the constellation Scorpius?

questions.text: Which is the smallest of the 88 modern constellations?

questions.text: Which constellation does the Sun pass through that is not one of the 12 traditional zodiac signs?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'serpent-bearer', and it is usually drawn as a man grasping a snake.

questions.text: Roughly how many light-years make up one parsec?
questions.fun_fact: It is the distance at which the Earth–Sun distance would span an angle of one arcsecond.

questions.text: What is the escape velocity from Earth's surface?

questions.text: What is the effect that makes the Moon always show the same face to Earth called?

questions.text: In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole in which galaxy?

questions.text: Which ESA space observatory, launched in 2013, charted the positions of about a billion stars?

questions.text: The Gran Telescopio Canarias, a giant optical telescope, stands on which island?
questions.fun_fact: Its segmented main mirror is 10.4 m across.

questions.text: Which country became the third to launch a satellite on its own rocket, with Astérix in 1965?
questions.fun_fact: It was launched on a Diamant A rocket from Hammaguir, in Algeria.

questions.text: What was the name of the Soviet space shuttle that made a single uncrewed orbital flight in 1988?

questions.text: Who was the Soviet 'Chief Designer' behind Sputnik 1 and Gagarin's Vostok flight?
questions.fun_fact: During his lifetime he was publicly identified only by the title 'Chief Designer'.

questions.text: Which two Soviet dogs became the first to orbit Earth and return alive, in 1960?
questions.fun_fact: They shared the flight with a gray rabbit, 42 mice, two rats, flies and some plants.

questions.text: Who made the first American spacewalk, during the Gemini 4 mission in 1965?

questions.text: Which moon of Saturn sprays plumes of water from cracks near its south pole?

questions.text: In 1973, which probe made the first flyby of Jupiter?
questions.fun_fact: It was also the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt, and one of the first set on a path out of the Solar System.

questions.text: What is a word formed by rearranging all the letters of another, as 'silent' is from 'listen'?
questions.fun_fact: Robert Hooke first published his law of elasticity in the form of a scrambled Latin anagram.

questions.text: What is a phrase that joins contradictory terms, like 'deafening silence', called?

questions.text: What are words like 'knight' and 'night', which sound alike but differ in meaning, called?

questions.text: Which script is used to write Russian?

questions.text: The word 'boomerang' comes from an Aboriginal language of which country?

questions.text: The word 'igloo' comes from the language of which people?

questions.text: The word 'cookie' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: It comes from 'koekje', meaning 'little cake'.

questions.text: The word 'alphabet' comes from the first two letters of which alphabet?
questions.fun_fact: Alpha and beta in turn came from Phoenician aleph ('ox') and bet ('house').

questions.text: Which of these languages is written from right to left?
questions.fun_fact: In everyday speech, Urdu and Hindi are largely mutually intelligible.

questions.text: Afrikaans developed mainly from which European language?
questions.fun_fact: Once seen as a Dutch dialect, it eventually replaced Standard Dutch as an official language in South Africa.

questions.text: Which of these Eastern European languages is a Romance language?
questions.fun_fact: Its grammar keeps noun cases and attaches the definite article to the end of words.

questions.text: English belongs to which branch of the Indo-European language family?
questions.fun_fact: Its closest relatives include Scots, Low Saxon and Frisian.

questions.text: Which German word means pleasure taken in someone else's misfortune?
questions.fun_fact: Literally, it means 'harm-joy'.

questions.text: The French phrase 'déjà vu' literally means what?
questions.fun_fact: French philosopher Émile Boirac first used the term in 1876.

questions.text: The invitation abbreviation 'RSVP' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: It stands for a phrase meaning, literally, 'respond if it pleases you'.

questions.text: What is a slip of the tongue like 'blushing crow' for 'crushing blow' called?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after William Archibald Spooner, an Oxford don said to make such slips often.

questions.text: The word 'motel' blends 'motor' with which other word?
questions.fun_fact: The term traces back to the Milestone Mo-Tel in San Luis Obispo, California.

questions.text: Which English writer coined the word 'utopia' in 1516?
questions.fun_fact: It comes from Greek and literally means 'no place'.

questions.text: Which canal completes the palindrome 'A man, a plan, a canal...'?
questions.fun_fact: That palindrome dates from 1948; 'Madam, I'm Adam' goes back to 1861.

questions.text: What are the two dots over German letters like ä, ö and ü called?
questions.fun_fact: In German, ä, ö and ü are not counted as separate letters of the alphabet.

questions.text: 'Saudade', a word for deep nostalgic longing, is most associated with which language?
questions.fun_fact: The word is also used in Galician, a close relative of Portuguese.

questions.text: The name 'Australia' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Explorer Matthew Flinders popularized the name from 1804; it replaced 'New Holland'.

questions.text: The word 'piano' is short for an Italian name meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: The full early name described a 'harpsichord with soft and loud'.

questions.text: Thursday takes its name from the thunder deity known in Norse mythology as whom?
questions.fun_fact: Most Romance languages name the day after Jupiter instead, as in French 'jeudi'.

questions.text: The Latin phrase 'et cetera' literally means what?
questions.fun_fact: It is a calque of the Koine Greek phrase 'kai ta hetera'.

questions.text: Hiragana and katakana are writing systems used for which language?
questions.fun_fact: Hiragana first gained popularity among women, who generally had less access to education than men.

questions.text: The word 'shampoo' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: Indian traveler Dean Mahomed is credited with bringing 'shampooing' baths to Britain.

questions.text: The word 'pajamas' comes from Persian words meaning what kind of garment?
questions.fun_fact: The word reached English by way of Hindustani.

questions.text: The word 'mentor' comes from a character in which ancient epic?
questions.fun_fact: In the poem, the goddess Athena takes Mentor's form to guide Odysseus's son Telemachus.

questions.text: Charles Boycott, whose name gave English the word 'boycott', was a land agent in which country?
questions.fun_fact: He had first come to Ireland as an officer in the British Army.

questions.text: The leotard is named after Jules Léotard, a 19th-century French what?
questions.fun_fact: He was famous for his daring performances on the trapeze.

questions.text: The name of the ancient cuneiform script comes from the Latin word for what?
questions.fun_fact: Cuneiform was used to write many languages, including Sumerian, Akkadian and Hittite.

questions.text: The Greek alphabet was adapted from the script of which ancient people?
questions.fun_fact: Greek was the first known alphabet to write vowels as well as consonants systematically.

questions.text: Which Japanese script is mainly used to write foreign loanwords?
questions.fun_fact: Its use is often compared to italics in English, as it can also mark emphasis.

questions.text: Which language of Ethiopia is written in the Ge'ez script?
questions.fun_fact: Ge'ez is an abugida: each character stands for a consonant plus a vowel.

questions.text: Basque, spoken in Spain and France, is classified as what kind of language?
questions.fun_fact: It is the only surviving language of Paleo-European origin.

questions.text: Persian (Farsi) belongs to which language family?
questions.fun_fact: It is written in a script derived from Arabic in Iran, but in Cyrillic in Tajikistan.

questions.text: Tamil, spoken mainly in southern India, belongs to which language family?
questions.fun_fact: It is also an official language of Sri Lanka and Singapore.

questions.text: Hawaiian, Māori and Tagalog all belong to which language family?
questions.fun_fact: By some estimates, the family contains about 1,257 languages.

questions.text: Romansh is a national language of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It gained that status in 1938 and, like Italian, descends from Latin.

questions.text: Whose 1828 dictionary helped establish American spellings such as 'color' and 'center'?
questions.fun_fact: Most of those spellings already existed; he chose them for simplicity and analogy.

questions.text: The Académie française, guardian of the French language, was founded in which century?
questions.fun_fact: Its 40 members are known as 'les immortels', the immortals.

questions.text: Besides collecting fairy tales, the Brothers Grimm began a huge dictionary of which language?
questions.fun_fact: Begun in 1838, it was still unfinished at their deaths and was completed by later scholars.

questions.text: Peter Mark Roget is famous for compiling what kind of reference book?
questions.fun_fact: It began as a list for his own use and was published in 1852.

questions.text: What is a misheard phrase, especially from a song or poem, called?

questions.text: Georges Perec's 1969 novel La Disparition never uses which letter?
questions.fun_fact: Its English translation, A Void, also manages without the letter.

questions.text: Denim takes its name from which French city?

questions.text: The Canary Islands take their name from a Latin phrase meaning 'Islands of the' what?

questions.text: What is the small hook under the 'c' in 'façade' called?

questions.text: The old letter þ, called thorn, is still used in which modern language?

questions.text: The runic alphabet known as the 'futhark' is named after what?
questions.fun_fact: The oldest form, the Elder Futhark, had 24 runes.

questions.text: In 1821, Sequoyah completed a syllabary for which Native American language?

questions.text: What is the official system for writing Standard Chinese in the Latin alphabet?

questions.text: In 1928, Turkey replaced the Arabic script with which alphabet?
questions.fun_fact: The new alphabet was introduced as part of Atatürk's reforms.

questions.text: The abbreviation 'e.g.' stands for which Latin phrase?

questions.text: The word 'emoji' comes from Japanese words meaning what?

questions.text: The word 'coach' comes from Kocs, a town in which country?

questions.text: The word 'window' comes from Old Norse words meaning what?

questions.text: The word 'calculate' comes from the Latin 'calculus', meaning what?

questions.text: 'Serendipity' was coined from Serendip, an old Persian name for which island?

questions.text: Guarani is an official language, alongside Spanish, of which country?

questions.text: The Italian greeting 'ciao' comes from a Venetian phrase meaning what?

questions.text: The word 'silhouette' comes from Étienne de Silhouette, who held which post in France?

questions.text: The word 'kangaroo' comes from which Aboriginal Australian language?

questions.text: Writing that alternates direction from one line to the next is called what?

questions.text: The Tifinagh script is used to write which group of languages?
