questions.fun_fact: Some unicellular organisms contain many nuclei in their single cell, such as the seaweed Caulerpa.

questions.text: Amoebas and ciliates belong to which mostly single-celled group of eukaryotes?
questions.fun_fact: Protists are not a natural group: they are all eukaryotes that are not animals, land plants or fungi.

questions.text: What is a visible clump of identical bacterial cells grown from one parent cell on a solid dish called?
questions.fun_fact: Single-celled slime molds can gather into colonies when food is hard to find.

questions.text: What do we call slimy communities of microbes that stick to surfaces such as river stones?
questions.fun_fact: A biofilm's slimy matrix can hold many times its dry weight in water.

questions.text: Which American biologist published the 1967 paper 'On the Origin of Mitosing Cells'?
questions.fun_fact: Her paper was rejected by about fifteen journals before it was published.

questions.text: Which single-celled algae cause the bluish flashes of light seen in some ocean water at night?
questions.fun_fact: Botanists once called them Pyrrophyta, or 'fire algae', after their glowing forms.

questions.text: Chalk deposits such as the White Cliffs of Dover are made largely of plates from which microscopic algae?
questions.fun_fact: Their calcium carbonate plates are transparent, so the algae can still photosynthesize underneath.

questions.text: Which Romanian-American cell biologist first described ribosomes, in 1955, and shared a 1974 Nobel Prize?
questions.fun_fact: His work with electron microscopy and cell fractionation helped lay the foundations of modern molecular cell biology.

questions.text: Which German physicist shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics for designing the first electron microscope?
questions.fun_fact: Ruska received half of the 1986 prize; Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer shared the rest for the scanning tunneling microscope.

questions.text: What are small circular DNA rings that bacteria can pass to each other called?
questions.fun_fact: Scientists use artificial plasmids as vectors to carry DNA into host cells.

questions.text: What was the original name of the archaea, before they were recognized as a separate domain?
questions.fun_fact: When archaea were first recognized as a separate group, the only ones known were the methane-making methanogens.

questions.text: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn nitrogen gas from the air into which compound?
questions.fun_fact: Lightning can also fix nitrogen, with no living things involved.

questions.text: Which network of folded membranes in a cell helps make and transport proteins and lipids?
questions.fun_fact: Reticulum is Latin for 'little net'.

questions.text: Which type of cell, found in animals, plants and fungi, has a true nucleus?
questions.fun_fact: The oldest known eukaryote fossils may be from China's Ruyang Group, dated to about 1.8 to 1.6 billion years ago.

questions.text: Which type of microscope can show viruses, which are too small for light microscopes?
questions.fun_fact: Electron microscopes resolve about 0.1 nm, compared with about 200 nm for light microscopes.

questions.text: Which mesh-like polymer of sugars and amino acids strengthens bacterial cell walls?
questions.fun_fact: The peptidoglycan layer is much thicker in gram-positive bacteria (20 to 80 nm) than in gram-negative ones (7 to 8 nm).

questions.text: What is it called when a single bacterial cell divides into two cells?
questions.fun_fact: In E. coli, cells typically divide about every 20 minutes at 37 °C.

questions.text: Which part of a microscope do you put your eye to?
questions.fun_fact: On microscopes, eyepieces are usually interchangeable, letting users change the magnification.

questions.text: Which bacterium commonly lives in the human gut and is a standard laboratory organism?
questions.fun_fact: Some E. coli strains benefit their hosts by producing vitamin K2 in the gut.

questions.text: What is the protein coat that surrounds a virus's genetic material called?
questions.fun_fact: The visible 3D subunits of a capsid are called capsomeres.

questions.text: What do we call organisms that thrive in very salty places such as the Dead Sea?
questions.fun_fact: Some halophiles give off a red color from carotenoid compounds.

questions.text: Which heat treatment, named after a French scientist, makes milk keep longer by reducing microbes?
questions.fun_fact: Heating wine to preserve it was already known in China by AD 1117, centuries before Pasteur.

questions.text: What is the pressure of water pushing a plant cell's membrane against its wall called?
questions.fun_fact: When turgor pressure is low, the cell goes flaccid, which is why plant leaves and stalks wilt.

questions.text: Julius Petri, who gave the Petri dish its name, was an assistant to which German physician?
questions.fun_fact: Petri made the final changes to the dish in 1887, and it is now the most common type of culture plate.

questions.text: A cell membrane's basic structure is a double layer of which molecules?
questions.fun_fact: Their water-loving heads face outward, while the fatty-acid tails point toward the middle.

questions.text: What network of protein fibers gives a cell its shape and helps move its parts?
questions.fun_fact: Even bacteria and archaea have a cytoskeleton.

questions.text: What double membrane, dotted with pores, surrounds the nucleus of a cell?
questions.fun_fact: The gap between its inner and outer membranes is about 10 to 50 nm wide.

questions.text: What is programmed cell death, in which a cell neatly takes itself apart, called?
questions.fun_fact: The name, Greek for 'falling off', was suggested in 1972 by James Cormack, a professor of Greek at the University of Aberdeen.

questions.text: In photosynthesis, plants use light to turn carbon dioxide and water into oxygen and which sugar?
questions.fun_fact: Photosynthetic organisms convert around 100-115 billion tons of carbon into biomass every year.

questions.text: What is it called when cells use energy to move substances across a membrane against a concentration gradient?
questions.fun_fact: Jens Christian Skou won the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on the sodium-potassium pump.

questions.text: Which freshwater organism forms spherical colonies of up to 50,000 green algal cells?
questions.fun_fact: Volvox was first reported by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in 1700.

questions.text: Which small squid hosts glowing bacteria in a special light organ?
questions.fun_fact: The squid feeds its bacteria a solution of sugar and amino acids.

questions.text: Which microbiologist discovered chemoautotrophy, showing that microbes can live on inorganic chemicals?
questions.fun_fact: He is best known in school science for the Winogradsky column, a way to study sediment microbes.

questions.text: What do scientists call adding dye to cells so their parts stand out under a microscope?
questions.fun_fact: Staining is also used outside biology, for example to study the structure of some polymers.

questions.text: Bacteria swap DNA by conjugation through a tube-like structure. What is it called?
questions.fun_fact: The best-studied conjugative pilus is the F-pilus of E. coli, built from fibrous pilin proteins.

questions.text: The slime mold Physarum polycephalum can grow into one giant cell containing many what?
questions.fun_fact: Its bright yellow, network-shaped stage can grow to 30 cm (a foot) or more in diameter.

questions.text: Which organelle takes its name from the hydrogen peroxide it produces and breaks down?
questions.fun_fact: Christian de Duve and Pierre Baudhuin identified them as organelles in 1966; they were earlier known as microbodies.

questions.text: Spirulina, a food the Aztecs harvested from Lake Texcoco, is the dried biomass of which organisms?
questions.fun_fact: The Aztecs called it tecuitlatl, and one of Cortés' soldiers described it being sold as cakes.

questions.text: What is it called when bacteria coordinate their behavior by sensing how many of them are nearby?
questions.fun_fact: The term was introduced in 1994 by Fuqua, Winans and Greenberg.

questions.text: Which bacterium makes the carbon dioxide that forms the 'eyes' in Swiss-type cheeses?
questions.fun_fact: Its fermentation also makes propionate and acetate, which add nutty and sweet flavors to the cheese.

questions.text: What are the folds of a mitochondrion's inner membrane called?
questions.fun_fact: In typical liver mitochondria, the inner membrane has about five times the area of the outer membrane.

questions.text: Which bacterium is nicknamed 'Conan the Bacterium'?
questions.fun_fact: Guinness World Records listed it in 1998 as the most radiation-resistant bacterium.

questions.text: What is a batch of microbes deliberately grown in a lab on a nutrient medium called?
questions.fun_fact: Bacteriophages are grown by letting them infect a 'lawn' of bacteria spread across a plate.

questions.text: Which microscope sweeps an electron beam over a specimen to give a 3D-looking view of its surface?
questions.fun_fact: Manfred von Ardenne invented an early high-resolution scanning microscope in 1937.

questions.text: What name is given to live microbes in foods like yogurt that are eaten for possible gut benefits?
questions.fun_fact: The modern idea is generally credited to Russian Nobel laureate Élie Metchnikoff, around 1907.

questions.text: Which cylinder-shaped structures help organize the spindle when animal cells divide?
questions.fun_fact: Each centriole is made of nine sets of short microtubule triplets arranged in a cylinder.

questions.text: Which device sterilizes lab equipment and culture media with high-pressure steam?
questions.fun_fact: It was invented by Charles Chamberland in 1879; a typical cycle uses steam at 121 °C for at least 15 minutes.

questions.text: Which Scottish botanist gave the cell nucleus its name in 1831?
questions.fun_fact: He also observed the jittery motion of tiny particles that is now called Brownian motion.

questions.text: Which Dutch botanist was one of three scientists who rediscovered Mendel's work around 1900?
questions.fun_fact: In 1886 De Vries discovered new forms among evening primroses growing wild near Hilversum.

questions.text: In 1961 Nirenberg and Matthaei found that the RNA code UUU specifies which amino acid?
questions.fun_fact: Marshall Nirenberg shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for cracking the genetic code.

questions.text: In which English town was Charles Darwin born in 1809?
questions.fun_fact: He was the fifth of six children; his father Robert Darwin was a wealthy doctor and financier.

questions.text: Bird wings and insect wings do the same job but evolved separately. What are such structures called?
questions.fun_fact: Similarly, the wings of a sycamore maple seed and the wings of a bird are analogous, as they develop from quite different structures.

questions.text: Which biologist wrote the 1976 book 'The Selfish Gene'?
questions.fun_fact: Dawkins coined the word 'meme' in this book.

questions.text: Broccoli, kale, cabbage and cauliflower were all bred from which single wild plant?
questions.fun_fact: The same species also gave rise to Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi, through selection of different plant parts.

questions.text: Darwin's last book, from 1881, was about the soil-making work of which animals?
questions.fun_fact: It sold thousands of copies within weeks of its release in October 1881.

questions.text: Which organism became the first eukaryote to have its genome fully sequenced, in 1996?
questions.fun_fact: Baker's yeast has about 12 million base pairs of DNA spread over 16 chromosomes.

questions.text: The 1958 Meselson–Stahl experiment supported which model of DNA replication?
questions.fun_fact: They grew E. coli on heavy nitrogen-15 so that old and new DNA strands had different densities.

questions.text: What are the short DNA pieces made on the lagging strand during copying called?
questions.fun_fact: They are named after Reiji Okazaki and Tsuneko Okazaki, who found them in the 1960s.

questions.text: What term describes random shifts in the frequency of gene variants from one generation to the next?
questions.fun_fact: The Wright-Fisher model of genetic drift is named after Sewall Wright and Ronald Fisher.

questions.text: What is the term for a variant form of the same gene?
questions.fun_fact: The word 'allele' is short for 'allelomorph', from Greek words meaning 'other form'.

questions.text: Whales and dolphins belong to which class of vertebrates?
questions.fun_fact: Even the largest whales are warm-blooded and breathe air with lungs, so they must surface regularly.

questions.text: Neanderthals are named after a valley in which country, where the first recognized fossil was found in 1856?
questions.fun_fact: A local schoolteacher, Johann Carl Fuhlrott, recognized that the bones were distinct from modern humans.

questions.text: What was the name of Charles Darwin's paternal grandfather, who wrote about evolution in 'Zoonomia'?
questions.fun_fact: He was a founding member of the Lunar Society, a Birmingham group of thinkers and inventors.

questions.text: When red and white snapdragons are crossed and produce pink flowers, what is this called?
questions.fun_fact: Incomplete dominance is also called partial dominance or semi-dominance; the heterozygote's look is intermediate between the parents'.

questions.text: What is a trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment called?
questions.fun_fact: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace proposed that adaptation is explained by natural selection.

questions.text: Which German biologist cut the tails off mice for five generations to test whether acquired traits are inherited?
questions.fun_fact: No mouse was born without a tail; his germ plasm theory says inheritance passes only through egg and sperm cells.

questions.text: What is it called when humans choose which plants or animals breed to get wanted traits?
questions.fun_fact: Darwin bred pigeons himself and used the results of breeders as evidence for his theory.

questions.text: The Red Queen hypothesis, named for a character of Lewis Carroll, says species must constantly do what?
questions.fun_fact: The biologist Leigh Van Valen proposed the hypothesis in 1973.

questions.text: Which of these traits did Mendel study in his pea plants?
questions.fun_fact: Mendel tracked seven traits, including flower color, pod color and plant height.

questions.text: What is the term for the specific position of a gene on a chromosome?
questions.fun_fact: The plural of locus is loci, and an ordered list of loci in a genome is called a gene map.

questions.text: In biological classification, which rank sits between class and family?
questions.fun_fact: Some mammal classifications add extra ranks, called grandorder and mirorder, between superorder and order.

questions.text: Among the three main types of rock, in which are fossils most commonly found?
questions.fun_fact: These rocks form at temperatures and pressures that do not destroy the remains of living things.

questions.text: Identical twins develop from how many fertilized eggs?
questions.fun_fact: Their scientific name, monozygotic, means they come from one zygote that splits to form two embryos.

questions.text: In 1848 Wallace and Henry Walter Bates set out to collect specimens in which river basin?
questions.fun_fact: Wallace lost most of his specimens when the ship carrying them home caught fire in 1852.

questions.text: Mitochondrial DNA is normally passed down from which parent?
questions.fun_fact: Mitochondrial DNA is thought to come from the circular genomes of bacteria engulfed by early eukaryotic cells.

questions.text: Which German entomologist founded cladistics, classifying organisms by shared derived traits?
questions.fun_fact: His book 'Phylogenetic Systematics' was translated into English in 1966.

questions.text: Mendel's law of what states that different traits are inherited independently of one another?
questions.fun_fact: Many deviations from independent assortment occur because of genetic linkage.

questions.text: Darwin's finches of the Galápagos differ from each other mainly in the size and shape of which body part?
questions.fun_fact: The ornithologist John Gould, not Darwin, first realized the birds formed a new group of 12 species.

questions.text: What is the passing of genetic traits from parents to their offspring called?
questions.fun_fact: Biologists also call heredity 'biological inheritance'.

questions.text: Which enzyme, discovered in 1970 by Temin and Baltimore, builds DNA from an RNA template?
questions.fun_fact: Temin and Baltimore shared the 1975 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Renato Dulbecco.

questions.text: In 1969 Robert Whittaker proposed a system of how many kingdoms of life?
questions.fun_fact: Whittaker also designed a well-known diagram sorting biomes by temperature and rainfall.

questions.text: What kind of diagram shows the evolutionary relationships among species, with branches from common ancestors?
questions.fun_fact: Darwin included a diagrammatic evolutionary tree in his 1859 book On the Origin of Species.

questions.text: Which species was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, in 1998?
questions.fun_fact: The hermaphrodite worm's nervous system has exactly 302 neurons, and all their connections have been mapped.

questions.text: What is the technique called that uses the steady pace of DNA changes to estimate when species diverged?
questions.fun_fact: Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling introduced the idea in the early 1960s.

questions.text: What is a sharp drop in a population's size, which cuts its genetic diversity, called?
questions.fun_fact: Northern elephant seals fell to about 30 animals in the 1890s, and their genetic variation is still very low.

questions.text: Photo 51, a 1952 X-ray image of DNA, was taken by Raymond Gosling while working under which scientist?
questions.fun_fact: It got its name because it was the 51st diffraction photograph that Gosling had taken.

questions.text: Which scientist won Nobel Prizes in Chemistry for sequencing both a protein, insulin, and DNA?
questions.fun_fact: His 1977 chain-termination method was the main way to read DNA for decades.

questions.text: Wallace's 1858 essay on natural selection, sent to Darwin, is named after which Indonesian island?
questions.fun_fact: Darwin received the essay on 18 June 1858.

questions.text: Richard Lenski's long-running evolution experiment, begun in 1988, follows populations of which microbe?
questions.fun_fact: Between generations 31,000 and 31,500, one population evolved the ability to use citrate as food.

questions.text: In a famous Siberian breeding experiment started in 1959, which animal was bred for tameness?
questions.fun_fact: Many of the tamed foxes had floppy ears and short or curly tails.

questions.text: Which American geneticist won the 1946 Nobel Prize for showing that X-rays can cause mutations?
questions.fun_fact: Muller got hooked on fruit fly genetics through Thomas Hunt Morgan's famous 'fly lab'.

questions.text: What are the thread-like structures of DNA and protein in a cell's nucleus called?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from Greek words for 'color' and 'body', because chromosomes take up stains strongly.

questions.text: Which enzyme copies a gene's DNA sequence into messenger RNA?
questions.fun_fact: Roger Kornberg won the 2006 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for revealing how it works in detail.

questions.text: Cave-dwelling populations of the Mexican tetra, a small fish, have lost which body feature?
questions.fun_fact: Cave and surface forms of the Mexican tetra belong to the same species and can still interbreed.

questions.text: The 1952 Hershey–Chase experiments are nicknamed after which kitchen appliance used in them?
questions.fun_fact: They showed that a bacteriophage's DNA, not its protein coat, enters the bacteria it infects.

questions.text: When Mendel crossed two hybrid pea plants, dominant and recessive traits appeared in roughly what ratio?
questions.fun_fact: Between 1856 and 1863 Mendel grew and tested some 28,000 plants, most of them peas.

questions.text: The full title of Darwin's 1859 book says species originate 'by Means of' what?
questions.fun_fact: All editions of the book end with the word 'evolved'.

questions.text: Birds are the living descendants of which group of dinosaurs?
questions.fun_fact: Fossils of more than thirty non-avian dinosaur species with preserved feathers have been found.

questions.text: The Burgess Shale, famed for its Cambrian fossils, is found in which country?
questions.fun_fact: By 1924 Charles Walcott had collected over 65,000 specimens from the shale.

questions.text: In biological classification, which rank comes directly above species?
questions.fun_fact: The plural of genus is genera.

questions.text: About how many base pairs of DNA are in one complete set of human chromosomes?
questions.fun_fact: The Human Genome Project, begun in 1990, was an international effort to read the sequence of this DNA.

questions.text: What is the process called by which organisms with helpful inherited traits tend to leave more descendants?
questions.fun_fact: Darwin and Wallace first presented the idea of natural selection together in 1858.

questions.text: What is the rapid diversification of one ancestor into many species filling different niches called?
questions.fun_fact: Hawaiian honeycreepers form a highly diverse group of birds that began radiating early in Hawaii's history.

questions.text: What is the change in the inherited traits of populations over many generations called?
questions.fun_fact: Darwin first used the word 'evolution' only in the sixth edition of On the Origin of Species.

questions.text: Which principle says allele frequencies stay constant from generation to generation unless evolutionary forces act?
questions.fun_fact: Godfrey Hardy, an English mathematician, and Wilhelm Weinberg, a German physician, formulated it independently in 1908.

questions.text: Which biologist, nicknamed 'Darwin's Bulldog', defended evolution in public debates?
questions.fun_fact: His grandson Aldous Huxley wrote the novel 'Brave New World'.

questions.text: Alfred Russel Wallace spent eight years of the 1850s and 1860s collecting specimens in which region?
questions.fun_fact: His total of 125,660 specimens included more than 83,000 beetles.

questions.text: What is a scientist who studies genes, heredity and variation in living things called?
questions.fun_fact: Geneticists often run experiments on model organisms such as fruit flies, zebrafish and the worm C. elegans.

questions.text: Which small flowering weed, a favorite lab organism, was the first plant to have its genome sequenced?
questions.fun_fact: It grows from seed to seed in about six weeks and has a small genome, which makes it ideal for research.

questions.text: Which English surveyor used fossils to match rock layers and published a pioneering geological map of Britain in 1815?
questions.fun_fact: Simon Winchester's 2001 biography of Smith is titled 'The Map That Changed the World'.

questions.text: Which enzymes, used in genetic engineering, cut DNA at specific recognition sites?
questions.fun_fact: Werner Arber, Daniel Nathans and Hamilton Smith shared the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for them.

questions.text: During the Beagle voyage, Darwin worked out a theory of how which ring-shaped islands form?
questions.fun_fact: In 1896-1898 the Royal Society drilled on Funafuti atoll in Tuvalu to investigate how coral reefs form.

questions.text: What is it called when two species, such as a flower and its pollinator, evolve in response to each other?
questions.fun_fact: In 1964 Paul Ehrlich and Peter Raven described how butterflies and the plants they eat drive each other's evolution.

questions.text: Which 'master control' gene, shared by flies and mice, starts eye development in both?
questions.fun_fact: Mouse Pax6 can trigger eye development in fruit flies, though insect and vertebrate eyes look very different.

questions.text: Which family of genes controls the layout of body segments along the head-to-tail axis in animals?
questions.fun_fact: Mutations in Hox genes can make a fruit fly grow legs where its antennae should be.

questions.text: In biology, what does the abbreviation GMO stand for?
questions.fun_fact: The first genetically modified plant was produced in 1983.

questions.text: Which living reptiles are the closest relatives of birds?
questions.fun_fact: Birds and crocodilians both have four-chambered hearts.

questions.text: Who wrote the 1973 essay 'Nothing in Biology Makes Sense Except in the Light of Evolution'?
questions.fun_fact: The essay first appeared in the journal American Biology Teacher.

questions.text: Who was the captain of HMS Beagle during Darwin's famous voyage?
questions.fun_fact: FitzRoy later founded what became the Met Office and coined the term 'forecast' for his weather predictions.

questions.text: Which term describes new species forming when a geographic barrier splits a population?
questions.fun_fact: Moritz Wagner first proposed the idea of geographic speciation in 1868, calling it 'Separationstheorie'.

questions.text: What is the largest group of organisms in which any two can produce fertile offspring together?
questions.fun_fact: This is the biological species concept, one of several competing definitions of a species.

questions.text: What is a permanent change in the DNA sequence of an organism called?
questions.fun_fact: Mutagens such as UV rays and X-rays can increase the rate of mutation.

questions.text: Comparing matching DNA letter by letter, humans and chimpanzees are about how similar?
questions.fun_fact: Counting insertions, deletions and non-coding DNA as well, the difference grows to about 12.5% to 13.3%.

questions.text: Java Man, found by Eugène Dubois in 1891, belonged to which species?
questions.fun_fact: Dubois first called it Anthropopithecus erectus, then renamed it Pithecanthropus erectus.

questions.text: The Denisovans were first identified from a finger bone found in a cave in which mountain range?
questions.fun_fact: DNA from Denisovans is still found in some people of Oceania and Southeast Asia.

questions.text: Golden Rice was genetically engineered to make which pigment, which the body can turn into vitamin A?
questions.fun_fact: The rice was developed by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer.

questions.text: What is an organism that is a genetically identical copy of another called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Greek for 'twig' and was coined by Herbert J. Webber in 1903.

questions.text: Which Japanese geneticist proposed the neutral theory of molecular evolution in 1968?
questions.fun_fact: Kimura was a pioneer in using diffusion equations to model how gene variants spread in populations.

questions.text: Which British biologist introduced the idea of 'inclusive fitness' in his 1964 papers on social behavior?
questions.fun_fact: John Maynard Smith first used the term 'kin selection' in 1964.

questions.text: Which early human species, described in 1964, has a name meaning 'handy man'?
questions.fun_fact: It lived in East and South Africa from about 2.4 to 1.65 million years ago.

questions.text: Animals with a notochord at some stage of life, including all vertebrates, belong to which phylum?
questions.fun_fact: Sea squirts are chordates too, but they show the notochord only as tadpole-like larvae.

questions.text: A Punnett square is a diagram used to predict what?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the British geneticist Reginald Punnett, who devised it in the early 1900s.

questions.text: Humans, chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans are together known as which group?
questions.fun_fact: All great apes share a common ancestor that lived roughly 14 million years ago.

questions.text: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix at the start of copying?
questions.fun_fact: Helicases use energy from ATP to pull the two DNA strands apart.

questions.text: Around which proteins is DNA wrapped to form nucleosomes?
questions.fun_fact: Around 146 base pairs of DNA wrap 1.65 times around each histone core.

questions.text: Which nitrogen base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.fun_fact: Uracil is essentially thymine without a methyl group.

questions.text: DNA is read in triplets of its four bases. How many different triplets, or codons, are possible?
questions.fun_fact: Three of the 64 codons act as stop signals; the others code for the 20 standard amino acids.

questions.text: Which sugar forms the backbone of DNA together with phosphate groups?
questions.fun_fact: Deoxyribose has one fewer oxygen atom than ribose, the sugar found in RNA.

questions.text: Which scientist worked with James Watson to propose the double-helix model of DNA in 1953?
questions.fun_fact: Crick, Watson and Maurice Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the structure of DNA.

questions.text: Which physicist's 1944 book 'What Is Life?' inspired Watson and Crick to study genes?
questions.fun_fact: In the book Schrödinger discussed the idea of a complex molecule carrying the genetic code of living things.

questions.text: In the central dogma of molecular biology, information flows from DNA to RNA to which product?
questions.fun_fact: Reverse transcription, in which RNA is copied into DNA, is a known exception to the usual flow.

questions.text: The Olduvai Gorge, a famous site for early human fossils, is in which country?
questions.fun_fact: In 1959 Mary Leakey found a skull there nicknamed Zinjanthropus, now usually called Paranthropus boisei.

questions.text: What is the process by which a cell makes an exact copy of its DNA called?
questions.fun_fact: DNA replication is all-or-none: once it begins, it proceeds to completion.

questions.text: Bread wheat is hexaploid, meaning it carries how many sets of chromosomes?
questions.fun_fact: Four of bread wheat's six chromosome sets come from emmer wheat and two from the wild grass Aegilops tauschii.

questions.text: At which university did Watson and Crick work out the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953?
questions.fun_fact: They worked at its Cavendish Laboratory, which is the university's Department of Physics.

questions.text: The Miller–Urey experiment of 1952 produced which building blocks of proteins from simple gases and sparks?
questions.fun_fact: Stanley Miller carried out the experiment in Harold Urey's lab at the University of Chicago.

questions.text: What is the term for the formation of new species from existing ones?
questions.fun_fact: The term 'speciation' was coined by the American biologist Orator F. Cook in 1906.

questions.text: What is the offspring of two different species, such as a lion and a tiger, called?
questions.fun_fact: A liger, from a male lion and a tigress, grows much larger than either of its parents.

questions.text: Which organ pumps blood around the human body?
questions.fun_fact: In humans the heart is roughly the size of a closed fist and sits in the chest between the lungs.

questions.text: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood out to the whole body?
questions.fun_fact: The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right one because it must push blood around the whole body.

questions.text: What is the thick muscular middle layer of the heart wall called?
questions.fun_fact: The heart wall has three layers, and the whole heart is also enclosed in a protective double-membraned sac.

questions.text: Which cluster of cells in the right atrium acts as the heart's natural pacemaker?
questions.fun_fact: Martin Flack first spotted the node in a mole's heart; he and Arthur Keith published the discovery in 1907.

questions.text: Which arteries supply blood to the heart muscle itself?
questions.fun_fact: The word coronary comes from the Latin for crown, because these arteries encircle the heart like a crown.

questions.text: What produces the 'lub-dub' sound of a normal heartbeat?
questions.fun_fact: The first sound comes from the mitral and tricuspid valves closing, the second from the aortic and pulmonary valves.

questions.text: Which arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs?
questions.fun_fact: They are unusual because nearly all other arteries in the body carry oxygen-rich blood.

questions.text: Which large veins return blood from the body to the heart's right atrium?
questions.fun_fact: The superior vena cava drains the upper body and the inferior vena cava drains the lower body.

questions.text: Which pair of arteries running up the sides of the neck supplies the head and neck with blood?
questions.fun_fact: Each common carotid artery splits in the neck into an external branch and an internal branch that travels up into the skull.

questions.text: What do mature human red blood cells lack, which leaves more room for hemoglobin?
questions.fun_fact: Each human red blood cell contains about 270 million hemoglobin molecules.

questions.text: Which hormone, made mainly in the kidneys, tells bone marrow to make more red blood cells?
questions.fun_fact: Erythropoietin was purified in 1977 by Eugene Goldwasser and Ching Kung.

questions.text: About how much blood does an average adult body contain?
questions.fun_fact: Blood makes up roughly 7% of a person's body weight.

questions.text: The Rh blood group system is named after which animal?
questions.fun_fact: The human Rh factor later proved not to be identical to the rhesus monkey factor, but the name had already stuck.

questions.text: Which blood type is often called the 'universal donor' for red blood cells?
questions.fun_fact: People with type AB Rh-positive blood are called universal recipients for red cell transfusions.

questions.text: Which instrument is used to measure blood pressure?
questions.fun_fact: Italian physician Scipione Riva-Rocci introduced an easier-to-use version in 1896.

questions.text: Which Dutch physiologist built the first practical electrocardiograph and won a 1924 Nobel Prize?
questions.fun_fact: Einthoven gave the waves of the heartbeat trace the letters P, Q, R, S and T that are still used in ECG traces.

questions.text: Which clear fluid, drained from body tissues, travels through the lymphatic system?
questions.fun_fact: Unlike blood, lymph has no central pump; it moves as nearby muscles squeeze the vessels and one-way valves keep it flowing.

questions.text: The circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of which organ?
questions.fun_fact: It is a circulatory anastomosis, so its arteries link up and blood can reach the brain by more than one route.

questions.text: Which tiny hair-like structures in the airways sweep mucus and trapped dust toward the throat?
questions.fun_fact: This sweeping movement is known as the mucociliary escalator.

questions.text: The windpipe divides into two airways, one leading into each lung. What are they called?
questions.fun_fact: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left one.

questions.text: The Adam's apple is formed by cartilage of which organ?
questions.fun_fact: The vocal cords sit inside the larynx and vibrate as air passes over them to make sound.

questions.text: What is the medical name for a sneeze?
questions.fun_fact: People cannot sneeze while asleep, because reflex signals are not relayed during the muscle atonia of REM sleep.

questions.text: Which organs take in oxygen when you breathe in?
questions.fun_fact: The left lung is slightly smaller than the right to leave room for the heart.

questions.text: Which brain structure, deep in the temporal lobe, is crucial for forming new memories?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Greek for seahorse, which the curved structure was thought to resemble.

questions.text: Which lobe of the brain contains the primary visual cortex?
questions.fun_fact: The occipital lobe is the smallest of the four main lobes of the cerebral cortex and sits at the back of the head.

questions.text: Which lobe of the brain, behind the forehead, is linked to planning and decision-making?
questions.fun_fact: It is the largest of the four main lobes of the human brain.

questions.text: Which part of the brainstem controls automatic actions such as breathing and heart rate?
questions.fun_fact: The medulla oblongata sits at the base of the brain, where the brain joins the spinal cord.

questions.text: Which chemical messenger do motor neurons release to make skeletal muscles contract?
questions.fun_fact: Otto Loewi showed in 1921 that the vagus nerve releases a substance, later identified as acetylcholine, that slows the heart.

questions.text: Which clear fluid cushions the brain and spinal cord?
questions.fun_fact: The body makes about 500 mL a day, but only about 125 mL is present at any moment, so it is replaced several times daily.

questions.text: A doctor taps the tendon just below the kneecap to test which reflex?
questions.fun_fact: The knee-jerk is a stretch reflex that is handled by the spinal cord, without needing the brain.

questions.text: Which structure runs down the back inside the spine and carries messages between brain and body?
questions.fun_fact: In adults the spinal cord ends around the first or second lumbar vertebra, well above the base of the spine.

questions.text: Wernicke's area, named after a German neurologist, is mainly involved in what?
questions.fun_fact: Carl Wernicke described the area in 1874; in most people it lies in the left hemisphere.

questions.text: Which egg-shaped brain structure acts as a relay station for most sensory signals?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Greek word for a chamber or inner room.

questions.text: Which Montreal-based neurosurgeon mapped the brain's sensory and motor areas, creating the 'homunculus'?
questions.fun_fact: Penfield co-founded the Montreal Neurological Institute in 1934 and became its first director.

questions.text: Which network of neurons lining the gut is nicknamed the 'second brain'?
questions.fun_fact: It can run gut movements by itself, but it also exchanges signals with the brain through the vagus nerve.

questions.text: Luigi Galvani's frog-leg experiments in the 1780s suggested that muscles respond to what?
questions.fun_fact: Galvani called it animal electricity, and the words galvanize and galvanometer come from his name.

questions.text: Hodgkin and Huxley's Nobel-winning work on nerve impulses used the giant axon of which animal?
questions.fun_fact: The squid giant axon is up to 1.5 mm wide, large enough for researchers to slide electrodes inside it.

questions.text: Pacinian corpuscles, found deep in the skin, detect which kind of stimulus?
questions.fun_fact: Abraham Vater first reported them in 1741, but they are named after Filippo Pacini, who rediscovered them in 1835.

questions.text: What name is given to the body's roughly 24-hour internal clock?
questions.fun_fact: The term comes from the Latin circa, around, and dies, day.

questions.text: What does the 'R' in REM sleep stand for?
questions.fun_fact: In 1953 Nathaniel Kleitman and his student Eugene Aserinsky defined rapid eye movement sleep and linked it to dreaming.

questions.text: Which part of the eye changes shape to focus on near and far objects?
questions.fun_fact: Many fish focus differently: they move the lens closer to or farther from the retina instead of changing its shape.

questions.text: Which tough white outer layer of the eyeball is often called 'the white of the eye'?
questions.fun_fact: In children the sclera is thinner and shows some of the pigment beneath it, so it can look slightly blue.

questions.text: Which jelly-like substance fills the large chamber behind the eye's lens?
questions.fun_fact: It makes up about four-fifths of the volume of the eyeball.

questions.text: The malleus, incus and stapes are tiny bones in which part of the body?
questions.fun_fact: Malleus, incus and stapes are Latin for hammer, anvil and stirrup, which describe their shapes.

questions.text: What is the visible, outer part of the ear called?
questions.fun_fact: The pinna is also called the auricle; its folds help the brain work out where a sound is coming from.

questions.text: The stapedius, the smallest skeletal muscle in the body, is found in which organ?
questions.fun_fact: It tightens in response to loud sounds, reducing the vibration passed to the inner ear.

questions.text: Which small organ tucked under the liver stores bile?
questions.fun_fact: Bile released from the gallbladder helps with the digestion of fats in food.

questions.text: What is the name for the wave-like muscle contractions that push food through the digestive tract?
questions.fun_fact: Earthworms use a similar wave of muscle contractions to crawl along.

questions.text: Which enzyme in gastric juice begins breaking down proteins in the stomach?
questions.fun_fact: Pepsin was one of the first enzymes ever discovered; Theodor Schwann described it in 1836.

questions.text: What is the first section of the small intestine, just after the stomach, called?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Latin for twelve, because it is about twelve finger-widths long.

questions.text: Which muscular ring controls the flow of food from the stomach into the small intestine?
questions.fun_fact: Pylorus comes from the Greek for gatekeeper.

questions.text: What is the community of trillions of microbes living in the human gut called?
questions.fun_fact: Gut bacteria ferment fibers that people cannot digest, producing short-chain fatty acids.

questions.text: Which slippery substance coats the stomach lining and shields it from its own acid?
questions.fun_fact: In humans the gastric mucosa, the stomach's inner lining, is only about one millimeter thick.

questions.text: Which part of plant foods cannot be digested by humans but helps keep the gut moving?
questions.fun_fact: Fiber comes in soluble and insoluble forms; oats and beans are rich in the soluble kind.

questions.text: Which simple sugar is the main fuel carried in the blood to the body's cells?
questions.fun_fact: The brain relies mostly on glucose for its energy.

questions.text: About how many bones does a typical adult human skeleton have?
questions.fun_fact: A newborn has around 270 bones; some of them fuse together during growth.

questions.text: Per gram, which nutrient supplies the most food energy?
questions.fun_fact: Fat gives about 9 kcal per gram, more than twice the roughly 4 kcal from protein or carbohydrate.

questions.text: Which vitamin does the skin make when it is exposed to sunlight?
questions.fun_fact: The skin makes it when UVB light strikes a cholesterol-related molecule in the skin.

questions.text: Which vitamin is essential for normal blood clotting?
questions.fun_fact: The K comes from the Danish word koagulation, meaning coagulation.

questions.text: Which vitamin is also known as ascorbic acid?
questions.fun_fact: Most animals make their own vitamin C, but humans and other higher primates, guinea pigs and most bats must get it from food.

questions.text: The body converts beta-carotene, the orange pigment in carrots, into which vitamin?
questions.fun_fact: Heinrich Wackenroder first isolated carotene from carrot juice and published it in 1831.

questions.text: Which mineral, plentiful in dairy foods, is the main mineral in bones?
questions.fun_fact: Roughly 99% of the calcium in the human body is in bone mineral, from which it can be released into the blood when needed.

questions.text: Which substance makes up the largest share of an adult's body weight?
questions.fun_fact: By weight the average adult is about 60% water, while a newborn baby can be as much as 75% water.

questions.text: What is the anatomical name for the breastbone?
questions.fun_fact: The upper ribs attach to the sternum through bars of costal cartilage.

questions.text: What is the anatomical name for the shoulder blade?
questions.fun_fact: The scapula is a triangular flat bone that connects the upper arm bone with the collarbone.

questions.text: Which tough bands of tissue connect one bone to another at a joint?
questions.fun_fact: Ligaments are viscoelastic: they strain gradually under tension and return to their original shape when it is removed.

questions.text: Bending of the elbow is done mainly by which type of joint?
questions.fun_fact: The knee is the largest hinge joint in the human body, although it also allows a little rotation.

questions.text: Which fluid lubricates the joints and feeds their cartilage?
questions.fun_fact: Its name probably comes from the Latin ovum, egg, because the fluid looks and feels a little like raw egg white.

questions.text: Which slender bone runs alongside the tibia in the lower leg?
questions.fun_fact: Fibula is Latin for a clasp or brooch; the bone carries almost none of the body's weight.

questions.text: Which triangular bone at the base of the spine is formed from fused vertebrae?
questions.fun_fact: Its five sacral vertebrae fuse together between the ages of about 18 and 30.

questions.text: Which bone cells break down old bone tissue?
questions.fun_fact: Osteoclasts are unusually large cells with many nuclei, formed when several cells fuse together.

questions.text: Which type of muscle is found only in the heart?
questions.fun_fact: Cardiac muscle cells are joined by intercalated discs, which let the whole heart contract in a coordinated way.

questions.text: Which broad back muscle, nicknamed the 'lats', pulls the arm down and back?
questions.fun_fact: Its Latin name means the broadest muscle of the back.

questions.text: Which facial muscle pulls up the corners of the mouth when you smile?
questions.fun_fact: It runs from the cheekbone, called the zygomatic bone, to the corner of the mouth.

questions.text: Which small muscles between the ribs help raise and lower the rib cage as you breathe?
questions.fun_fact: The intercostal muscles come in three layers: external, internal and innermost.

questions.text: Which protein is the most abundant in the bodies of humans and other mammals?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Greek kolla, glue, because animal skin and sinews were boiled to make glue.

questions.text: Which muscle at the front of the upper arm bends the elbow?
questions.fun_fact: Biceps is Latin for two-headed, because the muscle has two points of origin at the shoulder blade.

questions.text: Which organ is the largest in the human body by weight?
questions.fun_fact: Skin makes up roughly 16% of a person's body mass.

questions.text: Which layer of the skin lies directly beneath the epidermis?
questions.fun_fact: The dermis contains hair follicles, sweat glands, blood vessels and nerve endings.

questions.text: Which oily substance do the skin's sebaceous glands produce?
questions.fun_fact: Sebum is Latin for fat or tallow.

questions.text: What is the soft inner core of a tooth, containing nerves and blood vessels, called?
questions.fun_fact: Teeth are not made of bone; they are built from several tissues of differing hardness, including enamel, dentin and pulp.

questions.text: How many teeth are in a full set of children's baby teeth?
questions.fun_fact: Teething typically begins around the age of six months, and the last baby teeth usually come in by 25 to 33 months.

questions.text: Which pointed teeth, between the incisors and premolars, are used for tearing food?
questions.fun_fact: The upper canines have the longest roots of any human teeth.

questions.text: What is the small fleshy flap hanging at the back of the soft palate called?
questions.fun_fact: Uvula comes from the Latin for little grape.

questions.text: The heart, blood and blood vessels together make up which body system?
questions.fun_fact: In vertebrates the circulatory system is closed, which means blood never leaves the network of vessels.

questions.text: Which type of cell can develop into many other kinds of cells?
questions.fun_fact: Bone marrow holds stem cells that give rise to every type of blood cell.

questions.text: Which part of the skeleton houses and protects the brain?
questions.fun_fact: The bones of the skull are joined by immovable fibrous joints called sutures.

questions.text: A typical human body cell nucleus holds how many chromosomes?
questions.fun_fact: Other great apes have 24 pairs, but human chromosome 2 is the result of two ancestral chromosomes fusing end to end.

questions.text: Which tiny organelles in human cells break down worn-out cell parts using digestive enzymes?
questions.fun_fact: Lysosomes were discovered in the 1950s by Christian de Duve, who later won a Nobel Prize for the work.

questions.text: Which cells in the pancreas make insulin?
questions.fun_fact: Beta cells sit in clusters called the islets of Langerhans.

questions.text: Which hormone, released by the adrenal glands, is known as the 'stress hormone'?
questions.fun_fact: Cortisol levels follow a daily rhythm, rising in the early morning and falling during the day.

questions.text: Which hormone from the pancreas prompts the liver to release stored glucose into the blood?
questions.fun_fact: Glucagon and insulin act in opposite ways to keep blood sugar levels steady.

questions.text: Which tube carries urine from each kidney to the bladder?
questions.fun_fact: An adult ureter is typically 20 to 30 centimeters long and only 3 to 4 millimeters wide.

questions.text: Which Y-shaped proteins made by immune cells bind to specific invaders such as germs?
questions.fun_fact: Antibodies are made by plasma cells, which develop from B cells.

questions.text: Which Canadian physician, with Charles Best, helped discover insulin in 1921?
questions.fun_fact: Banting shared his 1923 Nobel Prize money with Best, who had not been named by the Nobel committee.

questions.text: Which Italian scientist was the first to see capillaries, in 1661?
questions.fun_fact: He saw them in a frog's lungs, revealing the link between arteries and veins that had eluded William Harvey.

questions.text: Which two British physiologists discovered the hormone secretin in 1902?
questions.fun_fact: Secretin is made by S cells in the lining of the duodenum and prompts the pancreas to release bicarbonate.

questions.text: Which American physiologist coined the term 'fight or flight' and developed the theory of homeostasis?
questions.fun_fact: Cannon also used X-rays to watch how food moves through the digestive tracts of animals.

questions.text: The hamstrings are a group of muscles at the back of which part of the body?
questions.fun_fact: There are three hamstring muscles: the semimembranosus, the semitendinosus and the biceps femoris.

questions.text: Which Greek physician of the Roman Empire wrote anatomy texts used in Europe for over a thousand years?
questions.fun_fact: Galen was born in Pergamon, in present-day Turkey, and served as personal physician to several Roman emperors.

questions.text: In temperate climates, a tree trunk usually adds one of what each year, which can be counted to estimate its age?
questions.fun_fact: Leonardo da Vinci is the first person known to have noted that trees form rings annually and that ring thickness reflects growing conditions.

questions.text: Which part of a flower is its male organ, which produces pollen?
questions.fun_fact: A stamen has an anther, where pollen develops, carried on a stalk called the filament.

questions.text: Which structures let dandelion seeds drift on the wind for long distances?
questions.fun_fact: Each dandelion seed is a single-seeded fruit called a cypsela, attached to a pappus of fine hair-like material.

questions.text: Which mushroom, with a bright red cap dotted with white warts, is a classic image in fairy tales and video games?
questions.fun_fact: Its name in many European languages is thought to come from its old use as an insecticide, sprinkled in milk to kill flies.

questions.text: The name of which common lawn flower is thought to come from 'day's eye', because its head closes at night and opens in the morning?
questions.fun_fact: Geoffrey Chaucer called the daisy the 'eye of the day'.

questions.text: Wine bottle corks are cut from the bark of which tree?
questions.fun_fact: Once a cork oak is about 25 years old, its bark can be harvested every 9 to 12 years without harming the tree.

questions.text: Which common plant is covered in hollow hairs that inject a stinging mix of chemicals when brushed against?
questions.fun_fact: The tips of its stinging hairs break off when touched, turning each hair into a tiny needle.

questions.text: Which African tree with a huge swollen trunk is nicknamed the 'upside-down tree'?
questions.fun_fact: Baobabs are native to mainland Africa, Madagascar and Australia, and are among the longest-lived vascular plants.

questions.text: Which Japanese art involves growing and shaping miniature trees in containers?
questions.fun_fact: Bonsai literally means 'pot planting'; similar arts include China's penjing and Korea's bunjae.

questions.text: What is the Japanese custom of gathering to enjoy cherry blossoms called?
questions.fun_fact: Japan's weather agency issues a yearly 'cherry blossom front' forecast, since the blossoms last only a week or two.

questions.text: The glossy brown seeds called conkers grow inside spiky green cases on which tree?
questions.fun_fact: The scars its leaves leave on twigs have a distinctive horseshoe shape, complete with seven 'nails'.

questions.text: Which single-celled fungus makes bread dough rise by producing gas?
questions.fun_fact: Baker's yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the same species used in brewing, though a different strain.

questions.text: Mushrooms spread by releasing microscopic what from the gills under their caps?
questions.fun_fact: Leaving a cap gill-side down overnight makes a spore print, whose color helps identify the mushroom.

questions.text: Which plant, nicknamed the 'shy plant', folds its leaflets inward when touched?
questions.fun_fact: Its leaflets re-open a few minutes later; it is a classic example of rapid plant movement.

questions.text: What is a plant called that completes its life cycle, from seed to seed, in a single growing season?
questions.fun_fact: Only about 6% of all plant species, and 15% of herbaceous plants, are annuals.

questions.text: What is growing plants in water-based nutrient solutions, with no soil, called?
questions.fun_fact: German botanists Julius von Sachs and Wilhelm Knop developed soilless cultivation between 1859 and 1875.

questions.text: Which botanic garden in Richmond, London, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003?
questions.fun_fact: Kew also runs a second garden, Wakehurst in Sussex, which is home to the Millennium Seed Bank.

questions.text: Which carnivorous plant has hinged leaf lobes that snap shut on insects?
questions.fun_fact: Its trap shuts only if trigger hairs are touched twice within about 20 seconds, which helps it ignore raindrops.

questions.text: What are trees called that keep green foliage all year round, such as most pines?
questions.fun_fact: Individual evergreen leaves last from a few months to decades; bristlecone pine needles can stay on for up to 45 years.

questions.text: What is the process called when a seed begins to sprout and grow?
questions.fun_fact: Some seeds that need winter cold are held dormant until they take in water in the fall and experience cooler temperatures.

questions.text: Which tree is known for white, papery bark that peels away in thin sheets?
questions.fun_fact: Birch bark is marked with long horizontal lenticels and often separates into thin, papery plates, especially on the paper birch.

questions.text: From which plant do we get the soft fibers spun into thread for denim jeans?
questions.fun_fact: Cotton fiber grows in a protective case called a boll around the seeds.

questions.text: Which green plants unfurl their young leaves from tightly coiled 'fiddleheads'?
questions.fun_fact: Ferns have neither seeds nor flowers, and they spend part of their life cycle as a tiny, short-lived gametophyte.

questions.text: The needles of a pine tree are what kind of plant organ?
questions.fun_fact: A waxy covering on conifer needles helps the tree minimize water loss.

questions.text: Bees, butterflies, birds and bats that carry pollen between flowers are collectively called what?
questions.fun_fact: Farms close to natural habitat tend to have higher crop yields because more pollinators visit them.

questions.text: Which colorful flower parts are often shaped or colored to attract pollinators?
questions.fun_fact: All the petals of one flower together are called the corolla.

questions.text: Most eucalyptus species are native to which country?
questions.fun_fact: The genus has more than 700 species, and every Australian state and territory has native eucalypts.

questions.text: Which tall plant with a big yellow flower head is grown for oil and edible seeds?
questions.fun_fact: Young sunflower buds track the sun across the sky, but mature heads point in a fixed, typically easterly direction.

questions.text: Which flowerless plants form soft green cushions on damp rocks and tree trunks?
questions.fun_fact: Mosses anchor themselves with threadlike rhizoids, which resemble root hairs rather than true roots.

questions.text: Which prickly plant stores water in a thick, fleshy stem to survive in deserts?
questions.fun_fact: Most cacti have lost true leaves, keeping only spines, and their enlarged stems carry out the photosynthesis.

questions.text: Which plant tissue carries sugars made in the leaves to the rest of the plant?
questions.fun_fact: Mature phloem sieve tube cells lack a nucleus and rely on neighboring companion cells for most of their metabolic needs.

questions.text: Which usually green flower parts protect the bud before it opens?
questions.fun_fact: All the sepals of a flower together are called the calyx.

questions.text: Which pigments give autumn leaves their yellow and orange colors once green chlorophyll fades?
questions.fun_fact: The yellow was there all along, masked by chlorophyll in summer; the reds come from anthocyanins gained as autumn sets in.

questions.text: Plants like grasses and lilies, whose seeds contain a single embryonic leaf, are called what?
questions.fun_fact: The single seed leaf is only one of several features of monocots, and it is not completely reliable for telling plant groups apart.

questions.text: Which carbohydrate is the main structural component of plant cell walls?
questions.fun_fact: The cellulose content of cotton fiber is about 90%.

questions.text: Apart from a single exception, cacti are native to which part of the world?
questions.fun_fact: The exception, Rhipsalis baccifera, is also found in Africa and Sri Lanka.

questions.text: Though it looks like a tree, a banana plant is botanically classified as what?
questions.fun_fact: What looks like a trunk is a pseudostem made of tightly packed leaf stalks growing from an underground corm.

questions.text: Which giant grass includes species reported to grow about 91 centimeters in a single day?
questions.fun_fact: Bamboo's fast growth depends on a unique rhizome-dependent system.

questions.text: Tulips reached northern Europe in the 1500s through diplomats who visited the court of which empire?
questions.fun_fact: The word tulip may come, via Ottoman Turkish, from a Persian word for turban.

questions.text: Natural rubber latex comes mainly from which tree, native to the Amazon basin?
questions.fun_fact: Hevea brasiliensis belongs to the spurge family and is now grown across the tropics.

questions.text: Where does the archaeological record suggest wheat was first cultivated, around 9600 BC?
questions.fun_fact: Well-known wheat species and hybrids include common wheat, spelt, durum, emmer, einkorn and Khorasan wheat.

questions.text: The stem fibers of which plant are woven into linen cloth?
questions.fun_fact: Flax seeds are called linseed, and the oil pressed from them is linseed oil.

questions.text: The Joshua tree of the Mojave Desert belongs to which plant genus?
questions.fun_fact: Its flowers are pollinated by the yucca moth, which spreads pollen while laying its eggs inside the flower.

questions.text: Botanically, the potato we eat is an underground storage structure derived from which plant part?
questions.fun_fact: The 'eyes' on a potato are arranged in a spiral and hold the buds from which new stems grow.

questions.text: What are the slim, dangling flower clusters of birch and willow trees called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from Middle Dutch katteken, meaning 'kitten', perhaps because long catkins resemble a kitten's tail.

questions.text: Which tree, the sole surviving species of its order, has fan-shaped leaves and is called a 'living fossil'?
questions.fun_fact: Its order, Ginkgoales, first appeared in the Permian, about 270 million years ago.

questions.text: The Wollemi pine, discovered in 1994 in a remote gorge, grows wild in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was found about 150 km north-west of Sydney, in Wollemi National Park in New South Wales.

questions.text: The monkey puzzle tree is Chile's national tree. In which neighboring country does it also grow wild?
questions.fun_fact: Its nearest living relative, Araucaria angustifolia, grows in Brazil and northeastern Argentina.

questions.text: Which fig tree grows aerial prop roots that thicken into extra trunks?
questions.fun_fact: Older banyans' aerial roots can become indistinguishable from the original trunk, as in the Great Banyan of Kolkata.

questions.text: Which tropical tree, grown mostly in Ecuador, gives the very light wood used in model aircraft?
questions.fun_fact: Balsa is classified as a hardwood even though its wood is the softest commercial hardwood.

questions.text: What is the red-orange fruit that forms on a rose after its flowers are pollinated?
questions.fun_fact: The hairs inside rose hips are irritating, and have been used as itching powder.

questions.text: Which carnivorous plants trap insects on stalked glands covered in glistening drops of mucilage?
questions.fun_fact: The name Drosera comes from Greek for 'dew'; sundews grow wild on every continent except Antarctica.

questions.text: What is the network of thread-like hyphae that forms the main body of most fungi called?
questions.fun_fact: A fungus secretes enzymes onto its food through the hyphae, then absorbs the broken-down nutrients.

questions.text: What tough material forms the cell walls of fungi?
questions.fun_fact: Chitin also forms the exoskeletons of arthropods such as insects and crustaceans.

questions.text: Genetically, fungi are more closely related to which group than to plants?
questions.fun_fact: Like animals, fungi are heterotrophs: they absorb food after digesting it outside their bodies.

questions.text: What is the partnership between fungal threads and plant roots, trading minerals for sugars, called?
questions.fun_fact: The fungus supplies minerals such as phosphorus, nitrogen or zinc, and the plant supplies sugars or lipids made by photosynthesis.

questions.text: Which edible spring fungus is known for a honeycomb-like pitted cap?
questions.fun_fact: Morels are sac fungi, close relatives of the anatomically simpler cup fungi.

questions.text: Which prized fungus grows underground near tree roots and was historically hunted with pigs?
questions.fun_fact: Truffles fruit underground, so wind cannot spread their spores; they depend on animals that eat them.

questions.text: Reindeer moss, a key food for caribou, is actually what kind of organism?
questions.fun_fact: It is extremely cold-hardy and grows mainly in areas of alpine tundra.

questions.text: Beatrix Potter, creator of Peter Rabbit, was also respected for her scientific paintings of what?
questions.fun_fact: Her interest in fungi deepened after she met the naturalist and amateur mycologist Charles McIntosh.

questions.text: Which East Asian vine, also called Japanese arrowroot, is invasive across the southeastern United States?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Japanese kuzu, and it belongs to the pea family.

questions.text: Which green, berry-bearing plant lives as a hemiparasite on the branches of host trees?
questions.fun_fact: Mistletoes attach through a structure called the haustorium, which draws water and nutrients from the host.

questions.text: A fig is a hollow structure lined with many tiny what, which fig wasps pollinate?
questions.fun_fact: More than 600 fig species have figs holding three types of flowers: male, short female and long female.

questions.text: Grasses and conifers rely mainly on which natural force to carry their pollen?
questions.fun_fact: Wind-pollinated plants such as grasses often have very small petals, or none at all.

questions.text: Which American agronomist developed high-yield semi-dwarf wheat in Mexico, helping launch the Green Revolution?
questions.fun_fact: Mexico became a net exporter of wheat by 1963, and yields in Pakistan and India nearly doubled between 1965 and 1970.

questions.text: Which southern African succulents, nicknamed 'living stones', are camouflaged to look like pebbles?
questions.fun_fact: Their leaves are mostly buried in the soil, with a translucent 'window' on top that lets light in for photosynthesis.

questions.text: Which Scottish plant collector introduced the Sitka spruce, sugar pine and ponderosa pine into British cultivation?
questions.fun_fact: He also gave his name to the Douglas fir, which he introduced into cultivation in 1827.

questions.text: Which Kenyan founded the Green Belt Movement, which focuses on planting trees?
questions.fun_fact: She encouraged women across Kenya to run tree nurseries, using seeds of native trees found in nearby forests.

questions.text: Which technique joins a cutting of one plant onto the rooted base of another so they grow together?
questions.fun_fact: The upper part of the joined plant is called the scion and the lower part is the rootstock.

questions.text: After fertilization, the ovule of a flowering plant matures into what?
questions.fun_fact: The ovule's outer layers, the integuments, develop into the seed coat.

questions.text: Which pairs of cells surround stomata and open or close the pore by changing how swollen they are?
questions.fun_fact: The pores are widest when water is plentiful and the guard cells are turgid, and closed when water is critically scarce.

questions.text: What is the embryonic root called, the first part of a seedling to emerge from a germinating seed?
questions.fun_fact: Together with the hypocotyl, the radicle forms the embryonic axis of the seed.
