questions.fun_fact: Silver is found in Earth's crust in a pure, free form known as native silver.

questions.text: Nitrogen's old French name, azote, comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: The name nitrogen was suggested in 1790, after the gas was found in nitric acid and nitrates.

questions.text: Which element, named in 1997, honors a scientist who was still alive at the time?
questions.fun_fact: Oganesson, element 118, was later also named after a living scientist, Yuri Oganessian.

questions.text: What is the largest number of electrons the first electron shell can hold?
questions.fun_fact: In general, the nth electron shell can hold up to 2n squared electrons.

questions.text: Which element, named in 2016, was the first named by a team of Asian physicists?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from Nihon, a common Japanese name for Japan.

questions.text: Which element did Clemens Winkler name after his homeland in 1886?
questions.fun_fact: Mendeleev had predicted this element years earlier and called it ekasilicon.

questions.text: Brass is an alloy of copper and which other metal?
questions.fun_fact: Changing the mix of copper and zinc changes brass's color and its mechanical, electrical, acoustic and chemical properties.

questions.text: In alchemy, which planet was linked with the metal lead?
questions.fun_fact: Gold was always linked with the Sun and silver with the Moon.

questions.text: Cerium, found in 1803, is named after which object discovered in 1801?
questions.fun_fact: Cerium was the first of the lanthanides to be discovered, at Bastnäs in Sweden.

questions.text: Which Greek philosopher from Sicily originated the theory of four classical elements?
questions.fun_fact: Empedocles proposed forces called Love and Strife that mix and separate the elements.

questions.text: Baking powder mixes a bicarbonate and a weak acid with a drying agent that stops them reacting early. Which drying agent is usual?
questions.fun_fact: Double-acting baking powder releases some gas when it gets wet and more when it is heated, which gives the batter a second rise in the oven.

questions.text: Lemon juice and vinegar both taste sour. What kind of substances are they?
questions.fun_fact: The word acid comes from the Latin acidus, meaning 'sour', and acidic solutions turn blue litmus paper red.

questions.text: Which natural gelling agent found in fruit makes jam set?
questions.fun_fact: Apples, quinces and citrus fruits are rich in pectin, and commercial pectin comes mainly from dried citrus peel and apple pomace.

questions.text: Which kitchen liquid is often brushed on cut apples to slow their browning?
questions.fun_fact: Browning is driven by the enzyme polyphenol oxidase, and acids such as citric acid and ascorbic acid slow it down.

questions.text: Which stretchy protein network gives bread dough its chewy structure?
questions.fun_fact: Kneading builds more gluten cross-links, while fat shortening blocks them, which keeps pie crust tender and flaky.

questions.text: Which natural sugar, found in honey and fruit, is the sweetest of all naturally occurring sugars?
questions.fun_fact: Fructose tastes roughly twice as sweet as glucose and is the most water-soluble of all the sugars.

questions.text: Which artificial sweetener was discovered in 1879 when a chemist noticed that his hand tasted sweet?
questions.fun_fact: Saccharin is about 500 times sweeter than sucrose but can leave a bitter or metallic aftertaste.

questions.text: Making margarine involves adding which gas to liquid vegetable oils so that they turn solid or soft?
questions.fun_fact: Raney nickel, a spongy nickel catalyst, was developed by Murray Raney in 1926 specifically for hydrogenating vegetable oils.

questions.text: Which plant compounds make strong tea and red wine feel dry and puckery in the mouth?
questions.fun_fact: The word tannin comes from the French term for crushed oak bark, which people used to tan animal hides into leather.

questions.text: Cream of tartar, used to stabilize whipped egg whites, is a salt of which acid found in grapes?
questions.fun_fact: Its crude form, called tartar or wine stone, is a by-product of winemaking that is deposited on must barrels.

questions.text: Gelatin, used in gummy candy and marshmallows, is made by partly breaking down which protein?
questions.fun_fact: A recipe for jelled meat broth, an early gelatin dish, appears in Le Viandier, written in or around 1375.

questions.text: Which family of proteins makes up about 80% of the protein in cow's milk?
questions.fun_fact: Casein paint, a fast-drying water-soluble medium, has been used by artists since ancient Egyptian times as a form of tempera.

questions.text: Crushing garlic triggers an enzyme that makes which sulfur compound, giving fresh garlic its aroma?
questions.fun_fact: Allicin is not present in intact garlic: the enzyme alliinase makes it from alliin only when the garlic's tissue is damaged.

questions.text: Which compound gives cinnamon its flavor and smell?
questions.fun_fact: French chemists Dumas and Péligot isolated it from cinnamon oil in 1834, and Luigi Chiozza first made it in the lab in 1854.

questions.text: Which compound gives orange peel its scent and is used in citrus-scented cleaners?
questions.fun_fact: Limonene dissolves oils, so it is used as an adhesive remover and degreaser, and it comes as a by-product of making orange juice.

questions.text: Safety matches ignite only when struck on a special strip. Which substance in that strip makes this work?
questions.fun_fact: Swedish inventor Gustaf Erik Pasch developed the separate striking surface in 1844 and patented the use of red phosphorus in it.

questions.text: Which compound gives tonic water its bitter taste and makes it glow under ultraviolet light?
questions.fun_fact: Quinine in tonic water even fluoresces visibly in direct sunlight against a dark background, but the glow stops once the UV source is removed.

questions.text: Which yellow pigment gives turmeric its color?
questions.fun_fact: Curcumin was named in 1815 when Vogel and Pelletier isolated a yellow coloring matter from turmeric rhizomes. It is food additive E100.

questions.text: Which red pigment gives tomatoes and watermelons their color?
questions.fun_fact: Processed tomato products such as tomato juice, sauce and ketchup contain more bioavailable lycopene than raw tomatoes.

questions.text: Disposable hand warmers make heat as which metal powder reacts with air and rusts?
questions.fun_fact: Air-activated hand warmers get their heat from the exothermic oxidation of iron, and salt is usually added to speed up the process.

questions.text: Which compound is known as washing soda?
questions.fun_fact: Soda ash is dissolved in water and crystallized to make washing soda, which is used to lower the hardness of water.

questions.text: What is the main active ingredient of household chlorine bleach?
questions.fun_fact: Household bleach is a 3-8% solution of sodium hypochlorite, with a little sodium hydroxide added to slow its breakdown.

questions.text: In nature, baking soda occurs almost exclusively as nahcolite or as part of which other, more common mineral?
questions.fun_fact: Baking soda has a slightly salty, alkaline taste that resembles the taste of washing soda.

questions.text: What name is given to compounds such as soap that lower the surface tension of water?
questions.fun_fact: Surfactants also work as wetting, foaming and emulsifying agents in products from paints to fabric softeners.

questions.text: One end of a soap molecule is attracted to water. What is the other end attracted to?
questions.fun_fact: Soap molecules form tiny spheres called micelles, which trap grease in a fat-loving core so that water can rinse it away.

questions.text: Dry ice, used to keep things very cold, is the solid form of which gas?
questions.fun_fact: At normal air pressure dry ice has no liquid state: it turns straight into gas, which is why it is used in theater fog machines.

questions.text: Which type of enzyme in laundry detergent breaks down protein stains such as egg, milk and grass?
questions.fun_fact: Enzymes were first used in laundry in 1913, but only became mainstream after heat-stable bacterial enzymes became available.

questions.text: Laundry brighteners absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit which color of light to make white clothes look whiter?
questions.fun_fact: The extra blue light offsets the yellow or brown tint of old fabric and paper, shifting its hue toward white.

questions.text: Which highly porous form of carbon is used in water filters to trap contaminants?
questions.fun_fact: Activated carbon has a surface area of over 3,000 square meters per gram, thanks to its microscopic pores.

questions.text: Which element is added to many public water supplies to kill germs?
questions.fun_fact: The first continuous use of chlorine to disinfect US drinking water began in 1908 at Boonton Reservoir, which supplied Jersey City.

questions.text: Which kitchen item, resting in a hot salty or baking soda bath with silverware, can reverse tarnish?
questions.fun_fact: The method reverses tarnish electrochemically instead of scrubbing it off, so no silver is removed.

questions.text: What is the thin green layer that forms on weathered copper roofs and statues called?
questions.fun_fact: The green patina on copper and bronze is sometimes called verdigris.

questions.text: What are the small silica gel packets found in shoe boxes and food packaging meant to absorb?
questions.fun_fact: Silica gel has a specific surface area of about 750 to 800 square meters per gram, which lets it absorb water readily.

questions.text: What is water with lots of dissolved calcium and magnesium, which makes soap lather poorly, called?
questions.fun_fact: In hard water, soap forms a white precipitate called soap scum instead of lather, and the same minerals build limescale in kettles.

questions.text: Epsom salt, sold for bath salts, is which compound?
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from a bitter saline spring in Epsom, Surrey, England, where the salt was first produced.

questions.text: Which super-absorbent polymer, able to hold hundreds of times its mass in water, fills disposable diapers?
questions.fun_fact: It can absorb 100 to 1,000 times its mass in water, and it is also used in hair gels and soaps.

questions.text: Which solvent, also called propanone, is the main ingredient in many nail polish removers?
questions.fun_fact: Acetone mixes completely with water and is also used as a solvent in paint thinner.

questions.text: Which gas, easily turned into a liquid under slight pressure, fuels most disposable lighters?
questions.fun_fact: Butane is also used as a propellant in aerosol sprays and as a feedstock for making petrochemicals by steam cracking.

questions.text: Which element, usually added in the form of fluoride, is the most common active ingredient in toothpaste?
questions.fun_fact: Fluoride was first added to toothpastes in the 1890s.

questions.text: Tooth enamel is made mostly of which mineral?
questions.fun_fact: Enamel is about 96% mineral, and fluoride can turn part of it into fluorapatite, which resists acid attack much better.

questions.text: Which white zinc compound is used in sunscreens to block UVA and UVB rays?
questions.fun_fact: Between 50% and 60% of all zinc oxide goes into the rubber industry, not into sunscreen.

questions.text: Which white compound is the most widely used pigment in white paint?
questions.fun_fact: It is used in about two-thirds of all pigments, and as a food coloring it carries the E number E171.

questions.text: In perfume, the fragrance oils are usually dissolved in which liquid?
questions.fun_fact: Eau de parfum holds 15-20% aromatic compounds, eau de toilette 5-15% and eau de cologne only 2-3%.

questions.text: Which sweet, syrupy compound, a by-product of soap-making, is used as a humectant in skin care?
questions.fun_fact: Splitting fats with sodium hydroxide gives soap plus glycerol, which is also used as a sweetener and may help preserve foods.

questions.text: Which glittering mineral is added to eye shadow and lipstick for shimmer?
questions.fun_fact: Mica powder also decorates Japanese woodblock prints, where it sparkles on wet ink in a technique called kirazuri.

questions.text: Tempered glass, used in car side windows and shower doors, is safer because of how it breaks. How does it shatter?
questions.fun_fact: Tempered glass is about four times stronger than ordinary annealed glass, because rapid cooling puts its outer surfaces under compression.

questions.text: Petroleum jelly, sold as Vaseline, was first refined from a waxy residue found on what?
questions.fun_fact: Chemist Robert Chesebrough took the drillers' 'rod wax' to his lab and found that distilling off lighter oils left a light-colored gel.

questions.text: Which red dye, used in lipstick and food, is made from crushed cochineal insects?
questions.fun_fact: About 70,000 cochineal insects are needed to make roughly half a kilogram of red dye.

questions.text: Which red-orange dye in the leaves of the henna plant stains skin and hair?
questions.fun_fact: Henna extracts have been used as hair and skin dye for more than 5,000 years, and lawsone is also found in common walnuts.

questions.text: Which blue dye is traditionally used to color denim jeans?
questions.fun_fact: A pair of blue jeans needs only about 3 to 12 grams of indigo dye.

questions.text: Flameless ration heaters warm military meals when water reacts with a powder of which metal, mixed with iron and salt?
questions.fun_fact: Development of the flameless ration heater began in 1973 at the US Army's Natick research center in Massachusetts.

questions.text: Which wax, now mostly made from petroleum and first created in Germany in 1830, became a cheap, clean-burning candle material?
questions.fun_fact: Dyed paraffin wax can be made into crayons, and paraffin candles burned more cleanly and reliably than the tallow candles they replaced.

questions.text: Which plastic, made from fermented plant starch such as corn, is used in compostable cups and packaging?
questions.fun_fact: PLA is mainly used for short-lived disposable packaging, and it can be biodegradable or long-lasting depending on how it is made.

questions.text: Which compound, found in sand, makes up about 70% of ordinary window and bottle glass?
questions.fun_fact: Obsidian is a natural volcanic glass, rich in silica, that forms when lava cools rapidly.

questions.text: Borosilicate laboratory glass resists sudden temperature changes because it has very low what?
questions.fun_fact: It is about 80% silica and 13% boric oxide, and it can withstand temperature differences of about 166 degrees Celsius without fracturing.

questions.text: Adding tiny amounts of which precious metal gives ruby or cranberry glass its red color?
questions.fun_fact: Cranberry glass is costly to make in bulk, so it is usually hand-blown; the gold is first dissolved in aqua regia to make gold chloride.

questions.text: Which metal's compounds have been used since antiquity to give glass and porcelain a deep blue color?
questions.fun_fact: Smalt, a blue pigment made by grinding cobalt-containing glass, was the main cobalt pigment before cobalt blue was developed.

questions.text: Which common rock is heated with clay in a kiln to make Portland cement?
questions.fun_fact: Joseph Aspdin patented it in 1824 and named it for its resemblance to pale Portland stone from Dorset, England.

questions.text: What liquid reacts with cement to make it harden into concrete?
questions.fun_fact: Hardening is a chemical reaction called hydration, not drying, so concrete can even be placed and cured underwater.

questions.text: Most clear plastic soft-drink bottles are made from which plastic?
questions.fun_fact: Recycled PET, called rPET, is used to make new bottles, clothing fibers, carpets and strapping.

questions.text: What does PVC, the plastic used for drain pipes, stand for?
questions.fun_fact: About half of all PVC made worldwide goes into pipes, and it is the third most widely produced plastic after polyethylene and polypropylene.

questions.text: Foam takeout boxes and cups are usually made from expanded which plastic?
questions.fun_fact: Polystyrene foams are 95-98% air, and the Koppers Company developed expanded polystyrene in 1954 under the name Dylite.

questions.text: Which common clothing fiber is a close chemical relative of the plastic in soda bottles?
questions.fun_fact: Polyester is also used to make sails (Dacron), tarpaulins, canoes and insulating tapes.

questions.text: Silicones are polymers whose backbone is a chain of alternating silicon atoms and atoms of which other element?
questions.fun_fact: English chemist Frederic Kipping coined the word silicone in 1901, by analogy with the formula of ketones.

questions.text: Which clear, shatter-resistant plastic, sold as Plexiglas, is often used instead of glass?
questions.fun_fact: Otto Röhm trademarked the name Plexiglas in 1933, after trying to make safety glass by polymerizing a liquid between two sheets of glass.

questions.text: LEGO bricks are molded from which plastic?
questions.fun_fact: ABS replaced cellulose acetate for LEGO bricks in 1963, and the plastic is heated to about 232 degrees Celsius before molding.

questions.text: Which stretchy fiber, invented in 1958 at DuPont, is used in leggings and swimwear?
questions.fun_fact: The name spandex is an anagram of 'expands', and it is the preferred name in North America.

questions.text: Which clay, also called china clay, is a key ingredient of fine porcelain?
questions.fun_fact: The word kaolin comes from Gaoling, meaning 'High Ridge', a village near Jingdezhen in China.

questions.text: Plaster of Paris is made by heating which mineral?
questions.fun_fact: It is named for a large gypsum deposit at Montmartre in Paris, and it sets into a hard mass when water is added.

questions.text: When you cook an egg white, its proteins unfold and clump together in a process called what?
questions.fun_fact: Ceviche 'cooks' raw fish without heat: an acidic citrus marinade denatures its proteins.

questions.text: Sterling silver is 92.5% silver, with the rest usually being which metal?
questions.fun_fact: Pure silver is too soft for most uses, so it is alloyed with copper to increase its hardness and strength.

questions.text: Which gas, stored as a liquid in pressurized tanks, is a popular fuel for barbecues and portable stoves?
questions.fun_fact: Propane was found dissolved in Pennsylvanian light crude oil by Edmund Ronalds in 1864.

questions.text: Pencil 'lead' is made mostly of graphite mixed with which binder?
questions.fun_fact: In 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté found that changing the graphite-to-clay ratio changes the hardness; less clay gives a softer core.

questions.text: Which black powder, made by burning oil or gas with little air, reinforces rubber in car tires?
questions.fun_fact: About 70% of all carbon black goes into tires, where it also conducts heat away from the tread and extends tire life.

questions.text: Which fiber, also called viscose, is made from regenerated cellulose, such as wood pulp?
questions.fun_fact: Rayon is called semi-synthetic: it is made from natural cellulose and has the same molecular structure as cellulose.

questions.text: Which metal powder forms the negative electrode of an ordinary alkaline AA battery?
questions.fun_fact: Compared with zinc-carbon batteries, alkaline batteries have a higher energy density and a longer shelf life at the same voltage.

questions.text: Which Canadian engineer invented the modern alkaline dry battery in the 1950s?
questions.fun_fact: Urry, Karl Kordesch and P. A. Marsal filed the US patent for the alkaline battery in October 1957, and it was granted in 1960.

questions.text: Which form of carbon is the usual material of the negative electrode in a lithium-ion battery?
questions.fun_fact: Lithium ions rock back and forth between the electrodes, so these cells are also called rocking-chair batteries.

questions.text: Which old photographic process, using iron salts and sunlight, produced the blue of blueprints?
questions.fun_fact: Anna Atkins used cyanotypes in her 1843-61 albums of British algae, effectively the first photographically illustrated books.

questions.text: Which chemist rediscovered cyanoacrylates in 1951 while working at Eastman Kodak, leading to super glue?
questions.fun_fact: Cyanoacrylate rapidly polymerizes in the presence of water, forming long, strong chains that join the bonded surfaces together.

questions.text: Hydrangea flowers can bloom blue in acidic soil because the plant takes up which metal?
questions.fun_fact: Soil with a pH of 5.5 or lower gives blue flowers, 6.5 or higher gives pink, and in between gives purple.

questions.text: Eyeglass lenses that darken in sunlight were first made of glass containing which silver compounds?
questions.fun_fact: These silver-based lenses became largely obsolete after photochromic organic compounds were introduced.

questions.text: In 1789 Claude Berthollet made a bleaching liquid at the Quai de Javel in Paris. By what French name is it known?
questions.fun_fact: He made the liquid by passing a gas through a solution of potash lye, and it was a weak solution of a hypochlorite salt.

questions.text: Which red dye, originally from madder roots, was the first natural dye ever made synthetically?
questions.fun_fact: Madder has been grown as a dye plant since antiquity in central Asia and Egypt, as early as 1500 BC.

questions.text: In 1934 Arnold Beckman was asked for a quick acidity test for the juice of which fruit, leading to the pH meter?
questions.fun_fact: Beckman registered the first patent for a complete pH measuring instrument in October 1934.

questions.text: On the pH scale, what is ocean water usually?
questions.fun_fact: Seawater pH typically stays between 7.5 and 8.4, and oceanographers use three different pH scales for it.

questions.text: Clean, unpolluted rain is slightly acidic because it contains dissolved molecules of which gas?
questions.fun_fact: Nitrogen oxides, which can make rain more acidic, are also produced naturally by lightning strikes.

questions.text: Spreading salt on icy roads works because of which effect?
questions.fun_fact: The same effect is used in ice cream makers and in car antifreeze made with ethylene or propylene glycol.

questions.text: Which of these is a mixture rather than a pure substance?
questions.fun_fact: Air can be described as a gaseous solution: oxygen and other gases dissolved in nitrogen, its major component.

questions.text: Which gas is used to fill party balloons so that they float?
questions.fun_fact: Helium is a non-flammable lifting gas, and sound travels nearly three times faster through it than through air.

questions.text: Which French scientist made the decisive discovery that bacteria are what turn alcohol into vinegar?
questions.fun_fact: A long fermentation can produce a slimy 'mother of vinegar', made of acetic acid bacteria and their cellulose biofilm.

questions.text: Which company's scientists invented neoprene, the synthetic rubber of wetsuits, in 1930?
questions.fun_fact: Wallace Carothers of DuPont took over commercial development after the company bought the patent rights from the University of Notre Dame.

questions.text: Smartphone cover glass is strengthened by swapping sodium ions for larger ions of which element?
questions.fun_fact: Steven Kistler developed the sodium-for-potassium ion exchange in 1962; the glass sits in a molten potassium-salt bath at about 400 degrees Celsius.

questions.text: Window glass is made by floating molten glass on a bath of which molten metal?
questions.fun_fact: The float process was developed in the 1950s by Sir Alastair Pilkington and Kenneth Bickerstaff at St Helens, England.

questions.text: Medieval iron gall ink was made from iron salts and tannins taken from which plant growths?
questions.fun_fact: Fermenting the gall extract releases gallic acid, which gives a darker purple-black ink as iron gallate forms.

questions.text: Which sulfur-containing gas, along with nitrogen oxides, is a main cause of acid rain?
questions.fun_fact: Acid rain forms when these gases react with water in the atmosphere to make sulfuric and nitric acids.

questions.text: Which of these is a chemical change rather than a physical change?
questions.fun_fact: Burning is a redox reaction between a fuel and an oxidant, usually oxygen from the air, that gives out heat.

questions.text: Which food component turns blue-black when iodine solution is added to it?
questions.fun_fact: The iodine-starch test was first described in 1814 by Colin and Gaultier de Claubry, and independently by Friedrich Stromeyer.

questions.text: Which type of glass accounts for around 90% of all manufactured glass?
questions.fun_fact: Glass density ranges from 2.2 grams per cubic centimeter for fused silica to 7.2 for dense flint glass.

questions.text: In the resin identification code on plastic items, which plastic is marked with the number 2?
questions.fun_fact: The Society of the Plastics Industry introduced the numbered triangle symbols in 1988; the number shows the resin, not that it is recyclable.

questions.text: Which French scribe, named in the first Harry Potter book, is said in legend to have made the philosopher's stone?
questions.fun_fact: The real Flamel lived in Paris in the 14th and 15th centuries; legends of his alchemy first appeared in the 17th century.

questions.text: Glauber's salt, named for a 17th-century alchemist, is which sodium compound?
questions.fun_fact: Johann Glauber called it sal mirabilis, 'wonderful salt', and its discovery in 1625 brought him fame.

questions.text: Which Flemish chemist introduced the word 'gas' into the vocabulary of science in the 1600s?
questions.fun_fact: He is also remembered for a five-year experiment in which he grew a willow tree.

questions.text: Which Swiss alchemist is probably the first to have given the element zinc its modern name, around 1526?
questions.fun_fact: The name likely comes from German 'zinke', meaning pointed, after the sharp look of zinc crystals.

questions.text: Alchemists dreamed of turning base metals such as lead into gold. What is such a change of one element into another called?
questions.fun_fact: Modern science says it is impossible by chemical means but possible by physical means, using nuclear reactions.

questions.text: Which woman, a perfumer in ancient Assur named on a tablet of about 1200 BC, is called one of the first recorded chemists?
questions.fun_fact: She used flowers, oil and calamus, and distilled and filtered the mixture several times.

questions.text: The word 'atom' comes from an ancient Greek word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Leucippus and his pupil Democritus developed the idea of atoms in the 5th century BC.

questions.text: What does 'aqua regia', the acid mixture that can dissolve gold, mean in Latin?
questions.fun_fact: Alchemists named it so because it can dissolve the noble metals gold and platinum, though not all metals.

questions.text: Which Dutch-born scientist won the 1936 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on dipole moments and X-ray diffraction in gases?
questions.fun_fact: He later moved to the United States and taught at Cornell University.

questions.text: Alchemists dreamed of an 'elixir of life'. What was it supposed to give the person who drank it?
questions.fun_fact: In the European tradition the elixir is closely linked to the creation of the philosopher's stone.

questions.text: Western alchemy is traced back to Hellenistic Egypt. Which city was its center of alchemical knowledge?
questions.fun_fact: The city kept its pre-eminence in alchemy through most of the Greek and Roman periods.

questions.text: In ancient Greek thought, matter was made of earth, air, fire and which fourth element?
questions.fun_fact: Aristotle added a fifth element, aether, to explain the unchanging heavens.

questions.text: Alchemists used an alembic, a still made of two vessels joined by a tube, for which process?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from Arabic al-inbiq, which in turn comes from Greek ambix, meaning 'cup' or 'beaker'.

questions.text: Which ancient pigment, made from silica, lime, copper and an alkali, is considered the first synthetic pigment?
questions.fun_fact: It was used in ancient Egypt for thousands of years.

questions.text: Which gas did Scottish chemist Joseph Black call 'fixed air'?
questions.fun_fact: Black is also known for discovering magnesium and latent heat.

questions.text: Which French chemist was the first to demonstrate the bleaching action of chlorine gas?
questions.fun_fact: He was also the first to develop a solution of sodium hypochlorite as a modern bleaching agent.

questions.text: Which German chemist won the 1910 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for pioneering work on alicyclic compounds?
questions.fun_fact: Much of his work studied terpenes, the fragrant compounds in essential oils.

questions.text: Which French chemist announced the law of combining volumes of gases in 1808?
questions.fun_fact: In 1804 he rose to 7,016 meters in a hydrogen balloon to study the atmosphere.

questions.text: In which German city was the first international conference of chemists held, in 1860?
questions.fun_fact: It was organized by August Kekulé and is known for helping to settle atomic weights.

questions.text: Which British chemist's 1794 'Essay on Combustion' described the idea of catalysis?
questions.fun_fact: She also discovered photoreduction and has been called the first solo woman researcher of modern chemistry.

questions.text: Which woman wrote 'Conversations on Chemistry', published anonymously in 1805?
questions.fun_fact: The book summarized the lectures of Humphry Davy and was one of the first elementary science textbooks.

questions.text: Which Frenchwoman wrote 'La Chymie charitable et facile, en faveur des dames', a chemistry treatise for women?
questions.fun_fact: Scholars argue it was the first chemistry or alchemy work written by a woman.

questions.text: Which deep blue pigment, probably first made in Berlin around 1706, is considered the first modern synthetic pigment?
questions.fun_fact: It was probably made by accident, when blood-tainted potash was used to make a red cochineal dye.

questions.text: Which Berlin chemist announced in 1747 that beets contain sugar and devised a way to extract it?
questions.fun_fact: His student Franz Achard later devised an economical industrial method to extract the sugar.

questions.text: Which English chemist discovered the elements iridium and osmium in 1803?
questions.fun_fact: He also helped to prove that diamond and charcoal are the same substance.

questions.text: Which German-Swiss chemist discovered ozone while experimenting with the electrolysis of water?
questions.fun_fact: He also invented the fuel cell, at the same time as William Robert Grove.

questions.text: Which French chemist first showed molecular chirality, using crystals of tartaric acid salts?
questions.fun_fact: It was also the first explanation of isomerism; he is better known for pasteurization.

questions.text: Which German professor at Giessen is called the 'father of the fertilizer industry'?
questions.fun_fact: He devised the modern laboratory-oriented teaching method for chemistry.

questions.text: Which English metallurgist created the first man-made plastic, shown at London's 1862 International Exhibition?
questions.fun_fact: He set up The Parkesine Company in 1866 to make his material.

questions.text: Celluloid, an early plastic, was long used to make what kind of film?
questions.fun_fact: American John Wesley Hyatt began working on it in the 1860s, hoping to replace ivory in billiard balls.

questions.text: Which Swedish chemist became the first Swede to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, in 1903?
questions.fun_fact: He was the first to use physical chemistry to estimate how rising carbon dioxide would warm Earth's surface.

questions.text: Which American chemist, known for the electron-pair idea of the covalent bond, gave his name to dot structures?
questions.fun_fact: He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 41 times but never won it.

questions.text: Which Swiss chemist won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and was the first inorganic chemist to do so?
questions.fun_fact: He was the only inorganic chemist to win the prize before 1973.

questions.text: Which French geologist arranged the elements by atomic weight on a spiral around a cylinder in 1862?
questions.fun_fact: He called it the telluric helix, because tellurium sat in the middle of his graph.

questions.text: Which chemist became the first woman admitted to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology?
questions.fun_fact: She was also the first American woman to earn a degree in chemistry, from Vassar College in 1870.

questions.text: In which German city was the chemical company BASF founded in 1865?
questions.fun_fact: BASF began as a dye maker; its name means Baden Aniline and Soda Factory.

questions.text: Which American chemical industrialist founded the Dow Chemical Company?

questions.text: Which Spanish archipelago has two joint capitals, Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria?

questions.text: The lilangeni, introduced in 1974 at par with the rand, is the currency of which country?

questions.fun_fact: The CFP franc was first issued in three separate forms for French Polynesia, New Caledonia and the New Hebrides.

questions.text: In which year did Australia replace the pound with the dollar?

questions.text: Which nickname is sometimes used for the New Zealand dollar in currency trading?

questions.text: In which year did New Zealand switch from the pound to the dollar?

questions.text: Governor Macquarie made the 'holey dollar' for New South Wales by punching the centers out of which coins?

questions.text: Mauritius was historically dependent on which crop?

questions.text: Which spice is sold as 'Bourbon' or 'Madagascar' type, after the Indian Ocean islands where it is grown?

questions.text: Which crop is the main agricultural product grown in Fiji?
questions.fun_fact: Fiji also grows coconuts, ginger, cassava, bananas, rice and pineapples.

questions.text: In the 1800s Lesotho supplied South African mining camps with grain and mohair, the hair of which animal?
questions.fun_fact: By the early 20th century Lesotho had become a net food importer and a labor reserve for South African mines.

questions.text: By the early 1870s New Zealand had about 10 million of which farm animal?
questions.fun_fact: Wool became the first staple export, initially shipped from the Wellington settlement in the late 1850s.

questions.text: In which year did Australia's goods and services tax come into effect?
questions.fun_fact: It replaced the federal wholesale sales tax and was meant to phase out state taxes such as stamp duty.

questions.text: Which Central American country uses the quetzal, named after a colorful bird, as its currency?
questions.fun_fact: The bird that gave the currency its name also appears on the flag of Guatemala.

questions.text: The lempira is the currency of which Central American country?
questions.fun_fact: Lempira was a 16th-century Lenca leader, renowned in Honduran folklore for leading resistance against Spanish forces.

questions.text: Nicaragua's currency, the córdoba, is named after which Spanish conquistador?
questions.fun_fact: Córdoba is credited as founder of Nicaragua and of the cities of León and Granada.

questions.text: Panama's currency is named after which Spanish explorer who crossed the isthmus in 1513?
questions.fun_fact: The balboa replaced the Colombian peso in 1904 and is tied to the US dollar, which is also legal tender in Panama.

questions.text: Which Chilean city became a major stopover for ships rounding Cape Horn in the 1800s?
questions.fun_fact: Valparaíso also gained importance supplying the California gold rush of 1848 to 1858.

questions.text: Peru's currency, the sol, shares its name with the Spanish word for what?
questions.fun_fact: The name actually comes from the Latin solidus; an earlier sol circulated from 1863 to 1985.

questions.text: The guaraní, named after an Indigenous people, is the currency of which South American country?
questions.fun_fact: The guaraní replaced the peso fuerte; the first guaraní notes and coins were issued in 1944.

questions.text: The gourde is the currency of which Caribbean country?
questions.fun_fact: The first gourde was introduced in 1813 and replaced the French livre.

questions.text: Which bird appears on Canada's one-dollar coin?
questions.fun_fact: The coin's nickname led Canadians to call the later two-dollar coin the toonie.

questions.text: In which year was the Canadian Pacific Railway's transcontinental line completed?
questions.fun_fact: The railway was a promise made to British Columbia when it joined Canada in 1871.

questions.text: The Grand Banks off Newfoundland were long famous as a rich fishing ground for which fish?
questions.fun_fact: The Canadian Grand Banks fishery was closed in 1992 after Atlantic cod collapsed.

questions.text: Ford's 1913 moving assembly line was developed to mass-produce which famous car?
questions.fun_fact: Ford cut production time for a car from about 12 and a half hours to 93 minutes by 1914.

questions.text: Which US farming region, centered on Iowa and Illinois, is famed for growing maize?
questions.fun_fact: Since the 1850s the region has dominated corn production in the United States.

questions.text: Which company was founded in 1939 in a Palo Alto garage now called the 'Birthplace of Silicon Valley'?
questions.fun_fact: Its first big contract supplied audio oscillators for Walt Disney's animated film Fantasia.

questions.text: The California gold rush began in 1848 when gold was found at which sawmill?
questions.fun_fact: The mill later became part of Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park in Coloma.

questions.text: Levi Strauss sold supplies to miners from which city, where his jeans company was based?
questions.fun_fact: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented riveted work trousers in 1873.

questions.text: The 1901 Spindletop gusher near which Texas city began the Texas oil boom?
questions.fun_fact: The Spindletop gusher blew for nine days at an estimated 100,000 barrels of oil per day.

questions.text: In which US state did Edwin Drake drill his 1859 oil well at Titusville?
questions.fun_fact: Drake bought a steam engine to ram the drill through the soil down to bedrock.

questions.text: In which city did John D. Rockefeller found Standard Oil in 1870?
questions.fun_fact: In 1911 the US Supreme Court found Standard Oil guilty of anticompetitive practices and ordered it broken up.

questions.text: Founded in 1848, the Chicago Board of Trade became the main marketplace for trading which goods?
questions.fun_fact: Its Art Deco tower is topped by a 9.5 m (31-foot) statue of Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain.

questions.text: What is the name of Argentina's currency?
questions.fun_fact: The peso introduced in 1992 replaced the austral at a rate of 10,000 to one.

questions.text: Ships in the Panama Canal are lifted by locks up to which artificial lake?
questions.fun_fact: When it was created in 1913, Gatún Lake was the largest man-made lake in the world.

questions.text: In which year did the North American Free Trade Agreement take effect?
questions.fun_fact: NAFTA linked the United States, Canada and Mexico into one of the world's largest free trade areas.

questions.text: In 2020, NAFTA was replaced by which trade agreement?
questions.fun_fact: Canada calls it CUSMA, and Mexico calls it T-MEC.

questions.text: Mercosur, the South American trade bloc founded in 1991, began with Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and which country?
questions.fun_fact: A second agreement, the Protocol of Ouro Preto, followed in 1994.

questions.text: The 1973 Treaty of Chaguaramas, which created CARICOM, was signed in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The treaty took effect on August 1, 1973.

questions.text: Juan Valdez is the advertising mascot of which Colombian product?
questions.fun_fact: The character has appeared in the federation's ads since 1958, representing a Colombian farmer.

questions.text: Cuba's economy was long highly dependent on exports of which crop?
questions.fun_fact: In the 19th century Cuba's sugar and tobacco exports made it one of the most prosperous countries in Latin America.

questions.text: Chiquita Brands descends from which company that dominated the Central American banana trade?
questions.fun_fact: The company was formed in 1899 by merging the Boston Fruit Company with Minor C. Keith's banana-trading businesses.

questions.text: Spanish silver dollars minted in Mexico and Peru were widely known by what nickname?
questions.fun_fact: Spanish dollars were legal tender in the United States until 1857.

questions.text: Which state-owned company, founded in 1938, is Mexico's national oil company?
questions.fun_fact: The 1938 nationalization of private oil companies made Pemex an enduring symbol of Mexican nationalism.

questions.text: The town of Tequila, famous for the spirit named after it, is in which Mexican state?
questions.fun_fact: The town and its surrounding agave fields were declared a World Heritage Site.

questions.text: Mexican border-area factories that assemble goods for export are known by what name?
questions.fun_fact: The program grew out of the Border Industrialization Program, which began in 1965.

questions.text: Brazil's 1994 Plano Real was designed mainly to end which economic problem?
questions.fun_fact: A temporary unit of value, the URV, was set at about one US dollar to break the cycle of daily price adjustments.

questions.text: The Bovespa, now part of B3, is the stock exchange of which Brazilian city?
questions.fun_fact: Bovespa was founded in 1890, and B3 was created in 2017 through a merger.

questions.text: The country Brazil is named after brazilwood, a tree prized by early traders as a source of what?
questions.fun_fact: Brazilwood is also the premier wood for making bows for stringed instruments.

questions.text: Argentina's vast grassland plains, the Pampas, are historically famous for raising which animals?
questions.fun_fact: The Pampas are also used for farming honey with European honeybees.

questions.text: In the 1800s, Chile's Atacama Desert was a major source of which fertilizer mineral?
questions.fun_fact: Two old nitrate works, Humberstone and Santa Laura, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.

questions.text: Simón Patiño, nicknamed 'The Andean Rockefeller', made his fortune from the tin mines of which country?
questions.fun_fact: In 1900 Patiño found a very rich tin vein, later called 'La Salvadora' (The Savior).

questions.text: Colombia is world-famous for exporting which green gemstone?
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's rare 'trapiche' emeralds are marked by ray-like spokes of dark impurities.

questions.text: The Museo del Oro, which holds thousands of pre-Hispanic gold objects, is in which city?
questions.fun_fact: Its displays include tumbaga, an alloy of gold and copper used in pre-Columbian times.

questions.text: Venezuela's main oil-producing area lies around which large lake?
questions.fun_fact: The lake is fed by many rivers, the biggest being the Catatumbo.

questions.text: Fishmeal, a major Peruvian export, is made mainly from which small fish?
questions.fun_fact: Since about 2005 more anchoveta has been eaten directly, fresh, canned or as salted fillets.

questions.text: The industrial landscape of Fray Bentos in Uruguay was built around making which product?
questions.fun_fact: The Liebig meat-extract plant opened in 1863 and closed in 1979.

questions.text: Brazil and Paraguay share the Itaipu hydroelectric dam on which river?
questions.fun_fact: Itaipu is named after a nearby island whose Guarani name refers to a 'sounding stone'.

questions.text: Jamaica has long been a major exporter of which aluminum ore?
questions.fun_fact: By the late 1960s Jamaica was producing about 21 percent of the world's bauxite output.

questions.text: George Eastman founded Kodak, maker of the Brownie camera, in which New York city?
questions.fun_fact: The first Kodak camera came loaded with a 100-exposure roll and was mailed to Rochester for processing.

questions.text: Which Caribbean territory, with its capital at George Town, is a well-known offshore financial center?
questions.fun_fact: Offshore finance mushroomed from the 1970s, while tourism had begun to flourish in the 1950s.

questions.text: The Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, which issues the Eastern Caribbean dollar, is based on which island?
questions.fun_fact: The bank was set up in 1983, succeeding the Eastern Caribbean Currency Authority.

questions.text: The National Theatre in San José, opened in 1897, was financed by taxes on exports of which crop?
questions.fun_fact: The theatre's front features statues of the playwright Calderón de la Barca and the composer Beethoven.

questions.text: The coat of arms of Belize shows woodcutters' tools and which tree, once vital to its economy?
questions.fun_fact: Its wreath of 50 leaves symbolizes 1950, when Belizeans began the struggle for independence.

questions.text: The Colón Free Trade Zone, a huge duty-free trading area, sits at which end of the Panama Canal?
questions.fun_fact: The zone started operations in 1948 and covers about 2.4 square kilometers.

questions.text: Which plant-based blue dye was El Salvador's most important crop in colonial times?
questions.fun_fact: Natural indigo was replaced by synthetic dyes in the late 19th century.

questions.text: Which dye, made from a tiny insect that lives on prickly pear cacti, became an important colonial export?
questions.fun_fact: Its dye, carmine, is still used as a colorant in food and lipstick.

questions.text: Hollywood, famous for the film industry, is a neighborhood of which US city?
questions.fun_fact: Hollywood was an independent municipality from 1903 until it consolidated with its neighbor in 1910.

questions.text: When Argentina launched its new currency in 1992, it was valued at one unit of which foreign currency?
questions.fun_fact: That one-to-one rate was maintained until early 2002.

questions.text: In which Canadian city is the Bank of Canada headquartered?
questions.fun_fact: Before the Bank of Canada existed, the Bank of Montreal acted as the government's banker.

questions.text: Where was the first United States Mint established in 1792?
questions.fun_fact: The Mint makes coins, while the Bureau of Engraving and Printing prints paper currency.

questions.text: The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, connected the Hudson River with which Great Lake?
questions.fun_fact: The canal gave New York City a strong advantage over all other US ports.

questions.text: The first US transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869 at which Utah location?
questions.fun_fact: A ceremonial gold 'Last Spike' was tapped with a silver hammer at Promontory Summit.

questions.text: From which country did the United States buy the Louisiana Territory in 1803?
questions.fun_fact: The $15 million deal roughly doubled the size of the United States.

questions.text: Under the 1862 Homestead Act, a settler could claim how many acres of public land?
questions.fun_fact: Homesteading ended in the lower 48 states in 1976 and in Alaska in 1986.

questions.text: In which state did Sam Walton open the first Walmart in 1962?
questions.fun_fact: The first store opened in Rogers; Walton's earlier five-and-dime in nearby Bentonville is now the Walmart Museum.

questions.text: In which state did the McDonald brothers open their first restaurant in 1940?
questions.fun_fact: The Golden Arches design was introduced in 1953.

questions.text: Boeing was founded in 1916 in which US city?
questions.fun_fact: William Boeing was a lumber industrialist before he founded the company.

questions.text: Joseph-Armand Bombardier, whose most famous invention was a snowmobile, founded his company in which province?
questions.fun_fact: Bombardier was born in Valcourt, Quebec, and opened his own garage there at age 19.

questions.text: Sudbury, Ontario, is famous for mining which metal?
questions.fun_fact: Before mining dominated, Sudbury was also a major lumber center.

questions.text: The St. Lawrence Seaway, opened in 1959, lets ocean ships sail from the Atlantic into which lakes?
questions.fun_fact: The seaway cost C$470 million, of which the Canadian government paid about C$336 million.

questions.text: Which US city earned the nickname 'Steel City' for its giant steel industry?
questions.fun_fact: Pittsburgh is also nicknamed the 'City of Bridges' for the many bridges across its three rivers.

questions.text: In which year was the Toronto Stock Exchange founded by 24 brokers?
questions.fun_fact: The 24 brokers met at the Masonic Hall on October 25, 1861.

questions.text: When William Durant formed General Motors in 1908, he borrowed its naming style from which company?
questions.fun_fact: GM's first acquisition was Buick, which Durant already owned, followed by Olds Motor Works in November 1908.

questions.text: The colonial town of Ouro Preto in Brazil grew rich mainly from which metal?
questions.fun_fact: Officially, 800 tons of gold were sent to Portugal from Brazil in the 1700s.

questions.text: Trinidad's famous Pitch Lake has long been mined for which material?
questions.fun_fact: Sir Walter Raleigh visited the lake in 1595 and used the pitch to caulk his ships.

questions.text: The Chisholm Trail was used to drive Texas cattle north to railheads in which state?
questions.fun_fact: The trail's wagon road was established around 1864 by Jesse Chisholm.

questions.text: Which Hawaiian island is nicknamed 'Pineapple Island' because of its past as a giant plantation?
questions.fun_fact: James Dole, head of Hawaiian Pineapple Company, bought the island and built the world's largest pineapple plantation.

questions.text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average began in 1896 with how many companies?
questions.fun_fact: Charles Dow's first stock average, in 1884, featured 11 stocks, mostly railroads.

questions.text: Which animal's skin was the Hudson's Bay Company's standard unit of trade value?
questions.fun_fact: In 1795, one made beaver could buy eight knives or one kettle.

questions.text: Washington State is best known for growing which fruit?
questions.fun_fact: Wenatchee calls itself the 'Apple Capital of the World'.

questions.text: Which US state is home to both Hollywood and Silicon Valley?
questions.fun_fact: The name 'Silicon Valley' was popularized by Don Hoefler's January 1971 article in Electronic News.

questions.text: Canada is world-famous for syrup made from the sap of which tree?
questions.fun_fact: Indigenous peoples made maple syrup long before European settlers arrived.

questions.text: Patagonia's economy was historically built on raising which animal?
questions.fun_fact: Sheep from the Falkland Islands were introduced there in the 1860s.

questions.text: The Uruguay Round of trade talks, launched in 1986, led to the creation of which organization?
questions.fun_fact: The round was launched in Punta del Este, Uruguay, in September 1986.

questions.text: Which beans were commonly used as money in pre-Hispanic Mesoamerica?
questions.fun_fact: The beans were used to buy small items such as tamales and rabbits.

questions.text: The Inca kept economic records with which device made of knotted cords?
questions.fun_fact: Quipus used knots in a base-10 system to record numbers.

questions.text: Which shell beads of Northeastern Woodlands peoples were used as currency in colonial trade?
questions.fun_fact: Wampum was legal tender in New England from 1637 to 1661, and Dutch colonists mass-produced it in workshops.

questions.text: The 1947 Leduc oil discovery transformed the economy of which Canadian province?
questions.fun_fact: The discovery set off a boom in petroleum exploration across Western Canada.

questions.text: Which Argentine river port, northwest of Buenos Aires, ships out wheat, flour and linseed?
questions.fun_fact: Rosario is called the 'Cradle of the Flag' because the Argentine flag was first raised there in 1812.

questions.text: Spanish treasure fleets gathered at which Cuban port before crossing the Atlantic to Spain?
questions.fun_fact: The convoy system began in the 1560s after French privateers sacked Havana.

questions.text: A rival to the Panama route, a proposed 19th-century canal would have crossed which large lake?
questions.fun_fact: Proposals for a canal across Nicaragua stretch back to the early colonial era.

questions.text: Bermuda is a major world center for which financial industry?
questions.fun_fact: Tourism is also a pillar of its economy, mostly from North America.

questions.text: Which financier bought Carnegie Steel in 1901 to help create U.S. Steel?
questions.fun_fact: The 1901 deal merged Carnegie Steel, Federal Steel and National Steel for $492 million.

questions.text: Which Michigan city is nicknamed 'Cereal City' for its breakfast cereal pioneers?
questions.fun_fact: Inspired by Kellogg's cereals, C. W. Post invented Grape-Nuts and founded his own cereal company in Battle Creek.

questions.text: The 'Rust Belt' in the northern United States got its name from the decline of which sector?
questions.fun_fact: Some people in the region consider the term 'Rust Belt' a pejorative.

questions.text: John Deere made his first steel plow in the 1830s in which US state?
questions.fun_fact: In 1848 Deere moved to Moline, Illinois, for access to the railroad and the Mississippi River.

questions.text: Microsoft was founded in 1975 in which city, before moving to the Seattle area?
questions.fun_fact: The company moved to Bellevue, Washington, in 1979.

questions.text: Amazon began in 1994 as an online seller of which product?
questions.fun_fact: Amazon began as 'Cadabra' and was renamed Amazon in November 1994.

questions.text: Grenada is nicknamed the 'Island of Spice' for which spice?
questions.fun_fact: Nutmeg was introduced to Grenada in 1843 from a merchant ship coming from the East Indies.

questions.text: Which Mexican colonial town is still famed for its silver jewelry?
questions.fun_fact: Tourism is now Taxco's main economic activity, as mining is no longer a mainstay.

questions.text: Which Oklahoma city held the nickname 'Oil Capital of the World' for most of the 20th century?
questions.fun_fact: Tulsa's population swelled to over 140,000 between 1901 and 1930.

questions.text: Which fruit is Florida's agriculture best known for?
questions.fun_fact: Florida's farms also produce strawberries, nuts, sugarcane and cattle.

questions.text: Which independence leader does Venezuela's national currency honor?
questions.fun_fact: It was introduced by the monetary reform of 1879, replacing the venezolano.

questions.text: What popular nickname did US paper money issued during the Civil War carry?
questions.fun_fact: Because it was fiat money, the greenback traded at a steep discount to gold.

questions.text: Which cash crop became the economic backbone of colonial Virginia?
questions.fun_fact: In 1610 John Rolfe arrived at Jamestown with a Caribbean strain milder than the harsh native plant.

questions.text: Google's founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin were PhD students at which university?
questions.fun_fact: In 1998 they used their friend Susan Wojcicki's garage as their first office.

questions.text: Procter & Gamble began as a partnership between a candlemaker and a maker of which product?
questions.fun_fact: William Procter was born in England and James Gamble in Ireland.

questions.text: Cemex, one of Mexico's biggest companies, mainly makes which building material?
questions.fun_fact: It traces back to a company opened in 1906 and became Cemex after a 1931 merger.

questions.text: Which Wisconsin city became famous for beer made by firms like Pabst, Schlitz and Miller?
questions.fun_fact: Because of its brewing past, the city earned the nickname 'Brew City'.

questions.text: Which inventor's company built the Pearl Street Station, an early power plant in New York City, in 1882?
questions.fun_fact: At the start it supplied 400 lamps to 82 customers.

questions.text: The Welland Canal in Ontario, opened in 1829, lets ships bypass which famous waterfall?
questions.fun_fact: The canal has followed four different routes since it opened.

questions.text: Which crop is the US state of Idaho best known for?
questions.fun_fact: Idaho's official state nickname is the 'Gem State'.

questions.text: Which Midwestern state is nicknamed 'America's Dairyland'?
questions.fun_fact: Research by Stephen Babcock at its state university helped build that reputation.

questions.text: William Wrigley Jr. built a Chicago business empire mainly on which product?
questions.fun_fact: He began by selling soap, then baking powder, using free gum as a premium that proved more popular.

questions.text: Rum, long tied to Caribbean plantations, is distilled from the juice or molasses of which crop?
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Navy gave its sailors a daily rum ration, called a tot, until 31 July 1970.

questions.text: Which domesticated Andean animal is prized for its fine, soft fleece?
questions.fun_fact: There are no known wild alpacas; the vicuña is their closest living relative.

questions.text: Tiffany & Co., founded in 1837, is best known for selling what?
questions.fun_fact: It became famous in the early 20th century under the artistic direction of the founder's son.

questions.text: Starbucks opened its first store in 1971 in which US city?
questions.fun_fact: The first store stood near Seattle's Pike Place Market.

questions.text: Ford, General Motors and which company formed Detroit's traditional 'Big Three' automakers?
questions.fun_fact: General Motors was founded in 1908 as a holding company for Buick.

questions.text: Colonel Harland Sanders began selling fried chicken from a roadside restaurant in which US state?
questions.fun_fact: Before chicken, he worked as an insurance salesman and filling station operator.

questions.text: George Washington Carver urged poor farmers to plant which crop to restore soil worn out by cotton?
questions.fun_fact: He also researched uses for sweet potatoes, soybeans and pecans.

questions.text: Milton Hershey built his chocolate factory and model town in which US state?
questions.fun_fact: The factory rose in dairy farmland, and houses, shops and roads grew up around it.

questions.text: Which company introduced the Oreo cookie in 1912?
questions.fun_fact: The first Oreos were made at a Nabisco factory in the Chelsea neighborhood of Manhattan, now Chelsea Market.

questions.text: Kona coffee, first planted there in 1828, is grown in which US state?
questions.fun_fact: The first coffee plants came to Kona as cuttings from Brazil.

questions.text: The Mexican city of Zacatecas began in the 1540s as a mining camp for which metal?
questions.fun_fact: Native peoples were already mining silver in the hills long before Europeans arrived.

questions.text: The Aztecs traded at the huge Tlatelolco market, beside which island capital?
questions.fun_fact: The conquistador Bernal Díaz del Castillo wrote about the market in his history of the conquest.

questions.text: Argentina's Mendoza region is especially known for growing which grape variety?
questions.fun_fact: In Cahors, in France, the Malbec grape is called Auxerrois or Côt Noir.

questions.text: Which US agency was created in 1933 to insure bank deposits after a wave of bank failures?
questions.fun_fact: It was created by the Banking Act of 1933, also known as the Glass-Steagall Act.

questions.text: Minnesota's Mesabi Range has long been one of America's main sources of which ore?
questions.fun_fact: The Ojibwe called the range Misaabe-wajiw, meaning "giant mountain".

questions.text: Intel was founded in 1968 by Robert Noyce and which co-founder?
questions.fun_fact: The name Intel stands for Integrated Electronics.

questions.text: Henry Ford's rubber-plantation town Fordlândia, founded in 1928, stood in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Ford's project failed and the town was abandoned.

questions.text: Which Ohio city, home of tire makers like Goodyear and Firestone, was nicknamed the 'Rubber Capital of the World'?
questions.fun_fact: B.F. Goodrich and General Tire were also headquartered in the city.

questions.text: The Indiana city of Gary was founded in 1906 as a company town by which corporation?
questions.fun_fact: Gary was named after Elbert Henry Gary, the founding chairman of the company.

questions.text: Butte, Montana, boomed in the late 1800s as a town for mining which metal?
questions.fun_fact: The Anaconda Copper Mining Company dominated the town, though Butte was never a company town.

questions.text: Hormel makes Spam, its famous canned meat, in the town of Austin in which US state?
questions.fun_fact: Austin is nicknamed "Spam Town USA".

questions.text: The Jack Daniel's whiskey brand comes from the town of Lynchburg in which state?
questions.fun_fact: The label says 'Est. & Reg. in 1866', but a biographer disputes that founding date.

questions.text: Cornelius Vanderbilt, nicknamed 'the Commodore', first rose in which business before building railroads?
questions.fun_fact: He built his wealth in railroads and shipping, starting with inland and coastal shipping.

questions.text: Peru's 19th-century guano boom centered on which islands off its coast?
questions.fun_fact: Spain occupied the islands in 1864, setting off the Chincha Islands War.

questions.text: John Jacob Astor made his fortune mainly in a monopoly of which trade?
questions.fun_fact: He also made money in New York City real estate.

questions.text: Banco do Brasil was founded in 1808 by the prince regent of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was created to finance the kingdom's public debt when the court moved from Europe to Brazil.

questions.text: Marquis, a famous wheat variety released in 1909, was developed in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It is a cross between Red Fife and Hard Red Calcutta.

questions.text: Canada Dry ginger ale brand was founded in 1904 in which Canadian city?
questions.fun_fact: It was created by John J. McLaughlin, who marketed it as "The Champagne of Ginger Ales".

questions.text: Inca Kola, a golden soft drink invented in 1935, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its main ingredient is lemon verbena.

questions.text: Santos, which long shipped São Paulo state's output, was the main export port for which Brazilian product until World War II?
questions.fun_fact: Santos grew to serve migrants who headed to São Paulo and its coffee farms.

questions.text: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange began in 1898 as the Chicago Butter and what Board?
questions.fun_fact: It was an agricultural commodities exchange in its early decades.

questions.text: Who, as director of New Netherland, is credited with the 1626 purchase of Manhattan Island?
questions.fun_fact: He also founded the Swedish colony of New Sweden on the Delaware.

questions.text: The Union Stock Yards, opened in 1865, made which US city a world center of meatpacking?
questions.fun_fact: The Yards closed on July 30, 1971.

questions.text: Which Connecticut city is nicknamed the 'Insurance Capital of the World'?
questions.fun_fact: It is also nicknamed 'America's filing cabinet'.

questions.text: Nantucket Island, in which state, was a whaling center in the 1800s?
questions.fun_fact: Its whaleships also employed Hawaiian Islanders and Wampanoags.

questions.text: The banking house that became Goldman Sachs was founded in 1869 in which US city?
questions.fun_fact: It was founded by the German immigrant Marcus Goldman.

questions.text: George Pullman's company became famous for building which kind of railroad car?
questions.fun_fact: At its peak in the early 20th century its cars accommodated 26 million people a year.

questions.text: Montgomery Ward, founded in 1872, began as which kind of business?
questions.fun_fact: Its common nickname was 'Monkey Wards'.

questions.text: Disneyland, opened by Walt Disney in 1955, is in which California city?
questions.fun_fact: Disney first imagined an attraction beside his studios in Burbank.

questions.text: In the late 1600s, playing cards served as emergency money in which French colony?
questions.fun_fact: Intendant Jacques de Meulles introduced it to pay soldiers when the colony faced insolvency.

questions.text: Which bank, founded in 1817, is considered Canada's oldest?
questions.fun_fact: It started life as the Montreal Bank.

questions.text: In which year was the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange founded?
questions.fun_fact: It is the successor to the Banco Mercantil, created in 1822 by Bernardino Rivadavia.

questions.text: In which year was Brazil's state oil company Petrobras created?
questions.fun_fact: It was created with the slogan 'The Oil is Ours' and a legal monopoly.

questions.text: The Comstock Lode, discovered in 1859, lies in which US state?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first major discovery of silver ore in the United States.

questions.text: William Colgate founded his starch, soap and candle business in 1806 in which city?
questions.fun_fact: His first factory stood on Dutch Street in Lower Manhattan.

questions.text: Nike began as Blue Ribbon Sports, founded by Phil Knight and which University of Oregon track coach?
questions.fun_fact: It first distributed Japanese Onitsuka Tiger shoes from Eugene, Oregon.

questions.text: H. J. Heinz began packing food in 1869 in Pennsylvania, selling which condiment first?
questions.fun_fact: He founded Heinz Noble & Company with his friend L. Clarence Noble.

questions.text: Richard Sears began the mail-order business that became Sears by selling which product?
questions.fun_fact: He later went into business with the watch repairman Alvah Curtis Roebuck.

questions.text: The first Tim Hortons donut shop opened in 1964 in which Ontario city?
questions.fun_fact: It was co-founded by the hockey player Tim Horton and Jim Charade.

questions.text: Yucatán's 19th-century boom came from henequen, a rope fiber from which plant?
questions.fun_fact: Henequen's leaf fiber is made into rope and twine.

questions.fun_fact: It was reorganized as the Tokyo Stock Exchange on 16 May 1949.

questions.text: Which business newspaper took over the Nikkei 225 index from the Tokyo Stock Exchange in 1970?

questions.text: Which country's Sar-i Sang mines have long supplied lapis lazuli?
