questions.text: What do economists call it when a firm's average cost per unit falls as its output grows?
questions.fun_fact: When growth pushes unit costs back up, a firm suffers diseconomies of scale.

questions.text: Whose 1871 'Principles of Economics' launched the Austrian School of economics in Vienna?
questions.fun_fact: He developed the idea of marginal utility around the same time as William Stanley Jevons in England.

questions.text: Which country is famous for strict bank client confidentiality, written into law in 1934?
questions.fun_fact: The 1934 Banking Act made it a criminal offense for bankers to reveal client information.

questions.text: To calculate GDP per capita, what do you divide a country's GDP by?
questions.fun_fact: 'Per capita' is Latin for 'by heads'.

questions.text: Which country issued a 100-trillion-dollar banknote during a famous hyperinflation?
questions.fun_fact: In April 2009 it stopped printing its own currency, and foreign currencies came into use.

questions.text: What is a loan used to buy real estate, secured by the property itself, called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from a Law French term meaning 'death pledge': the pledge ends, or 'dies', when the debt is paid or the property is lost.

questions.text: Which economic rule of thumb links a rise in unemployment to a loss of a country's output?
questions.fun_fact: Arthur Okun first proposed the relationship in 1962.

questions.text: Which investor from Nebraska is nicknamed the 'Oracle of Omaha'?
questions.fun_fact: His company, Berkshire Hathaway, began as a New England textile manufacturer.

questions.text: On a loan, what does 'APR' stand for?
questions.fun_fact: In the US, the Truth in Lending Act of 1968 requires lenders to disclose a loan's APR.

questions.text: Herbert Simon's idea that people decide with limited information, time and brainpower is known as what?
questions.fun_fact: Simon also coined 'satisficing', choosing an option that is good enough rather than the best.

questions.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein's 2008 book is named after which gentle way of steering people's choices?
questions.fun_fact: Thaler later won the 2017 Nobel Prize in economics for his work in behavioral economics.

questions.text: Until 1826, the English Exchequer recorded debts and payments using what kind of notched wooden record?
questions.fun_fact: Split tallies were common in medieval Europe, when coins were scarce, to document debts and exchanges.

questions.text: Which English city was nicknamed 'Cottonopolis' for its dominance of the textile trade in the 1800s?
questions.fun_fact: The Manchester Ship Canal, opened in 1894, turned the inland city into a major port.

questions.text: What is money called when it has value because a government declares it legal tender, not because it is backed by gold?
questions.fun_fact: 'Fiat' is Latin for 'let it be done'.

questions.text: Kenneth Arrow's 'impossibility theorem' concerns the design of which kind of procedure?
questions.fun_fact: It generalizes the Marquis de Condorcet's earlier finding that majority voting can produce cycles.

questions.text: The Nikkei 225 stock index peaked in December of which year, before Japan's 'lost decades'?
questions.fun_fact: The bubble was fueled by cheap credit in the years after the 1985 Plaza Accord.

questions.text: What does VAT, a consumption tax used in many countries, stand for?
questions.fun_fact: Unlike a simple sales tax, VAT is collected at each stage of production, and businesses reclaim the VAT they pay on inputs.

questions.text: Harry Markowitz's 1952 modern portfolio theory is built on which investing principle?
questions.fun_fact: Markowitz shared the 1990 Nobel Prize in economics for his work on portfolio choice.

questions.text: A 'laissez-faire' approach to the economy calls for what?
questions.fun_fact: The French phrase roughly means 'let do' and is linked to the physiocrats, 18th-century French economists.

questions.text: Which American engineer's 'scientific management' sought to raise factory efficiency by studying and timing tasks?
questions.fun_fact: His 1911 book 'The Principles of Scientific Management' made 'efficiency' a buzzword in factories around the world.

questions.text: What is a person who starts and runs a new business, taking on its financial risk, called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from French entreprendre, 'to undertake'; Richard Cantillon helped bring the idea into economics.

questions.text: A hyperinflation from 1992 to 1994, with monthly inflation peaking near 313 million percent, struck which country?
questions.fun_fact: Daily inflation reached about 62%, a rate of roughly 2% per hour.

questions.text: If demand for a product rises while its supply stays the same, what usually happens to its price?
questions.fun_fact: Where the supply and demand curves cross is the equilibrium, the price at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.

questions.text: What do economists call the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice?
questions.fun_fact: Opportunity costs also count non-money losses, such as lost time and pleasure, not just financial costs.

questions.text: What is it called when two companies combine into a single legal entity?
questions.fun_fact: In an acquisition, by contrast, one company takes ownership of another, which can be friendly or hostile.

questions.text: A standard London 'good delivery' gold bar weighs roughly how many troy ounces?
questions.fun_fact: That is about 12.4 kg, and the bar must be at least 99.5% pure gold.

questions.text: Which economist's 1937 essay 'The Nature of the Firm' asked why companies exist at all?
questions.fun_fact: Coase won the 1991 Nobel Prize in economics, partly for his work on transaction costs.

questions.text: The 'impossible trinity' says a country cannot have free capital movement, an independent monetary policy and what else at the same time?
questions.fun_fact: The idea was developed independently by John Marcus Fleming and Robert Mundell in the early 1960s.

questions.text: Which item did 'The Wealth of Nations' use to show how division of labor boosts output?
questions.fun_fact: French writer Duhamel du Monceau described the division of pin-making work in 1761, before 'The Wealth of Nations'.

questions.text: ASEAN was founded in 1967 in which capital city?
questions.fun_fact: On 7 January 1984, Brunei became its sixth member, the first newcomer after the five founders.

questions.text: Which British bank, founded in 1762, collapsed in 1995 after losses run up by a trader in Singapore?
questions.fun_fact: The Dutch group ING bought the bank for one pound and took over its debts.

questions.text: Wassily Leontief won the 1973 Nobel Prize in economics for developing which method?
questions.fun_fact: Four of his doctoral students, including Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow, also went on to win the prize.

questions.text: Which paradox asks why water, vital to life, is cheap while diamonds, far less useful, are expensive?
questions.fun_fact: Marginal utility theory in the 1870s resolved it: price reflects the value of the last unit, not total usefulness.

questions.text: What does the 'S&P' in the S&P 500 stock index stand for?
questions.fun_fact: The index was expanded to 500 companies on March 4, 1957.

questions.text: In his 1936 'General Theory', which phrase did the author use for the instincts that drive economic choices?
questions.fun_fact: George Akerlof and Robert Shiller revived the idea in a 2009 book titled 'Animal Spirits'.

questions.text: Whose portrait appears on the US $100 bill?
questions.fun_fact: As a printer in colonial Philadelphia, he produced paper money for the colony of Pennsylvania.

questions.text: Which financial market, open around the clock on weekdays, is the largest in the world by trading volume?
questions.fun_fact: Trading rolls from Sydney to Tokyo, London and New York as business hours move around the globe.

questions.text: Britain's 1840s investment bubble in a new transport technology is known as what?
questions.fun_fact: Britain's rail network grew several times over between 1840 and 1850.

questions.text: In which kind of auction does the price start high and fall until a bidder accepts?
questions.fun_fact: It suits goods that must be sold quickly, such as flowers, fresh produce and tobacco.

questions.text: The dot-com bubble in technology shares reached its peak in which year?
questions.fun_fact: The Nasdaq Composite peaked in March 2000 and then fell by roughly three quarters by 2002.

questions.text: What is a state-owned investment fund, often built from oil or trade surpluses, called?
questions.fun_fact: Many are funded by oil and gas exports, while others come from foreign currency reserves built up by trade surpluses.

questions.text: When you buy a government bond, what are you essentially doing?
questions.fun_fact: Bondholders usually receive regular interest, called the coupon, and get their face value back at maturity.

questions.text: Which idea says that if everyone tries to save more during a slump, total saving may actually fall?
questions.fun_fact: It was stated as early as 1714 in 'The Fable of the Bees' and later popularized by John Maynard Keynes.

questions.text: The G20 forum of finance ministers was created in 1999 after which crisis?
questions.fun_fact: The first G20 finance ministers' meeting was held in Berlin in December 1999.

questions.text: Governments use which two main tools in fiscal policy?
questions.fun_fact: Its partner tool, monetary policy, is run by a central bank rather than by the government.

questions.text: On 'Black Wednesday' in 1992, which currency was forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism?
questions.fun_fact: Investor George Soros famously made a huge profit by betting against it.

questions.text: Which economist gave his name to a curve linking tax rates to government tax revenue?
questions.fun_fact: Journalist Jude Wanniski popularized it; the curve was supposedly sketched on a napkin in 1974.

questions.text: How easily an asset can be sold quickly without lowering its price is known as its what?
questions.fun_fact: Cash is the most liquid asset of all, while property such as houses usually takes much longer to sell.

questions.text: In which year did Britain abandon the gold standard during the Great Depression?
questions.fun_fact: The US followed in 1933 by restricting private gold holdings.

questions.text: The Black–Scholes model, published in 1973, is used to price what kind of financial contract?
questions.fun_fact: Myron Scholes and Robert C. Merton received the 1997 Nobel Prize in economics for related work.

questions.text: Which French court physician created the 1758 'Tableau économique', an early model of economic flows?
questions.fun_fact: His physiocrat school held that agriculture alone produced a true surplus of wealth.

questions.text: How many companies make up the Dow Jones Industrial Average?
questions.fun_fact: The index is price-weighted, so companies with higher share prices move it more than cheaper ones.

questions.text: Which metaphor, used by an 18th-century Scottish thinker, describes how self-interest can end up benefiting society?
questions.fun_fact: The phrase appears just once in 'The Wealth of Nations', in a passage about investing at home rather than abroad.

questions.text: What is a business owned and run by its members, such as customers or workers, called?
questions.fun_fact: The 1844 Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers in England set out co-op principles that many cooperatives still follow.

questions.text: What does 'CEO', the title of a company's top manager, stand for?
questions.fun_fact: The term is attested as early as 1782, in a US congressional ordinance.

questions.text: Which steel magnate wrote 'The Gospel of Wealth' (1889), urging the rich to give away their fortunes?
questions.fun_fact: He devoted his later life to philanthropy, funding Carnegie Hall in New York and the Peace Palace in The Hague.

questions.text: Which Scottish economist gives his name to the Giffen good, whose demand can rise when its price rises?
questions.fun_fact: Classic examples are staple foods, such as bread or potatoes, for very poor households.

questions.text: Which American economist's 1879 bestseller 'Progress and Poverty' urged a single tax on land values?
questions.fun_fact: Progress and Poverty sold millions of copies worldwide, a huge number for an economics book of its day.

questions.text: Which 1890 US law was the first federal statute to outlaw monopolies and cartels?
questions.fun_fact: It is named for John Sherman of Ohio, its principal author, and it bans agreements that restrain trade.

questions.text: In 1873 Sweden and Denmark created a monetary union around which common unit name?
questions.fun_fact: Norway joined in 1875; each country kept its own notes but accepted the others' coins.

questions.text: Which branch of economics studies whole economies, such as growth, unemployment and inflation?
questions.fun_fact: Its topics are often split by time frame: short-term business cycles, medium-term unemployment and long-term growth.

questions.text: Which American economist won the 2008 Nobel Prize in economics for explaining trade patterns and where economic activity locates?
questions.fun_fact: He was the sole winner that year, and also wrote a long-running column for The New York Times.

questions.text: In a December 1996 speech, which phrase did Fed chair Alan Greenspan use to ask if asset prices were too high?
questions.fun_fact: Economist Robert Shiller later used the phrase as the title of a 2000 book on market bubbles.

questions.text: Which Scottish philosopher described the price–specie flow mechanism, showing how gold flows correct trade imbalances?
questions.fun_fact: He set out the argument in his essay 'Of the Balance of Trade' to counter mercantilist thinking.

questions.text: Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in economics for which approach to fighting global poverty?
questions.fun_fact: Banerjee and Duflo, who are married, co-founded the Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) at MIT.

questions.text: In which year did the IMF formally come into existence, after 29 countries ratified its Articles of Agreement?
questions.fun_fact: It began financial operations on 1 March 1947, and France was its first borrower.

questions.text: Which investment bank's economist coined the term 'BRIC' in 2001?
questions.fun_fact: Jim O'Neill's paper grouped Brazil, Russia, India and China; South Africa joined the BRICS name in 2010.

questions.text: Which Indian economist won the 1998 Nobel Prize for work on welfare economics and the causes of famines?
questions.fun_fact: He later served as master of Trinity College at the University of Cambridge.

questions.text: A secret 1910 meeting that shaped the US Federal Reserve took place on which Georgia island?
questions.fun_fact: The plan drafted there became the basis of the Aldrich Plan, later reworked into the Federal Reserve Act.

questions.text: Farming, fishing and mining belong to which sector of the economy?
questions.fun_fact: The three-sector model was developed in the 1930s by economists Allan Fisher and Colin Clark.

questions.text: Which British economist devised the IS–LM model in 1937 to summarize Keynes's ideas?
questions.fun_fact: Alvin Hansen later extended it, and it was the leading framework for macroeconomic analysis from the 1940s to the 1970s.

questions.text: Which economist quipped 'In the long run we are all dead' in his 1923 'Tract on Monetary Reform'?
questions.fun_fact: He was mocking advice that waits for the economy to fix itself over the long run.

questions.text: Which agency, founded in 1919 and now part of the UN, sets international labor standards?
questions.fun_fact: It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969, on its 50th anniversary.

questions.text: According to Engel's law, as household income rises, the share of spending on which category falls?
questions.fun_fact: Engel found that food spending rises in absolute terms as income grows, even as its share of the budget falls.

questions.text: Sales taxes are often called what kind of tax, because they take a bigger share of low incomes?
questions.fun_fact: Excise taxes on goods such as fuel and tobacco are also usually seen as regressive.

questions.text: Which new currency, introduced in November 1923, helped end Germany's hyperinflation?
questions.fun_fact: One Rentenmark was set equal to one trillion paper marks.

questions.text: In 1990 which country's central bank became the first to adopt formal inflation targeting?
questions.fun_fact: Canada and the United Kingdom followed in the early 1990s, and dozens of countries now use the approach.

questions.text: In which year was the Hong Kong dollar linked to the US dollar under its currency board system?
questions.fun_fact: It was adopted on 17 October 1983 in response to the 'Black Saturday' currency crisis.

questions.text: 'Dutch disease' describes how a natural resource boom can hurt which other part of an economy?
questions.fun_fact: A British magazine coined the term in 1977 after the Netherlands' natural gas boom.

questions.text: How many countries originally signed the GATT in 1947?
questions.fun_fact: It was signed in Geneva on 30 October 1947 and took effect on 1 January 1948.

questions.text: Which law says that 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure'?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after British economist Charles Goodhart, who expressed the idea in a 1975 paper on UK monetary policy.

questions.text: Which French economist popularized the 'law of markets', often summed up as 'supply creates its own demand'?
questions.fun_fact: His principal work, the Traité d'économie politique, appeared in 1803.

questions.text: A sudden collapse of asset prices after a long, debt-fueled boom is called a 'moment' named after which economist?
questions.fun_fact: Hyman Minsky's ideas on fragile finance were largely ignored until the 2008 crisis revived interest in them.

questions.text: Which effect explains why services with little productivity growth, such as live music, get steadily more expensive?
questions.fun_fact: William Baumol and William Bowen first described it in the 1960s, studying the cost of the performing arts.

questions.text: What does 'renminbi', the official name of China's currency, literally mean?
questions.fun_fact: The renminbi was first issued in December 1948, before the People's Republic was founded in 1949.

questions.text: When a country buys more goods and services from abroad than it sells abroad, it runs what?
questions.fun_fact: A country's balance of trade is a main part of its current account, which also counts income and transfers.

questions.text: UNCTAD, the UN body focused on trade and development, was set up in which year?
questions.fun_fact: Its first secretary-general was the Argentine economist Raúl Prebisch.

questions.text: In game theory, which classic puzzle shows two players who would both gain by cooperating but are each tempted to betray the other?
questions.fun_fact: Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the game at the RAND Corporation in 1950; Albert Tucker gave it its name.

questions.text: Which Houston energy company's 2001 collapse led to the 2002 Sarbanes–Oxley accounting reforms?
questions.fun_fact: Its auditor, Arthur Andersen, lost its clients and effectively shut down after the scandal.

questions.text: What does 'ATM', the cash-dispensing machine, stand for?
questions.fun_fact: In Britain the machines are often called cashpoints.

questions.text: In which year did the Bitcoin network go live, a few months after its 2008 white paper?
questions.fun_fact: The first block contained a newspaper headline about a second bank bailout, a hint at the motive behind Bitcoin.

questions.text: The Doha Round of world trade talks, launched in 2001, takes its name from the capital of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It was launched with a 'development' agenda meant to help poorer countries gain from trade.

questions.text: What is money that has already been spent and cannot be recovered called?
questions.fun_fact: Letting past spending drive new choices, like finishing a bad meal because you paid for it, is the sunk cost fallacy.

questions.text: Which Swedish mining company issued the oldest known surviving share certificate, in 1288?
questions.fun_fact: Its modern successor, the forestry group Stora Enso, is sometimes called the world's oldest limited liability company.

questions.text: In George Akerlof's 1970 paper 'The Market for Lemons', what do the 'lemons' stand for?
questions.fun_fact: Akerlof shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for showing how unequal information can make markets fail.

questions.text: Which volatility index, launched by the Chicago Board Options Exchange in 1993, is nicknamed the 'fear gauge'?
questions.fun_fact: It measures the stock market's expectation of volatility, based on S&P 500 index contracts.

questions.text: Which US president launched the New Deal, a set of programs to fight the Great Depression?
questions.fun_fact: His 'first hundred days' in 1933 produced a flood of new laws and made that phrase a standard way to judge new presidents.

questions.text: Which US hedge fund, with Nobel laureates Myron Scholes and Robert Merton on its board, needed a Fed-brokered rescue in 1998?
questions.fun_fact: A group of 14 banks put in about $3.6 billion to stop its collapse from spreading through the financial system.

questions.text: What is the maximum number of bitcoins that will ever exist, by design?
questions.fun_fact: New coins come from mining rewards, which halve every 210,000 blocks, roughly every four years.

questions.text: Which Italian-born swindler in 1920 Boston gave his name to a fraud that pays early investors with later investors' money?
questions.fun_fact: Ponzi promised 50% returns in 45 days, supposedly by trading international reply coupons.

questions.text: In finance, one basis point is equal to what?
questions.fun_fact: Interest rate changes are often quoted in basis points, so a rise of 25 basis points means a quarter of a percentage point.

questions.text: What is a fall in a currency's value against others in a floating market called?
questions.fun_fact: Heavy demand for imports can push a currency down, because buyers must first obtain foreign currency to pay for them.

questions.text: Which Russian author wrote the 1862 novel Fathers and Sons?
questions.fun_fact: Its young hero, Yevgeny Bazarov, champions a new philosophy called nihilism.

questions.text: In The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, what is the name of the great lion who rules Narnia?
questions.fun_fact: Like the other Narnia books, it was illustrated by Pauline Baynes.

questions.text: Which Egyptian architect championed mud-brick building and designed the village of New Gourna?
questions.fun_fact: His book on New Gourna, first published in 1969, was reissued in 1973 as Architecture for the Poor.

questions.text: Which architect designed the neo-Gothic Parliament Building on the Danube in Budapest?
questions.fun_fact: Construction ran from 1885 to 1904.

questions.text: Which Japanese architect designed the Yoyogi National Gymnasium for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics?
questions.fun_fact: In 1987 he became the first Japanese architect to win the Pritzker Prize.

questions.text: The Dancing House, by Frank Gehry and Vlado Milunić, stands in which city?
questions.fun_fact: Gehry first called it Ginger and Fred, after Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire, as it looks like a dancing couple.

questions.text: In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, which city does Dorothy travel to along the yellow brick road?
questions.fun_fact: The book's success led L. Frank Baum to write thirteen more Oz books as sequels.

questions.text: Which city became the world's first UNESCO City of Literature in 2004?
questions.fun_fact: It is the birthplace of Walter Scott, Robert Louis Stevenson and Arthur Conan Doyle.

questions.text: Which Austrian artist designed a colorful Vienna apartment block with wavy floors and trees growing from its windows?
questions.fun_fact: He was born Friedrich Stowasser and later changed his name.

questions.text: Which author created the honey-loving bear Winnie-the-Pooh?
questions.fun_fact: The name Winnie came from a black bear at London Zoo, herself named after the Canadian city of Winnipeg.

questions.text: In E. B. White's Charlotte's Web, what kind of animal is Charlotte?
questions.fun_fact: Garth Williams illustrated the 1952 book, and White asked him to draw a realistic spider, not one with a woman's face.

questions.text: What kind of animal is Miffy, the picture-book character created by Dutch artist Dick Bruna?
questions.fun_fact: The first Miffy book appeared in 1955, and more than thirty others have followed.

questions.text: Which playwright wrote The Importance of Being Earnest?
questions.fun_fact: Its subtitle is A Trivial Comedy for Serious People.

questions.text: Which Polish poet won the 1996 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.fun_fact: She is known for witty, ironic poems about everyday things.

questions.text: Which English author wrote the Famous Five adventure books?
questions.fun_fact: The five are Julian, Dick, Anne, George and their dog Timmy; the first book appeared in 1942.

questions.text: The Van Gogh Museum, with the world's largest collection of his works, is in which city?
questions.fun_fact: Architect Gerrit Rietveld designed the main building, which opened in 1973.

questions.text: Which author wrote the beginner reader The Cat in the Hat?
questions.fun_fact: It was written as a lively alternative to dull school primers, using a limited vocabulary.

questions.text: Johannes Vermeer lived and worked in which Dutch city?
questions.fun_fact: Only about three dozen paintings are generally attributed to him.

questions.text: The dot-painting movement of Western Desert Aboriginal artists began in 1971 at which community?
questions.fun_fact: It grew from a 1971 school mural of the Honey Ant Dreaming, encouraged by teacher Geoffrey Bardon.

questions.text: Which architect designed the Barcelona Pavilion for the 1929 International Exposition?
questions.fun_fact: His motto 'less is more' became a slogan of modern architecture.

questions.text: Which architect designed the glass pyramid at the Louvre in Paris?
questions.fun_fact: The pyramid opened in 1989 and uses 603 rhombus-shaped and 70 triangular glass segments.

questions.text: Which French author wrote The Three Musketeers?
questions.fun_fact: The title heroes are Athos, Porthos and Aramis; the young d'Artagnan hopes to join the Musketeers.

questions.text: Which German writer wrote the two-part play Faust?
questions.fun_fact: Its earliest version, known as the Urfaust, was written in the 1770s; Part Two appeared in 1832.

questions.text: Which Norwegian playwright wrote A Doll's House?
questions.fun_fact: The play premiered in Copenhagen in 1879.

questions.text: Which English author wrote Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol?
questions.fun_fact: Dickens published most of his novels in monthly or weekly installments.

questions.text: Which Swiss-French architect designed Villa Savoye near Paris?
questions.fun_fact: He was born Charles-Édouard Jeanneret.

questions.text: The Uffizi Gallery, a museum of Renaissance art, is in which Italian city?
questions.fun_fact: Building work began in 1560 and ended in 1581; it officially opened to the public in 1769.

questions.text: Which Prague-born writer wrote The Metamorphosis?
questions.fun_fact: The adjective 'Kafkaesque' is named after him.

questions.text: Which elephant becomes king in Jean de Brunhoff's 1931 picture book?
questions.fun_fact: The story grew from a bedtime tale that Brunhoff's wife, Cécile, invented for their children.

questions.text: Which Russian playwright wrote The Seagull and Uncle Vanya?
questions.fun_fact: The Seagull was booed at its 1896 premiere in Saint Petersburg but later became a triumph.

questions.text: Shakespeare and Company, famed for English-language books, is a bookshop in which city?
questions.fun_fact: American Sylvia Beach opened the first shop in 1919.

questions.text: Which Argentine cartoonist created the comic strip Mafalda?
questions.fun_fact: Mafalda ran as a newspaper strip from 1964 to 1973.

questions.text: Which English Romantic poet wrote 'Ode to a Nightingale'?
questions.fun_fact: According to his friend Charles Brown, Keats wrote it in one morning under a plum tree in their Hampstead garden.

questions.text: Which Chilean poet wrote Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair?
questions.fun_fact: Published in 1924, the collection made him famous at the age of 19.

questions.text: Which Icelandic author won the 1955 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.fun_fact: His novel Independent People follows a stubborn sheep farmer.

questions.text: Which Mexican poet and essayist won the 1990 Nobel Prize in Literature?
questions.fun_fact: His 1950 essay collection The Labyrinth of Solitude explores Mexican identity.

questions.text: Which Japanese novelist wrote Norwegian Wood and Kafka on the Shore?
questions.fun_fact: Murakami ran a jazz bar in Tokyo before he became a full-time novelist.

questions.text: Which Brazilian author wrote the 1899 novel Dom Casmurro?
questions.fun_fact: It is told by Bento Santiago, a jealous husband and a famously unreliable narrator.

questions.text: In Don Quixote, what is the name of the knight's loyal squire?
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish, 'panza' means 'belly'.

questions.text: Which German brothers published a famous collection of fairy tales including Hansel and Gretel?
questions.fun_fact: Their first collection, Children's and Household Tales, was published in 1812.

questions.text: Which comic book publisher first published Superman and Batman?
questions.fun_fact: The 'DC' originally stood for Detective Comics.

questions.text: Which manga artist, using the pen name Fujiko F. Fujio, created Doraemon?
questions.fun_fact: Doraemon, a robot cat from the 22nd century, first appeared in children's magazines in December 1969.

questions.text: Which American poet wrote the collection Leaves of Grass?
questions.fun_fact: Whitman paid for the first edition himself in 1855 and kept revising the book for decades.

questions.text: Which manga artist created Dragon Ball?
questions.fun_fact: Dragon Ball began running in the magazine Weekly Shōnen Jump in 1984.

questions.text: Which Argentine writer is famous for the short-story collection Ficciones?
questions.fun_fact: Borges was appointed director of Argentina's National Library in 1955.

questions.text: Which river do Huckleberry Finn and Jim travel down on a raft?
questions.fun_fact: Mark Twain published the book in 1884 as a follow-up to The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.

questions.text: Which Italian author wrote the novel The Name of the Rose?
questions.fun_fact: The 1980 book was his debut novel and has sold over 50 million copies.

questions.text: In which Italian city is Shakespeare's play Romeo and Juliet mainly set?
questions.fun_fact: Shakespeare drew on Arthur Brooke's 1562 poem The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet.

questions.text: What is Mr. Darcy's first name in Pride and Prejudice?
questions.fun_fact: Austen first drafted the novel in the 1790s under the title First Impressions.

questions.text: Which Italian cartoonist created the sailor-adventurer Corto Maltese?
questions.fun_fact: Corto Maltese first appeared in 1967 in the story The Ballad of the Salt Sea.

questions.text: Edward Hopper's Nighthawks, a late-night diner scene, hangs in which Chicago museum?
questions.fun_fact: Hopper painted Nighthawks in early 1942, and the Art Institute bought it within months.

questions.text: Which Polish-British novelist wrote the 1899 novella Heart of Darkness?
questions.fun_fact: It first appeared as a three-part serial in Blackwood's Magazine.

questions.text: What is the name of Tintin's white fox terrier?
questions.fun_fact: In the original French books, Snowy is called Milou.

questions.text: Which comic-strip cat is famous for loving lasagna and hating Mondays?
questions.fun_fact: Creator Jim Davis named the cat after his grandfather, James Garfield Davis.

questions.text: Which publishing house did Allen Lane found in 1935, bringing cheap paperbacks to a mass audience?
questions.fun_fact: The first ten Penguin paperbacks cost sixpence each.

questions.text: Which Italian author wrote The Adventures of Pinocchio?
questions.fun_fact: 'Collodi' is a pen name taken from the Tuscan village where his mother was born.

questions.text: Which Chinese writer wrote the novella The True Story of Ah Q (1921-22)?
questions.fun_fact: It first ran as a newspaper serial under the pen name Ba Ren, so few readers knew who wrote it.

questions.text: Which German author wrote The Neverending Story?
questions.fun_fact: In the first edition, the text is printed in two colors: red for the real world and green for Fantastica.

questions.text: Walter Frederick Morrison's 1955 flying disc design, the archetype of modern discs, was called the Pluto what?
questions.fun_fact: Morrison sold the rights to the toy company Wham-O on January 23, 1957.

questions.text: What does the '40' in the name of the spray WD-40 refer to?
questions.fun_fact: WD stands for 'Water Displacement'; the 1953 formula was first used to protect the skin of the Atlas missile from rust.

questions.text: The word 'yahoo', which inspired the name of the web company Yahoo, comes from creatures in which book?
questions.fun_fact: Jerry Yang and David Filo founded Yahoo in January 1994.

questions.text: The toy company Wham-O, maker of the Frisbee, took its name from the sound of which first product hitting a target?
questions.fun_fact: Founders Richard Knerr and Arthur Melin first promoted it with demonstrations of their own shooting skills.

questions.text: Netflix began in 1997 as a mail-based service renting out which items?
questions.fun_fact: Netflix launched its streaming service in 2007.

questions.text: The golden arches of the McDonald's logo form which letter?
questions.fun_fact: The arches began as a feature of the McDonald brothers' restaurant building, drawn up with architect Stanley Meston.

questions.text: John Kemp Starley's 1885 chain-driven 'safety bicycle' was given which name?
questions.fun_fact: Often called the first modern bicycle, the Rover was heavier than a penny-farthing but lighter and cheaper than the tricycles of its day.

questions.text: George Nissen named the trampoline after the Spanish word for what?
questions.fun_fact: Nissen heard the word trampolín on a demonstration tour in Mexico in the late 1930s.

questions.text: Dungeons & Dragons was created in 1974 by Gary Gygax and which co-creator?
questions.fun_fact: Its first rules were a variation of Chainmail, a 1971 miniature wargame.

questions.text: Converse's Chuck Taylor All Star sneakers were originally developed for which sport?
questions.fun_fact: A forerunner called Non-Skids appeared in 1917; the shoe is named after basketball player Chuck Taylor, who joined Converse as a salesman in 1921.

questions.text: Which company released the Xbox video game console in 2001?
questions.fun_fact: The Xbox was the first video game console with a built-in hard disk drive.

questions.text: Who designed the Apple logo, the apple with a bite taken out, in 1977?
questions.fun_fact: Rob Janoff also did design work for IBM and Intel.

questions.text: Which waterproof fabric did Thomas Burberry invent in 1879?
questions.fun_fact: In 1901 Burberry's Equestrian Knight logo was developed with the Latin word 'Prorsum', meaning 'forwards'.

questions.text: What was the profession of Alfred Butts, who invented Scrabble in the 1930s?
questions.fun_fact: Butts based it on an earlier word game he had invented, called Lexiko.

questions.text: The video game company Atari, founded by Nolan Bushnell, is named after a term from which board game?
questions.fun_fact: The Japanese word 'atari' means 'to hit a target'.

questions.text: The watch brand Swatch, launched in 1983, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The name Swatch is a contraction of 'second watch'.

questions.text: Which co-founder of Apple sold his 10% stake in 1976 for just $800?
questions.fun_fact: Wayne drew Apple's first logo, which showed Isaac Newton sitting under an apple tree.

questions.text: Victorinox, maker of the Swiss Army knife, is named after founder Karl Elsener's mother plus 'inox', short for what?
questions.fun_fact: Elsener named his brand Victoria in his mother's honor in 1909 and changed it to Victorinox in 1921.

questions.text: The block-building video game Minecraft was developed by a company from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Minecraft was first created by Markus 'Notch' Persson and was formally released in November 2011.

questions.text: Who came up with the name Coca-Cola and chose its flowing script logo?
questions.fun_fact: Robinson was the bookkeeper of the drink's creator, John Pemberton; the lettering style is called Spencerian script.

questions.text: WhatsApp's name is meant to sound like which everyday phrase?
questions.fun_fact: WhatsApp was bought by Facebook in February 2014 for about US$19.3 billion.

questions.text: Playmobil, the toy figures launched in 1974, comes from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The figures were invented by Hans Beck and are made by the company Geobra Brandstätter.

questions.text: French filmmaker Albert Lamorisse, director of The Red Balloon, invented which board game?
questions.fun_fact: Risk was invented in 1957 and became one of the most popular board games in history.

questions.text: Brazil's Havaianas flip-flops were inspired by which Japanese sandals?
questions.fun_fact: Havaianas is the Portuguese word for 'Hawaiians', and the brand was created and patented in 1962.

questions.text: The name Crayola combines French 'craie', meaning chalk, with a shortened form of which word?
questions.fun_fact: Alice Binney, a schoolteacher and wife of co-founder Edwin Binney, came up with the name.

questions.text: Which British engineer devised the Spirograph drawing toy, first sold in 1965?
questions.fun_fact: Fisher showed the toy at the 1965 Nuremberg Toy Fair, and the American company Kenner sold it from 1966.

questions.text: Which company created the video game character Sonic the Hedgehog?
questions.fun_fact: The character was created by Naoto Ohshima, Yuji Naka and Hirokazu Yasuhara.

questions.text: The energy drink Red Bull comes from a company in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Red Bull was launched in 1987 by the Austrian entrepreneur Dietrich Mateschitz.

questions.text: The Snurfer, an early forerunner of the snowboard, was invented by Sherman Poppen. What does its name blend with 'snow'?
questions.fun_fact: Poppen first made it on Christmas Day in 1965 for the amusement of his children.

questions.text: A standard Rubik's Cube has faces in how many different colors?
questions.fun_fact: On the classic cube, each of the six faces is covered by nine stickers.

questions.text: Pokémon creator Satoshi Tajiri was inspired by his childhood hobby of collecting what?
questions.fun_fact: Tajiri's company Game Freak began as a fanzine about video games.

questions.text: The name Xerox comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: The company began in 1906 in Rochester, New York, as the Haloid Photographic Company.

questions.text: Colonel Sanders is the face of which fried chicken chain?
questions.fun_fact: His title 'Colonel' was honorary, awarded by the governor of Kentucky in 1935.

questions.text: Earle Dickson invented the Band-Aid in the 1920s while working for which company?
questions.fun_fact: Dickson, a cotton buyer, first made the bandage for his wife Josephine, who often cut herself while cooking.

questions.text: The Japanese retailer Muji's full name, Mujirushi Ryōhin, means 'no-brand' what?
questions.fun_fact: Muji started in 1980 as a private label of the Japanese supermarket chain Seiyu.

questions.text: The sportswear brand ASICS takes its name from a Latin saying about a sound mind in a sound what?
questions.fun_fact: Kihachiro Onitsuka founded the company in Kobe in 1949, at first as Onitsuka Co.

questions.text: Häagen-Dazs founder Reuben Mattus made up the brand's name to sound like it came from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The ice cream brand was started in the Bronx, New York City, and its early labels showed an outline map of the country.

questions.text: The Roomba, first introduced by iRobot in 2002, is a robot that does which household job?
questions.fun_fact: The Roomba's early prototypes were built using LEGO bricks.

questions.text: The software company Adobe is named after a what near co-founder John Warnock's home?
questions.fun_fact: Warnock and Charles Geschke founded Adobe in 1982; the creek runs through Los Altos, California.

questions.text: The Hills Hoist, a rotary clothes line, is a famous icon of backyards in which country?
questions.fun_fact: From 1945, Hills Hoists were made in Adelaide, South Australia, based on designs Lance Hill bought from inventor Gerhard 'Pop' Kaesler.

questions.text: At which university was Mark Zuckerberg a student when he launched Facebook in 2004?
questions.fun_fact: Zuckerberg coded the site, known as TheFacebook, in January 2004.

questions.text: Marcel Bich created the name of the Bic pen brand by dropping which letter from his surname?
questions.fun_fact: The Bic Cristal ballpoint became the company's first product under the Bic name, in 1950.

questions.text: Mary Anderson, who patented a windshield wiper in 1903, came from which US state?
questions.fun_fact: Her design was a hand-operated blade that cleared snow, ice or sleet from the windshield.

questions.text: Instagram's name blends 'instant camera' with which older message technology?
questions.fun_fact: Instagram launched in October 2010 and was first available only on Apple's iOS.

questions.text: Sony's name blends the Latin word 'sonus' with the slang 'sonny'. What does 'sonus' mean?
questions.fun_fact: Sony's co-founders were the engineer Masaru Ibuka and the businessman Akio Morita.

questions.text: Lincoln Logs, a building toy invented around 1916, were created by John Lloyd Wright, son of which famous architect?
questions.fun_fact: The toy's mold was based on the Imperial Hotel in Tokyo, whose foundation used interlocking log beams.

questions.text: In YouTube's first video, 'Me at the zoo', co-founder Jawed Karim stands in front of which animals?
questions.fun_fact: The 19-second clip was uploaded on April 23, 2005.

questions.text: Sega's name is short for which two words?
questions.fun_fact: Sega began in Honolulu in 1940 as Standard Games, supplying coin-operated machines to US military bases.

questions.text: The air-cushioned soles of Dr. Martens boots were developed by a doctor from which country?
questions.fun_fact: The 1460 boot's name records its first sale date, 1 April 1960; Märtens was a German Army doctor.

questions.text: A sundial tells the time using what?
questions.fun_fact: The earliest known sundials are shadow clocks from ancient Egypt and Babylon, dated to about 1500 BC.

questions.text: Which day of the week is named after the Norse thunder deity Thor?
questions.fun_fact: Most Romance languages name the day after Jupiter, the Roman counterpart of Thor.

questions.text: What shape is a standard stop sign in most countries?
questions.fun_fact: The octagon was standardized in the US in 1922; its unique shape lets drivers facing the back of the sign tell it is a stop sign.

questions.text: About how many weeks are there in a year?
questions.fun_fact: Japan has used a ten-day period called the jun alongside the seven-day week.

questions.text: Which unit of weight is made up of 16 ounces?
questions.fun_fact: The abbreviation 'lb' comes from libra, the Latin word for scales or balance.

questions.text: How many teaspoons are in a US tablespoon?
questions.fun_fact: An Australian tablespoon is larger, at 20 milliliters, which equals four of its teaspoons.

questions.text: On the Fahrenheit scale, at what temperature does water freeze?
questions.fun_fact: Fahrenheit placed 0 degrees at the freezing point of a mix of ice, water and salt.

questions.text: Which unit is used to measure the loudness of sound?
questions.fun_fact: A decibel is a tenth of a bel, a unit named after Alexander Graham Bell.

questions.text: How many items make up a 'baker's dozen'?
questions.fun_fact: The Oxford Dictionary of English traces it to bakers giving retailers a thirteenth loaf, the extra loaf being the retailer's profit.

questions.text: How many years are in a 'score', as in 'four score and seven years ago'?
questions.fun_fact: A 'score' is also used as a large, indefinite number, as in the newspaper headline 'scores of people'.

questions.text: In which unit is household electricity usually billed?
questions.fun_fact: One kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 megajoules of energy.

questions.text: In traditional painting, which two colors are mixed to make green?
questions.fun_fact: Color printing uses a different set of primaries: cyan, magenta and yellow inks.

questions.text: Which month of the year has the fewest days?
questions.fun_fact: In leap years February gains a 29th day, called the leap day.

questions.text: Which color sits between yellow and blue in a rainbow?
questions.fun_fact: Isaac Newton chose to name seven rainbow colors, perhaps by analogy with the seven notes of the musical scale.

questions.text: What does 'SPF' on a sunscreen bottle stand for?
questions.fun_fact: The SPF number mainly rates protection against UVB rays, the kind that cause sunburn.

questions.text: Which unit measures how much visible light a lamp gives out?
questions.fun_fact: One candela of light spread evenly over one steradian gives out exactly one lumen.

questions.text: What does a barometer measure?
questions.fun_fact: Italian scientist Evangelista Torricelli is usually credited with inventing the mercury barometer in the 1640s.

questions.text: Most TV remote controls send their signals using which kind of invisible light?
questions.fun_fact: Zenith's 1956 'Space Command' remote used ultrasonic sound instead of light.

questions.text: What does a pedometer count?
questions.fun_fact: Leonardo da Vinci envisioned a mechanical pedometer, a device with military uses.

questions.text: What does the 'W' in 'WC', a common sign for a toilet, stand for?
questions.fun_fact: Inventor Joseph Bramah began his career installing water closets based on Alexander Cumming's patented design of 1775.

questions.text: In a standard Western place setting, on which side of the plate does the dinner fork go?
questions.fun_fact: Knives and spoons go on the right, with the knife's blade turned toward the plate.

questions.text: In Japan, 'meishi' are exchanged with a formal ritual. What are they?
questions.fun_fact: The receiver takes a meishi with both hands, reads it carefully and bows.

questions.text: Which of these countries drives on the left side of the road?
questions.fun_fact: Left-hand traffic is also used in the UK, India, Australia and South Africa.

questions.text: In chess, which piece moves in an L-shape?
questions.fun_fact: Knights and pawns are the only chess pieces that can move from the starting position.

questions.text: On a standard US Monopoly board, which property costs the most to buy?
questions.fun_fact: The property names come from real streets in Atlantic City, New Jersey.

questions.text: What is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes called?
questions.fun_fact: The word combines the Japanese 'ori', meaning folding, with 'kami', meaning paper.

questions.text: On a standard six-sided die, opposite faces always add up to which number?
questions.fun_fact: Some of the oldest known dice were found at the Burnt City, an archeological site in Iran dated to about 2800 to 2500 BCE.

questions.text: The saying 'once in a blue moon' describes something that happens how often?
questions.fun_fact: A 'blue moon' is also the name given to a second full moon in a single calendar month.

questions.text: The radio distress call 'Mayday' comes from which language?
questions.fun_fact: It was proposed in the 1920s by a radio officer at Croydon Airport near London.

questions.text: On a standard analog clock, which hand is the shortest?
questions.fun_fact: The short hour hand makes two revolutions a day, while the long minute hand makes one every hour.

questions.text: Which household appliance did Josephine Cochrane invent in the 1880s?
questions.fun_fact: Her company was sold to KitchenAid in 1926, and KitchenAid is now part of Whirlpool.

questions.text: Which company's lab created the weak glue used on Post-it Notes?
questions.fun_fact: The first Post-it Notes were yellow because the lab next door had only yellow scrap paper.

questions.text: The word 'denim' is thought to come from a fabric made in which French city?
questions.fun_fact: Denim is a twill weave: the warp threads are usually dyed indigo while the weft threads are left white.

questions.text: Which kitchen appliance was invented after Percy Spencer saw a candy bar melt near radar equipment?
questions.fun_fact: Raytheon's first microwave oven, the 1947 Radarange, stood almost 1.8 meters tall and weighed about 340 kilograms.

questions.text: Which household machine did British engineer Hubert Cecil Booth invent in 1901?
questions.fun_fact: Booth's huge horse-drawn machine, nicknamed 'Puffing Billy', was offered as part of a cleaning service.

questions.text: The first bristle toothbrush resembling the modern one, made with hog bristles, was found in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Earlier, people used chew sticks, twigs with frayed ends; the oldest known were found in Sumer, around 3500 BC.

questions.text: The kilogram was originally defined in 1795 as the mass of one liter of which liquid?
questions.fun_fact: Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined using the Planck constant instead of a physical object.

questions.text: How many feet are in a statute mile?
questions.fun_fact: The 5,280-foot mile was fixed in England by an act of Parliament in 1593.

questions.text: How many pounds make up one stone, a unit still used for body weight in the UK?
questions.fun_fact: The unit gets its name from the actual stones once used as weights on market scales.

questions.text: Which traditional unit, equal to four inches, is used to measure a horse's height?
questions.fun_fact: A horse is measured from the ground to the withers, the highest non-variable point of its skeleton.

questions.text: Which ISO paper size measures about 210 by 297 millimeters?
questions.fun_fact: Each A size is half the area of the next larger one, and all share a side ratio of the square root of 2.

questions.text: A ship's speed of one knot equals one nautical mile per what?
questions.fun_fact: Until the mid-19th century, ship speed was measured with a chip log, a wooden panel on a line let out behind the vessel.

questions.text: How many small calories are in one food Calorie (kilocalorie) on a nutrition label?
questions.fun_fact: One small calorie is the energy needed to warm one gram of water by one degree Celsius.

questions.text: Which metric unit of area equals 10,000 square meters?
questions.fun_fact: One hectare is about 2.47 acres.

questions.text: In CMYK color printing, the ink marked 'K' is which color?
questions.fun_fact: The K comes from 'key plate'; black ink also saves colored ink and gives more consistent dark tones than mixing C, M and Y.

questions.text: What color are aircraft flight recorders, the so-called 'black boxes', actually painted?
questions.fun_fact: The 'black box' name comes from World War II, when secret British electronic gear in aircraft was housed in non-reflective black boxes.

questions.text: Which month is named after Janus, the two-faced Roman deity?
questions.fun_fact: Numa Pompilius is said to have added January and February to the Roman calendar around 713 BC.

questions.text: In which year did the Gregorian calendar reform begin?
questions.fun_fact: Britain and the British Empire, including what became the eastern United States, did not adopt it until 1752.

questions.text: Which Roman leader introduced the Julian calendar in 45 BC?
questions.fun_fact: To realign the calendar, the year 46 BC was stretched to 445 days, known as the 'year of confusion'.

questions.text: The French day name 'mardi', meaning Tuesday, honors which Roman deity?
questions.fun_fact: English Tuesday honors Týr, whom the Germanic peoples equated with the Roman Mars.

questions.text: Which animal starts the 12-year Chinese zodiac cycle?
questions.fun_fact: In the legend, the Jade Emperor held a race, and the winner, the rat, received the first year of the cycle.

questions.text: The 'Ides of March' falls on which date?
questions.fun_fact: In the Roman calendar the Ides fell on the 15th in March, May, July and October, and on the 13th in other months.

questions.text: In 'a.m.' and 'p.m.', what does the 'a.m.' stand for?
questions.fun_fact: Because noon is neither before nor after midday, writing '12 a.m.' or '12 p.m.' often causes confusion.

questions.text: The universal recycling symbol was designed in 1970 for a contest tied to which event?
questions.fun_fact: Gary Anderson, then a university student, won the design contest with his three-arrow symbol.

questions.text: What do Scoville heat units measure?
questions.fun_fact: The scale is named after American pharmacist Wilbur Scoville, whose 1912 method relied on a subjective taste test.

questions.text: Which metal is traditionally linked to a 25th wedding anniversary?
questions.fun_fact: Linking anniversaries to precious metals is documented in Germanic countries since the 1500s.

questions.text: Which component generates the microwaves inside a microwave oven?
questions.fun_fact: A cavity magnetron introduced in England in 1940 improved on earlier versions and was used in early radar systems.

questions.text: Which metal is used for the filament in a traditional incandescent light bulb?
questions.fun_fact: In 1906 William Coolidge developed 'ductile tungsten' at General Electric, which began selling bulbs with tungsten filaments by 1911.

questions.text: The Māori greeting called the 'hongi' involves pressing which parts of two people together?
questions.fun_fact: In the hongi, people exchange the 'ha', the breath of life, in a symbolic show of unity.

questions.text: At midnight on New Year's Eve in Spain, people traditionally eat how many grapes?
questions.fun_fact: Each grape is said to stand for one of the twelve coming months of the year.

questions.text: In a traditional Japanese home, what is the entrance area where shoes are removed called?
questions.fun_fact: The genkan also serves as a spot for brief visits by people who are not invited further into the house.

questions.text: In Argentina, friends often pass around a shared gourd of which herbal drink?
questions.fun_fact: Everyone drinks from the same gourd through the same wooden or metal straw, called a bombilla in Spanish.

questions.text: On 'Dagen H' in 1967, which country switched from driving on the left to the right?
questions.fun_fact: All non-essential traffic was banned from the roads from 01:00 to 06:00 that Sunday morning.

questions.text: Which toy did naval engineer Richard James create in 1943 after a tension spring fell off a shelf?
questions.fun_fact: The first 400 Slinkys sold in 90 minutes at a demonstration at the Gimbels department store in Philadelphia.

questions.text: Which board game began as Elizabeth Magie's 'The Landlord's Game', patented in 1904?
questions.fun_fact: Magie created it to show that an economy rewarding individuals is better than one where monopolies hold all the wealth.

questions.text: The spades, hearts, diamonds and clubs used in English-speaking countries are the traditional suits of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Much of central Europe uses different suits: acorns, leaves, hearts and bells.

questions.text: The 'wai', a slight bow with the palms pressed together, is a traditional greeting in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It has its origin in the Indian Añjali Mudrā, as do the Indian namaste and the Burmese mingalaba.

questions.text: The strategy board game Go was first played in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The number of legal positions on a Go board is far greater than the number of atoms in the observable universe.

questions.text: Which toy became the first ever advertised on American television, in 1952?
questions.fun_fact: It first came as a set of plastic parts to push into a real potato or other vegetable.

questions.text: Which toy company popularized the plastic hula hoop in 1958?
questions.fun_fact: The hoop was named after the Hawaiian hula dance.

questions.text: Which American mechanic patented the safety pin in 1849?
questions.fun_fact: Hunt sold the patent for $400, then used some of the money to repay a $15 debt to a friend.

questions.text: In the 1890s Whitcomb Judson patented a 'clasp locker' that evolved into which everyday fastener?
questions.fun_fact: The name 'zipper' came from the B. F. Goodrich company, which used it for its rubber boots in the 1920s.

questions.text: Which scientist invented the vacuum flask in 1892?
questions.fun_fact: Dewar never patented his flask; German men who found its commercial use named it Thermos and claimed the trademark.

questions.text: Which American inventor patented a machine in 1871 that made flat-bottomed paper bags?
questions.fun_fact: She was granted at least 27 patents, and an obituary called her a 'woman Edison'.

questions.text: In which US state was sliced bread first sold, in 1928?
questions.fun_fact: Inventor Otto Rohwedder's first bread-slicer prototype was destroyed in a fire; his fully working machine was ready only in 1928.

questions.text: Which English courtier, a godson of Elizabeth I, described an early flush toilet in a 1596 book?
questions.fun_fact: He called his toilet the Ajax, a pun on 'jakes', then a slang word for toilet.

questions.text: The earliest recorded evidence of soap-making, from about 2800 BC, comes from which ancient civilization?
questions.fun_fact: Soap is made by saponification, in which an alkaline solution such as lye turns fats and oils into soap.

questions.text: Which English chemist invented the first commercially successful friction match in the 1820s?
questions.fun_fact: Walker declined to take out a patent, saying he hoped the invention would be a benefit to the public.

questions.text: Theophilus Van Kannel, who patented the revolving door in 1888, lived in which US city?
questions.fun_fact: A revolving door lets people pass without letting much wind in, which helps save heating costs.

questions.text: Table forks first became widely used in Western Europe in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Thomas Coryat described the fork in English in 1611, but it was long viewed as an unmanly Italian affectation.

questions.text: The square-socket Robertson screw drive was invented in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Peter L. Robertson's 1908 breakthrough was a socket shape that let screw heads be cold formed easily.

questions.text: Which pioneering aviator's complaint about pocket watches inspired Louis Cartier to create the Santos wristwatch?
questions.fun_fact: The Santos was Cartier's first men's wristwatch, created by Louis Cartier in 1911.

questions.text: The kaleidoscope was invented by a scientist from which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its inventor, David Brewster, named it from Greek words meaning 'beautiful form' and 'to see'.

questions.text: The Bluetooth logo combines the runic initials of which Danish king?
questions.fun_fact: Harald is remembered for uniting Danish tribes, which inspired the name for a technology that unites devices.

questions.text: In which year did Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patent their copper-riveted work pants?
questions.fun_fact: Davis, a tailor in Reno, Nevada, added copper rivets to the pocket corners to stop them from tearing.

questions.text: Chicle, an early chewing gum base, is tapped from trees of which genus?
questions.fun_fact: Chicle was well known to the Aztecs and the Maya, and tapping it resembles the tapping of latex from rubber trees.

questions.text: The French Republican Calendar of 1793 grouped days into weeks of how many days?
questions.fun_fact: Napoleon declared the calendar abolished, and its use ended on 1 January 1806.

questions.text: From which century does the first documented European hourglass date?
questions.fun_fact: A much older timekeeper, the water clock, is known to have existed in Babylon and Egypt as early as the 16th century BCE.

questions.text: The word 'calendar' comes from the Roman 'calends', which was which day of each month?
questions.fun_fact: On that day the pontiffs announced the number of days until the next month, and debtors had to pay off their debts.

questions.text: Which month was originally called Sextilis, Latin for 'sixth'?
questions.fun_fact: It was renamed for Emperor Augustus in 8 BC, reportedly because several of his great triumphs fell in that month.

questions.text: Ionization smoke detectors usually contain a tiny amount of which radioactive element?
questions.fun_fact: The americium's alpha particles ionize the air in a small chamber; smoke disrupts the resulting flow of electricity and sets off the alarm.

questions.text: On a multi-speed bicycle, which part moves the chain between sprockets?
questions.fun_fact: The French word it comes from literally means 'derailer', and its first recorded use was in 1930.

questions.text: In Georgia's traditional 'supra' feast, who is the toastmaster called?
questions.fun_fact: The term tamada is of Circassian origin and does not appear in historical records until the 19th century.

questions.text: In Scotland, 'first-footing' is a custom of which celebration?
questions.fun_fact: The first-foot is often a tall, dark-haired man who brings gifts such as coal, shortbread and whisky.

questions.text: The name of the board game Ludo comes from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Alfred Coller marketed it as 'Ludo' in England in 1896 and later sold it as 'Royal Ludo'.

questions.text: John Spilsbury, credited with commercializing jigsaw puzzles around 1760, made them to teach which subject?
questions.fun_fact: He mounted a map on wood and cut along the borders of countries to create the pieces.

questions.text: In which year was the first US patent for a can opener granted?
questions.fun_fact: England's first can-opener patent came earlier, in 1855, even though tin cans were in use decades before.

questions.text: The number puzzle Sudoku was first published in 1979 in a US magazine under which name?
questions.fun_fact: The Japanese publisher Nikoli later popularized it under the name Sudoku.

questions.text: In which city's newspaper did the word 'OK' first appear in print, in 1839?
questions.fun_fact: Most reference works trace it to 'oll korrect', a joke misspelling of 'all correct' from a Boston fad for comic abbreviations.

questions.text: The name of the stacking game Jenga comes from a Swahili word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Leslie Scott launched Jenga at the London Toy Fair in January 1983 and sold it through her own company.

questions.text: What shape is a yield sign in most countries?
questions.fun_fact: Denmark introduced a triangular yield sign in 1937, in red and white to match the Danish flag.

questions.text: What do British speakers usually call the tool that Americans call a wrench?
questions.fun_fact: A 'spanner in the works' is called a 'monkey wrench' in US English.

questions.text: What do the letters in 'DIY' stand for?
questions.fun_fact: The phrase 'do-it-yourself' has been linked to consumers since at least 1912, mainly for home improvement.

questions.text: Which emergency number is used across nearly all European Union countries?
questions.fun_fact: On GSM phones, 112 can be dialed even when the phone is locked, or in some countries with no SIM card.

questions.text: Chopsticks first came into use in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The first chopsticks were used for cooking and serving food, not as eating utensils.

questions.text: Which kitchen tool, full of small holes, is used to drain pasta?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Latin 'colum', meaning sieve.

questions.text: What does a weather vane show?
questions.fun_fact: The Tower of the Winds in Athens once had a bronze weather vane in the shape of Triton, from about 50 BC.

questions.text: In British English, tic-tac-toe is usually called what?
questions.fun_fact: With best play from both sides, the game always ends in a draw.

questions.text: How many cards are in a standard deck of playing cards, not counting jokers?
questions.fun_fact: Many countries use German, Italian, Spanish or Swiss-suited cards instead of the French-suited deck.

questions.text: A traditional wedding rhyme asks for something old, new, borrowed and something of which color?
questions.fun_fact: In the custom, a British silver sixpence is a symbol of prosperity.

questions.text: Many tall buildings in Western countries skip which number when numbering their floors?
questions.fun_fact: Skipped floors are often relabeled, for example as level 14, as '12A' or as 'M'.

questions.text: On which date is Valentine's Day celebrated?
questions.fun_fact: In ancient Rome, the festival of Lupercalia was held from 13 to 15 February.

questions.text: Which animal is a white-striped pedestrian crossing named after?
questions.fun_fact: The first zebra crossing in the world was installed in Slough, England, in 1951.

questions.text: Which day of the week is named after the Roman god Saturn?
questions.fun_fact: West Germanic peoples borrowed the Roman name directly, as no Germanic god matched Saturn.

questions.text: Each 25 January, Scots hold suppers to honor which national poet?
questions.fun_fact: The first Burns supper was held by the poet's friends at Burns Cottage in Ayrshire in 1801.

questions.text: What does a whistling kettle signal?
questions.fun_fact: The sound comes from steam passing through a device on the spout and making it vibrate.

questions.text: What is the British name for the board game Americans call checkers?
questions.fun_fact: The name 'draughts' comes from the verb 'to draw' or 'to move'.

questions.text: Before blowing out birthday candles, people traditionally do what?
questions.fun_fact: A German count's 1746 party had a giant cake with candles stuck in it.

questions.text: What do people usually save in a piggy bank?
questions.fun_fact: The oldest Western money box found is a 2nd-century BC temple-shaped one from Priene in Asia Minor.

questions.text: Which toy that spools down and back up a string appears on ancient Greek vases?
questions.fun_fact: The word 'yo-yo' probably comes from the Ilocano language of the Philippines.

questions.text: In Britain, the card game Americans call solitaire is traditionally known as what?
questions.fun_fact: 'Patience' is the earliest recorded name for these games in British and American sources.

questions.text: A US gallon is closest to how many liters?
questions.fun_fact: Until 1976, the British imperial gallon was defined as the volume of 10 pounds of water.

questions.text: The cubit, an ancient unit of length, is based on the distance from the elbow to which point?
questions.fun_fact: The forearm is still used in hedgelaying to set the gap between stakes.

questions.text: The word 'mile' comes from a Latin phrase for a thousand of what?
questions.fun_fact: A Roman pace was counted as the distance between two steps of the same foot.

questions.text: Knocking on wood is a custom meant to avoid doing what?
questions.fun_fact: Germanic belief held that three Norns sent fate up into the universe through a tree.

questions.text: A fathom, used to measure water depth, equals how many feet?
questions.fun_fact: It was originally the span of a man's outstretched arms.

questions.text: Playing cards were most likely invented in which country around the 9th century?
questions.fun_fact: The invention is linked to woodblock printing technology of the Tang dynasty.

questions.text: Which month began the year in the earliest Roman calendar?
questions.fun_fact: Its name honors Mars, whom the Romans counted as the father of Romulus and Remus.

questions.text: In the US customary system, a cup is half of which unit?
questions.fun_fact: A US cup of brewed coffee is usually just 4 fluid ounces.

questions.text: Before pumpkins, Halloween lanterns in parts of Britain and Ireland were hollowed from which vegetable?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from lights flickering over peat bogs, also called will-o'-the-wisps.

questions.text: In Groundhog Day lore, a groundhog seeing its shadow means how many more weeks of winter?
questions.fun_fact: The tradition came from German lands, where a badger was watched and four weeks were predicted.

questions.text: In France and Italy, a classic 1 April prank is sticking a paper what on someone's back?
questions.fun_fact: French poet Eloy d'Amerval wrote about the April prank in 1508, possibly its first mention.

questions.text: In Spain and Latin America, which animal collects children's lost baby teeth?
questions.fun_fact: The character first appeared in an 1894 tale by Luis Coloma for King Alfonso XIII.

questions.text: Furoshiki are traditional Japanese cloths used for what?
questions.fun_fact: The name means 'bath spread', from visitors who wrapped their belongings in cloth at bathhouses.

questions.text: On pencil grades, what does the 'B' in 'HB' commonly stand for?
questions.fun_fact: HB is the standard writing grade, while F is usually taken to mean fineness.

questions.text: What is the small plastic or metal sheath on the end of a shoelace called?
questions.fun_fact: Aglets were once made of metal, glass or stone, and many were ornamental.

questions.text: The word 'sideburns' is a twist on the name of which American Civil War general?
questions.fun_fact: Originally 'burnsides', the style linked thick side whiskers with a moustache and a clean chin.

questions.text: The necktie traces back to mercenaries from which country serving in France in the 1600s?
questions.fun_fact: Their neckerchiefs became known as 'cravats'; International Necktie Day is each 18 October.

questions.text: Mancala games are played by sowing what into pits or holes?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Arabic 'naqala', meaning 'to move'.

questions.text: What did the letters in the original 1906 distress signal SOS stand for?
options: Nothing; it was just a pattern
questions.fun_fact: SOS began in German maritime radio regulations that took effect on 1 April 1905.

questions.text: Which inventor is credited with popularizing 'hello' as a telephone greeting?
questions.fun_fact: Before telephones, greetings often named the time of day, such as 'good morning'.

questions.text: The word 'asterisk' comes from the Greek for what?
questions.fun_fact: Scholars at the Library of Alexandria developed the mark over 2,000 years ago.

questions.text: The word 'salary' comes from a Latin word linked to which substance?
questions.fun_fact: A popular claim that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is baseless.

questions.text: Which polished metal was used for mirrors in Mesopotamia from about 4000 BCE?
questions.fun_fact: Mirrors from ancient Egypt date from around 3000 BCE.

questions.text: Fika is a Swedish tradition of taking a break for what?
questions.fun_fact: After arriving in the 1680s, coffee was first sold in Swedish pharmacies as a medicinal product.

questions.text: The Wellington boot is named after which British general and statesman?
questions.fun_fact: He asked his shoemaker to modify the Hessian boot, a style of military footwear.

questions.text: Bloomers, a divided garment for women, are named after which 19th-century activist?
questions.fun_fact: Wearers called the style the 'reform costume' or 'American dress'; 'bloomers' was a derogatory name.

questions.text: The joker was created in the United States as a trump card for which card game?
questions.fun_fact: Since the 1950s, German and Austrian packs have usually included three jokers, for German Rummy.

questions.text: English shoe sizes are still based on which unit, equal to a third of an inch?
questions.fun_fact: A statute of 1300 set three dry, round barleycorns as the basis of the inch.

questions.text: Under the ISO 8601 standard, which weekday is the first day of the week?
questions.fun_fact: Virtually all cultures treat Saturday, Sunday or Monday as the first day of the week.

questions.text: One of the oldest known buttons, a shell about 5,000 years old, was found at Mohenjo-daro in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Many early buttons were ornaments or seals rather than fasteners.

questions.text: High-heeled shoes spread from the 10th-century riding boots of the cavalry of which empire?
questions.fun_fact: Persian envoys of Abbas the Great brought modern high heels to Europe in the early 1600s.

questions.text: Which French physicist invented the steam digester, forerunner of the pressure cooker, in 1679?
questions.fun_fact: Papin presented it to the Royal Society of London in 1681 and was later elected a member.

questions.text: In shogi, what can a player do with captured pieces?
options: Drop them back in as their own
Swap them for a lost piece
questions.fun_fact: Black and White only label the sides; all the pieces are the same color.

questions.text: A pure graphite deposit found in 1565 in what is now which English county made the pencil practical?
questions.fun_fact: The deposit, at Borrowdale, was so valuable that the mines were guarded and flooded between uses to prevent theft.

questions.text: The name 'grandfather clock' comes from an 1876 song by which American songwriter?
questions.fun_fact: Work wrote it after hearing a story about a tall clock at a hotel in Piercebridge, England.

questions.text: On a clothing care label, which shape stands for bleaching?
questions.fun_fact: In the US and Japan, other icons are used for natural or line drying.

questions.text: Which English writer popularized the expression 'red herring' in 1807?
questions.fun_fact: He told of dragging a smoked herring to throw hounds off a rabbit's trail.

questions.text: Frenchman Philippe de Girard had which British merchant take out the 1810 patent for tin-can food preservation?
questions.fun_fact: By 1813 canned food was being made for the Royal Navy at a factory in London.

questions.text: In which US city was the first yield sign erected, in 1950?
questions.fun_fact: Police officer Clinton Riggs designed it, at first in the shape of a keystone.

questions.text: A 'Hobson's choice' is named after a livery stable owner in which English city?
questions.fun_fact: Hobson had about 40 horses but made customers take the one nearest the door.

questions.text: Which computer scientist is credited with proposing the first smiley emoticon, in 1982?
questions.fun_fact: He proposed the smiley on a Carnegie Mellon bulletin board as a label for 'attempted humor'.

questions.text: Who patented the first adjustable mechanical alarm clock, in 1847?
questions.fun_fact: Levi Hutchins made the first American alarm clock in 1787; it rang only at 4 a.m.

questions.text: The first corkscrew patent, granted in 1795, went to which Englishman?
questions.fun_fact: His design added a disk, the 'Henshall Button', between the worm and the shank.

questions.text: Which Austrian maker of surgical instruments popularized the snow globe and won its first patent?
questions.fun_fact: A snow globe with a man holding an umbrella was shown at the 1878 Paris Exposition.

questions.text: Which scientist invented a precursor of the electric doorbell around 1831?
questions.fun_fact: William Murdoch installed a compressed-air doorbell in his Birmingham house in 1817.

questions.text: Which German city was an early center of thimble making in the 15th century?
questions.fun_fact: Elizabeth I is said to have given a lady-in-waiting a thimble set with precious stones.

questions.text: Japanese onigiri rice balls are usually wrapped in which dried seaweed?
questions.fun_fact: Traditional onigiri fillings are often salty or sour.

questions.text: Balsamic vinegar is made wholly or partly from the must, or crushed juice, of which fruit?
questions.fun_fact: The story of balsamic vinegar began in the 11th century in the city of Modena.

questions.text: The name of the Italian dairy product ricotta literally means what?
questions.fun_fact: Ricotta is made from the whey left over from making other cheeses, using sheep, cow, goat or buffalo milk.

questions.text: Which Italian dessert of coffee-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone has a name meaning "pick me up"?
questions.fun_fact: Tiramisu first appeared in an Italian dictionary in 1980 and in English in 1982.

questions.text: The cooking method sous vide gets its name from French words meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: French chef Georges Pralus adopted sous vide in 1974 for the Restaurant Troisgros in Roanne, France.

questions.text: The French word that gave us "sauté" means what, in reference to tossing food in the pan?
questions.fun_fact: Sautéing uses a small amount of oil or fat in a shallow pan over relatively high heat.

questions.text: What inside a popcorn kernel turns to steam and makes it burst when heated?
questions.fun_fact: A popped kernel expands to 20 to 50 times its original size.

questions.text: Muesli was first developed around 1900 as a dish for patients in a hospital in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Its creator was the physician Maximilian Bircher-Benner; Müesli is a Swiss German diminutive of Mus, meaning "mush".

questions.text: The Louisiana stew gumbo is often thickened with filé powder, made from the dried, ground leaves of which tree?
questions.fun_fact: Gumbo is often grouped by its thickener, either okra or filé powder.

questions.text: The French flavor base mirepoix is a mix of diced onions, carrots and which other vegetable?
questions.fun_fact: The traditional ratio is two parts onion to one part each of carrot and celery.

questions.text: Which round, yeast-leavened flatbread, often with an interior pocket, is also known as pocket bread?
questions.fun_fact: Pita is also known as Greek bread, Arabic bread, Syrian bread and Lebanese bread.

questions.text: Skewered, grilled satay is most commonly served with a sauce based on which nut?
questions.fun_fact: Besides chicken and beef, satay can be made with goat, pork or seafood, and is grilled over charcoal.

questions.text: A roux, used to thicken sauces, is made by cooking flour with what?
questions.fun_fact: Roux is typically made from equal parts flour and fat by weight and cooked to the desired level of brownness.

questions.text: The word "chai", as in chai latte, means what in Hindi?
questions.fun_fact: The term chai came from the Chinese word for tea, cha, through Hindustani.

questions.text: Cannoli, tube-shaped pastries filled with sweet ricotta, are a specialty of which Italian island?
questions.fun_fact: Cannoli were historically a treat during Carnival season before becoming a year-round staple.
