questions.text: Around 1810, which country's government awarded a prize to Nicolas Appert for his method of preserving food?
questions.fun_fact: The award had been offered to find a cheap method to preserve large amounts of food for military rations.

questions.text: The Granny Smith apple began as a chance seedling in which country?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Maria Ann Smith, who propagated the seedling, and dates to 1868.

questions.text: Tarte Tatin is a tart in which fruit is caramelized in butter and sugar. Which fruit is used most often?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the Tatin sisters, who served it as the signature dish of their hotel.

questions.text: Brazilian pão de queijo cheese bread is made with flour from which starchy root instead of wheat?
questions.fun_fact: Pão de queijo is a traditional recipe from the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais.

questions.text: The sweet orange is a hybrid of the mandarin and which other citrus fruit?
questions.fun_fact: The maternal line of the sweet orange is that of the pomelo, according to its chloroplast genome.

questions.text: Eggs poached in a spiced sauce of tomatoes, peppers and onion make which North African and Middle Eastern dish?
questions.fun_fact: Shakshouka is commonly spiced with cumin, paprika and cayenne pepper.

questions.text: A Spanish tortilla is an omelet made with eggs and which vegetable?
questions.fun_fact: The first known written reference to the tortilla in Spanish is in a Navarrese document from 1817.

questions.text: Camembert, the soft cow's milk cheese, was first made in a village in which region of France?
questions.fun_fact: Camembert was reportedly first made in 1791 by the Normandy farmer Marie Harel.

questions.text: What do bees mainly gather from flowers to make honey?
questions.fun_fact: Bees also make honey from honeydew, a sugary secretion of aphids.

questions.text: In botanical terms, bananas are classified as which type of fruit?
questions.fun_fact: In some countries, cooking bananas are called plantains to tell them apart from dessert bananas.

questions.text: The Italian bread ciabatta is named after which everyday item?
questions.fun_fact: Ciabatta was created in 1982 by a baker in Adria, Veneto, in response to the popularity of French baguettes.

questions.text: Croissants get flaky layers because the dough is folded repeatedly with butter. What is such dough called?
questions.fun_fact: The croissant was inspired by the shape of the Austrian kipferl.

questions.text: One theory traces the word "ketchup" to a Hokkien term for the brine of which pickled food?
questions.fun_fact: Another theory links ketchup to the Malay word kicap, originally meaning "soy sauce".

questions.text: Kobe beef comes from Wagyu cattle raised in which Japanese prefecture?
questions.fun_fact: Kobe beef comes from the Tajima strain of Japanese Black cattle.

questions.text: Spanish churros, ridged fried snacks, are made by piping which kind of dough into hot oil?
questions.fun_fact: Churros are often eaten for breakfast dipped in coffee, or in hot chocolate as an afternoon snack.

questions.text: Which creamy sauce usually forms the top layer of Greek moussaka?
questions.fun_fact: The modern Greek version of moussaka was created in the 1920s by Nikolaos Tselementes.

questions.text: Polenta, the Italian dish that can be cooled, sliced and then fried or grilled, is boiled from what?
questions.fun_fact: Polenta was historically made from other grains.

questions.text: Ghee, widely used in South Asian cooking, is a type of what?
questions.fun_fact: Ghee originated in the Indian subcontinent.

questions.text: Panettone, a sweet bread usually prepared for Christmas, is associated with which Italian city?
questions.fun_fact: Panettone is both a sweet bread and a fruitcake, and it is also baked in Eritrea.

questions.text: Swiss chocolatier Daniel Peter is credited with inventing which type of chocolate in the 1870s?
questions.fun_fact: Peter made it by adding powdered milk to chocolate; he was a neighbor of Henri Nestlé in Vevey.

questions.text: Lassi, a drink from the Indian subcontinent, is made by blending water and spices with which dairy product?
questions.fun_fact: In Punjab, where lassi originated, the yogurt is traditionally made from water buffalo milk.

questions.text: Paneer, a fresh non-melting South Asian cheese, is made by curdling milk with an acid, such as which?
questions.fun_fact: Paneer's origins are unknown; hypotheses include a Persian origin or a Portuguese introduction of acid-set cheese in the 17th century.

questions.text: What is deglazing in cooking?
options: Coating a pan with a layer of oil
Cooling a hot pan with cold water
Dissolving browned residue in a pan
questions.fun_fact: The sauce made from the browned bits is called fond, the French word for "base" or "foundation".

questions.text: Which Chinese spice mixture commonly contains star anise, cloves, Chinese cinnamon, Sichuan pepper and fennel seeds?
questions.fun_fact: The five flavors of the spices reflect the five traditional Chinese elements.

questions.text: Japanese mochi rice cakes are made by pounding steamed rice of which type?
questions.fun_fact: Mochi is traditionally made in a ceremony called mochitsuki.

questions.text: Tahini, the Middle Eastern seed butter, is made from ground what?
questions.fun_fact: The most common kind uses hulled seeds; unhulled seeds make a slightly bitter but more nutritious paste.

questions.text: In Italian, what does "macchiato", as in caffè macchiato, mean?
questions.fun_fact: A caffè macchiato is an espresso with a small amount of milk, usually foamed.

questions.text: The Italian dessert panna cotta has a name that literally means what?
questions.fun_fact: It is sweetened cream thickened with gelatin and molded, and may be flavored with coffee or vanilla.

questions.text: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil, an acid such as vinegar, and which main ingredient?
questions.fun_fact: Mayonnaise forms the base of other sauces, including tartar sauce, remoulade and ranch dressing.

questions.text: Onions, garlic, leeks and chives all belong to which plant genus?
questions.fun_fact: Scallions and shallots are also alliums with a long history of cultivation as food.

questions.text: What does the French kitchen term "mise en place" mean?
questions.fun_fact: It refers to the setup required before cooking and is often used in professional kitchens.

questions.text: Danish smørrebrød, an open-faced sandwich, is traditionally built on which dense, dark bread?
questions.fun_fact: Smørrebrød is topped with cold cuts, meat or fish, cheese or spreads, plus garnishes.

questions.text: Coffee beans are really seeds from a fruit commonly called a coffee what?
questions.fun_fact: Unlike a cherry, which usually has one pit, the coffee fruit most commonly holds two seeds with their flat sides together.

questions.text: After briefly boiling vegetables in the technique called blanching, cooks usually plunge them into what to stop the cooking?
questions.fun_fact: Plunging blanched food into cold water to halt cooking is known as shocking or refreshing.

questions.text: The tiny "seeds" on the outside of a strawberry are actually what?
questions.fun_fact: The garden strawberry was first bred in Brittany, France, in the 1750s.

questions.text: Which liquid ingredient reacts with baking soda to raise traditional Irish soda bread?
questions.fun_fact: Soda bread was developed in the early to mid-1800s, soon after bicarbonate of soda became available as a leavening agent.

questions.text: Takoyaki, the Japanese snack of batter balls, is typically filled with pieces of which sea animal?
questions.fun_fact: A street vendor named Tomekichi Endo is credited with inventing takoyaki in Osaka in 1935.

questions.text: Cashew trees are native to which continent?
questions.fun_fact: Portuguese explorers met cashews in the 16th century and spread them to India and other tropical regions.

questions.text: Poke, a dish of diced raw fish tossed in sauce, takes its name from which language?
questions.fun_fact: Poke means "to slice" or "cut crosswise into pieces"; it began as cut-offs from the catch, eaten raw with sea salt.

questions.text: The hard, nutty cheese Gruyère is named after a town in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Gruyère gained protected AOC status in 2001, which became AOP in 2013.

questions.text: The Italian cooking term "al dente", used for pasta, literally means what?
questions.fun_fact: The term also extends to firmly cooked vegetables.

questions.text: Gazpacho, a cold soup of raw blended vegetables, is also called by the name of which Spanish region?
questions.fun_fact: Gazpacho is both a cold soup and a drink; related dishes such as salmorejo and ajoblanco are often considered variants of it.

questions.text: Darjeeling tea comes from which Indian state?
questions.fun_fact: Tea was first planted in the Darjeeling area in 1841 by Archibald Campbell.

questions.text: Which Italian hard cheese, often grated over pasta, is aged for at least 12 months?
questions.fun_fact: The cheese is named after the Italian provinces of Parma and Reggio Emilia.

questions.text: Bouillabaisse, a traditional Provençal fish soup, originated in which French port city?
questions.fun_fact: It was originally made by fishermen from bony rockfish that they could not sell to restaurants or markets.

questions.text: Botanically, what type of fruit is a peppercorn?
questions.fun_fact: Black pepper comes from the still-green, unripe drupes, which are cooked briefly in hot water before being dried.

questions.text: Madeleines, small French sponge cakes, are baked in molds of which distinctive shape?
questions.fun_fact: Marcel Proust's memory of a madeleine dipped in tea made "Proustian" a word for something that evokes a forgotten memory.

questions.text: Pad thai, the Thai street-food dish, is made with which kind of stir-fried noodles?
questions.fun_fact: Stir-fried rice noodles reached Thailand from China centuries ago, but pad thai itself was created in the 20th century.

questions.text: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes and chili peppers all spread worldwide from which region?
questions.fun_fact: Old World crops such as rice, wheat and sugar cane spread the other way and became important in the New World.

questions.text: Bibimbap, a bowl of rice topped with seasoned vegetables and chili paste, is a dish from which cuisine?
questions.fun_fact: The name means "mixed rice": bibim means mixing and bap is cooked rice.

questions.text: Maize was domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from a wild grass called what?
questions.fun_fact: Native Americans planted maize with beans and squashes in the Three Sisters polyculture.

questions.text: White chocolate is made from sugar, milk solids and which ingredient from the cacao bean?
questions.fun_fact: It is ivory in color because it lacks the non-fat cocoa solids that darken other chocolate.

questions.text: Which Italian dish is made of wide, flat pasta sheets stacked in layers with fillings and sauce?
questions.fun_fact: Lasagna originated in Italy during the Middle Ages.

questions.text: Worcestershire sauce was invented in the first half of the 19th century by two men of which profession?
questions.fun_fact: It has been a generic term since 1876, when an English court ruled that Lea & Perrins did not own a trademark for the name.

questions.text: Brown sugar gets its color from the presence of what?
questions.fun_fact: It may be unrefined or partially refined sugar, or refined sugar with molasses added back.

questions.text: Mascarpone, the soft Italian dairy product, is made by heating which ingredient until it thickens?
questions.fun_fact: It is technically not a cheese, because it is made without rennet.

questions.text: The pasta name vermicelli comes from an Italian word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Vermicelli is round in section, like spaghetti, but usually thinner in English-speaking regions.

questions.text: Kombucha is a fizzy fermented drink made from sweetened what?
questions.fun_fact: It is fermented by a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast, called a SCOBY, often nicknamed a "mother" or "mushroom".

questions.text: What is the name of the process of soaking and cooking maize in an alkaline solution, used to make masa dough?
questions.fun_fact: Plain maize flour cannot form a dough with water, but nixtamalized maize can; the alkaline solution is usually limewater.

questions.text: Coffea canephora is more commonly sold under which name?
questions.fun_fact: Robusta has almost double the caffeine of arabica and is less susceptible to pests.

questions.text: Mexican tacos al pastor are based on a spit-roasted dish brought by Lebanese immigrants. Which dish?
questions.fun_fact: Al pastor combines the shawarma method with a traditional Mexican marinade called adobada.

questions.text: Skyr, a thick cultured dairy product with the texture of strained yogurt, is a tradition of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Skyr can be classified as a fresh sour milk cheese, though it is eaten like yogurt.

questions.text: Which coffee drink is made by adding hot water to a shot of espresso?
questions.fun_fact: The drink typically uses espresso and hot water in a ratio of 1:3 to 1:4.

questions.text: Which Italian word, meaning "frozen", is the everyday name for ice cream in Italy?
questions.fun_fact: Gelato typically contains 20 to 35 percent air and less butterfat than other frozen desserts.

questions.text: Tempeh, a cake of fermented soybeans, is a traditional food of which country?
questions.fun_fact: Tempeh is made by a natural culturing and controlled fermentation process that binds the soybeans into a cake.

questions.text: Commercially produced dry pasta is made almost entirely from which species of wheat?
questions.fun_fact: Durum is also called pasta wheat or macaroni wheat.

questions.text: Which French bread has a rich, tender crumb thanks to its high butter and egg content?
questions.fun_fact: Brioche is a viennoiserie, the same family of baked goods as the croissant.

questions.text: Which alkaline treatment gives pretzels their traditional skin and flavor?
questions.fun_fact: Salt is the most common pretzel topping, followed by mustard, cheese, sugar, chocolate or cinnamon.

questions.text: The French cooking method confit cooks food slowly at low temperature while it is submerged in what?
questions.fun_fact: For meat, the method requires the meat to be salted first, and the name comes from the French for "to preserve".

questions.text: Which nut gives the chocolate spread Nutella its main flavor besides cocoa?
questions.fun_fact: Nutella was introduced in 1964, although the first version dates to 1963.

questions.text: Which spice, sold in small seed pods that are triangular in cross-section, ranks among the most expensive by weight?
questions.fun_fact: Cardamom is made from the seeds of plants in two genera, Elettaria and Amomum.

questions.text: Which banana cultivar replaced Gros Michel as the main variety in the banana export trade?
questions.fun_fact: Gros Michel, nicknamed "Big Mike", has a thick peel that resists bruising, which made it the main export banana until the 1950s.

questions.text: Miso is made by fermenting soybeans with salt and which mold-based starter?
questions.fun_fact: Kōji is the mold Aspergillus oryzae; miso is also mixed with dashi stock to make miso soup.

questions.text: Which two ingredients are slowly simmered together to make a basic dulce de leche?
questions.fun_fact: The simmering takes between 1.5 and 2 hours of near-constant stirring, and baking soda can be added.

questions.text: The word empanada comes from a Spanish verb meaning to do what?
questions.fun_fact: The origin of empanadas is unknown, but they are thought to come from Galicia, a region in northwest Spain.

questions.text: Kimchi, the Korean fermented side dish, is most often made from which vegetable?
questions.fun_fact: Napa cabbage reached Korea only at the end of the 19th century, so older kimchi was made with other vegetables such as radish.

questions.text: Which vegetable is commonly mixed with wheat flour, egg and salt to make Italian gnocchi?
questions.fun_fact: Gnocchi are a varied family of pasta-like dumplings, and some variations add cheese or breadcrumbs.

questions.text: The part of a globe artichoke that people eat is the unopened what?
questions.fun_fact: The artichoke is a cultivated variety of a species of thistle.

questions.text: What makes black tea different from green tea?
options: It comes from a different plant
questions.fun_fact: Green, white, yellow, oolong and black teas are all made from the leaves of the same shrub or small tree.

questions.text: A julienne cut slices food, such as carrots, into which shape?
questions.fun_fact: A julienne cut is also called allumette or French cut.

questions.text: Pink Himalayan salt is mined mainly in which country?
questions.fun_fact: The salt is mostly mined at the Khewra Salt Mine, in the foothills of the Salt Range.

questions.text: What is done to a traditional bagel's dough just before it is baked?
options: It is briefly boiled in water
It is steamed in a basket
questions.fun_fact: Bagels were first mentioned in 1610 in Jewish community ordinances in Kraków, Poland.

questions.text: Paprika is a spice made from the dried, ground fruits of which plant?
questions.fun_fact: Like all capsicums, paprika descends from wild ancestors from the Amazon River region.

questions.text: The name of the samosa comes from a Middle Persian word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: Samosas are often served with chutney and have origins in the Middle Ages or earlier.

questions.text: Besides wild yeast, which group of bacteria lives in a sourdough starter and makes the bread sour?
questions.fun_fact: The fermentation produces lactic acid, which gives sourdough its distinctive sour taste and improves its keeping qualities.

questions.text: Which Greek hero of the Trojan War gave his name to a famous 'weak spot'?
questions.fun_fact: His mother Thetis is said to have dipped him in the River Styx, holding him by the heel.

questions.text: Which woman of Greek myth opened a jar that let troubles loose on the world?
questions.fun_fact: The jar became a 'box' through a 16th-century mistranslation, often credited to Erasmus.

questions.text: Who built the Labyrinth for King Minos of Crete in Greek myth?
questions.fun_fact: After leaving Crete, he is said to have found shelter in Sicily at the court of King Cocalus.

questions.text: Which enchantress is King Arthur's scheming half-sister in Malory's 'Le Morte d'Arthur'?
questions.fun_fact: Her Italian name, Fata Morgana, is also used for a complex kind of mirage seen near the horizon.

questions.text: Which creatures of Greek myth lured sailors with enchanting song?
questions.fun_fact: In the Odyssey, Odysseus had his crew plug their ears with beeswax and was tied to the mast.

questions.text: Which handsome youth of Greek myth fell in love with his own reflection?
questions.fun_fact: The word 'narcissism' comes from his name; in Ovid's telling, a narcissus flower grows where he had lain.

questions.text: Which sculptor of Greek myth fell in love with his own statue, which came to life?
questions.fun_fact: The statue has no name in Ovid's version; the now-familiar name Galatea was added in much later retellings.

questions.text: Which mortal weaver was turned into a spider after challenging Athena?
questions.fun_fact: The Roman poet Ovid tells her story in Book Six of the Metamorphoses; her name means 'spider' in Greek.

questions.text: How many Muses were there in the best-known Greek tradition?
questions.fun_fact: The word 'museum' comes from the Greek for a place sacred to the Muses.

questions.text: Which mythical creature has a woman's upper body and a fish's tail?
questions.fun_fact: A mermaid-like goddess called Atargatis, or Derceto, appears in ancient Greek and Roman writings.

questions.text: Which one-eyed giants does Odysseus meet in Homer's Odyssey?
questions.fun_fact: The name Cyclops is usually explained as meaning 'circle-eyed' in Greek.

questions.text: Which woman of Greek myth is called 'the face that launched a thousand ships'?
questions.fun_fact: The phrase comes from Christopher Marlowe's play Doctor Faustus, not from ancient sources.

questions.text: Which swift huntress of Greek myth joined the Calydonian boar hunt?
questions.fun_fact: In one tale she lost a footrace to Hippomenes, who slowed her by dropping golden apples.

questions.text: Which winged Greek goddess of victory inspired the name of a sportswear brand?
questions.fun_fact: The Nike of Samothrace, a Hellenistic masterpiece, shows her on the prow of a warship.

questions.text: Which Roman goddess of grain gave her name to the word 'cereal'?
questions.fun_fact: The Romans saw her as the counterpart of the Greek goddess Demeter.

questions.text: Which Roman goddess of the hearth had priestesses who kept her sacred fire burning?
questions.fun_fact: Her priestesses, the Vestal Virgins, vowed to serve her for at least 30 years.

questions.text: In a famous story told by Livy, which Roman left his plow to lead Rome in a crisis, then went back to his farm?
questions.fun_fact: Cincinnati, Ohio, is named after the Society of the Cincinnati, which honored him.

questions.text: The Chimera of Greek myth combined a lion, a goat and which other animal?
questions.fun_fact: It was said to breathe fire and to come from Lycia in Asia Minor.

questions.text: Which legendary ape-like creature is said to roam the forests of the Pacific Northwest?
questions.fun_fact: Bigfoot, also called Sasquatch, appears in both American and Canadian folklore.

questions.text: Which Norse god keeps watch at the rainbow bridge Bifröst?
questions.fun_fact: Heimdall owns the horn Gjallarhorn and is said to have extraordinary hearing and sight.

questions.text: Which serpent of Norse myth is said to encircle the world, biting its own tail?
questions.fun_fact: Thor once went fishing for it, using an ox head as bait.

questions.text: Odin's ravens Huginn and Muninn are named for 'thought' and which other mental power?
questions.fun_fact: The two ravens fly around the world bringing Odin information and gossip.

questions.text: Which day of the week is named after Odin, known to the Anglo-Saxons as Woden?
questions.fun_fact: Many Romance languages name the day after Mercury instead, as in French mercredi.

questions.text: Which Norse goddess, wife of Thor, was famed for her golden hair?
questions.fun_fact: Dwarfs forged her a new head of golden hair after Loki cut off the original.

questions.text: Which Old Norse poem, 'The Seeress's Prophecy', tells of the world's creation and its end?
questions.fun_fact: It survives in the Poetic Edda, and Snorri Sturluson quoted parts of it in his Prose Edda.

questions.text: Which giant bird of Arabian legend, said to carry off elephants, appears in the Sinbad tales?
questions.fun_fact: Marco Polo's account of a huge eagle-like bird led others to place the roc on Madagascar.

questions.text: Which giant sea monster of Scandinavian legend is often pictured as squid-like?
questions.fun_fact: Alfred Tennyson wrote an 1830 sonnet called 'The Kraken'.

questions.text: Which Greek hero tamed the winged horse Pegasus and went to face the Chimera?
questions.fun_fact: Athena gave him a golden bridle to tame Pegasus.

questions.text: Which mythical creature symbolized the emperor in imperial China?
questions.fun_fact: In the Yuan dynasty, the five-clawed dragon was reserved for the emperor.

questions.text: Which Egyptian goddess was the wife of Osiris and mother of Horus?
questions.fun_fact: Her name is linked to the Egyptian word for 'throne', which she wears as a headdress.

questions.text: Which Egyptian god, 'the hidden one', rose to become king of the gods in the New Kingdom?
questions.fun_fact: He was later merged with the sun god Ra and worshipped as Amun-Ra.

questions.text: Which Egyptian goddess, often shown with cow horns, was linked to music and joy?
questions.fun_fact: The Greeks identified her with their goddess Aphrodite.

questions.text: March is named after which Roman god of war?
questions.fun_fact: His sacred animals were the wolf and the woodpecker, and Romans called him father of Romulus and Remus.

questions.text: The ancient Egyptian ankh hieroglyph symbolizes what?
questions.fun_fact: The ankh is sometimes called the 'key of life'.

questions.text: In Irish myth, what is the otherworld of eternal youth called?
questions.fun_fact: In one tale the hero Oisín returns from it to find that 300 years have passed.

questions.text: Into which birds were the Children of Lir turned in the Irish legend?
questions.fun_fact: The curse lasts 900 years, in three stretches of 300 years on different waters.

questions.text: Which shape-shifting water spirit of Scottish folklore often takes the form of a horse?
questions.fun_fact: The Kelpies, two huge horse-head sculptures near Falkirk, honor this folklore.

questions.text: Which collection of medieval Welsh tales includes 'Culhwch and Olwen'?
questions.fun_fact: Lady Charlotte Guest popularized the title through her English translation of the 1840s.

questions.text: Which knight of the Round Table, Lancelot's son, is famed for his purity?
questions.fun_fact: Galahad first appears in the early 13th-century Lancelot-Grail cycle.

questions.text: Who is King Arthur's queen in the legends?
questions.fun_fact: Her Welsh name, Gwenhwyfar, can be translated as 'the White Fay' or 'White Ghost'.

questions.text: Who wrote 'Le Morte d'Arthur', printed by William Caxton in 1485?
questions.fun_fact: Caxton's edition divided the work into 21 books.

questions.text: Which 12th-century French poet wrote 'Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart'?
questions.fun_fact: He is the first writer known to mention the Holy Grail, in 'Perceval'.

questions.text: Which Victorian poet wrote 'Idylls of the King', a cycle of poems about King Arthur?
questions.fun_fact: The cycle has twelve narrative poems, published between 1859 and 1885.

questions.text: In which forest did Robin Hood and his Merry Men live, according to legend?
questions.fun_fact: Sherwood Forest lies in Nottinghamshire and is home to a famous old tree called the Major Oak.

questions.text: Which of Robin Hood's men has a name that jokes about his great height?
questions.fun_fact: In an old ballad he meets Robin on a narrow bridge and they fight with quarterstaffs.

questions.text: Who is Robin Hood's sweetheart in the legends?
questions.fun_fact: She appears in none of the earliest ballads and came from May Day games and plays.

questions.text: Which 14th-century poem contains the earliest clear mention of Robin Hood?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
questions.fun_fact: The poem is thought to have been composed in the 1370s.

questions.text: Which Swiss folk hero is said to have shot an apple off his son's head?
questions.fun_fact: The legend is set in Altdorf, in the canton of Uri, and is traditionally dated to 1307.

questions.text: Which legendary figure rose from poverty to become Lord Mayor of London, helped by his cat?
questions.fun_fact: The tale is based on a real merchant, Richard Whittington, who became Lord Mayor of London.

questions.text: Which giant lumberjack of American folklore had a blue ox named Babe?
questions.fun_fact: William B. Laughead's 1916 pamphlet for the Red River Lumber Company popularized his legend.

questions.text: Which American folk figure is remembered for planting apple orchards across the frontier?
questions.fun_fact: He was a real man, John Chapman, born in Massachusetts in 1774.

questions.text: Which Texan cowboy of tall tales supposedly used a rattlesnake as his lasso?
questions.fun_fact: His first known story appeared in The Century Magazine in October 1923.

questions.text: Which fairy-tale heroine lets down her long hair from a tower?
questions.fun_fact: Her name is that of a plant, cornsalad or rampion, which her mother craves.

questions.text: What is the witch's house made of in 'Hansel and Gretel'?
questions.fun_fact: Humperdinck's opera started the trend of picturing the witch's house as gingerbread.

questions.text: Which French writer published 'Cinderella' and 'Puss in Boots' in 1697?
questions.fun_fact: His collection was subtitled 'Tales of Mother Goose'.

questions.text: Which Italian writer's 'Pentamerone' (1630s) holds an early version of Cinderella?
questions.fun_fact: He wrote the book in Neapolitan dialect.

questions.text: Which Russian folklorist compiled the 1850s-60s collection 'Russian Fairy Tales'?
questions.fun_fact: His collection is often called the Russian counterpart of the Grimms' tales.

questions.text: Which nymph of Greek myth could only repeat the last words spoken to her?
questions.fun_fact: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, she falls in love with Narcissus but can only repeat his words.

questions.text: In which fairy tale does a girl carry food to her grandmother and meet a wolf in the woods?
questions.fun_fact: In the Grimms' version, a huntsman rescues the girl and her grandmother.

questions.text: In 'Sleeping Beauty', what does the princess prick her finger on?
questions.fun_fact: Perrault's 1697 version is called 'La Belle au bois dormant', the beauty sleeping in the wood.

questions.text: How many mattresses lie under the princess in Andersen's 'The Princess and the Pea'?
questions.fun_fact: It was one of Andersen's first fairy tales, published in 1835.

questions.text: What does the imp spin from straw in the Grimms' tale of Rumpelstiltskin?
questions.fun_fact: Similar tales include 'Tom Tit Tot' in England and 'Gilitrutt' in Iceland.

questions.text: In which German town does the legend of the Pied Piper take place?
questions.fun_fact: Robert Browning's 1842 poem made the tale famous in English.

questions.text: In Andersen's tale, who points out that the emperor is wearing no clothes?
questions.fun_fact: Andersen adapted the story from a 14th-century Spanish tale by Juan Manuel.

questions.text: In the Grimms' 'Snow White', how many dwarfs does she live with?
questions.fun_fact: The dwarfs were first given names in a 1912 Broadway play, then renamed in Disney's 1937 film.

questions.text: Who published the first known printed version of 'The Three Bears' in 1837?
questions.fun_fact: In his version the intruder was an old woman, not the girl Goldilocks.

questions.text: Who wrote the earliest known literary version of 'Beauty and the Beast' in 1740?
questions.fun_fact: A shorter 1756 version by Leprince de Beaumont became the one most often retold.

questions.text: In 'Jack and the Beanstalk', what does Jack get in exchange for the family cow?
questions.fun_fact: Joseph Jacobs's 1890 version in English Fairy Tales made the story widely known.

questions.text: Which French scholar's early 1700s translation added 'Aladdin' and 'Ali Baba' to the Nights?
questions.fun_fact: A storyteller from Aleppo, Hanna Diyab, told Galland fourteen more stories from memory.

questions.text: Which legendary maiden of a Rhine cliff is said to lure sailors with her song?
questions.fun_fact: Heinrich Heine's 1824 poem 'Die Lorelei' made her legend famous.

questions.text: In 'The Three Little Pigs', which material does the third pig build his house from?
questions.fun_fact: Printed versions date to the 1840s, and Joseph Jacobs's 1890 version is the best known.

questions.text: In which mountain range is the Yeti, or 'Abominable Snowman', said to roam?
questions.fun_fact: The name 'Abominable Snowman' was coined in 1921 during a British Everest reconnaissance.

questions.text: In folklore, what is a person who can change into a wolf called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Old English 'werwulf', meaning 'man-wolf'.

questions.text: Who is the Monkey King in the Chinese novel 'Journey to the West'?
questions.fun_fact: In the novel he is a monkey born from a stone who gains supernatural powers.

questions.text: Which Greek philosopher first described the legendary island of Atlantis?
questions.fun_fact: He did so in two dialogues, Timaeus and Critias, written around 360 BC.

questions.text: Which bird-like mountain goblins of Japanese folklore are often shown with long noses?
questions.fun_fact: Tengu were once pictured as birds of prey; the long nose came to define them later.

questions.text: In 'The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter', where does the old man find baby Kaguya?
questions.fun_fact: It is considered the oldest surviving Japanese prose narrative, from about the 10th century.

questions.text: Tanuki, shape-shifters of Japanese folklore, are based on which real animal?
questions.fun_fact: Raccoon dogs have played a big part in Japanese folklore since ancient times, and are often shown in statues.

questions.text: Which horned ogres of Japanese folklore are driven out with thrown beans at Setsubun?
questions.fun_fact: Oni are often shown wearing tiger-skin loincloths and carrying iron clubs.

questions.text: Which Japanese folk hero visits an undersea Dragon Palace after rescuing a turtle?
questions.fun_fact: Given a mysterious box, he opens it and suddenly ages.

questions.text: Which mythical bird of Chinese tradition is sometimes called the 'Chinese phoenix'?
questions.fun_fact: The name joins feng and huang, once the male and female of the pair.

questions.text: Which Chinese moon goddess lives on the Moon with a jade rabbit in legend?
questions.fun_fact: China's Chang'e lunar missions are named after her.

questions.text: In Chinese myth, which goddess molded the first humans from yellow clay?
questions.fun_fact: She also mended the broken sky with colored stones.

questions.text: In the Chinese legend of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, what forms the yearly bridge?
questions.fun_fact: The lovers are linked to the stars Altair and Vega and the Qixi Festival.

questions.text: In Korea's founding myth, which animal becomes a woman and mother of Dangun?
questions.fun_fact: Both the bear and a tiger were told to eat only mugwort and garlic, but the tiger gave up after about 20 days.

questions.text: The Epic of Manas is a national treasure of which Central Asian country?
questions.fun_fact: Traditional performers called manaschi recite the epic from memory.

questions.text: Which ferryman of Greek myth carries the souls of the dead across the river to the underworld?
questions.fun_fact: Coins known as Charon's obols were sometimes placed in or near the mouths of the dead to pay his fee.

questions.text: In Welsh legend, which enchantress swallows Gwion Bach, who is then reborn from her as the poet Taliesin?
questions.fun_fact: Medieval Welsh poems say she owned the cauldron of poetic inspiration, called Awen.

questions.text: Which ancient Sanskrit animal-fable collection reached the Arab world as 'Kalila and Dimna'?
questions.fun_fact: Tradition says it was written to teach three princes the art of wise government.

questions.text: Which giant mythical bird of Native American tradition makes thunder with its wings?
questions.fun_fact: In Algonquian tellings, it also makes lightning by flashing its eyes.

questions.text: Which benevolent giant bird of Persian myth raises the abandoned hero Zal in the 'Shahnameh'?
questions.fun_fact: It gave Zal a feather to burn whenever he needed its help, and he later used it to summon the bird.

questions.text: Which K'iche' Maya book recounts the Hero Twins and a creation story?
questions.fun_fact: A Spanish friar, Francisco Ximénez, copied and translated it in the early 1700s.

questions.text: The legend of the chupacabra took off in 1995 with sightings on which Caribbean island?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'goat-sucker' in Spanish, after the livestock it supposedly attacks.

questions.text: Which Colombian lake is tied to the El Dorado legend of a king covered in gold dust?
questions.fun_fact: El Dorado means 'the golden one' in Spanish.

questions.text: Which West African oral poets traditionally recite the Epic of Sundiata?
questions.fun_fact: The epic tells of Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire in the 13th century.

questions.text: What does the Icelandic folk term 'huldufólk' mean?
questions.fun_fact: They are said to live in a parallel world and can make themselves visible at will.

questions.text: Which glowing bird of Russian folklore is hunted by Prince Ivan in a famous tale?
questions.fun_fact: A single glowing feather of the Firebird was said to light up a large room.

questions.text: Which legendary Czech ruler is said to have foretold the founding of Prague?
questions.fun_fact: Smetana's opera about her premiered in 1881 at the opening of Prague's National Theatre.

questions.text: Which mythical bird of prey is linked to Hungary's Árpád dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: In the legend of Emese, a turul appears in her dream while she is pregnant with Álmos.

questions.text: Which mythical creature stands opposite the lion on the royal coat of arms of the United Kingdom?
questions.fun_fact: On the arms the lion wears a crown, while the unicorn is shown in chains.

questions.text: In legend, Alexander the Great solved which famous puzzle by slicing through it with his sword?
questions.fun_fact: Legend said that whoever untied the knot on an ox-cart at Gordium in Phrygia would rule all of Asia.

questions.text: Kissing which stone at a castle near Cork, Ireland, is said to give you the 'gift of the gab'?
questions.fun_fact: The stone was set into a tower of Blarney Castle in 1446; to kiss it you must lean backward over the parapet.

questions.text: In the Japanese tale of Momotarō, which animals join the hero on his quest?
options: A fox, a crane and a turtle
A dog, a monkey and a pheasant
A bear, a deer and an owl
A cat, a rat and a rooster
questions.fun_fact: They agree to help in return for kibi dango, millet dumplings.

questions.text: In 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves', which magic words open the robbers' cave?
questions.fun_fact: The cave seals itself again on the words 'close sesame'.

questions.text: Which country's folklore tells of the bunyip, a creature said to lurk in swamps and billabongs?
questions.fun_fact: An early form of the word, 'bahnyip', appeared in the Sydney Gazette in 1812, for a seal-like animal with a terrible voice.

questions.text: In Andersen's 'Thumbelina', which seed does a woman plant to grow the flower that holds the tiny heroine?
questions.fun_fact: The tale was first published on 16 December 1835 in Copenhagen, in Fairy Tales Told for Children.

questions.text: Which mythical animal of North American folklore is a jackrabbit with antelope horns?
questions.fun_fact: Two taxidermist brothers popularized it in the 1930s in Douglas, Wyoming, by mounting deer antlers on jackrabbits.

questions.text: In the Grimms' tale of the poor shoemaker, what do he and his wife make for the little night helpers as thanks?
questions.fun_fact: The tale is number 39 in the Grimms' collection and is really three short stories under one title.

questions.text: In the Grimms' 'The Frog Prince', what does the princess drop into a well?
questions.fun_fact: It is the first tale in the Grimms' collection; the kiss that breaks the spell first appeared in English translations.

questions.text: In European folklore, a 'fairy ring' is a natural circle of what?
questions.fun_fact: Folklore sees them as lucky signs or dangerous places; they are also called elf circles or pixie rings.

questions.text: In the Grimms' tale, a donkey, a dog, a cat and which bird set out to become town musicians?
questions.fun_fact: Despite the title, the animals never reach Bremen: they scare off robbers and move into the robbers' cottage.

questions.text: Which mythical creature, armed with a sword and shield, appears on the coat of arms of Warsaw?
questions.fun_fact: An early coat of arms from 1390 showed a scaly, bird-legged creature; the first true mermaid dates from 1622.

questions.text: How many tails does the gumiho, a fox spirit of Korean folktales, have?
questions.fun_fact: In everyday Korean, calling someone a gumiho can mean that they are sly or cunning.

questions.text: For how many years does Rip Van Winkle sleep in the Catskill Mountains in Washington Irving's story?
questions.fun_fact: Irving wrote the story in England and admitted he had never been to the Catskills when he wrote it.

questions.text: Which ghostly flickering light, said to mislead travelers over bogs and marshes, appears in European folklore?
questions.fun_fact: Its Latin name, ignis fatuus, means 'foolish fire'.

questions.text: Which legendary ghost ship of sailors' lore is said to be doomed never to make port and to sail the seas forever?
questions.fun_fact: The oldest known written version of the legend dates from the late 18th century; sighting the ship was said to foretell doom.

questions.text: Which goat-legged Greek god of shepherds and wild places gave his name to the word 'panic'?
questions.fun_fact: His home was rustic Arcadia, and he was also the god of flocks, groves and rustic music.

questions.text: In the Norse poem Þrymskviða, how does Thor disguise himself to win back his stolen hammer?
questions.fun_fact: The god Heimdallr proposed the plan, and Loki came along disguised as a maidservant.

questions.text: In the Prose Edda, from what do the gods make the first man and woman, Ask and Embla?
questions.fun_fact: Old Norse askr means 'ash tree'; the pair also appear in the Völuspá, in the Poetic Edda.

questions.text: In which year did the Brothers Grimm publish the first volume of their fairy-tale collection?
questions.fun_fact: The first volume held 86 tales; UNESCO later listed the collection in its Memory of the World Registry.

questions.text: Which Aesop fable gave English the phrase 'sour grapes'?
questions.fun_fact: La Fontaine adapted the fable, and the Roman writer Phaedrus told a terse Latin version.

questions.text: The lake monster Ogopogo is said to live in Okanagan Lake in which Canadian province?
questions.fun_fact: 'Ogopogo' is a palindrome, and the lore says the creature looks the same from either end.

questions.text: Which wise-fool hero of Turkish and Central Asian humorous tales has a festival in Akşehir each July?
questions.fun_fact: UNESCO listed the tradition of comic tales about Nasreddin Khoja in 2022, after a joint bid by seven countries.

questions.text: Which hoofed creature of Chinese legend came to be identified with the giraffe after Zheng He's voyages?
questions.fun_fact: In modern Japanese, the related word kirin also means giraffe.

questions.text: Which 17th-century French poet is best known for verse Fables, many drawing on Aesop?
questions.fun_fact: Madame de Sévigné called his second collection of Fables, published in 1678, divine.

questions.text: Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis for the Golden Fleece. In which modern country was Colchis?
questions.fun_fact: Colchis was also the home of the sorceress Medea.

questions.text: Which winged female spirits of Greek myth, whose name means 'snatchers', were said to steal food from people?
questions.fun_fact: Hesiod pictured them as fair-haired winged maidens that kept pace with the blowing winds.

questions.text: In Homer's Odyssey, what happens to visitors who eat the lotus fruit on the Lotus-eaters' island?
options: They forget home and want to stay
questions.fun_fact: Figuratively, a 'lotus-eater' is a person who prefers pleasure and ease to practical concerns.

questions.text: Which stringed instrument does Finland's mythic hero Väinämöinen create?
questions.fun_fact: In the Kalevala he is an old, wise man whose magical singing voice is famous.

questions.text: In the medieval Reynard stories, what animal is the fox's main enemy, Isengrim?
questions.fun_fact: The first surviving versions of the Reynard cycle date from the second half of the 12th century.

questions.text: Which early Greek poet's 'Theogony' describes the origins and family trees of the gods?
questions.fun_fact: It begins with Chaos, a dark void, and is the first known Greek mythical cosmogony.

questions.text: In the Grimms' 'Frau Holle', what falls to Earth when the old woman shakes out her bed?
questions.fun_fact: In Hesse, people have said 'Hulda is making her bed' when it snows.

questions.text: In Japanese folklore, what is said to happen to a tool or object when it reaches 100 years old?
questions.fun_fact: The kanji for the word tsukumogami can be read as 'ninety-nine spirits'.

questions.text: In Perrault's 'Puss in Boots', what title does the clever cat invent for his miller's-son master?
questions.fun_fact: The oldest written version is by Straparola, around 1550, where the cat is a disguised fairy.

questions.text: Which Greek symbol of abundance is called the 'horn of Amalthea'?
questions.fun_fact: In another myth, Heracles tore a horn off the river god Achelous, and that horn became the cornucopia.

questions.text: In the Odyssey, what does King Aeolus give Odysseus tied up in a bag?
questions.fun_fact: Opening the bag blew the crew off course when they were nearly in sight of Ithaca.

questions.text: Which magical binding, forged by dwarves from things like a cat's footfall and a woman's beard, holds the wolf Fenrir?
questions.fun_fact: Though as thin as a silken ribbon, it is stronger than any iron chain.

questions.text: In Vietnamese legend, which creature rose from a Hanoi lake to reclaim a magic sword from Emperor Lê Lợi?
questions.fun_fact: The lake's name, Hoàn Kiếm, means 'Lake of the Returned Sword'.

questions.text: Which forest guardian of Brazilian folklore is famous for having feet that point backward?
questions.fun_fact: Its first written mention dates to 1560, in São Vicente, Brazil, by Joseph of Anchieta.

questions.text: Which supernatural race of Irish myth did early texts call 'the tribe of the gods'?
questions.fun_fact: Their full name is usually translated 'folk of the goddess Danu'.

questions.text: Which Cornish coastal castle did Geoffrey of Monmouth link to the origins of King Arthur?
questions.fun_fact: Digs in 2016 and 2017 found the outlines of a palace from the 5th or early 6th century.

questions.text: Which half-serpent water spirit of French folklore is said to be an ancestor of the House of Lusignan?
questions.fun_fact: Jean d'Arras wrote the most famous literary version of her tale in 1393.

questions.text: What are the strong, knight-like heroes of Russian and East Slavic epic poems called?
questions.fun_fact: Some, like the giant Svyatogor, are purely fictional, while others are thought to be historical figures.

questions.text: Which Slovak highwayman of legend is said to have robbed the rich to give to the poor, like a Slovak Robin Hood?
questions.fun_fact: A 7.5 m metal statue of him by Ján Kulich, made in 1988, stands near his home town of Terchová.

questions.text: In medieval tales, which imaginary land of plenty is a peasant's dream of ease, with skies that rain cheese?
questions.fun_fact: Edward Elgar used the name for his 1901 concert overture 'Cockaigne (In London Town)'.

questions.text: In an ancient tale of Rhodopis, seen as an early Cinderella story, what does an eagle snatch from her?
questions.fun_fact: The geographer Strabo first recorded the story around the turn of the 1st century.
