questions.fun_fact: The Grossglockner reaches 3,798 m and a scenic high alpine road leads close to its foot.

questions.text: Which Swedish island is home to the medieval walled town of Visby?
questions.fun_fact: Visby was a major Hanseatic trading town, and its ring wall still stands.

questions.text: Which is the largest of the Greek islands?
questions.fun_fact: Crete was the heart of the Bronze Age Minoan civilization.

questions.text: Saint Petersburg lies at the head of which gulf?
questions.fun_fact: The Neva River drains into the gulf at Saint Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city.

questions.text: Which body of water separates southern England from France?
questions.fun_fact: The Channel is about 560 km long and narrows to 34 km in the Strait of Dover.

questions.text: What is the fan-shaped landform called where a river splits into branches before entering the sea?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the triangle-shaped Greek capital letter delta (Δ), which the Nile Delta resembles.

questions.text: What is the nickname of the place in the ocean that lies farthest from any land?
questions.fun_fact: The three nearest landmasses, including an islet beside Easter Island, are each about 2,688 km away.

questions.text: Which ocean is named after a country?
questions.fun_fact: Asian monsoons cause seasonal changes in its currents, even reversing the Somali Current.

questions.text: What is the name of the deepest known point of the Mariana Trench?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after two British survey ships: HMS Challenger of the 1870s and HMS Challenger II of the early 1950s.

questions.text: What do we call a piece of land surrounded by water on three sides?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from Latin words meaning 'almost an island'.

questions.text: Which is the world's largest inland body of water by surface area?
questions.fun_fact: Its water is brackish, with roughly one-third the salinity of typical ocean water.

questions.text: Which continent has the highest average elevation?
questions.fun_fact: Most of the continent is covered by an ice sheet that averages 1.9 km in thickness.

questions.text: Which is the smallest continent by land area?
questions.fun_fact: The Australian continent is also the lowest and flattest continent on Earth.

questions.text: Which country lies in all four hemispheres: northern, southern, eastern and western?
questions.fun_fact: In 1995 Kiribati moved the International Date Line far to the east so that the whole country shares one date.

questions.text: What is the study and practice of making maps called?
questions.fun_fact: Modern cartography provides much of the foundation of geographic information systems (GIS).

questions.text: Together with the 180th meridian, which line divides Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres?
questions.fun_fact: The modern IERS Reference Meridian differs slightly from the historic meridian at Greenwich.

questions.text: Measured from its base on the ocean floor, which mountain is the tallest on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Only about 4,207 meters of Mauna Kea rise above sea level; most of its height is underwater.

questions.text: Which is the longest continental mountain range in the world?
questions.fun_fact: The Andes run through seven countries, from Venezuela in the north to Chile and Argentina in the south.

questions.text: Which country holds the largest share of the Amazon rainforest?
questions.fun_fact: The Amazon rainforest spans nine countries, but about 60 percent of it lies within Brazil.

questions.text: Why is Earth slightly wider at the equator than from pole to pole?
questions.fun_fact: The equatorial diameter is about 43 km greater than the polar diameter.

questions.text: What is the part of a map that explains its symbols and colors called?
questions.fun_fact: A legend is also called a key.

questions.text: What is the U-shaped lake that forms when a wide bend of a river is cut off called?
questions.fun_fact: In Australia, oxbow lakes are called billabongs.

questions.text: What is either of the two moments each year when the Sun is directly above the equator called?
questions.fun_fact: On an equinox the Sun rises almost exactly due east and sets almost exactly due west.

questions.text: What type of plate boundary is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
questions.fun_fact: At the ridge, new seafloor forms as the plates move apart by a few centimeters a year.

questions.text: The San Andreas Fault forms the boundary between which two tectonic plates?
questions.fun_fact: The fault runs for roughly 1,200 km through California.

questions.text: The Himalayas rose from a collision between the Eurasian Plate and which other plate?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from Sanskrit and means 'abode of snow'.

questions.text: Which is the largest tectonic plate on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: It first formed as a microplate about 190 million years ago.

questions.text: The Hawaiian Islands were built as the Pacific Plate moved slowly over what feature in the mantle?
questions.fun_fact: The islands grow older toward the northwest, where the chain continues as the Emperor Seamounts.

questions.text: Which of these landmasses was NOT part of the ancient supercontinent Gondwana?
questions.fun_fact: Remnants of Gondwana make up around two-thirds of the present-day continental area.

questions.text: Tectonic plates are pieces of which rigid outer layer of Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Beneath the lithosphere lies the softer, slowly flowing asthenosphere.

questions.text: Iceland lies on the boundary between which two tectonic plates?
questions.fun_fact: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, so the plates pulling apart power its volcanoes and hot springs.

questions.text: The Andes rose largely as which plate sinks beneath the western edge of South America?
questions.fun_fact: The plate is named after the Nazca region of southern Peru.

questions.text: What is it called when one tectonic plate slides beneath another?
questions.fun_fact: Subduction has created most of Earth's continental crust.

questions.text: The Tropic of Cancer lies at about what latitude?
questions.fun_fact: It marks the northernmost latitude where the Sun can be directly overhead, at the June solstice.

questions.text: What is the ridge or heap of rock debris carried and dumped by a glacier called?
questions.fun_fact: Terminal moraines form at a glacier's foot and mark the farthest point it advanced.

questions.text: In the Köppen climate classification, which letter group stands for polar climates?
questions.fun_fact: The system was first published by Wladimir Köppen in 1884 and has been revised many times since.

questions.text: Which of these regions has a Mediterranean climate of mild wet winters and hot dry summers?
questions.fun_fact: Besides the Mediterranean Basin, such climates occur in parts of California, Chile, South Africa and Australia.

questions.text: What do sailors call the belt of calm, light and shifting winds that lies near the equator?
questions.fun_fact: Scientists call it the Intertropical Convergence Zone; it encircles Earth near the thermal equator and shifts with the seasons.

questions.text: Which steady east-to-west winds near the tropics helped sailing ships cross the Atlantic?
questions.fun_fact: Here 'trade' comes from an old word meaning 'track' or 'course', not from commerce.

questions.text: What is the dry area on the downwind side of a mountain range called?
questions.fun_fact: Death Valley lies in the rain shadow of several mountain ranges, which helps make it so dry.

questions.text: The tropics lie between which two lines of latitude?
questions.fun_fact: The tropics receive the most direct sunlight and make up about 40 percent of Earth's surface.

questions.text: What is the phenomenon called when the Sun stays above the horizon around the clock in summer near the poles?
questions.fun_fact: At the North Pole itself, the Sun stays above the horizon for about six months of the year.

questions.text: What is a route that crosses a mountain range at a low point between the peaks called?
questions.fun_fact: Mountain passes have played a key role in trade, war and the migration of people and animals throughout history.

questions.text: About how long is Earth's circumference around the equator?
questions.fun_fact: The meter was originally defined as one ten-millionth of the arc from the pole to the equator.

questions.text: What is a slowly moving river of ice, flowing down a valley under its own weight, called?
questions.fun_fact: Glacial ice, together with the ice sheets, holds about 69 percent of the world's fresh water.

questions.text: Which coordinate measures how far north or south a place is from the equator?
questions.fun_fact: Lines of latitude are called parallels because they run parallel to the equator and never meet.

questions.text: In which year did an international conference in Washington, D.C., choose Greenwich as the world's prime meridian?
questions.fun_fact: France abstained from the vote and kept using the Paris meridian for its own time until 1911.

questions.text: What is the place where a river begins called?
questions.fun_fact: A river's source is also called its headwater.

questions.text: Counting its overseas territories, which country has the most time zones?
questions.fun_fact: France has 12 time zones, or 13 if its Antarctic claim is counted.

questions.text: Climbers who reach the top of the highest mountain on every continent complete which challenge?
questions.fun_fact: American businessman Dick Bass was the first to climb the Seven Summits, completing the list in 1985.

questions.text: Which country uses a standard time that is UTC+5:45?
questions.fun_fact: Nepal adopted Indian Standard Time in 1920, then moved its clocks forward 15 minutes in 1986.

questions.text: Ideally, how many degrees of longitude does one time zone span?
questions.fun_fact: In practice, national borders bend the zone lines, and some places use half-hour or 45-minute offsets.

questions.text: On a weather map, what are the lines joining places of equal air pressure called?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Ancient Greek word 'baros', meaning 'weight'.

questions.text: Which Scottish-Canadian railway engineer proposed worldwide standard time zones in the 1870s?
questions.fun_fact: Fleming also designed Canada's first postage stamp, the Threepenny Beaver of 1851.

questions.text: On a standard Mercator world map, which of these looks far bigger than it really is?
questions.fun_fact: On Mercator maps Greenland looks about as big as Africa, which is really roughly 14 times larger.

questions.text: Which Flemish cartographer introduced, in 1569, a map projection in which compass bearings are straight lines?
questions.fun_fact: His famous 1569 world map is inscribed with over five thousand words in fifteen legends.

questions.text: Which property does the Gall–Peters world map, promoted by Arno Peters in the 1970s, preserve?
questions.fun_fact: Scottish clergyman James Gall had described the same projection in 1855, well before Peters.

questions.text: Which map projection did the National Geographic Society adopt for its world maps in 1998?
questions.fun_fact: It replaced the Robinson projection, which the Society had used since 1988.

questions.text: The map on the United Nations emblem is centered on the North Pole in which type of projection?
questions.fun_fact: The map is flanked by olive branches, a symbol of peace.

questions.text: On a map with the scale 1:50,000, two centimeters represent what real distance?
questions.fun_fact: A large-scale map shows a small area in great detail, while a small-scale map covers a large area.

questions.text: What do we call a line on a map that joins places of equal elevation?
questions.fun_fact: Where contour lines lie close together, the slope is steep.

questions.text: What is the angle between magnetic north and true north at a given place called?
questions.fun_fact: The angle can change over time, so navigators need up-to-date values for their location.

questions.text: What is the whole area of land drained by a river and its tributaries called?
questions.fun_fact: In North America it is often called a watershed; elsewhere that word means the dividing ridge between basins.

questions.text: Under the UN Law of the Sea, up to how far from its coast can a country's exclusive economic zone extend?
questions.fun_fact: Within the first 12 nautical miles, the territorial sea, a coastal state has full sovereignty.

questions.text: Which scholar wrote the Geography in Alexandria around AD 150, describing the places of the known world?
questions.fun_fact: Its gazetteer gave latitude and longitude coordinates for every place the work described.

questions.text: What are the huge circular systems of ocean currents, such as the North Pacific one, called?
questions.fun_fact: There are five major ocean gyres, including the North Atlantic and South Pacific gyres.

questions.text: Which strait separates mainland South America from Tierra del Fuego?
questions.fun_fact: Magellan first sailed through it in 1520 and named it the Strait of All Saints.

questions.text: Which cape at the southern tip of South America was the dreaded route for sailing ships between the Atlantic and Pacific?
questions.fun_fact: The cape is named after the Dutch town of Hoorn, not after an animal's horn.

questions.text: Which New Zealand entomologist first proposed modern daylight saving time, in 1895?
questions.fun_fact: In 1907, Briton William Willett proposed British Summer Time as a way to save energy.

questions.text: What is the scientific study of landforms and how they evolve called?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from Greek words meaning 'earth', 'form' and 'study'.

questions.text: Which scholar made the 1154 world map known as the Tabula Rogeriana for King Roger II of Sicily?
questions.fun_fact: The map was drawn with south at the top, the opposite of modern convention.

questions.text: Which Italian navigator, sailing for England's Henry VII, reached the coast of North America in 1497?
questions.fun_fact: For the voyage's 500th anniversary, Canada and Britain named Cape Bonavista, Newfoundland, as his landing site.

questions.text: Which Spanish navigator captained the Victoria on the first voyage around the world, completed in 1522?
questions.fun_fact: Only the Victoria completed the voyage, reaching Seville with 18 Europeans and 3 Moluccans aboard.

questions.text: Which type of map shows the shape and height of the land's surface in detail?
questions.fun_fact: Traditional definitions require a topographic map to show both natural and human-made features.

questions.text: In 1492, Columbus first landed in the Americas on an island in which group?
questions.fun_fact: Columbus called the island San Salvador; its local name was Guanahani.

questions.text: Which ship, shaped so that crushing sea ice would push it upward, carried Nansen's Arctic drift expedition of 1893-96?
questions.fun_fact: Fram is preserved as a museum ship at the Fram Museum in Oslo, Norway.

questions.text: Which ocean opened up as Pangaea broke apart, between the Americas and Europe and Africa?
questions.fun_fact: It is still widening by a few centimeters a year as the seafloor spreads along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

questions.text: The Beaufort scale, devised in 1805, rates what?
questions.fun_fact: Royal Navy hydrographer Francis Beaufort devised it; forces 13 to 17 were added in 1946 for special cases such as typhoons.

questions.text: Which climate zones lie between the tropics and the polar circles?
questions.fun_fact: Their warmest parts, from about 23.5 to 35 degrees of latitude, are often called subtropical.

questions.text: Which German naturalist explored Latin America from 1799 to 1804 and has an ocean current named for him?
questions.fun_fact: In 1817 he drew isothermal lines, joining places of equal temperature, to compare climates around the world.

questions.text: What is a large area of high, flat land raised sharply above the land around it called?
questions.fun_fact: Plateaus are also called tablelands or high plains.

questions.text: Which supercontinent existed about a billion years ago, long before Pangaea?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Russian word 'rodina', meaning 'motherland'.

questions.text: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis effect deflects moving air and water to which side?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the French scientist Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who described it in 1835.

questions.text: What is the term for deep, cold, nutrient-rich water rising to the surface, as off Peru?
questions.fun_fact: Coastal upwelling zones cover a small part of the ocean but support some of its richest fisheries.

questions.text: What are the fast, narrow bands of wind high in the atmosphere called?
questions.fun_fact: Jet streams flow mainly from west to east, which is why transatlantic flights are quicker eastbound.

questions.text: Which German merchant made the Erdapfel in 1492, the oldest surviving terrestrial globe?
questions.fun_fact: Because it was made before Columbus's return, the Erdapfel shows no Americas.

questions.text: What is a chain or cluster of islands called?
questions.fun_fact: The word first referred to the Aegean Sea and its many islands.

questions.text: Which Ottoman admiral drew a 1513 world map that shows the coast of South America?
questions.fun_fact: It was rediscovered in 1929; the surviving third of the map is kept at Topkapı Palace in Istanbul.

questions.text: What is a crescent-shaped sand dune whose two horns point downwind called?
questions.fun_fact: Russian naturalist Alexander von Middendorf introduced the Kazakh-derived term in 1881.

questions.text: Which Flemish cartographer published the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum in 1570, often called the first modern atlas?
questions.fun_fact: The first edition contained 53 maps.

questions.text: Which continent is the world's largest cold desert?
questions.fun_fact: Antarctica's Dry Valleys almost never get snow.

questions.text: What is the point on Earth directly opposite another point called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Greek for 'opposite feet'; the plural, antipodes, is the older form.

questions.text: The shortest route between two points on a globe follows what kind of line?
questions.fun_fact: Any two points that are not exactly opposite each other lie on one unique great circle.

questions.text: What is the circle of latitude at about 66.5° N called?
questions.fun_fact: At the June solstice, the Sun does not set anywhere north of this line.

questions.text: Marshes, swamps and bogs are all types of which kind of landscape?
questions.fun_fact: The Ramsar treaty counts marine waters less than six meters deep at low tide as wetlands.

questions.text: What is the vast temperate grassland of Eurasia, stretching from Hungary to Mongolia, called?
questions.fun_fact: It was home to many nomadic peoples and empires, including the Scythians, the Huns and the Mongols.

questions.text: Which American geologist proposed the idea of seafloor spreading in the early 1960s?
questions.fun_fact: Hess used echo-sounding data collected as a US Navy officer to study the ocean floor.

questions.text: Which is the longest mountain chain on Earth, mostly hidden under the sea?
questions.fun_fact: It winds about 65,000 km around the globe, like the seam of a baseball.

questions.text: Which of the major oceans has the highest average salinity?
questions.fun_fact: Its salinity peaks near 25 degrees north and south, where rainfall is low and evaporation is high.

questions.text: About what share of Earth's surface is covered by water?
questions.fun_fact: More than 97 percent of all the water on Earth is salty.

questions.text: What is the shallow, gently sloping seabed around a continent called?
questions.fun_fact: Shelves end at the continental slope, usually at a depth of around 140 meters.

questions.text: What is a fertile spot in a desert, where water lets plants grow, called?
questions.fun_fact: Most oases are largely artificial, relying on wells and irrigation channels made by people.

questions.text: What name is given to the Ice Age land bridge that once joined Siberia and Alaska?
questions.fun_fact: At its greatest extent the land bridge was up to about 1,000 km wide.

questions.text: Which landmass, about 94 percent underwater, includes New Zealand and New Caledonia?
questions.fun_fact: Zealandia broke away from Gondwana between about 83 and 79 million years ago.

questions.text: Collections of maps are called atlases after which figure of Greek myth?
questions.fun_fact: Atlas was later identified with the Atlas Mountains of northwest Africa.

questions.text: Which volcano's 1815 eruption helped cause the 'Year Without a Summer' in 1816?
questions.fun_fact: It is on the island of Sumbawa in Indonesia.

questions.text: Which city lies near 6.5° N, 3.4° E?
questions.fun_fact: Lagos is the most populous city in Nigeria.

questions.text: What is a mountain peak that sticks up through an ice sheet called, using an Inuit word?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Greenlandic 'nunataq'.

questions.text: About how long is one degree of latitude on Earth's surface?
questions.fun_fact: A degree of longitude shrinks from about 111 km at the Equator to zero at the poles.

questions.text: Which city lies near 48.9° N, 2.3° E?
questions.fun_fact: The Seine River flows through the city.

questions.text: What is an area of open water surrounded by sea ice called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from a Russian term meaning 'open water'.

questions.text: What is the term for the process of mountain building?
questions.fun_fact: It comes from the Greek words for 'mountain' and 'birth'.

questions.text: Which city lies near 55.8° N, 37.6° E?
questions.fun_fact: The city is named after the Moskva River.

questions.text: How many continents are recognized in most English-speaking countries?
questions.fun_fact: Most English-speaking countries teach seven; other models join Europe and Asia, or the Americas, giving fewer.

questions.text: What is the gradual sinking of the land's surface called?
questions.fun_fact: Pumping groundwater or oil from underground can make the ground sink.

questions.text: At least how many GPS satellites must a receiver hear to fix its 3D position and time?
questions.fun_fact: A fourth satellite is needed to correct the receiver's clock.

questions.text: What does the abbreviation GMT stand for?
questions.fun_fact: GMT is the local mean time at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London.

questions.text: What is a long, narrow and very deep valley in the ocean floor called?
questions.fun_fact: Most of the deepest trenches lie around the edges of the Pacific Ocean.

questions.text: What is a long, steep slope or cliff separating two flatter levels of land called?
questions.fun_fact: An escarpment is also called a scarp.

questions.text: What is an ice-cored mound that pushes up through the permafrost in Arctic regions called?
questions.fun_fact: The word means 'conical hill' in Inuvialuktun; Canada's Tuktoyaktuk Peninsula has about 1,350 of them.

questions.text: Which of these cities lies south of the Equator?
questions.fun_fact: Nairobi began in 1898 as a rail depot on the Uganda-Kenya Railway.

questions.text: What do we call a country with no coastline on the open ocean?
questions.fun_fact: Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan are 'doubly landlocked', surrounded only by landlocked countries.

questions.text: Which free, editable world map project was founded by Steve Coast in 2004?
questions.fun_fact: It is often described as the 'Wikipedia of maps'.

questions.text: Which city lies near 40.7° N, 74° W?
questions.fun_fact: The city has five boroughs.

questions.text: About how much does air temperature drop for every kilometer you climb in the lower atmosphere?
questions.fun_fact: This average rate is called the environmental lapse rate.

questions.text: Which German mapmaker's 1507 world map was the first to use the name 'America'?
questions.fun_fact: Only one copy of the map survives; the US Library of Congress bought it in 2003.

questions.text: What is a map that shades regions by a value, such as population density, called?
questions.fun_fact: Choropleth comes from Greek words for 'area' and 'multitude'.

questions.text: What is the star-shaped figure on a map that shows compass directions called?
questions.fun_fact: A compass rose is also known as a wind rose.

questions.text: What is a narrow ridge of sand or gravel that juts out from the coast into the water called?
questions.fun_fact: Spits often grow as waves drift sand along the shore.

questions.text: What are north, east, south and west together called?
questions.fun_fact: The points halfway between them, such as northeast, are called ordinal or intercardinal directions.

questions.text: What is a steep rock face along the coast, often shaped by waves, called?
questions.fun_fact: Sandstone, limestone, chalk and dolomite are the rocks most likely to form cliffs.

questions.text: What is the loose, broken rock that piles up at the foot of a cliff called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from an Old Norse word for 'landslide'.

questions.text: What is a continent-sized mass of glacial ice covering more than 50,000 square kilometers called?
questions.fun_fact: Only Antarctica and Greenland hold ice sheets of this size.

questions.text: At what latitude is the North Pole?
questions.fun_fact: At the North Pole every direction points south.

questions.text: Which is the largest sea in the world by area?
questions.fun_fact: It covers an estimated 5 million square kilometers, east of the Philippines.

questions.text: What is a low, wet area dominated by grasses and reeds, often flooded by shallow water, called?
questions.fun_fact: A marsh with woody plants is sometimes called a carr.

questions.text: What is the raised bank built or formed along a river to hold back floodwater called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the French for 'raised'.

questions.text: What do we call a drainage basin that has no outlet to the sea?
questions.fun_fact: The Caspian Sea and the Dead Sea lie in endorheic basins.

questions.text: Which city lies near 33.9° S, 18.4° E?
questions.fun_fact: Cape Town is nicknamed the 'Mother City'.

questions.text: What is the fan-shaped deposit of sediment at the foot of a mountain slope called?
questions.fun_fact: Alluvial fans often form where a mountain stream suddenly reaches flat ground.

questions.text: What is a drowned river valley that forms a long, branching inlet on a coast called?
questions.fun_fact: The Kingsbridge Estuary in Devon, England, is an extreme example of a ria.

questions.text: About how salty is average seawater, as a share of its mass?
questions.fun_fact: Most of the dissolved salt is sodium and chloride ions.

questions.text: Measuring a coastline with ever-smaller rulers makes it longer. What is this puzzle called?
questions.fun_fact: Lewis Fry Richardson first noticed the effect.

questions.text: Which satellite navigation system is run by the European Union?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei.

questions.text: What is the elevation above which snow stays on the ground all year called?
questions.fun_fact: Near the Equator the snow line sits at about 4,500 meters above sea level.

questions.text: Which city lies near 19.4° N, 99.1° W?
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City is the oldest capital city in the Americas.

questions.text: What is a flat-topped underwater mountain called?
questions.fun_fact: Harry Hess first recognized guyots in 1945, using echo-sounding data.

questions.text: What is a long line of connected mountains called?
questions.fun_fact: Several linked ranges form a mountain system or belt.

questions.text: What is a long chain of mountain ranges, as along the western Americas, called?
questions.fun_fact: The word is borrowed from Spanish and is related to 'cuerda', meaning 'cord'.

questions.text: Which mountain belt runs from Spain through the Alps and the Himalayas toward Indonesia?
questions.fun_fact: It is the world's second most seismically active belt after the Pacific Ring of Fire.

questions.text: What do we call a high, steep piece of land that juts out into the sea?
questions.fun_fact: A headland is a type of promontory, and a large one is often called a cape.

questions.text: What do geographers call a compact group of mountains forming an uplifted block, like Mont Blanc?
questions.fun_fact: The word is French and means 'massive'.

questions.text: What is a mound or ridge of sand piled up by the wind called?
questions.fun_fact: Dunes form not only in deserts but also on beaches.

questions.text: What do we call the slow rise of land after the weight of ice sheets has melted away?
questions.fun_fact: It is still raising parts of Scandinavia and Canada.

questions.text: Greenland is considered part of which continent?
questions.fun_fact: Politically it is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.

questions.text: Which of these countries does the Prime Meridian cross?
questions.fun_fact: The meridian also touches Antarctica, at Queen Maud Land.

questions.text: What is the place where a river flows into a sea or a lake called?
questions.fun_fact: A river mouth may take the form of a delta or an estuary.

questions.text: Which 17th-century French canal links the Garonne river with the Mediterranean?
questions.fun_fact: It was designed by Pierre-Paul Riquet.

questions.text: Which city lies near 34.6° S, 58.4° W?
questions.fun_fact: The city stands on the western shore of the Río de la Plata estuary.

questions.text: Which wind-blown yellow silt blankets large areas of northern China?
questions.fun_fact: China's Loess Plateau is covered by loess deposits hundreds of meters thick.

questions.text: What does the abbreviation GIS stand for in mapping?
questions.fun_fact: Roger Tomlinson, who built a Canadian GIS in the 1960s, is called its father.

questions.text: What is a small mountain lake that fills a cirque carved by a glacier called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Old Norse 'tjörn', meaning 'pond'.

questions.text: What is a boulder carried by a glacier and left far from the bedrock it broke off from called?
questions.fun_fact: Big Rock, an erratic near Okotoks in Alberta, Canada, weighs about 16,500 tonnes.

questions.text: What word describes the wearing away of rock and soil by wind, water or ice?
questions.fun_fact: Weathering breaks rock down where it sits; erosion also carries the loose material away.

questions.text: Which of these cities lies in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres?
questions.fun_fact: Lima lies in the valleys of the Chillón, Rímac and Lurín rivers.

questions.text: What term, coined by Patrick Geddes, describes a region where neighboring cities have merged into one urban area?
questions.fun_fact: Geddes coined it in 1915.

questions.text: What is the flat land beside a river that floods in high water called?
questions.fun_fact: Regular flooding leaves fertile silt, which is why floodplains are good farmland.

questions.text: Which city lies near 30° N, 31° E?
questions.fun_fact: Cairo is nicknamed 'the city of a thousand minarets'.

questions.text: Which city lies near 1.35° N, 103.8° E?
questions.fun_fact: It sits on an island at the tip of the Malay Peninsula.

questions.text: What do we call frozen seawater that floats on the polar oceans?
questions.fun_fact: Sea ice covers roughly 7 percent of Earth's surface.

questions.text: What do we call a tall column of rock left standing in the sea after waves erode a headland?
questions.fun_fact: Stacks often begin as arches, which collapse and leave a pillar offshore.

questions.text: What are the north-south lines on a globe called?
questions.fun_fact: The word meridian comes from the Latin for 'midday'.

questions.text: Which navigational instrument measures the angle between the horizon and the Sun or a star?
questions.fun_fact: The instrument's principle was first put to use around 1731 by John Hadley and Thomas Godfrey.

questions.text: Glaciers carve valleys with which cross-section shape?
questions.fun_fact: Rivers usually cut V-shaped valleys instead.

questions.text: Which English cathedral displays the Mappa Mundi, a world map made around 1300?
questions.fun_fact: East is at the top, with Jerusalem at the center.

questions.text: What is a long, winding ridge of sand and gravel left by a meltwater stream under a glacier called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Irish 'eiscir', meaning 'ridge'.

questions.text: Which city lies near 34° S, 151° E?
questions.fun_fact: Sydney stands on Port Jackson, a large natural harbor.

questions.text: How many longitudinal zones does the UTM coordinate system divide the world into?
questions.fun_fact: Each zone is 6 degrees of longitude wide.

questions.text: Which city lies near 35.7° N, 139.7° E?
questions.fun_fact: Tokyo was originally called Edo and became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603.

questions.text: What do we call a narrow channel of water that connects two larger bodies of water?
questions.fun_fact: The Strait of Gibraltar links the Atlantic Ocean with the Mediterranean Sea.

questions.text: What is a sandbar that joins an island to the mainland called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from Italian, where it means 'pillow' or 'cushion'.

questions.text: What is a looping bend in a river called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Maeander River in Turkey, famous for its winding course.

questions.text: The Peutinger Table is an ancient scroll map showing what?
questions.fun_fact: The map is a medieval copy of a Roman original.

questions.text: What do we call a long, narrow sandy island that runs parallel to the mainland coast?
questions.fun_fact: Barrier islands protect coastlines by absorbing wave energy.

questions.text: What do we call an intense dust storm driven by a thunderstorm's downdraft, as seen in Sudan?
questions.fun_fact: In Khartoum, haboobs have reached about 2,000 m high.

questions.text: What is a glacier-smoothed bedrock knob, gently sloped on one side and rough on the other, called?
questions.fun_fact: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure coined the term in 1786, likening the rocks to wigs smoothed with mutton fat.

questions.text: What is a lone rocky hill that rises abruptly from a flat plain, as Uluru does, called?
questions.fun_fact: The German word means 'island mountain'.

questions.text: Which US satellite program has photographed Earth's land continuously since 1972?
questions.fun_fact: The first satellite was launched as the Earth Resources Technology Satellite and renamed Landsat 1 in 1975.

questions.text: What name is given to the irregular shape that Earth's mean sea level would take without winds and tides?
questions.fun_fact: The geoid is lumpy because gravity is not the same everywhere.

questions.text: Which American designer created the Dymaxion map, which unfolds the globe into triangles?
questions.fun_fact: Fuller patented the map in 1946.

questions.text: What process moves sand along a beach at an angle, carried by waves?
questions.fun_fact: It builds spits and carries sand along the coast.

questions.text: Which Indonesian volcano's huge 1883 eruption was heard thousands of kilometers away?
questions.fun_fact: Its eruption was heard as far away as Rodrigues, near Mauritius, about 4,800 km off.

questions.text: Which of these cities lies farthest north?
questions.fun_fact: Reykjavik is the northernmost capital of a sovereign state.

questions.text: What is a small, low island of sand or coral on a reef called?
questions.fun_fact: The word cay is pronounced 'key', as in the Florida Keys.

questions.text: Which geodetic datum, introduced in 1984, is the reference frame used by GPS?
questions.fun_fact: It defines an ellipsoid and a reference meridian slightly east of Greenwich.

questions.text: What is the opening in Earth's crust from which lava, ash and gas can erupt called?
questions.fun_fact: Most volcanoes are found along the boundaries of tectonic plates.

questions.text: What is the sharp, knife-edged ridge between two glacial valleys or cirques called?
questions.fun_fact: In the Alps such ridges are often called by the German term Grat.

questions.text: A country's single dominant city, far larger than any other, is called what kind of city?
questions.fun_fact: Geographer Mark Jefferson introduced the term in 1939.

questions.text: Which two properties of seawater drive the deep-ocean 'global conveyor belt' circulation?
questions.fun_fact: Thermohaline means 'heat-salt'.

questions.text: What is a smaller river that flows into a larger one called?
questions.fun_fact: Many tributaries together form a river's drainage network, which feeds the main stem.

questions.text: What do we call water dropping over a steep ledge in a river's course?
questions.fun_fact: Below a waterfall, the falling water digs a deep pool called a plunge pool.

questions.text: What do we call a region that receives very little rain each year, typically under 250 mm?
questions.fun_fact: Deserts cover about one-third of Earth's land surface.

questions.text: What do we call a deep, steep-sided valley cut into the land by a river?
questions.fun_fact: The English word comes from the Spanish 'cañón'.

questions.text: What is a shallow body of water cut off from the open sea by a sandbar or reef called?
questions.fun_fact: Lagoons form along coasts and also inside coral atolls.

questions.text: What is the vast, flat part of the deep ocean floor, usually 3,000 to 6,000 m down, called?
questions.fun_fact: Abyssal plains are among the flattest and smoothest places on Earth.

questions.text: The word 'geography' comes from Greek words meaning roughly what?
questions.fun_fact: The Greek scholar Eratosthenes is credited with coining the word.

questions.text: What name is used for a tropical cyclone in the northwest Pacific Ocean?
questions.fun_fact: In the Indian Ocean and South Pacific the same kind of storm is usually called a cyclone.

questions.text: What is a flat, dry desert lakebed that sometimes floods after rain called?
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word playa literally means 'beach'.

questions.text: What is a landmass smaller than a continent and surrounded by water called?
questions.fun_fact: Islands are usually grouped as continental islands or oceanic islands.

questions.text: What do we call a round model of Earth that shows its continents and oceans?
questions.fun_fact: Unlike a flat map, a globe shows the shapes and sizes of landmasses without distortion.

questions.text: What is a smooth, oval hill of glacial debris, shaped like an upturned spoon, called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Irish 'droim', meaning 'ridge'.

questions.text: What is a stream that branches off a river and flows away from it, as in a delta, called?
questions.fun_fact: It is the opposite of a tributary, which flows toward and into a larger stream.

questions.text: What do we call a narrow strip of land with water on both sides that joins two larger landmasses?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Greek for 'neck'.

questions.text: What is the single huge landmass made up of Europe and Asia called?
questions.fun_fact: Adding Africa to it gives Afro-Eurasia, the largest contiguous landmass.

questions.text: What are lines joining points of equal water depth on a chart called?
questions.fun_fact: They are the underwater counterpart of contour lines on land.

questions.text: What is the wide part of a river where fresh water meets the tides of the sea called?
questions.fun_fact: Chesapeake Bay in the United States is one of the largest estuaries in the world.

questions.text: Which continent straddles both the Equator and the Prime Meridian?
questions.fun_fact: It is bordered by the Mediterranean Sea, the Red Sea, the Indian Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.text: What is the zone between the high-tide and low-tide marks on a shore called?
questions.fun_fact: It is also called the littoral zone or foreshore.

questions.text: Bondi Beach is in which Australian city?
questions.fun_fact: The beach lies about 7 km east of the city center and gave its name to the TV series Bondi Rescue.

questions.text: Which tiny animals build the coral structure of the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.fun_fact: The Great Barrier Reef was selected as a World Heritage Site in 1981.

questions.text: Whitehaven Beach, famous for its white silica sand, lies on which of the Whitsunday Islands?
questions.fun_fact: The beach is seven kilometers long, and its bright white sand is about 98 percent pure silica.

questions.text: The name of Australia's Nullarbor Plain comes from Latin words meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: The plain is the world's largest single exposure of limestone bedrock.

questions.text: Which salt lake in South Australia holds the lowest natural point in the country?
questions.fun_fact: On the rare occasions it fills completely, it is the largest lake in Australia.

questions.text: Which mountain chain runs roughly parallel to the east coast of Australia?
questions.fun_fact: It is the fifth-longest land-based mountain chain in the world and the longest entirely within one country.

questions.text: Which Australian state capital lies furthest south?
questions.fun_fact: Founded in 1804 as a penal colony, Hobart is Australia's second-oldest capital city after Sydney.

questions.text: Which city is the capital of Australia's Northern Territory?
questions.fun_fact: The city is named after the naturalist Charles Darwin, although he never visited the area himself.

questions.text: Perth, on Australia's west coast, faces which ocean?
questions.fun_fact: Perth was founded in 1829 and named after the city of Perth in Scotland.

questions.text: Which American architect won the competition to design Canberra?
questions.fun_fact: He developed his style in partnership with his wife, the architect Marion Mahony Griffin.

questions.text: What nickname do Sydneysiders give the Sydney Harbour Bridge?
questions.fun_fact: The bridge, which opened in 1932, carries rail, vehicle, bicycle and pedestrian traffic.

questions.text: The Three Sisters rock formation is a landmark of which mountain range near Sydney?
questions.fun_fact: The range's blue haze is thought to come from oils released by its eucalyptus trees scattering sunlight.

questions.text: Which striped, beehive-shaped sandstone towers are the highlight of Purnululu National Park?
questions.fun_fact: The towers rise in the Kimberley region and are made of sandstones and conglomerates.

questions.text: Which Australian island is the largest sand island in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Lake McKenzie on the island is a perched lake sitting on compact sand about 100 m above sea level.

questions.text: Which island off Perth is famous for its friendly quokkas?
questions.fun_fact: Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh called it 'rats' nest island' in 1696 after the quokkas.

questions.text: What was Uluru's European name, given to it in 1873?
questions.fun_fact: It was named for Sir Henry Ayers, then Chief Secretary of South Australia.

questions.text: Which is the largest desert in Australia?
questions.fun_fact: Explorer Ernest Giles named it after Queen Victoria after crossing it in 1875.

questions.text: Which peninsula in Australia's far north ends at the continent's northernmost mainland point?
questions.fun_fact: In 1606 the Dutch sailor Willem Janszoon reached the peninsula, the first recorded European landing in Australia.

questions.text: Which strait separates the northern tip of Australia from the Papuan coast?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the navigator Luís Vaz de Torres, who sailed through it in 1606 on a Spanish expedition.

questions.text: Which Australian island territory is known for its annual red crab migration?
questions.fun_fact: The red crab is found only on Christmas Island and the nearby Cocos (Keeling) Islands.

questions.text: Big Ben, an active volcano, rises on which remote Australian subantarctic territory?
questions.fun_fact: Its summit, at 2,745 m, is higher than any peak on the Australian mainland.

questions.text: Australia's Dingo Fence, among the longest structures on Earth, was built to protect which animals?
questions.fun_fact: The fence stretches 5,614 km, from the Darling Downs to the Nullarbor cliffs above the Great Australian Bight.

questions.text: Which huge underground water source lies beneath about a fifth of Australia?
questions.fun_fact: It is the largest and deepest artesian basin in the world, covering 1.7 million square kilometers.

questions.text: Hamelin Pool, famous for living stromatolites, is part of which World Heritage bay?
questions.fun_fact: Stromatolites, dome-shaped microbial colonies, are said to be among the oldest life forms on Earth.

questions.text: Which Australian state is the largest by area?
questions.fun_fact: It is also the second-largest subdivision of any country on Earth.

questions.text: What is the common name for Australia's remote, sparsely populated interior?
questions.fun_fact: Despite its dry image, the Outback includes tropical as well as arid climate zones.

questions.text: Which nickname describes the arid heart of Australia around Alice Springs?
questions.fun_fact: It is commonly taken to cover an area up to 600 km from Alice Springs.

questions.text: Which large, enclosed bay is surrounded by Melbourne and Geelong?
questions.fun_fact: The bay is horsehead-shaped and almost completely enclosed, with a narrow entrance called The Rip.

questions.text: Which is the highest mountain in Tasmania?
questions.fun_fact: At 1,617 m, it stands in the Pelion Range within Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair National Park.

questions.text: Which tropical rainforest, home to the southern cassowary, lies north of Cairns?
questions.fun_fact: It is part of the Wet Tropics of Queensland, the largest continuous area of tropical rainforest in Australia.

questions.text: Which continent is known as the driest inhabited one?
questions.fun_fact: Australia is also described as the world's flattest inhabited continent.

questions.text: What does the Māori name Aotearoa, used for New Zealand, usually translate as?
options: Land of the long white cloud
questions.fun_fact: The name was originally used by the Māori only for the North Island.

questions.text: Which strait separates New Zealand's North and South Islands?
questions.fun_fact: At its narrowest the strait is 22 km wide and has a reputation for unpredictable weather.

questions.text: Which is the tallest mountain in New Zealand?
questions.fun_fact: A 1991 collapse of rock and ice from its northern peak lowered its height.

questions.text: Despite its name, Milford Sound is actually which type of landform?
questions.fun_fact: Rudyard Kipling called Milford Sound the eighth wonder of the world.

questions.text: Which New Zealand city is famous for geysers, hot springs and bubbling mud pools?
questions.fun_fact: The city sits inside the Rotorua Caldera, the source of its geothermal activity.

questions.text: What kind of landform does New Zealand's Lake Taupō fill?
questions.fun_fact: The Oruanui eruption about 25,600 years ago was the largest known eruption of the past 70,000 years.

questions.text: Which symmetrical volcano, also called Mount Egmont, rises on the North Island's west coast?
questions.fun_fact: Its secondary cone on the south side is called Fanthams Peak.

questions.text: Which active volcano is the highest point on New Zealand's North Island?
questions.fun_fact: Its highest peak, Tahurangi, reaches 2,797 m, and it has a hot crater lake.

questions.text: Franz Josef Glacier, in New Zealand's West Coast region, is on which island?
questions.fun_fact: Its Māori name is Kā Roimata o Hine Hukatere, and the Waiho River flows out from its end.

questions.text: Which is New Zealand's longest glacier?
questions.fun_fact: Its meltwater flows through Tasman Lake and the Tasman River into Lake Pukaki.

questions.text: Queenstown, hub of New Zealand's adventure tourism, lies on which lake?
questions.fun_fact: At 80 km, Lake Wakatipu is the longest lake in New Zealand.

questions.text: Which island, also known as Rakiura, lies south of New Zealand's South Island?
questions.fun_fact: Rakiura means 'glowing skies' in Māori.

questions.text: Which New Zealand island group lies about 800 km east of the South Island?
questions.fun_fact: The islands have their own time zone, 45 minutes ahead of mainland New Zealand.

questions.text: Which New Zealand city is nicknamed the 'City of Sails'?
questions.fun_fact: The urban core sits on a narrow isthmus between the Manukau and Waitematā harbours.

questions.text: Which mountain range runs the length of New Zealand's South Island?
questions.fun_fact: The mountains are still being raised by tectonic pressure along the Alpine Fault.

questions.text: Which New Zealand national park was founded in 1942, 300 years after a Dutch explorer's visit?
questions.fun_fact: Its popular coast track runs for about 60 km along the park's eastern and northern shores.

questions.text: Which spherical boulders lie scattered along Koekohe Beach on New Zealand's Otago coast?
questions.fun_fact: The largest boulders measure up to about 2.2 meters across.

questions.text: Dunedin's name comes from the Scottish Gaelic name of which city?
questions.fun_fact: Dunedin comes from Dùn Èideann, meaning 'fort of Edin'.

questions.text: Which is New Zealand's longest river?
questions.fun_fact: The 425-km river flows through Lake Taupō and creates the Huka Falls.

questions.text: What creates the starry glow in the caves around Waitomo, New Zealand?
questions.fun_fact: The glowworm there is Arachnocampa luminosa, which is actually a fungus gnat.

questions.text: The Antipodes Islands are named for lying near the antipodes of which city?
questions.fun_fact: They are the southeasternmost point of land in the world outside Antarctica.

questions.text: Which large gulf on Australia's north coast lies just east of Arnhem Land?
questions.fun_fact: The gulf was dry land during the last ice age, when a large, shallow lake filled its center.

questions.text: Which sea separates Australia from New Zealand?
questions.fun_fact: The sea measures about 2,800 km from north to south.

questions.text: Which island in the Hawaiian chain is nicknamed the Big Island?
questions.fun_fact: The island holds 63 percent of the Hawaiian archipelago's total land area.

questions.text: Which Hawaiian island is nicknamed the Garden Isle?
questions.fun_fact: Kauai is home to Waimea Canyon State Park and Nā Pali Coast State Park.

questions.text: On which Hawaiian island is the state capital, Honolulu?
questions.fun_fact: Oʻahu is often nicknamed 'The Gathering Place'.

questions.text: Haleakalā, a huge volcano on Maui, has a name that means what?
questions.fun_fact: Its tallest point, Puʻu ʻUlaʻula or Red Hill, is 3,055 m high.

questions.text: Which mountain is the highest peak on any island on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Its other name, Carstensz Pyramid, honors Dutch explorer Jan Carstenszoon, who saw its glaciers in 1623.

questions.text: Which island, shared by two countries, is the world's second-largest island?
questions.fun_fact: The border between its western and eastern halves runs mostly along the 141st meridian east.

questions.text: Which is the largest island of Fiji?
questions.fun_fact: Viti Levu means 'Great Fiji' and is home to most of the country's people.

questions.text: Tahiti, Moorea and Bora Bora belong to which French Pacific territory?
questions.fun_fact: The territory is divided into five island groups, including the Society Islands and Marquesas.

questions.text: Which three island groups mark the corners of the Polynesian Triangle?
questions.fun_fact: The triangle is often used as a simple way to define Polynesia.

questions.text: The ancient stone city of Nan Madol was built on artificial islets off which Micronesian island?
questions.fun_fact: Nan Madol means 'within the intervals' and has 92 artificial islets separated by tidal canals.

questions.text: On which Vanuatu island can visitors approach the nearly constantly erupting Mount Yasur?
questions.fun_fact: Yasur has erupted nearly continuously for several hundred years, often several times an hour.

questions.text: Upolu and Savai'i are the two main islands of which Pacific country?
questions.fun_fact: Early European explorers called the island group the 'Navigator Islands' for its people's seafaring skills.

questions.text: Which material was strip-mined on the Pacific island of Nauru for about a century?
questions.fun_fact: At just 21 square kilometers, Nauru is the third-smallest country in the world.

questions.text: Roughly 70 percent of the world's fresh water is frozen on which continent?
questions.fun_fact: The Antarctic ice sheet that covers most of the continent averages about 1.9 km thick.

questions.text: Which ocean encircles Antarctica?
questions.fun_fact: The National Geographic Society officially recognized it as an ocean only in June 2021.

questions.text: Seen in skies near Antarctica, the southern lights are known by which Latin name?
questions.fun_fact: Australis comes from Auster, the ancient Roman name for the south wind.

questions.text: If you stand exactly at the South Pole, which way is every direction?
questions.fun_fact: The ice sheet at the pole slowly moves, so the marker for the geographic South Pole is moved several meters each year.

questions.text: What name is given to ground that stays frozen for two or more years in a row?
questions.fun_fact: The deepest permafrost reaches more than 1,500 m below the surface.

questions.text: What lies beneath the ice at the geographic North Pole?
questions.fun_fact: A Russian submersible measured the sea depth there at 4,261 m in 2007.

questions.text: Which Arctic sea route through Canada's islands links the Atlantic and Pacific oceans?
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, European explorers searched for this route as a possible trade route to Asia.

questions.text: Which is the southernmost active volcano on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Its summit crater holds a long-lived lava lake that has been present since at least the early 1970s.

questions.text: Which research station stands at the geographic South Pole?
questions.fun_fact: Built in 1956, it has been occupied ever since; there the Sun stays up for six months and then down for six.

questions.text: Shackleton sailed the lifeboat James Caird from Elephant Island to which island to seek help?
questions.fun_fact: Shackleton and five companions sailed about 1,300 km to get rescue for the stranded main party.

questions.text: Who led the Australasian Antarctic Expedition of 1911-14?
questions.fun_fact: Its sledging parties covered around 4,180 km of unexplored territory.

questions.text: Who led the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition of the 1950s?
questions.fun_fact: The expedition completed the first overland crossing of Antarctica, via the South Pole.

questions.text: McMurdo Station, a major Antarctic research hub, sits on which island?
questions.fun_fact: It takes its name from McMurdo Sound, named in 1841 after Lieutenant Archibald McMurdo of HMS Terror.

questions.text: Which is the highest mountain in Antarctica?
questions.fun_fact: Mount Vinson, at 4,892 m, lies in the Sentinel Range of the Ellsworth Mountains.

questions.text: Lake Vostok in Antarctica lies beneath roughly how much ice?
questions.fun_fact: The lake surface lies about 500 m below sea level, under the ice.

questions.text: Which long arm of Antarctica reaches out toward South America?
questions.fun_fact: Chile calls it O'Higgins Land, while Argentina calls it Tierra de San Martín.

questions.text: Which mountain range forms the boundary between East and West Antarctica?
questions.fun_fact: About 3,500 km long, it is one of the longest mountain ranges on Earth.

questions.text: Which Antarctic region of ice-free valleys is among the driest places on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: It is the largest ice-free region in Antarctica.

questions.text: What name is given to gravity-driven winds that rush downslope off ice sheets?
questions.fun_fact: Dense, cold air builds up over elevated ice sheets and then drains downhill.

questions.text: What do sailors call the strong westerly winds between 40 and 50 degrees south?
questions.fun_fact: They helped ships sail the Brouwer Route from Europe to the East Indies in the Age of Sail.

questions.text: Scott Base is an Antarctic research station of which country?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Captain Robert Falcon Scott, who led two British expeditions to the Ross Sea area.

questions.text: Which Antarctic island is the flooded caldera of an active volcano, entered through Neptune's Bellows?
questions.fun_fact: The island once held a whaling station and is now a popular stop for tourist ships.

questions.text: Which ice-free Russian Arctic port lies on Kola Bay?
questions.fun_fact: The city lies about 100 km from the border with Norway and about 1,930 km from Moscow.

questions.text: On which Arctic island did woolly mammoths survive until around 4,000 years ago?
questions.fun_fact: Wrangel Island has the highest density of polar bear dens in the world.

questions.text: Which remote subantarctic archipelago, administered by France, is nicknamed the Desolation Islands?
questions.fun_fact: The islands are among the most isolated places on Earth and part of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands.

questions.text: Which landmass holds the second-largest body of ice in the world?
questions.fun_fact: The ice sheet stretches almost 2,900 km from north to south.

questions.text: Brisbane is the capital of which Australian state?
questions.fun_fact: The city takes its name from the Brisbane River, named after Sir Thomas Brisbane, a governor of New South Wales.

questions.text: Which Indigenous people of northern Scandinavia are best known for semi-nomadic reindeer herding?
questions.fun_fact: Their homeland, Sápmi, was formerly known as Lapland and stretches across four countries.

questions.text: What does the Svalbard Global Seed Vault safeguard?
questions.fun_fact: It stands on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in the Arctic Svalbard archipelago.

questions.text: In which year was the Antarctic Treaty opened for signature?
questions.fun_fact: The 12 original signatories were countries active in Antarctica during the International Geophysical Year.

questions.text: Which engineer designed the pioneering steamship SS Great Britain, launched in 1843?
questions.fun_fact: In 1845 she became the first iron steamer to cross the Atlantic, taking 14 days.

questions.text: Which giant steamship laid the first lasting transatlantic telegraph cable in 1866?
questions.fun_fact: At 692 feet, her length was not surpassed by any other ship until 1899.

questions.text: The first transatlantic telegraph cable of 1858 ran from Valentia Island, Ireland, to which place?
questions.fun_fact: That first cable worked for only about three weeks before it failed.

questions.text: Samuel Morse, co-developer of the telegraph code named after him, first made his name as what?
questions.fun_fact: He returned from England in 1815 to start a full-time career as a painter.

questions.text: Introduced in 1839, which early photographic process made images on silver-coated plates?
questions.fun_fact: Each image was a one-of-a-kind positive, so it could not be printed from a negative.

questions.text: Which English inventor introduced the calotype, a paper-based photographic process, in 1841?
questions.fun_fact: Its translucent paper negative could be used to make many positive prints.

questions.text: Which British reformer proposed the Penny Black, the first adhesive postage stamp, issued in 1840?
questions.fun_fact: Before it, the recipient normally paid the postage when a letter was delivered.

questions.text: Which city opened the world's first underground passenger railway in January 1863?
questions.fun_fact: Its first trains were steam-powered and ran through cut-and-cover tunnels.

questions.text: Which city opened continental Europe's first electrified underground railway in 1896?
questions.fun_fact: Only London's City and South London Railway of 1890 is an older electrified underground.

questions.text: Which river does the Brooklyn Bridge, opened in 1883, cross?
questions.fun_fact: When it opened, its 1,595-foot main span made it the longest suspension bridge in the world.

questions.text: Which English inventor patented a process in the 1850s for cheap steel, blowing air through molten iron?
questions.fun_fact: His first licensees failed to make good steel, so he bought the licenses back.

questions.text: Which Frenchman patented a loom attachment in 1804 that used punched cards to weave complex patterns?
questions.fun_fact: Using replaceable punched cards to control a sequence is seen as an important step in computing history.

questions.text: Which Scottish veterinary surgeon developed the practical pneumatic tire in the late 1880s?
questions.fun_fact: He spent most of his career in Ireland and sold his tire rights for a small sum.

questions.text: Which luxury train service, created in 1883, eventually linked Paris with Istanbul?
questions.fun_fact: It was created by the Belgian company Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits; its first run in 1883 went from Paris to Vienna.

questions.text: Which railway, opened in north-east England in 1825, was the world's first public railway to use steam locomotives?
questions.fun_fact: Coal wagons were steam-hauled from the start, but passengers rode in horse-drawn coaches until 1833.

questions.text: Which Scottish geologist wrote Principles of Geology (1830-33)?
questions.fun_fact: The book argued that Earth was shaped by the same slow natural processes that still operate.

questions.text: In 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie discovered which element, named after Marie's native country?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first element discovered purely because of its strong radioactivity.

questions.text: Which London bridge, opened in 1894, has a middle section that opens to let ships through?
questions.fun_fact: It combines bascule and suspension bridge designs and was designed by Horace Jones.

questions.text: Which young woman traveled with the Lewis and Clark Expedition from North Dakota to the Pacific Ocean?
questions.fun_fact: She joined the expedition in her teens and helped it make contact with other peoples.

questions.text: Which British navigator led the first inshore circumnavigation of mainland Australia, then called New Holland?
questions.fun_fact: He is credited as the first person to use the name Australia for the whole continent.

questions.text: Which British explorer reached Lake Victoria in 1858 and named it in honor of his queen?
questions.fun_fact: He was most associated with the search for the source of the Nile.

questions.text: Which missionary and explorer did Henry Morton Stanley find at Ujiji, near Lake Tanganyika, in 1871?
questions.fun_fact: His famous greeting is missing from his journal: the pages after the meeting were torn out, and he likely invented the line later.

questions.text: Which British Romantic painter created Rain, Steam and Speed - The Great Western Railway (1844)?
questions.fun_fact: It shows a locomotive crossing Maidenhead Railway Bridge; no academic painter had used a train as a subject before.

questions.text: Which painter created The Potato Eaters in 1885?
questions.fun_fact: He painted it in Nuenen, Netherlands; it now hangs in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.

questions.text: Which decorative style of 1890-1910, inspired by sinuous plant forms, is linked to Alphonse Mucha and Victor Horta?

questions.fun_fact: The Saturday Evening Post bought the serial rights for $750 in 1903.

questions.text: Which boxer became the first Black world heavyweight champion by beating Tommy Burns in Sydney in 1908?
questions.fun_fact: Police stepped into the ring in the 14th round, stopping the fight in front of over 20,000 spectators.

questions.text: Henry Ford founded the Ford Motor Company in 1903 in which US state?
questions.fun_fact: Its first cars were built a few a day by small teams at a factory on Mack Avenue in Detroit.

questions.text: Which Swedish author became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1909?
questions.fun_fact: She published her first novel, Gösta Berling's Saga, at the age of 33.

questions.text: In which sport did American Margaret Abbott win an Olympic title at the 1900 Paris Games?
questions.fun_fact: Abbott never realized that she had won an Olympic event; her prize was a porcelain bowl.

questions.text: In which city was the firm later known as Rolex founded in 1905?
questions.fun_fact: It began as Wilsdorf and Davis and registered Rolex as its brand name in 1908.

questions.text: In which city did Antoni Gaudí remodel the Casa Batlló between 1904 and 1906?
questions.fun_fact: Its arched roof has been likened to the back of a dragon.

questions.text: Which Austrian painter completed Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I, rich in gold leaf, in 1907?
questions.fun_fact: It sold in 2006 for US$135 million, at the time a record price for a painting.

questions.text: Which Shakespeare play gave Elgar the title phrase for his Pomp and Circumstance marches?
questions.fun_fact: The trio of the first march (1901) contains the tune later known as "Land of Hope and Glory".

questions.text: Which German physicist introduced the idea of energy quanta in 1900, founding quantum theory?
questions.fun_fact: In 1948 the Kaiser Wilhelm Society, which he had twice led, was renamed the Max Planck Society.

questions.text: In Selma Lagerlöf's 1906 book, the shrunken boy Nils travels across Sweden on which bird's back?
questions.fun_fact: The Swedish title means "Nils Holgersson's wonderful journey across Sweden".

questions.text: In 1905, the year of his four groundbreaking papers, where did Albert Einstein work?
questions.fun_fact: He had acquired Swiss citizenship in 1901 and kept it for the rest of his life.

questions.text: In which Indian city did the Taj Mahal Palace hotel open in December 1903?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the Taj Mahal in Agra, about 1,050 km away.

questions.text: In which city did Charles Rennie Mackintosh design the Willow Tearooms, which opened in 1903?
questions.fun_fact: They are the only surviving tearooms that Mackintosh designed for his patron, Miss Catherine Cranston.

questions.text: Which engineer designed an air-conditioning system for a Brooklyn printing plant in 1902?
questions.fun_fact: Humid summers made the paper swell and shrink, spoiling color prints that needed up to four passes.

questions.text: Which team won the first modern World Series, in 1903?
questions.fun_fact: Boston came back from a three-games-to-one deficit in the best-of-nine series.

questions.text: In which city was the Harley-Davidson Motor Company founded in 1903?
questions.fun_fact: The first Harley-Davidson was assembled in a 10-by-15-foot shed in the Davidson family's backyard.

questions.text: Which ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire was begun by Darius I around 518 BC?
questions.fun_fact: Visitors entered through the Gate of All Nations, guarded by huge stone bulls with human heads.

questions.text: Which Chinese dynasty gave its name to China's largest ethnic group?
questions.fun_fact: A census of AD 2 under the Han counted more than 57 million people.

questions.text: Arthur Evans excavated which Minoan palace on Crete?
questions.fun_fact: Evans began large-scale digging in 1900 at Knossos, the largest and best-known center of Minoan civilization.

questions.text: In the 'Eternal Treaty' of about 1259 BC, Ramesses II of Egypt made peace with which Bronze Age empire?
questions.fun_fact: A copy of the treaty is displayed at the United Nations headquarters in New York as an early peace agreement.

questions.text: The Royal Game of Ur is named after an ancient city in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: Its rules were pieced together from a Babylonian clay tablet written in 177 BC.

questions.text: In an ancient Greek city, what was the agora?
options: A fortified citadel on a hilltop
An open square for markets and meetings
questions.fun_fact: The word agora literally means 'gathering place' or 'assembly'.

questions.text: The Maya wrote numbers with dots and bars. What did a shell symbol stand for?
questions.fun_fact: Maya numbers were base 20, and just three symbols, a shell, a dot and a bar, could write every digit from 0 to 19.

questions.text: In the ancient Mediterranean, what was an amphora?
questions.fun_fact: In Rome, Monte Testaccio is a hill made from the broken remains of discarded amphorae.

questions.text: Which Greek sailing guide of the 1st century AD lists trade ports from the Red Sea to India?
questions.fun_fact: It credits Hippalus with finding a direct sailing route across the open ocean from the Red Sea to India.

questions.text: What was the bound-page book format that gradually replaced the scroll in Roman times?
questions.fun_fact: Early codices were made of papyrus or parchment sheets folded and stitched together at one edge.

questions.text: Which statesman led Athens in the 5th century BC and championed the building of the Parthenon?
questions.fun_fact: His building program also gave the Acropolis its monumental gateway, the Propylaea.

questions.text: Which philosopher of Athens was the teacher of Plato?
questions.fun_fact: Socrates wrote nothing himself; we know him mainly through his students Plato and Xenophon.

questions.text: Mesopotamia lay between which two rivers?
questions.fun_fact: Early settlers in the region used wooden plows to grow crops such as barley, onions and turnips.

questions.text: Which English city, famous for its hot springs, grew from the Roman town of Aquae Sulis?
questions.fun_fact: The Romans built a bathing complex and temple around the hot spring, which visitors can still see as the Roman Baths.

questions.text: Which Iranian empire, ruling from about 247 BC to AD 224, lay between Rome and China on the Silk Road?
questions.fun_fact: Parthian horse archers were famed for the 'Parthian shot': feigning retreat, then turning in the saddle to shoot at pursuers.

questions.text: Vindobona, a Roman fortress on the Danube, grew into which modern capital?
questions.fun_fact: Its legionary fortress was probably built around AD 100, since the oldest dated building inscriptions are from 103.

questions.text: Which ancient people, whose lands covered roughly modern Tuscany, ruled central Italy before Rome rose?
questions.fun_fact: The Etruscans developed their writing from the Euboean Greek alphabet, which was used in southern Italy.

questions.text: The word 'paradise' goes back to an Old Iranian word with which literal meaning?
questions.fun_fact: The word came to mean the walled gardens of Persian kings, and Xenophon used the Greek paradeisos for their royal parks.

questions.text: Which Assyrian king gathered a vast library of clay tablets at Nineveh?
questions.fun_fact: Many Mesopotamian works, including the Epic of Gilgamesh, survive thanks to copies kept in his library.

questions.text: Which calendar, introduced in 45 BC, added a leap day every fourth year?
questions.fun_fact: Its 365.25-day average year is slightly longer than the solar year, a drift that the Gregorian reform of 1582 corrected.

questions.text: Cleopatra VII belonged to a dynasty founded by a general of which conqueror?
questions.fun_fact: Though descended from Greek rulers, Cleopatra is the only Ptolemaic ruler known to have learned the Egyptian language.

questions.text: Which month is named after Julius Caesar?
questions.fun_fact: July was originally Quintilis, Latin for fifth, because the old Roman year began in March.

questions.text: Which Bronze Age Greek citadel was entered through the Lion Gate?
questions.fun_fact: Its relief of two lions is the only surviving monumental sculpture of Mycenaean Greece and the largest of the Aegean Bronze Age.

questions.text: The colonists who founded Carthage came from which Phoenician city?
questions.fun_fact: Carthage grew into a major power of the western Mediterranean during the first millennium BC.

questions.text: Who is credited as the architect of the Step Pyramid at Saqqara?
questions.fun_fact: Rising in six steps to about 62 m, the Step Pyramid is described as the earliest colossal stone building in Egypt.

questions.text: Which thinker of Miletus is often called the first Greek philosopher, claiming all is water?
questions.fun_fact: He is said to have worked out the height of a pyramid by measuring its shadow.

questions.text: Which Roman road, begun in 312 BC, was nicknamed the 'queen of roads'?
questions.fun_fact: It linked Rome with Brindisi, a port on the Adriatic coast of southern Italy.

questions.text: Lothal, an Indus Valley site in India, is famed for a brick basin often seen as one of the earliest known what?
questions.fun_fact: Lothal's trade in beads, gems and ornaments reached West Asia and Africa.

questions.text: Which of these is NOT one of China's traditional 'Four Great Inventions'?
questions.fun_fact: Francis Bacon first praised three great inventions: printing, gunpowder and the compass; later writers added paper.

questions.text: Which animal's body does the Great Sphinx of Giza have?
questions.fun_fact: The Sphinx is carved from the limestone bedrock of the Giza Plateau, which also served as the quarry for the nearby pyramids.

questions.text: Which scholar of Alexandria estimated Earth's circumference around 240 BC?
questions.fun_fact: He compared the Sun's shadows at Alexandria and Syene (modern Aswan), and he also served as chief librarian at Alexandria.

questions.text: According to Greek myth, Athens was named after which goddess?
questions.fun_fact: In the myth, Athena won the city by offering its people the first domesticated olive tree.

questions.text: Which board game played with black and white stones began in ancient China?
questions.fun_fact: A standard Go board has 19 by 19 lines, giving 361 points on which to play.

questions.text: In which year did the Romans traditionally date the founding of their city?
questions.fun_fact: Ancient historians computed several founding dates, but 753 BC, from the Varronian chronology, became the standard one.

questions.text: The Library of Celsus stands in the ruins of which ancient city in Turkey?
questions.fun_fact: It was the third-largest library of the Greco-Roman world, after Alexandria and Pergamum, and held around 12,000 scrolls.

questions.text: Which huge city, with the Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon, flourished near modern Mexico City?
questions.fun_fact: At its zenith, perhaps between AD 1 and 500, it was the largest city in the Americas, with about 100,000 people.

questions.text: Which 4th-century BC theater in the Peloponnese is famed for its exceptional acoustics?
questions.fun_fact: Its capacity was 13,000 to 14,000 spectators, and it hosted music, singing and dramatic games.

questions.text: Which epic poet is traditionally credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey?
questions.fun_fact: Ancient editors divided each of the two epics into 24 books.

questions.text: Which Greek thinker gave his name to the theorem about the sides of a right triangle?
questions.fun_fact: Babylonian clay tablets show the relationship was known more than 1,000 years before Pythagoras.

questions.text: What is a qanat, an ancient Persian engineering feat?
options: A windmill tower for grinding grain
A tunnel carrying groundwater to fields
questions.fun_fact: Some qanats in Iran are still in use and are protected as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

questions.text: Cloth found at Mohenjo-daro in the Indus Valley is among the earliest evidence of which fiber's use?
questions.fun_fact: The Indus Valley region is a likely site for the first cultivation of tree cotton, which may have been an important export.

questions.text: Which Roman author wrote Natural History, an encyclopedia of 37 books?
questions.fun_fact: Completed around AD 77, his encyclopedia is one of the largest works to survive from the Roman Empire.

questions.text: The Behistun Inscription, key to deciphering cuneiform, was carved for which Persian king?
questions.fun_fact: It gives the same text in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian.

questions.text: Which Greek historian is called the 'Father of History' for his work The Histories?
questions.fun_fact: He was born in Halicarnassus, a Greek city in what is now Turkey.

questions.text: What was the original name of the Colosseum?
questions.fun_fact: The name Colosseum probably came from a nearby colossal statue of Nero.

questions.text: What did Mesopotamians roll over wet clay to leave a repeating picture as a mark of ownership?
questions.fun_fact: Most seals had a hole through the center, so they could be worn on a necklace and always be at hand.

questions.text: Which adviser of Chandragupta Maurya is credited with the Arthashastra, a guide to statecraft?
questions.fun_fact: The text was thought lost until a manuscript turned up in 1905, and it was first published in 1909.

questions.text: Which Roman silver coin gave British money its old abbreviation 'd' for pence?
questions.fun_fact: One gold aureus was worth 25 silver denarii, or 100 bronze sestertii.

questions.text: Which high priestess of Ur, around 2300 BC, is often celebrated as the earliest known named author?
questions.fun_fact: She was a daughter of Sargon of Akkad, and hymns to the goddess Inanna are attributed to her, though scholars debate her authorship.

questions.text: Which volcanic ash, mixed with lime, helped Roman concrete set even underwater?
questions.fun_fact: In Roman harbor concrete, seawater reacted with the volcanic ash to grow rare tobermorite crystals that may resist cracking.

questions.text: Which sculptor made the huge ivory-and-gold Statue of Zeus at Olympia?
questions.fun_fact: The seated statue was about 12 m tall and was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

questions.text: What are the stepped temple towers of ancient Mesopotamia called?
questions.fun_fact: A ziggurat had a core of sun-baked bricks faced with fired bricks that were often glazed in different colors.

questions.text: The Great Hypostyle Hall, with 134 columns in 16 rows, is part of which Egyptian temple complex?
questions.fun_fact: The hall covers about 5,000 square meters, and its central columns are far taller than the rest.

questions.text: Which pharaoh had the rock temples of Abu Simbel carved into a cliff?
questions.fun_fact: In 1968 the whole complex was moved to higher ground to keep it from being flooded by Lake Nasser.

questions.text: What is the circular opening at the top of the Pantheon's dome called?
questions.fun_fact: The height to the oculus equals the dome's interior diameter, 43 m.

questions.text: Which philosopher tutored the young Alexander the Great?
questions.fun_fact: Aristotle later founded his own school in Athens, known as the Lyceum.

questions.text: Which early Mesoamerican civilization carved colossal stone heads?
questions.fun_fact: The basalt slabs used for the heads were transported more than 150 km, a huge effort for the Olmec.

questions.text: What does Mare Nostrum, the Roman name for the Mediterranean, mean?
