questions.fun_fact: Romans also called it Mare Internum, meaning the inner sea.

questions.text: Which Greek explorer from Massalia sailed to northern Europe around 325 BC?
questions.fun_fact: He described Thule, an island six days' sail north of Britain, and is the first person on record to describe the midnight sun.

questions.text: Which pharaoh sent Phoenician sailors around Africa about 600 BC, according to Herodotus?
questions.fun_fact: The sailors reportedly said that during the voyage the Sun was on their right.

questions.text: Which Greek city-state's strict way of life gave us the word 'spartan'?
questions.fun_fact: Sparta was famed for its Laconic wit, a term drawn from Laconia, the region around the city.

questions.text: Which modern Indian city stands on the site of Pataliputra, capital of the Maurya Empire?
questions.fun_fact: The Greek ambassador Megasthenes described the city in his book Indica.

questions.text: What was the Roman system of underfloor heating called?
questions.fun_fact: Hot air from a furnace flowed beneath raised floors and up through hollow walls to warm bathhouses and villas.

questions.text: Which garment, a long draped wool cloth, was the formal dress of Roman citizens?
questions.fun_fact: Boys and some officials wore the toga praetexta, which had a purple border.

questions.text: In Roman numerals, which number does the letter D stand for?
questions.fun_fact: Roman numerals had no symbol for zero.

questions.text: Which Chinese waterway, begun in the 5th century BC, is the world's longest canal?
questions.fun_fact: It links Beijing in the north with Hangzhou in the south over about 1,800 km.

questions.text: According to legend, what fell into Empress Leizu's tea and led her to discover silk?
questions.fun_fact: Leizu is traditionally credited with teaching the Chinese how to raise silkworms and weave silk.

questions.text: The earliest known chocolate drink in ancient Mesoamerica was made from beans of which tree?
questions.fun_fact: Cacao beans were so valued in Maya and Aztec lands that they also served as currency.

questions.text: Which Roman emperor was born in Leptis Magna, in what is now Libya?
questions.fun_fact: Leptis Magna began as a Punic settlement before 500 BC, and its ruins are among the best-preserved Roman sites.

questions.text: Early Chinese compasses were made with which naturally magnetic material?
questions.fun_fact: The magnetic compass began as a divination device in Han-dynasty China and was adopted for navigation by the Song.

questions.text: On which island did the Colossus, a giant bronze statue of Helios, stand?
questions.fun_fact: The statue, finished in 280 BC, stood about 33 m high and was among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

questions.text: The giant Nazca Lines, etched into a desert plain, are in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Among the figures are a hummingbird, a monkey and a spider.

questions.text: Which ancient Greek storyteller is credited with the fable of the tortoise and the hare?
questions.fun_fact: Early sources say Aesop was a slave on the island of Samos, though whether he really lived is uncertain.

questions.text: Which ancient people originated the base-60 number system behind our 60-minute hour?
questions.fun_fact: Base 60 also lies behind the 360 degrees of a circle.

questions.text: The Pont du Gard, a three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge, stands in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: The bridge stands almost 49 m high and was built largely without mortar.

questions.text: The rust-resistant Iron Pillar of Delhi dates from the time of which dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: It now stands in Delhi's Qutb complex, but it was probably first erected elsewhere and moved there in the 11th century.

questions.text: Oracle bones, bearing the earliest known significant body of Chinese writing, come from which dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: The inscriptions were scratched onto ox shoulder blades and turtle shells.

questions.text: Which Roman poet wrote the Aeneid?
questions.fun_fact: In Dante's Divine Comedy, Virgil appears as the poet's guide through Hell and Purgatory.

questions.text: The Maya city of Tikal, with its towering temple-pyramids, lies in which modern country?
questions.fun_fact: Tikal's ruins were used as a filming location in the 1977 film Star Wars.

questions.text: Which Han historian wrote the Records of the Grand Historian?
questions.fun_fact: His history runs for more than two thousand years, beginning with the legendary Yellow Emperor.

questions.text: Which irrigation project of about 256 BC still waters the Chengdu Plain in Sichuan?
questions.fun_fact: Its builder Li Bing split the Min River with a fish-mouth levee instead of damming it.

questions.text: Naples began in the 8th century BC as a Greek colony called what?
questions.fun_fact: In the 6th century BC the colony was refounded as Neápolis, the Greek name that gave us Naples.

questions.text: Which Alexandrian engineer described the aeolipile, a spinning steam-jet device, in the 1st century AD?
questions.fun_fact: He also described what may be the first wind-powered machine, a windwheel driving an organ.

questions.text: Which philosopher founded the Academy, a famous school just outside Athens?
questions.fun_fact: The school took its name from Akademia, a grove outside the city walls of Athens.

questions.text: Which Peruvian site, inhabited from about 2600 BC, is among the oldest cities in the Americas?
questions.fun_fact: Caral's upper half has six monumental complexes, each with a pyramid, an open plaza and residential buildings.

questions.text: Which Greek scientist of Syracuse is linked with shouting 'Eureka!' in his bath?
questions.fun_fact: By drawing polygons with 96 sides around and inside a circle, he showed that pi lies between about 3.1408 and 3.1429.

questions.text: Which metal's Latin name, plumbum, gave us the word plumbing?
questions.fun_fact: Romans carried water to homes and baths through lead pipes, and a plumber was originally a worker in lead.

questions.text: What event was Rome's Circus Maximus mainly built for?
questions.fun_fact: The Circus Maximus was 621 m long and could hold over 150,000 spectators.

questions.text: Which Babylonian king rebuilt his capital and raised the glazed-brick Ishtar Gate?
questions.fun_fact: A reconstruction of the Ishtar Gate, using original glazed bricks, stands in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.

questions.text: Londinium, the Roman forerunner of London, was founded on which river?
questions.fun_fact: Londinium's forum basilica was one of the largest structures north of the Alps in Hadrian's day.

questions.text: How many days did the ancient Egyptian civil calendar have in a year?
questions.fun_fact: With no leap years, the civil calendar lost about one day every four years relative to the Julian calendar.

questions.text: The Valley of the Temples, with well-preserved Greek temples, is in which Sicilian city?
questions.fun_fact: Its temples are among the largest and best-preserved ancient Greek buildings outside Greece itself.

questions.text: Which Roman emperor ordered a wall across northern Britain from AD 122?
questions.fun_fact: The wall ran about 117 km (73 miles) across the width of northern England.

questions.text: Which Roman emperor wrote the philosophical notebook known as Meditations?
questions.fun_fact: He wrote it in Greek as private notes to himself, and its original title is unknown.

questions.text: Which Persian highway ran from Sardis to Susa and let couriers cross the empire quickly?
questions.fun_fact: Herodotus' praise of the royal couriers is often linked to the unofficial motto of the US postal service.

questions.text: Which ruler standardized Chinese writing, coins and measures after unifying China?
questions.fun_fact: He invented the title huangdi, meaning emperor, instead of reusing the old title for king.

questions.text: Which Greek engineer dug a tunnel on Samos in the 6th century BC, working from both ends at once?
questions.fun_fact: The tunnel, about 1 km long, carried water into the city of Samos and is a feat of ancient geometry.

questions.text: On how many hills was Rome traditionally said to be built?
questions.fun_fact: The hills include the Palatine, the Capitoline and the Aventine.

questions.text: Which board game with a grid of 30 squares was played in ancient Egypt?
questions.fun_fact: Senet game sets were buried in tombs, and one was found in Tutankhamun's.

questions.text: Which Greek tragedian wrote Oedipus Rex?
questions.fun_fact: Sophocles is said to have won first prize at the Athenian drama festival around 24 times.

questions.text: Which young English astronomer was the first to show that the Moon moves around Earth in an elliptical orbit?
questions.fun_fact: His friend William Crabtree was the only other person to observe the rare planetary transit that Horrocks predicted for 1639.

questions.text: Which Edo-period poet wrote the travel diary 'The Narrow Road to the Deep North', mixing prose and haiku?
questions.fun_fact: His disciples planted a banana plant, bashō, beside his hut, and he took his pen name from it.

questions.text: Which Dutch jurist wrote 'Mare Liberum' ('The Free Seas'), an influential work on the law of the sea?
questions.fun_fact: He has been called the 'father of international law' for his writings on the law of nations.

questions.text: Which color combination made Chinese Ming dynasty porcelain famous around the world?
questions.fun_fact: The blue designs were painted with cobalt, which was often imported from Persia.

questions.text: Versailles began as a hunting lodge built in 1623 for which French king?
questions.fun_fact: The royal court officially moved there in 1682, and the palace grew to contain about 2,300 rooms.

questions.text: Which Florida city, founded by Spain in 1565, is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded settlement in the contiguous US?
questions.fun_fact: Admiral Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, Florida's first governor, founded it on 8 September 1565.

questions.text: Which French navigator led the first French circumnavigation, in 1766-69, and gave his name to a flowering vine?
questions.fun_fact: Botanist Philibert Commerson sailed with him and named the plant bougainvillea in his honor.

questions.text: What is the widespread transfer of plants, animals and goods between the Americas and the Old World after 1492 called?
questions.fun_fact: It is named after Christopher Columbus; historian Alfred W. Crosby coined the term in his 1972 book of the same name.

questions.text: Topkapı Palace, the main residence of Ottoman sultans for centuries, stands in which city?
questions.fun_fact: The palace treasury displays the Spoonmaker's Diamond, one of the largest diamonds in the world.

questions.text: In 1752, which American proposed flying a kite in a thunderstorm to show that lightning is electrical?
questions.fun_fact: In May 1752, Thomas-François Dalibard carried out Franklin's proposed lightning experiment at Marly-la-Ville in France.

questions.text: The name Pacific, given to the ocean by Magellan's expedition, comes from a word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface, more than all of the planet's land combined.

questions.text: Which Danish castle on the Øresund, rebuilt in the 1570s and 1580s, inspired Elsinore in Shakespeare's 'Hamlet'?
questions.fun_fact: The Danish crown demanded Sound Dues from ships entering or leaving the Baltic through the Øresund.

questions.text: In Edo-period Japan, a daimyo's wealth was measured in koku, a unit of what?
questions.fun_fact: One koku was roughly the amount of rice needed to feed one person for a year.

questions.text: In 1710 a royal porcelain factory opened in which Saxon town, the first in Europe to make hard-paste porcelain?
questions.fun_fact: Johann Friedrich Böttger brought the porcelain to market, financed by Augustus the Strong, King of Poland and Elector of Saxony.

questions.text: Which northwestern Anatolian town produced the blue, turquoise and red tiles that decorated Ottoman buildings in the 1500s?
questions.fun_fact: Its potters introduced a distinctive bole red to replace purple, and a bright emerald green to replace sage green.

questions.text: Which drink, enjoyed by the Aztecs, was brought to Europe from Mexico and was a luxury for nobles by the 1600s?
questions.fun_fact: Chocolate drinks were already an essential part of Aztec culture by about 1400.

questions.text: Which Dutch captain left an inscribed pewter plate on an island off Western Australia in 1616?
questions.fun_fact: Eighty years later, in 1697, Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh found the plate half-buried in sand on the same island.

questions.text: Which English mathematician introduced the × symbol for multiplication, in his 1631 'Clavis Mathematicae'?
questions.fun_fact: He is also credited with inventing the slide rule around 1622, though Richard Delamain disputed his priority.

questions.text: The 18th-century European movement that stressed reason and science is called the Age of what?
questions.fun_fact: Immanuel Kant's 1784 essay 'What Is Enlightenment?' contains the Latin phrase sapere aude, 'dare to know'.

questions.text: Which performer is traditionally credited with starting kabuki theater in Kyoto around 1603?
questions.fun_fact: Women were banned from the kabuki stage in 1629, so male actors took over all female roles.

questions.text: Which Qing emperor commissioned the Siku Quanshu, a vast imperial book collection begun in 1772?
questions.fun_fact: Seven copies were produced, and the finished collection runs to 36,381 volumes.

questions.text: Which Mughal empress had coinage struck in her name and is seen by some historians as the real power behind the throne?
questions.fun_fact: Her name, given to her after she married the emperor, means 'Light of the World' in Persian.

questions.text: Which Ethiopian city, founded by Emperor Fasilides in 1636, is known for its royal castles?
questions.fun_fact: Its Fasil Ghebbi royal compound has been nicknamed the 'Camelot of Africa'.

questions.text: Which Spanish explorer gave Florida its name in 1513?
questions.fun_fact: He called it La Florida, partly for its flowering plants and partly because it was Easter season, Pascua Florida.

questions.text: Which Prussian king had Sanssouci built at Potsdam in the 1740s as his summer palace?
questions.fun_fact: Sanssouci is French for 'without worry'.

questions.text: The Uffizi, begun in 1560 by Giorgio Vasari for Cosimo I de' Medici, was first built to house what?
questions.fun_fact: The top floor became a gallery for the Medici family's art, and construction was completed in 1581.

questions.text: Which London palace began as a house that King George III bought for Queen Charlotte in 1761?
questions.fun_fact: It became the monarch's London residence only in 1837, when Queen Victoria came to the throne.

questions.text: Which prolific Spanish playwright of the early 1600s was credited in 1636 with about 1,800 full-length plays?
questions.fun_fact: Of those plays, only about 450 are known to survive.

questions.text: The Red Fort in Delhi takes its name from the color of its massive walls, built of which stone?
questions.fun_fact: Its design is attributed to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, who was also the architect of the Taj Mahal.

questions.text: Which Polynesian navigator joined Cook's Endeavour at Tahiti in 1769 and drew a chart of the Pacific islands?
questions.fun_fact: His chart showed 130 islands within a radius of about 3,200 kilometers, and he could name 74 of them.

questions.text: Which Elizabethan playwright, baptized in 1564 like Shakespeare, wrote 'Tamburlaine' and 'Doctor Faustus'?
questions.fun_fact: He was the first to win a critical reputation for blank verse, which became the standard form of Elizabethan drama.

questions.text: Which English botanist joined Cook's Endeavour voyage in 1768 and later advised King George III on Kew Gardens?
questions.fun_fact: The plant genus Banksia is named after him, and he is credited with introducing eucalyptus and acacia to the Western world.

questions.text: Which English naval official kept a famous private diary from 1660 to 1669?
questions.fun_fact: He wrote it in a form of shorthand called tachygraphy, devised by Thomas Shelton.

questions.text: Which Italian physicist invented the mercury barometer in 1643?
questions.fun_fact: The pressure unit called the torr is named in his honor.

questions.text: Which architect designed Flamsteed House, the original building of the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, begun in 1675?
questions.fun_fact: Commissioned by King Charles II, it was the first purpose-built scientific research facility in Britain.

questions.text: In which Dutch city did William of Orange found the Netherlands' oldest surviving university, in 1575?
questions.fun_fact: The university's Hortus Botanicus is the oldest botanical garden in the Netherlands.

questions.text: Which Ottoman traveler spent over 40 years on the ten-volume 'Seyahatname', a record of journeys across and beyond the empire?
questions.fun_fact: The first volume deals only with Constantinople, and the final volume with Egypt.

questions.text: Galileo taught geometry, mechanics and astronomy at the university of which city from 1592 to 1610?
questions.fun_fact: In March 1610, his last year there, he published his first telescope observations in 'Sidereus Nuncius'.

questions.text: Schönbrunn Palace, rebuilt in its present form in the 1740s and 1750s under Empress Maria Theresa, is in which city?
questions.fun_fact: The zoo in its gardens, Tiergarten Schönbrunn, claims to be the oldest zoo in the world.

questions.text: Hwaseong Fortress, built in 1794-96 with stone and brick, stands in which South Korean city?
questions.fun_fact: Builders used efficient pulleys and cranes, reflecting the Silhak school's interest in practical science.

questions.text: Catherine the Great began the collection of which famous museum in 1764 by buying paintings from a Berlin merchant?
questions.fun_fact: The museum marks its founding each year on 7 December, Saint Catherine's Day.

questions.text: Which Mughal emperor commissioned the Taj Mahal, completed around 1653?
questions.fun_fact: Its white marble came from quarries at Makrana in Rajasthan, and a vast crew of artisans worked on the complex.

questions.text: Which Danish astronomer built the observatory Uraniborg on the island of Hven in the 1570s?
questions.fun_fact: King Frederick II gave Tycho the island of Hven, and Uraniborg became the first large observatory in Christian Europe.

questions.text: Which English captain completed a voyage around the world in 1580 and was knighted aboard his own ship?
questions.fun_fact: His flagship Pelican was renamed Golden Hind to honor his backer Sir Christopher Hatton, after Hatton's coat of arms.

questions.text: Which Dutch explorer named Easter Island after the day he landed there, in 1722?
questions.fun_fact: On the same voyage he became the first European to find Bora Bora and Maupiti in the Society Islands.

questions.text: Which French king began building the Château de Chambord in 1519?
questions.fun_fact: It is the largest château in the Loire Valley, and its double-spiral staircase has two flights that never meet.

questions.text: Which Qing emperor, who took the throne in 1661, ruled for 61 years, one of the longest reigns in Chinese history?
questions.fun_fact: His court also compiled the Complete Tang Poems anthology and the Kangxi Dictionary of Chinese characters.

questions.text: In 1500, a Portuguese fleet under Pedro Álvares Cabral reached which South American land?
questions.fun_fact: Cabral's fleet of 13 ships was bound for India when it sailed far to the west and sighted the Brazilian coast.

questions.text: Which Renaissance artist wrote most of his notebooks in mirror-image cursive, running from right to left?
questions.fun_fact: Because he wrote with his left hand, writing from right to left was probably easier for him.

questions.text: Which French writer popularized the essay as a literary form with his 'Essais', first published in 1580?
questions.fun_fact: He wrote much of the Essais in a tower of his château, where his library was kept.

questions.text: Which Scottish mathematician published the first table of logarithms in 1614 to simplify calculations?
questions.fun_fact: He also invented 'Napier's bones', a set of rods used to speed up multiplication.

questions.text: Which instrument did Dutch spectacle-maker Hans Lipperhey try to patent in 1608?
questions.fun_fact: He got no patent because other spectacle-makers claimed the same invention, but the Dutch government paid him well for copies.

questions.text: Which 17th-century Mexican writer, nicknamed the 'Tenth Muse', became one of colonial Latin America's greatest poets?
options: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
questions.fun_fact: At 17, to test her learning, the viceroy had her answer questions from a panel of scholars, philosophers and poets.

questions.text: In December 1773, protesters threw chests of East India Company tea into the harbor of which American city?
questions.fun_fact: Disguised as Native Americans, they dumped about 340 chests of tea into the water.

questions.text: Which French king was nicknamed the 'Sun King'?
questions.fun_fact: He reigned for 72 years and 110 days, the longest reign of any monarch in history.

questions.text: Which Spanish explorer led the first known descent of the whole Amazon River, in 1541-42?
questions.fun_fact: He reached the river's mouth on 24 August 1542, and he also founded the city of Guayaquil in what is now Ecuador.

questions.text: Which ship carried about 100 passengers from England to North America in 1620?
questions.fun_fact: Before landing, the passengers signed the Mayflower Compact, an early agreement on governing their new colony.

questions.text: Which Russian polymath from the far north of Russia helped found Moscow University in 1755?
questions.fun_fact: His discoveries included the conservation of mass in chemical reactions and a theoretical prediction of Antarctica.

questions.text: Which chief architect of Ottoman sultans, including Suleiman the Magnificent, designed over 300 major structures?
questions.fun_fact: His works include the Kanuni Sultan Suleiman Bridge at Büyükçekmece.

questions.text: Which Swiss mathematician, born in 1707, introduced the notation f(x) for a function and solved the Königsberg bridge problem?
questions.fun_fact: His solution to the Seven Bridges of Königsberg is regarded as the birth of graph theory.

questions.text: Which French philosopher wrote the famous line 'I think, therefore I am'?
questions.fun_fact: He is credited as the father of analytic geometry, and the Cartesian coordinate system is named after him.

questions.text: Which Italian-born astronomer discovered the gap in Saturn's rings that now bears his name, in 1675?
questions.fun_fact: He also discovered four of Saturn's moons: Iapetus, Rhea, Tethys and Dione.

questions.text: Shakespeare's Globe Theatre, built in 1599, stood on the south bank of which river?
questions.fun_fact: The open-air Globe was a round theater that could hold about 3,000 spectators.

questions.text: Daniel Defoe's 1719 novel 'Robinson Crusoe' was probably inspired in part by a sailor marooned on which island group?
questions.fun_fact: In 1966 Chile renamed one of the islands Robinson Crusoe Island.

questions.text: What is the name of the Tokugawa policy of strictly limiting foreign contact from the 1630s to the 1850s?
questions.fun_fact: Even under sakoku, trade continued with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki, and with Korea and the Ryukyu Kingdom.

questions.text: Which Flemish painter created 'Hunters in the Snow' in 1565?
questions.fun_fact: It is one of a series of works, five of which survive, that depict different times of the year.

questions.text: Which Mughal emperor founded the capital city of Fatehpur Sikri in 1571?
questions.fun_fact: Akbar used it as his capital only from 1571 to 1585, and the city was completely abandoned by 1610.

questions.text: Which French philosopher edited the 'Encyclopédie', published from 1751 to 1772, with Jean le Rond d'Alembert?
questions.fun_fact: The first edition had seventeen folio volumes of text, accompanied by eleven volumes of engravings.

questions.text: In 1660 scientists in London founded which society, one of the oldest scientific academies still active?
questions.fun_fact: Its motto, 'Nullius in verba', is usually taken to mean 'take nobody's word for it'.

questions.text: Which 17th-century queen of Ndongo and Matamba, in present-day Angola, became famed for her diplomacy with the Portuguese?
questions.fun_fact: A statue of her stands in Kinaxixi Square in Angola's capital, Luanda.

questions.text: In 1607, English colonists founded Jamestown in what is now which US state?
questions.fun_fact: Jamestown was named for King James I and became the first permanent English settlement in the Americas.

questions.text: Which Florentine wrote the political treatise 'The Prince' in 1513?
questions.fun_fact: The Prince circulated in manuscript and was not printed until 1532, five years after its author's death.

questions.text: In 1609 Henry Hudson explored the river now named for him while sailing for which company?
questions.fun_fact: His ship on that voyage was the Halve Maen, or Half Moon.

questions.text: Which animal, reintroduced to the Americas by Europeans in the 1500s, transformed life for many Plains peoples?
questions.fun_fact: Native horses had died out in the Americas more than 10,000 years earlier, so Plains peoples long lived without them.

questions.text: Which Flemish Baroque painter, based in Antwerp, was also a diplomat knighted by the kings of Spain and England?
questions.fun_fact: Besides paintings, he designed tapestry cartoons for Flemish workshops and title pages for Antwerp publishers.

questions.text: Which Spanish king built the huge palace-monastery of El Escorial near Madrid in the 1500s?
questions.fun_fact: Construction began in 1563 and was finished in 1584, and the complex also holds a famous library.

questions.text: What is the Japanese name for the Edo-period study of Western science and medicine through Dutch books?
questions.fun_fact: The 1774 'New Text on Anatomy', led by Sugita Genpaku and based on a Dutch book, became a key reference.

questions.text: Which English architect designed the Banqueting House in Whitehall and the Queen's House in Greenwich?
questions.fun_fact: He also designed stage sets for several dozen court masques, many in collaboration with the writer Ben Jonson.

questions.text: Which French playwright, born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, wrote the 1668 comedy 'The Miser'?
questions.fun_fact: In French, a greedy, stingy person is called a harpagon, after the play's main character.

questions.text: Which English king acquired Hampton Court Palace from Cardinal Wolsey in 1529 and enlarged it?
questions.fun_fact: The palace's hedge maze was planted in the 1690s for William III.

questions.text: Which South American capital was founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1535 as the 'City of the Kings'?
questions.fun_fact: Lima's flag shows three gold crowns beneath a star, recalling its old name, City of the Kings.

questions.text: Fort Jesus, built by the Portuguese in 1593 to guard a key East African harbor, stands in which port?
questions.fun_fact: It was designed by the Italian architect Giovanni Battista Cairati.

questions.text: Which Flemish-Dutch mathematician popularized decimal fractions in his 1585 booklet 'De Thiende'?
questions.fun_fact: He also invented a land yacht, a carriage with sails, whose model was kept at Scheveningen until 1802.

questions.text: Which Chinese port did Portuguese traders settle in the 1550s, using it as a gateway to Ming China and Japan?
questions.fun_fact: From Macau, Portuguese ships carried Chinese silk to Japan and brought Japanese silver back to China.

questions.text: Shakespeare was born in 1564 in which English market town?
questions.fun_fact: His exact birth date is unknown; 23 April is traditional because his baptism was recorded on 26 April 1564.

questions.text: Elizabeth I of England, who reigned from 1558 to 1603, belonged to which royal house?
questions.fun_fact: She reigned longer than any other Tudor monarch, and her era is named the Elizabethan era.

questions.text: The world's first public opera house, the Teatro San Cassiano, opened in 1637 in which city?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first to open opera to a paying audience; until then opera had been a private show for courts and nobles.

questions.text: Which early modern empire, with lands in Europe, the Americas and Asia, was called 'the empire on which the sun never sets'?
questions.fun_fact: At its greatest extent, in the late 1700s and early 1800s, it covered about 13.7 million square kilometers.

questions.text: Which jewel-studded Mughal throne, ordered in the 1600s, took about seven years to build?
questions.fun_fact: It is said to have cost twice as much as building the Taj Mahal.

questions.text: Vitus Bering, the explorer in Russian service who gave his name to the Bering Strait, was born in which country?
questions.fun_fact: He was born in the port town of Horsens in 1681, and the Bering Sea and Bering Island are also named after him.

questions.text: Which German polymath developed calculus independently of Newton and designed a stepped calculating machine?
questions.fun_fact: His notation for calculus came to be favored as the conventional one, over the notation Newton used.

questions.text: Which ruined city in Karnataka was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire?
questions.fun_fact: Visiting in 1520, the Portuguese traveler Domingo Paes wrote that the city was as large as Rome.

questions.text: Which French explorer founded Quebec City in 1608?
questions.fun_fact: Lake Champlain, on the border between the US and Canada, is named after him.

questions.text: Which Venetian printer pioneered italic-style type and small portable books around 1500?
questions.fun_fact: His Aldine Press used a printer's mark of a dolphin wrapped around an anchor.

questions.text: Which German artist painted 'The Ambassadors' in 1533, with a strange distorted shape in the foreground?
questions.fun_fact: The painting shows a lute with a broken string among many scientific instruments.

questions.text: Which Vienna-born archduchess married the future King Louis XVI of France in 1770?
questions.fun_fact: She was the 15th child and youngest daughter of Empress Maria Theresa.

questions.text: Which Ming scholar wrote the 1637 technology encyclopedia 'Tiangong Kaiwu', covering farming, crafts and industry?
questions.fun_fact: The title is often translated 'The Exploitation of the Works of Nature'.

questions.text: In 1698 Peter the Great taxed what to push Russian men toward Western European fashions?
questions.fun_fact: People who paid the tax received a 'beard token' to show it had been paid.

questions.text: The 1600s, when Dutch trade, science and painting flourished, are known as the Dutch what?
questions.fun_fact: The era is usually dated from 1588, when the Dutch Republic was established, to 1672.

questions.text: Which Italian architect's 1570 treatise 'The Four Books of Architecture' inspired the Palladian style across Europe and America?
questions.fun_fact: His Villa Capra, known as La Rotonda, inspired many later buildings, including Thomas Jefferson's Monticello.

questions.text: Which Royal Navy captain led the First Fleet of eleven ships to Botany Bay in 1788?
questions.fun_fact: He found the Botany Bay site unsuitable and searched for a better one.

questions.text: Which German scientist and mayor used the Magdeburg hemispheres in 1654 to show the force of air pressure?
questions.fun_fact: Teams of horses could not pull the emptied hemispheres apart until a valve let air back in.

questions.text: Which French explorer canoed down the lower Mississippi in 1682 and claimed its basin for France?
questions.fun_fact: He named the region La Louisiane, in honor of Saint Louis and Louis XIV.

questions.text: The stone Rialto Bridge, completed in 1591 and lined with shops, crosses the Grand Canal in which city?
questions.fun_fact: It is the oldest of the four bridges that span the Grand Canal.

questions.text: Which British naval officer led the expedition that charted North America's northwest Pacific coast from 1791?
questions.fun_fact: The expedition also explored the Hawaiian Islands and the southwest coast of Australia.

questions.text: Which English inventor patented the flying shuttle for hand looms in 1733?
questions.fun_fact: Worried for their livelihoods, Colchester weavers petitioned the King to stop his inventions.

questions.text: On Cook's first voyage, the Endeavour went to Tahiti in 1769 to observe the transit of which planet?
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Navy and Royal Society expedition also hunted for the postulated southern land Terra Australis Incognita.

questions.text: Which Italian city's botanical garden, founded in 1545, is the world's oldest academic one still in its original place?
questions.fun_fact: It was founded by the Venetian Republic and is run by the University of Padua.

questions.text: Which Venetian playwright wrote the comedy 'The Servant of Two Masters'?
questions.fun_fact: His plays make rich use of the Venetian language and everyday colloquialisms.

questions.text: Which astronomer from Danzig (Gdańsk) charted the Moon in his 1647 work 'Selenographia'?
questions.fun_fact: He described ten new constellations, seven of which astronomers still use.

questions.text: Which English landscape architect earned his nickname by telling clients their estates had 'capability' for improvement?
questions.fun_fact: He is most famous for the landscaped parks of English country houses, many of which survive.

questions.text: Which French inventor built 'The Digesting Duck', an automaton that seemed to eat and digest grain?
questions.fun_fact: He is credited with inventing the first flexible rubber tube while building the duck's intestines.

questions.text: Which French explorer mapped the Gulf of St. Lawrence in the 1530s and gave Canada its name?
questions.fun_fact: His first voyage, in 1534, began after he was introduced to King Francis I.

questions.text: Which former royal palace in Paris opened as a public museum in 1793?
questions.fun_fact: It opened on 10 August 1793 with an exhibition of 537 paintings.

questions.text: Which composer wrote the 'Water Music', premiered on the Thames in 1717 at King George I's request?
questions.fun_fact: The collection opens with a French overture and is often published as three suites.

questions.text: In which city is the Trevi Fountain, completed in 1762?
questions.fun_fact: At 26.3 meters high, it is the largest Baroque fountain in the world.

questions.text: Which English scientist said he was inspired to formulate his theory of gravitation by watching an apple fall?
questions.fun_fact: He was born at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire on 25 December 1642 by the old calendar.

questions.text: Which queen of Castile helped finance Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage across the Atlantic?
questions.fun_fact: She ruled Castile and León from 1474 until her death in 1504.

questions.text: Which Dutch inventor built the first navigable submarine in 1620 while working for the English Royal Navy?
questions.fun_fact: Around 1604 his family moved to England, probably at the invitation of King James I.

questions.text: Which French scientist, best known for studying insects, invented a thermometer scale in 1731?
questions.fun_fact: His interest in meteorology began in 1731, the year he devised the scale that bears his name.

questions.text: Which Swedish warship sank barely 1,300 meters into her maiden voyage in 1628?
questions.fun_fact: She was salvaged in 1961 after spending 333 years on the seabed.

questions.text: Spanish treasure fleets carried riches from the New World in which type of large sailing ship?
questions.fun_fact: Spanish captains Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and Álvaro de Bazán designed the definitive galleon in the 1550s.

questions.text: The Iron Bridge, opened in 1781 as the world's first major cast-iron bridge, spans which English river?
questions.fun_fact: Abraham Darby III was responsible for its ironwork.

questions.text: Which French painter of the late Rococo created the playful scene 'The Swing'?
questions.fun_fact: He produced more than 550 paintings, known for their exuberance.

questions.text: On Cook's second voyage, which ship was first to cross the Antarctic Circle, in January 1773?
questions.fun_fact: Cook's most southerly crossing, on 3 February 1774, reached latitude 71°10' south.

questions.text: Which architect designed the Royal Crescent in Bath, built between 1767 and 1774?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first crescent of terraced houses ever built and has 114 Ionic columns.

questions.text: Which architect is most closely linked to the Elizabethan Baroque style of the Winter Palace in Saint Petersburg?
questions.fun_fact: The palace's green-and-white principal façade is 215 meters long.

questions.text: In which country was the metre first introduced, in the 1790s?
questions.fun_fact: In 1791 a commission defined it as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole.

questions.text: In which Shakespeare tragedy, first staged around 1606, do three witches prophesy a Scottish general's rise?
questions.fun_fact: It is Shakespeare's shortest tragedy.

questions.text: Which US college, founded in 1636, is the oldest institution of higher learning in the country?
questions.fun_fact: It was named Harvard College in 1639 for its first benefactor, the clergyman John Harvard.

questions.text: Which London museum, founded in 1753, is considered the world's first public national museum?
questions.fun_fact: It grew from the collection of the physician and naturalist Sir Hans Sloane.

questions.text: Andrea Palladio's last design, the Teatro Olimpico of 1580 to 1585, stands in which Italian city?
questions.fun_fact: Its onstage scenery from 1585 is the oldest surviving stage set still in existence.

questions.text: Built from 1788 to 1791 for a Prussian king, the Brandenburg Gate stands in which city?
questions.fun_fact: The bronze quadriga on top is the work of the sculptor Johann Gottfried Schadow.

questions.text: Which traditional Japanese puppet theater, founded in Osaka, rose to fame through the playwright Chikamatsu Monzaemon?
questions.fun_fact: The chanter Takemoto Gidayu founded the Takemoto puppet theater in Osaka in 1684.

questions.text: Which palace complex near Saint Petersburg did Peter the Great commission as a response to Versailles?
questions.fun_fact: He began expanding the grounds after visiting the French royal court in 1717.

questions.text: Under Sultan Ismail, who reigned 1672-1727, which Moroccan city became the capital and got a vast palace complex?
questions.fun_fact: The Almoravids founded it in the 11th century as a military settlement.

questions.text: Which Prussian king gave the Amber Room to Tsar Peter the Great in 1716?
questions.fun_fact: It was designed by sculptor Andreas Schlüter and Danish amber craftsman Gottfried Wolfram.

questions.text: Which Enlightenment writer published the satire 'Candide' in 1759?
questions.fun_fact: The story ends with the practical advice 'we must cultivate our garden'.

questions.text: Which Anglo-Irish writer published the satire 'Gulliver's Travels' in 1726?
questions.fun_fact: The book popularized the fictional island of Lilliput, whose tiny people Gulliver meets.

questions.text: Which Japanese castle, rebuilt from 1601 to 1609, is nicknamed 'White Heron Castle'?
questions.fun_fact: In 1993 it became one of the first UNESCO World Heritage Sites registered in Japan.

questions.text: In which city did Elizabeth I found Trinity College, Ireland's oldest university, in 1592?
questions.fun_fact: Its original name was the College of the Holy and Undivided Trinity of Queen Elizabeth near Dublin.

questions.text: The Spanish Steps, which climb up from the Piazza di Spagna, are in which city?
questions.fun_fact: The monumental stairway has 135 steps.

questions.text: Which Dutch cartographer of the East India Company published the 11-volume Atlas Maior in 1662?
questions.fun_fact: His 1648 world map was the first to incorporate the heliocentric theory.

questions.text: Which Hungarian inventor is known for 'The Turk', a chess-playing automaton that proved to be a hoax?
questions.fun_fact: He was born in 1734 in Pressburg (now Bratislava), then part of the Kingdom of Hungary.

questions.text: Which 1623 book collected 36 of Shakespeare's plays, prepared by his colleagues Heminges and Condell?
questions.fun_fact: It was published about seven years after Shakespeare's death.

questions.text: Which Ottoman scholar built an observatory in Istanbul after Sultan Murad III invited him in 1574?
questions.fun_fact: He used his instruments to observe the Great Comet of 1577.

questions.text: Which library of the University of Oxford, founded in 1602, is one of the oldest libraries in Europe?
questions.fun_fact: It was founded by Sir Thomas Bodley, from whom it takes its name.

questions.text: Which Italian painter of the Venetian school created 'Venus of Urbino', which was sold in 1538?
questions.fun_fact: Its reclining pose derives from the Dresden Venus of about 1510, attributed to Giorgione.

questions.text: A fire that began in a Pudding Lane bakery in 1666 gutted the medieval heart of which city?
questions.fun_fact: The fire burned from Sunday 2 September to Wednesday 5 September 1666.

questions.text: Which king of Ayutthaya, who ruled Siam from 1656 to 1688, exchanged embassies with Louis XIV's France?
questions.fun_fact: He is arguably the most famous king of the Prasat Thong dynasty.

questions.text: Which English potter founded a pottery company in 1759 and developed creamware and jasperware?
questions.fun_fact: He led the industrialization of European pottery through systematic experiments.

questions.text: Which English monarch, who never married, was nicknamed the 'Virgin Queen'?
questions.fun_fact: The colony of Virginia was perhaps named in her honor.

questions.text: Which Russian tsar founded Saint Petersburg in 1703?
questions.fun_fact: Russians have long called the city their 'Window to Europe'.

questions.text: The Tsar Bell, a giant bell commissioned by Empress Anna Ivanovna, is displayed in which Moscow complex?
questions.fun_fact: It has never been in working order, hung up or rung.

questions.text: Which garden designer laid out the gardens of Versailles for Louis XIV?
questions.fun_fact: Before Versailles, he worked with Louis Le Vau and Charles Le Brun on the park at Vaux-le-Vicomte.

questions.text: Mapungubwe Hill, capital of a medieval kingdom on the Limpopo River, lies in which present-day country?
questions.fun_fact: Its elite moved to the hilltop around 1220, and by 1250 the kingdom's capital had about 5,000 people.

questions.text: What name is given to medieval associations of merchants or craftsmen that set standards and trained apprentices?
questions.fun_fact: Craft guilds passed on skills through a formal system of apprenticeship, journeyman years and mastery.

questions.text: The brick Gothic Holstentor gate, begun in 1464, is a landmark of which northern German Hanseatic city?
questions.fun_fact: An inscription gives 1477 as its date, but the gate's correct completion date is now known to be 1478.

questions.text: The University of Bologna, with roots in 1088, is located in which country?
questions.fun_fact: By the late 1100s it was organized as 'universitas scholarium', or guilds of students.

questions.text: Which clear script, developed at Frankish monasteries around 800, is the ancestor of modern lowercase letters?
questions.fun_fact: It fell out of use until Italian Renaissance humanists modeled a new script on it, humanist minuscule.

questions.text: Which Persian mathematician and astronomer is also famous for his 'Rubaiyat' quatrains?
questions.fun_fact: He designed the Jalali calendar, whose very precise 33-year leap cycle became the basis of the Persian calendar.

questions.text: The Varangian Guard, made up largely of Scandinavians, served as elite bodyguards of which empire's emperors?
questions.fun_fact: Formed around 988, it later recruited many Anglo-Saxons, especially after 1066.

questions.text: Which language gradually replaced Latin for official use in the Byzantine Empire?
questions.fun_fact: Even so, its citizens called themselves Romans and their state the Roman Empire.

questions.text: Which caliph ordered the palace-city of Medina Azahara built near Córdoba in the 900s?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'the radiant city', and the remains of the palace-city form a major archaeological site.

questions.text: Troubadours, the poet-singers of courtly love, composed their songs mainly in which language?
questions.fun_fact: The tradition began in the late 11th century in Occitania, then spread to Italy and the Iberian Peninsula.

questions.text: Which 11th-century Italian music teacher devised the syllables 'ut, re, mi' for teaching singing?
questions.fun_fact: He is regarded as the inventor, or by some the developer, of modern staff notation.

questions.text: What was the deep, broad ditch dug around many medieval castles, often filled with water, called?
questions.fun_fact: Moats left only a few narrow crossings, such as drawbridges or causeways, which made a castle easier to defend.

questions.text: In which year was Cologne Cathedral, begun in 1248, finally completed?
questions.fun_fact: Work was halted around 1560 and resumed in the 1800s; it was then finished to its original medieval plan.

questions.text: Which Tuscan hill town is famous for preserving about a dozen of its medieval tower houses?
questions.fun_fact: Its historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the town is also known for its Vernaccia white wine.

questions.text: Which poet wrote 'The Knight in the Panther's Skin', the Georgian national epic, around 1200?
questions.fun_fact: Little is known of his life, but he is said to have served Tamar of Georgia as finance minister from 1191.

questions.text: Which Heian court lady wrote 'The Pillow Book', a collection of lists, essays and observations?
questions.fun_fact: She served Empress Teishi, and the book is famous for its witty lists, such as 'Hateful Things'.

questions.text: About 1,000 medieval letters written on birch bark have been dug up in which Russian city?
questions.fun_fact: Most were written by ordinary people in a local dialect, Old Novgorodian, between the 11th and 15th centuries.

questions.text: Hedeby was a major Viking Age trading town on the Jutland peninsula. Its ruins lie in which present-day country?
questions.fun_fact: The town minted its own coins from 825, and the traveler Ibrahim ibn Yaqub visited it around 965.

questions.text: Charles University, founded in 1348 by Charles IV, stands in which city?
questions.fun_fact: Students there were grouped into four 'nations': Bohemian, Bavarian, Saxon and Polish.

questions.text: Li Bai and Du Fu, two of China's greatest poets, lived during which dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: The anthology 'Complete Tang Poems' includes over 48,900 poems by more than 2,200 poets.

questions.text: The medieval Ghana Empire of West Africa grew rich on trade in which precious metal?
questions.fun_fact: Modern Ghana, further southeast, took its name from the empire when it gained independence in 1957.

questions.text: Which instrument, refined by medieval Islamic astronomers, measured the altitude of stars and helped tell time?
questions.fun_fact: It could also find latitude, identify stars and planets, and be used to survey land.

questions.text: Which French cathedral, rebuilt after 1194, is famous for its largely original medieval stained glass?
questions.fun_fact: The majority of its original stained glass windows survive intact, and the building has changed little since the early 13th century.

questions.text: Machu Picchu is believed to have been built as a royal estate for which Inca emperor?
questions.fun_fact: The site was abandoned roughly a century later, and it sits at an elevation of about 2,430 meters.

questions.text: Scholars from which English town founded the University of Cambridge in 1209?
questions.fun_fact: Peterhouse, the oldest Cambridge college, was founded in 1284.

questions.text: In which medieval sport did two knights on horseback charge at each other with lances?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from Old French 'joster', ultimately from Latin 'iuxtare', meaning 'to approach, to meet'.

questions.text: The English name 'Korea' comes from which medieval Korean dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: Founded in 918 by the general Wang Kŏn, it ruled the Korean Peninsula until Joseon was established in 1392.

questions.text: Prague's Orloj, a medieval astronomical clock dating to 1410, is mounted on the southern wall of which building?
questions.fun_fact: Its oldest part, the clock and astronomical dial, was made by horologist Mikuláš of Kadaň and professor Jan Šindel.

questions.text: Which member of a 921 Abbasid embassy to the Volga Bulgars wrote a famous account of the journey?
questions.fun_fact: He also described the Volga Vikings and the Oghuz Turks, and his writings inspired a Michael Crichton novel.

questions.text: Which medieval dynasty built the Brihadisvara Temple in Thanjavur, completed in 1010?
questions.fun_fact: It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site known as the 'Great Living Chola Temples'.

questions.text: Iceland's national parliament, first founded at Þingvellir in 930, is called what?
questions.fun_fact: Its name means 'general meeting', and Þingvellir, about 45 km east of Reykjavík, means 'assembly fields'.

questions.text: Which Peruvian civilization built Chan Chan, a vast adobe city near the Pacific coast, as its capital?
questions.fun_fact: Covering about 20 square km, it is the largest adobe city in the Americas; UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1986.

questions.text: On which lake was the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan founded, traditionally in 1325?
questions.fun_fact: Causeways linked the city to the mainland, with gaps spanned by bridges that let canoes pass.

questions.text: The 1274 and 1281 invasions of Japan, foiled partly by typhoons, were launched by which Mongol ruler?
questions.fun_fact: The typhoons that wrecked the invasion fleets gave Japanese the word 'kamikaze', meaning 'divine wind'.

questions.text: In the Middle Ages, what was a knight's young attendant, who cared for his horse, weapons and armor, called?
questions.fun_fact: The word is short for 'esquire', from the Anglo-French 'esquier', meaning 'shield bearer'.

questions.text: According to the sagas, which Norse explorer founded the first European settlement in Greenland in the 980s?
questions.fun_fact: He gave the island the name 'Greenland', hoping an attractive name would draw settlers.

questions.text: Which capital city is home to a Kremlin whose red-brick walls and towers were built in the late 1400s?
questions.fun_fact: Its walls as they now appear were built between 1485 and 1495, partly designed by Pietro Antonio Solari.

questions.text: Which animal carried most goods on the medieval trans-Saharan caravans?
questions.fun_fact: The caravans were guided by highly paid Berbers who knew the desert.

questions.text: The 12th-century Lewis chessmen, found in Scotland in 1831, are mostly carved from what?
questions.fun_fact: Most of the pieces are in the British Museum in London, while 11 are at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh.

questions.text: Which farm tool, with wheels and a moldboard, let medieval farmers till the dense soils of northern Europe?
questions.fun_fact: Wheels let heavy plows carry a larger, metal-faced moldboard; iron moldboards did not appear in Europe until the 10th century.

questions.text: Before printing, medieval books were copied by hand in which room or workshop, often in a monastery?
questions.fun_fact: Monastic scriptoria selectively preserved the West's literary history; the first European monastic writing dates from 517.

questions.text: Which Silk Road city in present-day Uzbekistan was the capital of Timur's empire?
questions.fun_fact: Timur made it his capital in 1370 and over the next 35 years rebuilt most of the city with great artisans and craftsmen.

questions.text: Which noble clan dominated Japan's Heian court by marrying daughters to emperors and serving as regents?
questions.fun_fact: Fujiwara no Michinaga was grandfather of three emperors and father of six empresses or imperial consorts.

questions.text: Heian-kyō, now Kyoto, was laid out on a grid modeled on which Chinese capital?
questions.fun_fact: Its main north-south axis was Suzaku Avenue, and the imperial palace stood in the northern center of the city.

questions.text: Which Castilian king, nicknamed 'the Wise', sponsored the Alfonsine Tables of planetary positions?
questions.fun_fact: He is sometimes nicknamed 'the Astrologer', and the Moon's Alphonsus crater is named after him.

questions.text: Which Spanish city was the center of a medieval 'school' that translated Arabic scientific and philosophical works into Latin?
questions.fun_fact: Its first period was led by Archbishop Raymond of Toledo in the 12th century.

questions.text: Which 15th-century Hungarian king assembled one of Europe's largest libraries in Buda?
questions.fun_fact: Only 216 volumes of the library are known to survive.

questions.text: At a medieval royal court, what was the main job of a jester?
questions.fun_fact: Besides telling jokes, jesters entertained with song, music, storytelling, acrobatics and juggling.

questions.text: Which Holy Roman Emperor, raised in Sicily, wrote a famous treatise on falconry?
questions.fun_fact: The treatise's Latin title is 'De arte venandi cum avibus', meaning 'The Art of Hunting with Birds'.

questions.text: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, an 11th-century Castilian knight, is better known by which name?
questions.fun_fact: The name comes from the Arabic honorific 'as-Sayyid', meaning 'the Lord' or 'the Master'.

questions.text: What name is given to the system of designing and displaying coats of arms, popular among medieval knights?
questions.fun_fact: Heraldry lost its military role when firearms made the mounted knight obsolete, and it became a decorative art.

questions.text: Which Old French epic poem tells of a Frankish leader's stand at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778?
questions.fun_fact: Written in the 11th century, it is the oldest surviving major work of French literature.

questions.text: Whose 'Book of Optics', written about 1011-1021, argued that we see when light enters the eye?
questions.fun_fact: Called 'the father of modern optics', he also studied the camera obscura, which forms an image through a small hole.

questions.text: Which storyteller narrates the tales of 'One Thousand and One Nights' to her husband, the king?
questions.fun_fact: It is often called 'The Arabian Nights' in English, after the first English edition of about 1706-1721.

questions.text: Medieval manuscripts were mostly written on parchment. What is parchment made from?
questions.fun_fact: Parchment first meant sheep or goat skin; the finer calfskin version was called vellum, from Latin 'vitulus', calf.

questions.text: Fibonacci's 1202 book 'Liber Abaci' helped introduce which number system to Europe?
questions.fun_fact: Fibonacci learned the numerals as a boy in Bugia, now Béjaïa in Algeria, where his father worked at a customs house.

questions.text: Which king of Wessex (871-899) promoted learning and had Latin works translated into Old English?
questions.fun_fact: Alfred is the only native-born English monarch to be called 'the Great'.

questions.text: Which author, born in Venice and writing in France, wrote 'The Book of the City of Ladies' in 1405?
questions.fun_fact: Her independence in producing her books earned her the title of first professional woman of letters in Europe.

questions.text: Which sturdy, broad-hulled Norse ship carried cargo and settlers across the North Atlantic?
questions.fun_fact: Knarrs were wider, deeper and shorter than longships, and could be operated by smaller crews.

questions.text: Which people settled the Carpathian Basin in the late 800s and early 900s, an event called the 'land-taking'?
questions.fun_fact: Before settling there, they were sometimes hired as horsemen by the First Bulgarian Empire, East Francia and Moravia.

questions.text: Which warrior class emerged in Japan during the Heian period?
questions.fun_fact: Besides swordsmanship, archery and horsemanship, samurai also studied literature, calligraphy and Confucian philosophy.

questions.text: What are the carved stone figures on Gothic buildings that channel rainwater off the walls called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from Old French 'gargoule', a water conduit, built on roots meaning 'throat'.

questions.text: In which city did King Casimir III the Great found Poland's oldest university in 1364?
questions.fun_fact: Nicolaus Copernicus studied there, and the university holds his landmark manuscript 'De revolutionibus'.

questions.text: Which wind-powered machines for grinding grain spread across northern Europe from the 12th century?
questions.fun_fact: The earliest European windmills were post mills, whose whole body turned on a central post to face the wind.

questions.text: Which city on the Niger River was the capital of the Songhai Empire?
questions.fun_fact: Ibn Battuta reached Gao by boat in 1353 and praised it as one of the finest, biggest and most fertile cities of the region.

questions.text: Which Egyptian city, whose name means 'the Vanquisher', was founded in 969 by the Fatimid dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: Parts of its medieval walls survive at Bab Zuwayla, Bab al-Futuh and Bab al-Nasr.

questions.text: Which Moroccan city, founded around 1070 as the Almoravid capital, is nicknamed the 'Red City'?
questions.fun_fact: Its red walls were built by Ali ibn Yusuf in 1122-1123.

questions.text: Which poet's 'Divine Comedy' helped make the Tuscan dialect the basis of standard Italian?
questions.fun_fact: Dante chose the everyday Tuscan vernacular over Latin and wrote a treatise defending the vernacular.

questions.text: Which Mississippian city near modern St. Louis was home to the giant earthen Monks Mound?
questions.fun_fact: At its peak around 1100 it had 15,000 to 20,000 people; in the 12th century it may have been larger than London or Paris.

questions.text: Eleanor of Aquitaine was queen consort of France and which other kingdom?
questions.fun_fact: Many writers dedicated works to her, including Wace, author of the 'Roman de Brut'.

questions.text: How were the 11-meter-high walls of Great Zimbabwe's Great Enclosure built?
questions.fun_fact: Smaller ruins of the same kind, called 'zimbabwes' or 'houses of stone', number more than 400 across southern Africa.

questions.text: Which London fortress, founded after the Norman Conquest of 1066, is home to the Crown Jewels?
questions.fun_fact: Its central White Tower, built by William the Conqueror in 1078, gives the castle its name.

questions.text: Timbuktu, a medieval hub of trade and learning, lies on the southern edge of which desert?
questions.fun_fact: The city's Ahmed Baba Institute held about 30,000 manuscripts.

questions.text: Normandy in northern France is named after which people who settled there in the early 900s?
questions.fun_fact: A 10th-century treaty between King Charles the Simple of France and the Viking leader Rollo confirmed the settlement.

questions.text: Which Sicilian city was capital of the Norman Kingdom of Sicily, with art blending Arab, Byzantine and Norman styles?
questions.fun_fact: Its Arab-Norman buildings, including the Cappella Palatina in the Norman Palace, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.text: Which Gothic cathedral on the Île de la Cité in Paris was begun in 1163?
questions.fun_fact: Its pioneering use of the rib vault and flying buttress helped set Gothic apart from the earlier Romanesque style.

questions.text: Which collection of Roman law, enacted from 529 to 534 under Emperor Justinian I, shaped legal systems across Europe?
questions.fun_fact: At Bologna it was taught by Pepo and then Irnerius, whose method was to read a passage aloud.

questions.text: Vikings, the seafaring traders and explorers of the early Middle Ages, came mainly from which region?
questions.fun_fact: Viking exports included weapons, walrus ivory, wax, salt and cod, and sometimes hunting birds.

questions.text: Which legendary sailor from 'One Thousand and One Nights' made seven voyages?
questions.fun_fact: In the tales he comes from Baghdad during the early Abbasid Caliphate, in the 8th and 9th centuries.

questions.text: Which Byzantine emperor had the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople built between 532 and 537?
questions.fun_fact: When completed in 537 it was the world's largest interior space, with a vast dome carried on pendentives.

questions.text: Which French walled city, restored in the 1800s by Viollet-le-Duc, has two rings of walls and 52 towers?
questions.fun_fact: Its Cité was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1997 for the exceptional preservation of its medieval fortifications.

questions.text: At which 1066 battle did William, Duke of Normandy, defeat the English army of King Harold Godwinson?
questions.fun_fact: It was fought about 11 km northwest of Hastings, close to the present-day town of Battle in East Sussex.

questions.text: Why did the Tower of Pisa begin to lean while it was still being built?
questions.fun_fact: Pauses in building, during wars with Genoa, Lucca and Florence, let the soil settle; otherwise it would likely have toppled.

questions.text: Which Japanese theater form, with masks and slow, stylized movement, was shaped by Kan'ami and his son Zeami in the 1300s?
questions.fun_fact: Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu supported them, which helped make Noh the most prominent theater art of its time.

questions.text: The Nibelungenlied, an epic poem written around 1200, is in which language?
questions.fun_fact: Its anonymous poet was likely from the Passau region; Old Norse parallels appear in the Poetic Edda and Völsunga saga.

questions.text: Which Portuguese prince, a son of King John I, sponsored 15th-century voyages down West Africa's coast?
questions.fun_fact: Using the new caravel ship, he directed early Portuguese exploration and trade along Western Africa.

questions.text: Which short-lived dynasty (581-618) reunified China and built the Grand Canal?
questions.fun_fact: Its mega-projects forcibly conscripted millions of workers, and the dynasty lasted only 37 years.

questions.text: Which language was the common language of scholars and universities in medieval Western Europe?
questions.fun_fact: Medieval Latin had an enlarged vocabulary that freely borrowed from other sources.

questions.text: Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses are signature features of which medieval building style?
questions.fun_fact: The term began as a put-down: Vasari wrote of a 'barbarous German style' in 1550, blaming the Goths.

questions.text: Which Frankish king was crowned Emperor of the Romans in the year 800?
questions.fun_fact: He made Aachen his imperial capital, where his Palatine Chapel is now part of Aachen Cathedral.

questions.text: Who wrote 'The Canterbury Tales' in Middle English in the late 1300s?
questions.fun_fact: Chaucer worked as a courtier and diplomat, and he left the Tales unfinished.

questions.text: The best-known sections of the Great Wall of China were built by which dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: Ming builders used bricks and stone instead of rammed earth, and up to 25,000 watchtowers may have been built.

questions.text: What sport drew huge crowds to the Hippodrome of Constantinople?
questions.fun_fact: Teams were backed by factions called the Blues, Greens, Reds and Whites; the Blues and Greens grew dominant.

questions.text: The Bayeux Tapestry, about 70 meters long, is actually what kind of textile work?
questions.fun_fact: It is embroidered in wool yarn on linen and shows the events that led to the Norman conquest of England.

questions.text: Which ship type, long and narrow with a shallow hull, let Vikings sail across seas and up rivers?
questions.fun_fact: Longships were clinker-built, meaning their hulls were made of overlapping planks.

questions.text: In a medieval motte-and-bailey castle, what was the 'motte'?
questions.fun_fact: These castles spread across northern Europe from the 10th century, starting in Normandy and Anjou.

questions.text: Which Iranian polymath estimated Earth's radius by measuring a mountain's height and the dip of the horizon?
questions.fun_fact: His study of India, finished around 1030, is the work on which his reputation as an Indologist chiefly rests.

questions.text: The Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) was fought mainly between England and which kingdom?
questions.fun_fact: Despite its name, it spanned 116 years and was often interrupted by long truces.

questions.text: Which Mongol khanate, also called the Ulus of Jochi, was centered on Sarai near the Volga?
questions.fun_fact: It was also known as the Kipchak Khanate, and it grew greatly in size under Batu Khan.

questions.text: Which South Pacific island country was first settled by Polynesian voyagers in the 13th or 14th century?
questions.fun_fact: They brought food plants from eastern Polynesia, including sweet potatoes, called kūmara, and taro.

questions.text: What name is given to the heavy latticed gate that slid down grooves to seal a medieval castle entrance?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from Old French 'porte coleice', meaning 'sliding gate'.

questions.text: What was the large fortified tower at the heart of many medieval castles, a last refuge, called?
questions.fun_fact: The first keeps were timber towers in motte-and-bailey castles that emerged in Normandy and Anjou in the 10th century.

questions.text: Which castle feature could be raised from inside to block the entrance across the moat?
questions.fun_fact: In American English the word often covers any movable bridge, but historically it meant a defensive bridge at a castle or tower.

questions.text: Which type of armor, made of small linked metal rings, protected European soldiers for many centuries?
questions.fun_fact: Mail was widely used in European militaries from the 3rd century BC to the 16th century AD.

questions.text: What were medieval peasants called who were bound to work a lord's land and could not be sold individually?
questions.fun_fact: Serfs were entitled to protection, justice and the right to cultivate certain fields for their own subsistence.

questions.text: What was a medieval lord's rural estate, worked by peasants and serfs, called?
questions.fun_fact: The manor system was slowly replaced by a money-based market economy; the last feudal dues in France ended at the French Revolution.

questions.text: In which language was the epic poem Beowulf composed?
questions.fun_fact: Its only surviving manuscript dates from between AD 975 and 1025, and the poem has 3,182 alliterative lines.

questions.text: What name is given to handwritten books decorated with borders and miniature illustrations?
questions.fun_fact: Most surviving examples are from the Middle Ages, and the earliest date from between 400 and 600 CE.

questions.text: What name is given to the medieval code of conduct associated with knighthood?
questions.fun_fact: It developed in France between 1170 and 1220 and was popularized in literature about Charlemagne's companions and King Arthur's knights.

questions.text: Which curved, single-edged Japanese sword was used by samurai in feudal Japan?
questions.fun_fact: The word means 'one-sided blade', and the sword was worn with its edge facing upward.

questions.text: What was a medieval scribe's quill pen made from?
questions.fun_fact: Quills hold no ink, so the writer had to dip them into an inkwell from time to time.

questions.text: What is the narrow vertical opening in a castle wall, used for firing arrows, called?
questions.fun_fact: A common cross-shaped version let defenders use both the longbow and the crossbow.

questions.text: Which siege engine used a swinging arm and a heavy counterweight to hurl stones?
questions.fun_fact: The counterweight trebuchet appeared around the Mediterranean in the 12th century and was carried to China by the Mongols in the 13th.

questions.text: In the Middle Ages, what was a young male attendant or messenger serving a nobleman called?
questions.fun_fact: At weddings, a page boy is often a symbolic attendant who carries the rings.

questions.text: In a medieval castle, what is the leveled courtyard enclosed by a curtain wall called?
questions.fun_fact: A bailey is also called a ward, and some castles had more than one.

questions.text: Which Italian city is home to the Ponte Vecchio, a medieval stone bridge lined with shops?
questions.fun_fact: Butchers, tanners and farmers first occupied its shops; jewelers, art dealers and souvenir sellers now do.

questions.text: Which dynasty took over China in 1368 from the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: The Yuan rulers retreated to the Mongolian Plateau and continued as the Northern Yuan until 1635.

questions.text: The Qutb Minar, begun by Qutb ud-Din Aibak around 1200, is a famous minaret in which Indian city?
questions.fun_fact: Its shaft has 399 steps, and Firuz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the top parts and added a cupola in 1368.

questions.text: The cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, built by Ancestral Puebloans, lie in which US state?
questions.fun_fact: Mesa Verde is Spanish for 'green table', and the park holds about 600 cliff dwellings among more than 5,000 sites.

questions.text: Which small, fast sailing ship, rigged with lateen sails, did Portuguese and Spanish explorers use in the 1400s?
questions.fun_fact: It grew out of fishing craft from Galicia, Portugal and Atlantic Andalusia and was noted for sailing well into the wind.

questions.text: Who led the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
questions.fun_fact: He led a group of rebels from Canterbury to London to oppose the collection of a poll tax.

questions.text: Which woman, once a Tang dynasty empress, ruled China in her own right as emperor from 690 to 705?
questions.fun_fact: She reformed the civil service system to promote merit and patronized literature and the arts.

questions.text: Which English king began building Caernarfon Castle in north Wales in 1283?
questions.fun_fact: The castle and town walls cost between 20,000 and 25,000 pounds from the start until work ended in 1330.

questions.text: Which medieval building style, dominant in the 11th and 12th centuries, features semicircular arches and thick walls?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first pan-European architectural style since Imperial Roman architecture, and it developed into Gothic.

questions.text: What title did the leader of the Republic of Venice hold?
questions.fun_fact: Doges were chosen for life through a complex voting process, and the republic lasted from 697 to 1797.

questions.text: By what name is Shangdu, the Yuan dynasty's summer capital, known in the West?
questions.fun_fact: Designed by the architect Liu Bingzhong, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.

questions.text: In feudal law, what was the property, often land, that a lord granted to a vassal in return for loyalty?
questions.fun_fact: A fief could also be a watermill, a government office, or rights to hunt, fish or fell trees.

questions.text: The European lute shares a common ancestor with which modern Middle Eastern instrument?
questions.fun_fact: Short-necked lutes from Gandhara were the predecessors of the Islamic, Sino-Japanese and European lute families.

questions.text: What does 'Minnesang', the name of the medieval German courtly song tradition, literally mean?
questions.fun_fact: Its performers, the Minnesänger, are comparable to Occitan troubadours but are 'an original German contribution to courtly lyric'.

questions.text: What did the Norse call the poets who composed ornate verses honoring kings in the Viking Age?
questions.fun_fact: More than 5,500 skaldic verses survive in over 700 manuscripts, including in Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda.

questions.text: Which German city, near the Belgian and Dutch borders, was Charlemagne's main royal residence?
questions.fun_fact: From 936 to 1531, 31 Holy Roman Emperors were crowned Kings of the Germans there.

questions.text: Which Chinese dynasty did Kublai Khan officially proclaim in 1271?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first dynasty founded by a non-Han ethnicity that ruled all of China proper.

questions.text: Malbork Castle, a vast Brick Gothic fortress built by the Teutonic Order, stands in which present-day country?
questions.fun_fact: Built from 1274 to 1406, it was the world's largest brick castle when completed.

questions.text: Sukhothai, a kingdom founded in 1238, was centered in what is now which country?
questions.fun_fact: Some historians credit King Ram Khamhaeng (1279-1298) with introducing the first Thai script.

questions.text: What are the solid, tooth-like sections between the gaps in a castle's battlement called?
questions.fun_fact: Late medieval English builders often crenellated tower tops purely as decoration, not for defense.

questions.text: Cheomseongdae, an ancient star-gazing tower in Gyeongju, was built under which Korean kingdom?
questions.fun_fact: Built under Queen Seondeok (r. 632-647), it is the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in Asia, and possibly the world.

questions.text: Amalfi, Pisa and Venice were, with which port city, the four best-known Italian maritime republics?
questions.fun_fact: Since 1947 their coats of arms have appeared on the flags of the Italian Navy and Merchant Navy.

questions.text: Which 19th-century composer's Norse operas helped popularize the image of Vikings in horned helmets?
questions.fun_fact: No Viking Age text mentions horned helmets, and the few Viking Age helmets found have no horns.

questions.text: The Yongle Encyclopedia, completed by 1408, was commissioned by an emperor of which Chinese dynasty?
questions.fun_fact: Fewer than 400 of its 11,095 volumes survive.

questions.text: Which sultanate was ruled from 1236 to 1240 by Razia, its only woman sultan?
questions.fun_fact: She administered Delhi in 1231-1232 while her father, Iltutmish, was away on campaign.

questions.text: The tall 'Atlantean' warrior statues at Tula once stood in the capital of which Mesoamerican people?
questions.fun_fact: Tula reached its height between the fall of Teotihuacan and the rise of Tenochtitlan.

questions.text: Tiwanaku, a large pre-Columbian site near Lake Titicaca, lies in which present-day country?
questions.fun_fact: It may have housed 10,000 to 20,000 people around AD 800, yet its builders had no written language.

questions.text: Which woman reigned over Georgia from 1184 to 1213, the peak of its Golden Age?
questions.fun_fact: Medieval Georgian sources gave her the title 'mepe', meaning 'king', stressing she was the first woman to rule in her own right.

questions.text: Which Byzantine princess wrote the Alexiad, a history of her father Emperor Alexios I's reign?
questions.fun_fact: It is the most important primary source for Byzantine history of the late 11th and early 12th centuries.

questions.text: In which medieval state was the early Cyrillic alphabet developed, at the Preslav Literary School?
questions.fun_fact: With Bulgaria's accession in 2007, Cyrillic became the third official script of the European Union.

questions.text: According to tradition, which Varangian chieftain was invited to reign in Novgorod in 862?
questions.fun_fact: His line, the Rurik dynasty, ruled Kievan Rus' and later Russia until 1598.

questions.text: Which union, begun in 1397, put Denmark, Sweden and Norway under a single monarch?
questions.fun_fact: Sweden left for good in 1523, when Gustav Vasa became its king.

questions.text: Which Tang-era writer produced 'The Classic of Tea', the first definitive work on growing and drinking tea?
questions.fun_fact: He is respected as the 'Sage of Tea' for his contribution to Chinese tea culture.

questions.text: What was the relay-station postal system of the Mongol Empire, expanded by Ögedei Khan, called?
questions.fun_fact: Its messengers covered 200 to 300 kilometers a day, changing to spare horses at stations.

questions.text: In the 13th century, which ship type progressively replaced Viking-style knarrs in northern waters?
questions.fun_fact: Their flat bottoms let cogs settle level in harbor, making them easier to load and unload.

questions.text: The Treaty of Verdun of 843 divided which empire among three sons of Louis I?
questions.fun_fact: It was the first of four partition treaties, followed by those of Prüm, Meerssen and Ribemont.

questions.text: Which 1356 decree, issued under Emperor Charles IV, set out how the prince-electors chose the Holy Roman Emperor?
questions.fun_fact: It was named for the golden seal it carried, and it shaped the empire's constitution for more than 400 years.

questions.text: Who founded the Kamakura shogunate and became its first shogun in 1192?
questions.fun_fact: He set up his government in Kamakura, far from the imperial court in Kyoto.

questions.text: Which Grand Prince of Moscow defeated a Golden Horde army at the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380?
questions.fun_fact: His nickname Donskoy means 'of the Don', after the river where the battle was fought.

questions.text: Which dynasty's first emperor began building Hanoi's Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long in 1010?
questions.fun_fact: Most of the surviving structure dates from a rebuilding ordered by Gia Long in 1805.

questions.text: Which king of Serbia was proclaimed Emperor of the Serbs in 1346?
questions.fun_fact: His constitution, known as Dušan's Code, is considered perhaps the most important literary work of medieval Serbia.

questions.text: What is the study of the origin and history of words called?
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Ancient Greek étymon, meaning "true sense".

questions.text: What is a person who compiles dictionaries called?
questions.fun_fact: Lexicographers must work out how words with many meanings can be defined clearly.

questions.text: Besides Maltese, which language is official in Malta?
questions.fun_fact: The Maltese alphabet consists of 30 letters based on the Latin alphabet.

questions.text: How many letters does the modern Greek alphabet have?
questions.fun_fact: The 24-letter Ionic-based alphabet became standard across the Greek world by the end of the 4th century BC.

questions.text: Which variety of Chinese is dominant in Hong Kong?
questions.fun_fact: Before 1859 English speakers often called it "the Canton dialect".

questions.text: Which of these is a Slavic language?
questions.fun_fact: Common Slavic nasal vowels survive only in modern Polish, apart from a few little-known dialects.

questions.text: Luxembourgish, French and which other language are official in Luxembourg?
questions.fun_fact: Luxembourgish is a West Germanic language, but it differs from the German also used in the country.
