questions.text: The English word "language" comes from a Latin word for which body part?
questions.fun_fact: It reached English through Old French; the Latin lingua meant both "language" and "tongue".

questions.text: What is a word that means the opposite of another word called?
questions.fun_fact: Gradable antonyms, such as hot and cold, lie on a continuous spectrum between two extremes.

questions.text: What is a word like "smog", blended from two other words, called?
questions.fun_fact: Lewis Carroll first applied the luggage term to word blends in Through the Looking-Glass (1871).

questions.text: Which of these languages is tonal, using pitch to tell words apart?
questions.fun_fact: Most African languages, including Hausa and Yoruba, are tonal too.

questions.text: English, Malay, Mandarin and which other language are official in Singapore?
questions.fun_fact: English is the common language and the only one used exclusively in many public services.

questions.text: Besides Hindi, which language does India's central government use for official work?
questions.fun_fact: The 1950 constitution allowed English for only 15 more years, but a 1963 act kept it in use alongside Hindi.

questions.text: Which letter appears most often in typical written English?
questions.fun_fact: Edgar Allan Poe's story "The Gold-Bug" has a hidden treasure found by cracking a cipher with English letter frequencies.

questions.text: What is a word adopted from another language, like "café" in English, called?
questions.fun_fact: "Calque" is a loanword from French, while "loanword" itself is a calque of the German Lehnwort.

questions.text: The Rosetta Stone carries one decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and which other language?
questions.fun_fact: A French officer found it in July 1799 at Fort Julien, near the town of Rashid (Rosetta).

questions.text: Which two digraphs did Spanish dictionaries once alphabetize as single letters?
questions.fun_fact: Since a 1994 decision, chico is alphabetized after centro instead of after all words starting with cu-.

questions.text: Around 405 AD, Mesrop Mashtots devised a new alphabet for which language?
questions.fun_fact: The script originally had 36 letters; two more were added in the 13th century.

questions.text: Scottish Gaelic is most closely related to which of these languages?
questions.fun_fact: Scottish Gaelic developed out of Old Irish and became a distinct language in the 13th century.

questions.text: How many letters are in the basic Arabic alphabet?
questions.fun_fact: It is written right to left in a cursive style, and most letters have different forms by position.

questions.text: The Occitan language, or "langue d'oc", is named after its word for what?
questions.fun_fact: Dante contrasted the languages of òc, oïl and sì, named for the word for "yes" in Occitan, French and Italian.

questions.text: Bislama, an English-based creole, is a national language of which Pacific country?
questions.fun_fact: Its earlier French name was bichelamar.

questions.text: Under Ireland's constitution, what is the country's name in the Irish language?
questions.fun_fact: From 1922 to 1937 its legal names were the Irish Free State and, in Irish, Saorstát Éireann.

questions.text: What is the oldest known Slavic alphabet?
questions.fun_fact: Cyrillic later replaced it in most places, but medieval Croatia kept using it alongside Cyrillic and Latin script.

questions.text: In which of these Canadian places is Inuktitut an official language?
questions.fun_fact: It is one of the languages written with Canadian Aboriginal syllabics.

questions.text: What is the small v-shaped mark over letters like č and š called?
questions.fun_fact: Slovenes call it a "little roof" (strešica), and Lithuanians a "little bird" (paukščiukas).

questions.text: Outside astronomy, what does the Russian word "sputnik" mean?
questions.fun_fact: In astronomy it means "satellite", and it can also mean "spouse".

questions.text: Which law says the most common word occurs about twice as often as the second most common?
questions.fun_fact: In the Brown Corpus, "the" accounts for nearly 7% of all word occurrences.

questions.text: What is the smallest meaningful unit of language, such as "un-" or "-ness"?
questions.fun_fact: The word "unbreakable" contains three morphemes: un-, break and -able.

questions.text: Which of these became an official language of New Zealand in 2006?
questions.fun_fact: The 2006 Act created rights to use it throughout the legal system.

questions.text: Nicaraguan Sign Language, which emerged in the 1970s and 1980s, was developed by whom?
questions.fun_fact: Before the 1970s, deaf people in Nicaragua were generally isolated from one another.

questions.text: Which Madrid institution, founded in 1713, works to keep the Spanish language stable?
questions.fun_fact: It was founded to "fix" the Castilian language in its greatest propriety, elegance and purity.

questions.text: What are Ireland's officially recognized Irish-speaking districts called?
questions.fun_fact: They were first officially recognized in the 1920s, after the Gaelic revival.

questions.text: What is a simplified contact language with no native speakers called?
questions.fun_fact: The word "pidgin" itself derives from a Chinese pronunciation of the English word "business".

questions.text: Spoken Hindi is largely mutually intelligible with which language?
questions.fun_fact: Hindustani is sometimes written in the Latin script, called Roman Urdu or Romanized Hindi.

questions.text: The name of the constructed language Ido means what in Esperanto?
questions.fun_fact: Ido was meant to fix perceived flaws of Esperanto, which had been created 20 years earlier.

questions.text: Which logical constructed language did James Cooke Brown begin developing in 1955?
questions.fun_fact: It was designed for linguistic research, notably on the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis.

questions.text: Which linguist, who studied Native American languages, created Klingon for Star Trek?
questions.fun_fact: His first Star Trek job was dubbing Vulcan dialogue into Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan.

questions.text: The 19th-century constructed language Solresol is built on what?
questions.fun_fact: Its creator, Jean-François Sudre, was a French music teacher and composer who began it in 1817.

questions.text: "Boondocks", slang for remote countryside, comes from a Tagalog word meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: US troops brought the term into American English during the Philippine–American War (1899–1902).

questions.text: The word "bungalow" derives from a word for which region of South Asia?
questions.fun_fact: The first house in England classified as a bungalow was built in 1869.

questions.text: Which West African script for Manding languages did Solomana Kanté devise in 1949?
questions.fun_fact: "N'ko" means "I say" in all Manding languages.

questions.text: Rotokas, spoken on Bougainville Island, is written with only how many Latin letters?
questions.fun_fact: Central Rotokas has an extremely small consonant inventory and lacks phonemic nasals.

questions.text: Which Bronze Age script of Minoan Crete has never been deciphered?
questions.fun_fact: Linear A was adapted into Linear B, which the Mycenaeans used to write an early form of Greek.

questions.text: Extinct Tocharian manuscripts were found around the edge of which Asian basin?
questions.fun_fact: Their discovery upset the idea of an east–west centum and satem split in Indo-European.

questions.text: Which Chinese-character-based script was formerly used to write Vietnamese?
questions.fun_fact: The Tale of Kiều, one of the best-known works of Vietnamese literature, was written in it by Nguyễn Du.

questions.text: Dozens of scripts across South and Southeast Asia descend from which ancient Indian script?
questions.fun_fact: One survey counted 198 scripts that ultimately derive from it.

questions.text: Al-Sayyid Bedouin Sign Language arose in a village in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Deafness is so common there that deaf and hearing villagers share the language, and deaf people are not stigmatized.

questions.text: Michif, a mixed language of Canada's Métis, pairs Plains Cree verbs with nouns from which language?
questions.fun_fact: Its French-origin nouns keep their gender, while its Cree-origin verbs keep much of their complex structure.

questions.text: Which change in English pronunciation, mostly between 1400 and 1700, is a main reason spelling often mismatches speech?
questions.fun_fact: English spelling standardization began in the 15th and 16th centuries, before the shift finished.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich kaufe ein ___ Haus."?
questions.fun_fact: Neu is cognate with English new; the ending -es shows a neuter noun after ein.

questions.text: Which German word means "thunderstorm"?
questions.fun_fact: Gewitter is ge- plus Wetter, "weather", and is documented since the 9th century.

questions.text: What does the German word "verschlimmbessern" mean?
options: Make worse by trying to improve
questions.fun_fact: It blends verschlimmern, "to worsen", and verbessern, "to improve", and is attributed to Lichtenberg.

questions.text: Which German word means "experience"?
questions.fun_fact: Erfahrung is erfahren plus the noun suffix -ung; Old High German already had the form irfarunga.

questions.text: Which German word means "hedgehog"?
questions.fun_fact: Igel is a diminutive of an ancient word for hedgehog that also appears in Lithuanian and Armenian.

questions.text: What does the German word "Augenblick" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Augenblick literally means "glance of the eye", like English "blink of an eye"; the time sense dates to about 1300.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Er hat ___ Brille vergessen."?
questions.fun_fact: Brille comes from Middle High German berille, from Latin beryllus, "beryl"; it can also mean a toilet seat, short for Klobrille.

questions.text: What does the German word "bekommen" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Bekommen is cognate with English become, but the meanings drifted: German "get", English "turn into".

questions.text: Which German word means "unfortunately"?
questions.fun_fact: Leider began as the comparative of the old adjective leid, "distressing", still heard in "Es tut mir leid".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Er hat mir ein Buch ___."?
questions.fun_fact: Schenken originally meant "to pour a drink", as still seen in einschenken.

questions.text: Which German word means "umbrella"?
questions.fun_fact: Regenschirm is Regen, "rain", plus Schirm, "screen"; Schirm alone can also mean umbrella.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Er interessiert sich ___ Kunst."?
questions.fun_fact: Interessieren works both ways: "Kunst interessiert mich", or reflexively with für: "Ich interessiere mich für Kunst".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Du ___ nicht so laut sprechen."?
questions.fun_fact: Dürfen is irregular: ich darf, du darfst, but wir dürfen, with an umlaut in the plural.

questions.text: What does the German word "Zufall" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Zufall is a calque of Latin accidens, "that which befalls"; compare zufallen.

questions.text: What does the German word "Gedächtnis" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Gedächtnis comes from gedacht, "thought of"; a Gedächtnislücke is a gap in one's memory.

questions.text: Which German word means "responsibility"?
questions.fun_fact: Verantwortung is ver- plus Antwort, "answer": to be responsible is to answer for something.

questions.text: Which German word means "shoe"?
questions.fun_fact: Schuh is cognate with English shoe and Dutch schoen.

questions.text: Which German word means "to develop"?
questions.fun_fact: Entwickeln is a calque of French développer: ent-, "un-", plus wickeln, "to wrap".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Das Auto ___ Lehrerin ist rot."?
questions.fun_fact: The suffix -in marks feminine forms: Lehrer, Lehrerin; the feminine genitive article is der.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich habe ihn gestern ___."?
questions.fun_fact: Anrufen is separable, so the participle's ge- goes between prefix and stem: an-ge-rufen.

questions.text: Which German word means "grandma"?
questions.fun_fact: Oma is shared with Dutch; both languages say Opa for grandpa.

questions.text: Which German word means "kitchen"?
questions.fun_fact: Küche and English kitchen both trace back to Late Latin cocina.

questions.text: What does the German word "Sehnsucht" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Sehnsucht joins sehnen, "to long", with Sucht, once "sickness" and now "addiction".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich putze ___ die Zähne."?
questions.fun_fact: German Zahn and English tooth are cognates; the High German consonant shift turned t into z.

questions.text: Which German word means "weekend"?
questions.fun_fact: The modern Wochenende copies English weekend and spread in German around 1920.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Wir ___ heute ins Kino."?
questions.fun_fact: Gehen is cognate with English go; both descend from a Proto-Germanic verb.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Wenn ich reich wäre, ___ ich ein Haus kaufen."?
questions.fun_fact: Würde plus an infinitive is the everyday way to form the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) in German.

questions.text: Which German word means "habit"?
questions.fun_fact: Gewohnheit is gewohn, an old variant of gewohnt, "accustomed", plus the suffix -heit; Old High German had giwonaheit.

questions.text: What does the German word "Rucksack" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Rucksack literally means "back sack", and English borrowed the word unchanged.

questions.text: What does the German word "Fernweh" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Fernweh, literally "far pain", is the counterpart of Heimweh, homesickness.

questions.text: Which German word means "apple"?
questions.fun_fact: Apfel is cognate with English apple and Dutch appel.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich wünschte, ich ___ mehr Zeit."?
questions.fun_fact: Hätte is the Konjunktiv II of haben and expresses wishes that are contrary to fact.

questions.text: Which German word means "exception"?
questions.fun_fact: Ausnahme comes from ausnehmen, "to take out"; Keine Regel ohne Ausnahme means "no rule without exception".

questions.text: What does the German word "Handschuh" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Handschuh is literally "hand shoe", and Dutch handschoen is built the same way.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich habe keine Lust, heute früh ___."?
questions.fun_fact: With separable verbs, zu slips between prefix and stem: auf-zu-stehen is written as one word.

questions.text: Which German word means "lightning"?
questions.fun_fact: Blitz is related to English bleak and bleach, from an old root meaning "shine" or "flash".

questions.text: Which German word means "bakery"?
questions.fun_fact: Bäckerei adds -ei to Bäcker, "baker"; the same ending gives Metzgerei, the butcher's shop.

questions.text: What does the German word "Schlüssel" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Schlüssel comes from a root meaning "to close", also behind schließen; English slot is a cousin.

questions.text: What does the German word "Chef" mean?
questions.fun_fact: German Chef is borrowed from French chef, "head, boss"; it is a false friend, since a cook in German is a Koch.

questions.text: What does the German word "Kindergarten" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Friedrich Fröbel coined Kindergarten in 1840 for a place where children grow, not a literal garden.

questions.text: Which German word means "to forget"?
questions.fun_fact: Vergessen is cognate with English forget; both come from a root meaning "to get".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Wie ___ du?"?
questions.fun_fact: Heißen is related to the archaic English hight, which also meant "to be named".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Weil ich müde ___, gehe ich ins Bett."?
questions.fun_fact: Weil comes from the noun Weile, "while"; after it the verb moves to the end of the clause.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Wegen ___ Regens blieben wir zu Hause."?
questions.fun_fact: Wegen formally takes the genitive, though in everyday speech many people use the dative.

questions.text: What does the German word "Briefkasten" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Briefkasten is literally "letter box": Brief, "letter", plus Kasten, "box".

questions.text: What does the German word "Fledermaus" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Fledermaus joins an Old High German word for "wing" with Maus, "mouse", though bats are not rodents.

questions.text: Which German word means "challenge"?
questions.fun_fact: Herausforderung comes from herausfordern: heraus, "out", plus fordern, "to demand".

questions.text: Which German word means "prerequisite"?
questions.fun_fact: Voraussetzung comes from voraussetzen, "to presuppose", plus the noun suffix -ung.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Das Haus ___ 1990 gebaut."?
questions.fun_fact: Werden is the passive auxiliary; it is cognate with the obsolete English worth, as in "woe worth the day".

questions.text: What does the German word "gemütlich" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Gemütlich comes from Gemüt, "mind, disposition"; Gemütlichkeit names a warm, relaxed coziness.

questions.text: What does the German word "Kummerspeck" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Kummerspeck is literally "grief bacon": Kummer is sorrow and Speck is fat.

questions.text: What does the German word "Fingerspitzengefühl" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Literally "fingertip feeling", it describes sure instinct in handling delicate situations.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Es ist kalt, ich brauche ___ Mantel."?
questions.fun_fact: Mantel came via Old High German mantal from Latin mantellum; as a masculine noun it takes einen in the accusative.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Das Wetter war so schlecht, ___ wir zu Hause blieben."?
questions.fun_fact: The conjunction dass and the article das are historically one word; the spelling split is a convention.

questions.text: What does the German word "Feierabend" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Feierabend first meant the evening before a holiday; "Schönen Feierabend!" wishes someone a good evening off.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Das ist ___ Buch."?
questions.fun_fact: Mein is cognate with English my and mine; neuter nouns like Buch take mein with no ending.

questions.text: What does the German word "Lebensmittel" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Lebensmittel is literally "means of life": Leben, a linking -s-, and Mittel.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Der Kurs beginnt ___ Montag."?
questions.fun_fact: Am is a contraction of an dem, and German uses it for a specific day of the week: am Montag, am Freitag.

questions.text: Which German word means "dog"?
questions.fun_fact: Hund is cognate with English hound, which once meant any dog.

questions.text: What does the German word "Bürgersteig" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Bürgersteig, "citizen path", was introduced in the 19th century as a native alternative to Trottoir.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Wir fahren mit ___ Zug."?
questions.fun_fact: Mit always takes the dative; its Old High German ancestor was miti.

questions.text: What does the German word "Torschlusspanik" mean?
options: Fear of missing your last chance
questions.fun_fact: Torschluss was the shutting of the town gate at nightfall, leaving latecomers outside.

questions.text: Which German word means "to learn"?
questions.fun_fact: Lernen is cognate with English learn, while lehren means "to teach".

questions.text: Which German word means "although"?
questions.fun_fact: Obwohl is ob, once "if", plus wohl, "well"; obgleich and obschon are close cousins.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich ___ heute früh aufgestanden."?
questions.fun_fact: Verbs of movement or change of state, such as aufstehen, form the perfect with sein, not haben.

questions.text: What does the German word "Weltschmerz" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Jean Paul coined Weltschmerz, "world pain", and English borrowed it for a gloomy sense that the world falls short.

questions.text: Which German word means "job interview"?
questions.fun_fact: Vorstellungsgespräch joins Vorstellung, "introduction", with Gespräch, "conversation".

questions.text: What does the German word "Heimat" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Heimat comes from Old High German heimōti and carries an emotional sense of belonging that is hard to translate.

questions.text: What does the German word "Briefmarke" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Briefmarke is Brief, "letter", plus Marke, "mark"; collecting them is called Briefmarkensammeln.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Gestern ___ ich im Kino."?
questions.fun_fact: War is a past form of sein taken from the older verb wesan, which sein replaced as the infinitive.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Wir haben uns lange nicht ___."?
questions.fun_fact: Sehen is cognate with English see; the participle gesehen is formed with ge- and -en.

questions.text: Which German word means "environment"?
questions.fun_fact: Umwelt is um, "around", plus Welt, "world"; its biological sense was first used by Jakob von Uexküll in 1909.

questions.text: Which German word means "tomorrow"?
questions.fun_fact: Morgen means both "tomorrow" and "morning", and is related to English morrow.

questions.text: What does the German word "tschüss" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Tschüss came from Low German adjüs, which goes back to Spanish adiós or French adieu.

questions.text: Which German word means "income"?
questions.fun_fact: Einkommen is ein, "in", plus kommen, "to come": money coming in.

questions.text: Which German word means "pillow"?
questions.fun_fact: Its standard form Kissen avoids sounding like küssen, "to kiss".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Der Mann, ___ Hund laut bellt, ist mein Nachbar."?
questions.fun_fact: Dessen is the genitive relative pronoun and is followed directly by a noun without an article.

questions.text: What does the German word "Kopfkino" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Kopfkino, "head cinema", fits any daydream or worry that plays out in your mind like a film.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Er ___ gern Fußball."?
questions.fun_fact: Spielen covers playing a game, an instrument or a role, so one verb does many jobs.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Meine Schwester ___ Lehrerin."?
questions.fun_fact: Sein is irregular: its forms (bin, ist, war) come from several different ancient roots.

questions.text: What does the German word "Zeitgeist" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Zeitgeist is a calque of Latin genius saeculi, credited to Herder; English borrowed the word too.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich habe ___ Katze."?
questions.fun_fact: Katze is akin to English cat; Old High German had the form kazza.

questions.text: Which German word means "quickly"?
questions.fun_fact: Schnell is related to snell, an obsolete English word for quick or keen.

questions.text: What does the German word "Flughafen" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Flughafen is Flug, "flight", plus Hafen, "port": an airport is a "flight harbor".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Das Kind ___ Milch."?
questions.fun_fact: Trinken is cognate with English drink and is attested in Old High German since the 8th century.

questions.text: Which German word means "window"?
questions.fun_fact: Fenster goes back through Old High German fenstar to a West Germanic loan from Latin; it can also mean a time frame, as in Zeitfenster.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich ___ mich auf die Ferien."?
questions.fun_fact: Freuen comes from froh, "glad"; English frolic is a distant relative.

questions.text: What does the German word "wahrscheinlich" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Wahrscheinlich, literally "true-seeming", came via Dutch waarschijnlijk, a loan translation of French vraisemblable or Latin verisimilis.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Er ___ sehr gut schwimmen."?
questions.fun_fact: Können originally meant "to know", just as English can once did.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich komme ___ Deutschland."?
questions.fun_fact: Aus is cognate with English out; both come from the same Germanic word.

questions.text: What does the German word "Bahnhof" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Bahnhof joins Bahn, "track, railway", with Hof, "yard"; Hauptbahnhof means main station.

questions.text: Which German word means "cheese"?
questions.fun_fact: Käse goes back to Old High German kāsi; informally, Käse can also mean nonsense, as in "Das ist doch Käse!"

questions.text: Which German word means "to remember"?
questions.fun_fact: Erinnern comes from innar, "inner": to remember is to bring something inward.

questions.text: What does the German word "Quatsch" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Quatsch is built from quatschen, "to babble"; "So ein Quatsch!" means "What nonsense!"

questions.text: What does the German word "Krankenhaus" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Krankenhaus is literally "house of the sick": Kranker plus Haus.

questions.text: Which German word means "advantage"?
questions.fun_fact: Vorteil is vor, "before", plus Teil, "part"; its opposite is Nachteil.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Heute ist das Wetter ___ als gestern."?
questions.fun_fact: Besser is cognate with English better; the comparative of gut is irregular, just like good and better.

questions.text: What does the German word "Glühwürmchen" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Glühwürmchen is literally "little glowing worm": glühen, "to glow", Wurm and the diminutive -chen.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich warte ___ den Bus."?
questions.fun_fact: Warten takes auf plus the accusative, and is cognate with English ward, as in "to keep ward".

questions.text: Which German word means "to open"?
questions.fun_fact: Öffnen is related to English open.

questions.text: Which German word means "to complain"?
questions.fun_fact: Beschweren is related to schwer, "heavy": it first meant "to weigh down", and the sense "to complain" grew from "to burden oneself".

questions.text: Which German word means "circumstance"?
questions.fun_fact: Umstand goes back to Middle High German umbestand, a calque of Latin circumstans, "standing around".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich habe mich ___ meinen Chef geärgert."?
questions.fun_fact: Sich ärgern über, sich wundern über and sich freuen über all take über.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich habe gestern lange ___."?
questions.fun_fact: Schlafen is a strong verb: schlafen, schlief, geschlafen.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Heute ___ es den ganzen Tag."?
questions.fun_fact: Regnen comes from the noun Regen, which is cognate with English rain.

questions.text: What does the German word "Ohrwurm" mean?
options: Catchy tune stuck in your head
questions.fun_fact: Ohrwurm also names the earwig insect; English borrowed the tune sense as earworm.

questions.text: What does the German word "Ausflug" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Ausflug comes from ausfliegen, "to fly out", though no plane is involved.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Wo ___ du?"?
questions.fun_fact: Wohnen means to live in a place; leben means to be alive, so ask "Wo wohnst du?".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Wenn es morgen regnet, ___ wir zu Hause."?
questions.fun_fact: Bleiben forms its perfect with sein: "Wir sind zu Hause geblieben."

questions.text: What does the German word "Wortschatz" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Wortschatz is literally "word treasure"; Dutch has the same idea in woordenschat.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich ___ Hunger."?
questions.fun_fact: German says "I have hunger" where English says "I am hungry".

questions.text: What does the German word "Fremdschämen" mean?
options: Embarrassment on behalf of someone else
questions.fun_fact: It joins fremd, "external", with sich schämen, "to be ashamed".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich habe ihn nicht ___ können."?
questions.fun_fact: With a modal in the perfect, a replacement infinitive stands in for the participle.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich habe ___ Geschwister."?
questions.fun_fact: Geschwister means "siblings" and is almost always plural; for one, Germans say Bruder or Schwester.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich ___ jeden Morgen ein Brötchen."?
questions.fun_fact: Essen is irregular (du isst, er isst), and Essen is also the noun for "food" or "meal".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich ___ gern einen Kaffee."?
questions.fun_fact: Möchte is the Konjunktiv II of mögen and works as a polite "would like".

questions.text: What does the German word "Eselsbrücke" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Eselsbrücke, literally "donkey bridge", is a calque of Latin pons asinorum; Dutch says ezelsbrug.

questions.text: Which German word means "train or bus ticket"?
questions.fun_fact: Fahrkarte combines fahren, "to travel", with Karte, "card"; Fahrschein is a synonym.

questions.text: Which German word means "to disappoint"?
questions.fun_fact: Enttäuschen is ent- plus täuschen, "to deceive", a calque of French détromper.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich träume ___ einem Urlaub am Meer."?
questions.fun_fact: Träumen is cognate with Dutch dromen and English dream.

questions.text: Which German word means "brother"?
questions.fun_fact: Bruder is cognate with English brother and Dutch broer.

questions.text: What does the German idiom "Das ist mir Wurst" mean?
questions.fun_fact: A related idiom, "Es geht um die Wurst", means that something decisive is at stake.

questions.text: What does the German word "Schule" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Schule is cognate with English school and Dutch school.

questions.text: What does the German word "Besserwisser" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Besserwisser is besser, "better", plus Wisser, "knower".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich habe Angst ___ Spinnen."?
questions.fun_fact: English borrowed Angst from German; German pairs it with vor: Angst vor.

questions.text: Which German word means "to apply (for a job)"?
questions.fun_fact: Bewerben shares its root with werben, which can mean "to court" or "to advertise".

questions.text: What does the German word "Mogelpackung" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Mogelpackung joins mogeln, "to cheat", with Packung, "package".

questions.text: Which German word means "nevertheless"?
questions.fun_fact: Trotzdem is trotz, "despite", fused with dem, "that".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Die Kinder ___ im Garten."?
questions.fun_fact: Kind forms its plural with -er, Kinder; many nouns add an umlaut too, as in Buch, Bücher.

questions.text: What does the German word "Freund" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Freund is cognate with English friend; the feminine form is Freundin.

questions.text: What does the German word "Zwickmühle" mean?
options: Dilemma with no good way out
questions.fun_fact: Zwickmühle is also a double-mill position in the board game Nine Men's Morris.

questions.text: What does the German word "Fahrrad" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Fahrrad is fahren, "to ride", plus Rad, "wheel"; people often just say Rad.

questions.text: What does the German word "Entschuldigung" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Entschuldigung is built on Schuld, "guilt" or "debt"; the verb is entschuldigen.

questions.text: Which German word means "advertising"?
questions.fun_fact: Werbung comes from werben, which also means "to recruit" or "to court".

questions.text: Which German word means "frequent"?
questions.fun_fact: Häufig comes from häufen, "to heap up": frequent things pile up.

questions.text: Which German word means "neighbor"?
questions.fun_fact: Nachbar is nah, "near", plus an old word for "dweller", so a near dweller.

questions.text: What does the German word "Erdgeschoss" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Erdgeschoss literally means "earth floor"; the floor above it is the erste Stock.

questions.text: Which German word means "street"?
questions.fun_fact: Straße and English street both go back to Latin strata, a paved road.

questions.text: What does the German idiom "Ich drücke dir die Daumen" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Germans press their thumbs where English speakers cross their fingers.

questions.text: What does the German word "Tisch" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Tisch is cognate with English dish; both go back to Latin discus via West Germanic *disk.

questions.text: What does the German word "Gleichgewicht" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Gleichgewicht is gleich, "equal", plus Gewicht, "weight".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Wir haben den Termin auf Freitag ___."?
questions.fun_fact: Verschieben is strong: verschieben, verschob, verschoben.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Das Buch, ___ ich gestern gelesen habe, war spannend."?
questions.fun_fact: A relative pronoun copies the noun's gender and number but takes its case from its own clause.

questions.text: Which German word means "to forbid"?
questions.fun_fact: Verbieten is cognate with English forbid and Dutch verbieden.

questions.text: Which German word means "reliable"?
questions.fun_fact: Zuverlässig is built from zu, verlassen and -ig; sich verlassen auf means "to rely on".

questions.text: What does the German word "Geschäft" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Geschäft means both "shop" and "business deal", which is why Geschäftsmann is a businessman.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich habe keine Zeit, ___ ich muss arbeiten."?
questions.fun_fact: Denn is a coordinating conjunction, so the verb keeps its normal second position.

questions.text: What does the German word "Vorfreude" mean?
questions.fun_fact: A German saying goes: Vorfreude ist die schönste Freude.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Mit meinem ___ Freund gehe ich ins Kino."?
questions.fun_fact: After a possessive in the dative, a masculine adjective takes -en.

questions.text: What does the German word "Mitbewohner" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Mitbewohner is mit, "with", plus Bewohner, "inhabitant"; a woman is a Mitbewohnerin.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich frage mich, ___ er kommt."?
questions.fun_fact: Ob introduces an indirect yes-or-no question, like English "whether".

questions.text: Which German word means "meanwhile"?
questions.fun_fact: Inzwischen is in plus zwischen, "between"; it can also mean "by now".

questions.text: Which German word means "water"?
questions.fun_fact: Wasser is cognate with English water; both share a Proto-Germanic root.

questions.text: Which German word means "red"?
questions.fun_fact: Rot is cognate with English red and Dutch rood.

questions.text: Which German word means "to pick up (someone)"?
questions.fun_fact: Abholen is separable: "Ich hole dich um acht ab."

questions.text: Which German word means "to cancel (an appointment)"?
questions.fun_fact: Absagen is separable: "Ich sage den Termin ab."

questions.text: Which German word means "to swim"?
questions.fun_fact: Schwimmen is cognate with English swim and Dutch zwemmen.

questions.text: What does the German word "Hausaufgaben" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Hausaufgaben is Haus plus Aufgaben, "tasks", and is almost always plural.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Er hat sein Studium ___."?
questions.fun_fact: Abbrechen is separable and strong: abbrechen, brach ab, abgebrochen.

questions.text: Which German word means "to deliver (goods)"?
questions.fun_fact: A Lieferdienst is a delivery service; the noun Lieferung means "delivery".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich bin ___ meiner Arbeit sehr zufrieden."?
questions.fun_fact: Zufrieden is built from zu and Frieden, "peace": literally "at peace".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Im Sommer ___ ich nach Berlin."?
questions.fun_fact: Fahren changes its vowel: ich fahre, du fährst, er fährt.

questions.text: Which German word means "cold"?
questions.fun_fact: Kalt is cognate with English cold; the Dutch word is koud.

questions.text: What does the German word "Mittagessen" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Mittagessen is Mittag, "midday", plus Essen, "meal"; the evening meal is Abendessen.

questions.text: What does the German word "Staubsauger" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Staubsauger is literally "dust sucker", from Staub and saugen.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Je mehr ich lerne, ___ besser verstehe ich."?
questions.fun_fact: Je ... desto means "the more ... the more"; umso works too.

questions.text: Which German word means "bread"?
questions.fun_fact: Brot is cognate with English bread and Dutch brood.

questions.text: What does the German word "Geborgenheit" mean?
options: Feeling of being safe and cared for
questions.fun_fact: Geborgenheit is geborgen, "sheltered", plus -heit, and is hard to translate in one word.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Das Problem muss sofort ___ werden."?
questions.fun_fact: With a modal, the passive uses the participle plus werden: gelöst werden.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Ich danke ___ für die Blumen."?
questions.fun_fact: Danken, helfen and gefallen take the dative, so it is "Ich danke dir", never dich.

questions.text: What does the German word "Treppenwitz" mean?
options: Clever retort thought of too late
questions.fun_fact: Treppenwitz, "staircase wit", calques French esprit de l'escalier; it now more often means an absurd irony.

questions.text: Which German word means "to believe"?
questions.fun_fact: Glauben is related to English believe and Dutch geloven, and it can also mean "to think".

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Das Kind wurde von ___ Lehrer gelobt."?
questions.fun_fact: In the passive, the doer is introduced by von plus dative, often contracted: vom.

questions.text: Which German word means "car"?
questions.fun_fact: Auto is short for Automobil; German also gave English the word Autobahn.

questions.text: Which German word means "behavior"?
questions.fun_fact: Verhalten is the verb sich verhalten, "to behave", used as a noun; its root halten means "to hold".

questions.text: Which German word means "to hesitate"?
questions.fun_fact: "Ohne zu zögern" means "without hesitation".

questions.text: What does the German word "Wehmut" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Wehmut is Weh, "woe", plus Mut, here "mood"; the adjective is wehmütig.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Sie schreibt ___ Freundin eine Karte."?
questions.fun_fact: Schreiben takes a dative for the recipient, so a feminine noun needs ihrer.

questions.text: German: which word fills the gap in "Die Frau, mit ___ ich gesprochen habe, ist Ärztin."?
questions.fun_fact: Relative pronouns look like articles except in the genitive and the dative plural.

questions.text: What does the German word "Wecker" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Wecker comes from wecken, "to wake", a cousin of English wake.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "She has lived here ___ 2010."?
questions.fun_fact: Since is a contraction of Middle English sithens; it is cognate with German seit.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "He is good ___ playing chess."?
questions.fun_fact: At is cognate with Latin ad.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "There aren't ___ apples left."?
questions.fun_fact: Any is built from one plus the suffix -y.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "If it ___ tomorrow, we will stay home."?
questions.fun_fact: Beyond Old English and Germanic, the origin of rain is uncertain.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "My brother is taller ___ me."?
questions.fun_fact: Than and then are doublets: two forms of one old Germanic word.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "We ___ to the beach last Sunday."?
questions.fun_fact: The old past of go, yode, was replaced by went, the past of wend, in the 15th century.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "There is ___ umbrella on the table."?
questions.fun_fact: An comes from Old English an, the same word as one.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "I look forward ___ seeing you."?
questions.fun_fact: After look forward to, use a noun or an -ing form, as in "looking forward to having".

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "She is the girl ___ won the race."?
questions.fun_fact: In who, the /hw/ sound simplified to /h/ without a spelling change, so the w is silent.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "The film was so boring that I fell ___ during it."?
questions.fun_fact: Asleep is a plus sleep, where a once meant in or on.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "He didn't ___ the answer."?
questions.fun_fact: Know is remotely related to ken and to German kennen.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "The meeting is ___ Monday."?
questions.fun_fact: On is cognate with Dutch aan and German an.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "I'd rather ___ tea than coffee."?
questions.fun_fact: Rather began as the comparative of the old word rathe, meaning quick.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "I wish I ___ more time."?
questions.fun_fact: Wish is cognate with German wünschen.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "By the time we arrived, the film ___."?
questions.fun_fact: Pluperfect comes from Latin plus quam perfectum, meaning more than perfect.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "She is interested ___ astronomy."?
questions.fun_fact: Interested has a second sense, having a stake, as in "all interested parties".

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "He is the ___ student in the class."?
questions.fun_fact: Tall goes back to Old English ġetæl; the Oxford English Dictionary calls its sense development remarkable.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "I have never ___ sushi."?
questions.fun_fact: Eaten is eat plus -en, the old ending for past participles.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "I enjoy ___ to music."?
questions.fun_fact: Listen comes from Old English hlysnan, and is cognate with Swedish lyssna.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "He suggested ___ a taxi."?
questions.fun_fact: Suggest was coined from Latin suggestus, the participle of suggero.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "I'm not used ___ getting up early."?
questions.fun_fact: In "be used to", used is the past participle of an archaic verb use, meaning "to be in the habit of".

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "Hardly ___ arrived when it started to rain."?
questions.fun_fact: Hardly goes back to Old English heardlīce, built from hard plus -ly.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "Not only ___ she sing, but she also dances."?
questions.fun_fact: The same inversion turns "She can swim" into the question "Can she swim?"

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "The book, ___ cover is red, is mine."?
questions.fun_fact: Whose comes from Old English hwæs, the genitive of the word for who.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "I need to ___ a shower."?
questions.fun_fact: Take came into late Old English as tacan, probably borrowed from Old Norse taka, "to touch, take".

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "The movie was ___ good that we watched it twice."?
questions.fun_fact: So is cognate with Dutch zo and German so.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "Can you give me some ___ about hotels?"?
questions.fun_fact: The d in advice was added in the 15th century, influenced by advise and the prefix ad-.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "She has very ___ friends in the city."?
questions.fun_fact: Few is related to Latin paucus and pauper, and so to poor.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "We were ___ by the amazing view."?
questions.fun_fact: Amazed is often followed by at, with or by.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "A cat ___ four legs."?
questions.fun_fact: Have is related to heave, even though the two look quite different.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "I'm afraid ___ spiders."?
questions.fun_fact: Afraid began as the past participle of the Middle English verb afraien.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "Look! It ___ outside."?
questions.fun_fact: English weather verbs like snow take the dummy subject it, as in "it is snowing".

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "I'm looking ___ my glasses. Have you seen them?"?
questions.fun_fact: Look for can also be an archaic verb meaning to expect.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "This is the ___ book I have ever read."?
questions.fun_fact: Best is cognate with Dutch best and German beste.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "Tom ___ tennis every Saturday."?
questions.fun_fact: The origin of play beyond Old English plegian is uncertain.

questions.text: What does the English word "ubiquitous" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Ubiquitous is built on Latin ubique, which combines ubi, "where", with -que.

questions.text: What does the English word "reluctant" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Reluctant comes from Latin reluctor, "to struggle against".

questions.text: What does the idiom "break the ice" mean?
questions.fun_fact: The idiom treats the social distance between strangers as ice.

questions.text: What does the idiom "a piece of cake" mean?
questions.fun_fact: It is attested since 1936, originally in American English.

questions.text: What does the idiom "once in a blue moon" mean?
questions.fun_fact: The phrase is first recorded around 1833.

questions.text: What does the English verb "procrastinate" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Procrastinate comes from Latin pro- plus crastinus, "of tomorrow".

questions.text: In "We have run out of milk," what does "run out of" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Run out can also mean to expire or come to an end.

questions.text: In "She looks after her grandmother," what does "looks after" mean?
questions.fun_fact: The oldest sense of look after, from the 10th century, is to follow someone with your eyes as they leave.

questions.text: In "They put off the trip until May," what does "put off" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Put off can also mean to distract or disturb someone's concentration.

questions.text: What does the English word "ephemeral" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Ephemeral comes from Greek ephemeros, built from epi and hemera, "day".

questions.text: What does the English word "serendipity" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Horace Walpole coined it in 1754, after a Persian story about the Three Princes of Serendip.

questions.text: What does the English word "mellifluous" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Mellifluous joins Latin mel, "honey", and fluere, "to flow".

questions.text: What does the English word "gregarious" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Gregarious was borrowed from Latin gregarius in the 1680s.

questions.text: What does the English word "benevolent" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Benevolent displaced the Old English word welwillende, literally "well-wishing".

questions.text: What does the English word "frugal" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Frugal displaced the Old English spærhende, literally "spare-handed".

questions.text: What does the English word "bilingual" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Bilingual is bi-, "two", plus lingual, from Latin lingua, "tongue".

questions.text: What does the idiom "cost an arm and a leg" mean?
questions.fun_fact: The idiom is usually used after cost, but also after charge, pay and spend.

questions.text: What does the idiom "hit the nail on the head" mean?
questions.fun_fact: An English text from 1593 already says "hitteth the nayle on the head".

questions.text: What does the idiom "spill the beans" mean?
questions.fun_fact: One guess links it to Greek voting with colored beans, but that may be a folk etymology.

questions.text: What does the idiom "on the fence" mean?
questions.fun_fact: A longer version is "sit on the fence".

questions.text: In "She was brought up in Spain," what does "brought up" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Bring up comes from the older Middle English upbryngen, with the word order flipped.

questions.text: In "He turned down the job offer," what does "turned down" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Turn down can also mean to lower the volume, heat or light.

questions.text: What does the English word "tentative" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Tentative is related to tempt and tent through Latin tentare.

questions.text: What does the English word "ambiguous" mean?
options: Open to more than one meaning
questions.fun_fact: Latin ambiguus meant "moving from side to side" or "of doubtful nature".

questions.text: What does the English word "meticulous" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Latin meticulosus meant "fearful"; the "precise" sense arrived later via French.

questions.text: What does the English word "resilient" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Resilient comes from Latin resilio, "to jump back", which comes from salio, "to leap".

questions.text: What does the English word "scrumptious" mean?
questions.fun_fact: It probably comes from scrimp plus -ious.

questions.text: What does the English word "glimpse" mean?
questions.fun_fact: The verb comes from an earlier glimse, probably from Middle English glimsen.

questions.text: What does the English word "knack" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Knack may be imitative in origin, like crack.

questions.text: What does the English verb "eavesdrop" mean?
questions.fun_fact: The listening sense comes from standing where water drips off the eaves.

questions.text: What does the English word "naive" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Naive is a doublet of native, as both trace back to Latin.

questions.text: What does the English word "mischievous" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Mischievous comes from Old French mes- plus chever, from chef, "head".

questions.text: What does the English word "lukewarm" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Luke alone once meant lukewarm, so lukewarm says "warm" twice.

questions.text: Which English word means "to receive something to use for a while"?
questions.fun_fact: Borrow is cognate with Dutch borgen.

questions.text: Which English word means "to have an influence on"?
questions.fun_fact: Affect goes back to Latin afficere, "to act upon", built from ad- and facere, "to do".

questions.text: Which English word means "paper, envelopes and pens"?
questions.fun_fact: Spelled with -ary, stationary means "not moving"; stationery is the writing supplies.

questions.text: Which English word means "a basic rule or belief that guides behavior"?
questions.fun_fact: Principle comes from Latin princeps, built from primus, "first", plus -ceps, "catcher".

questions.text: Which English word means "to come before something else"?
questions.fun_fact: Precede combines Latin prae-, "before", and cedo, "to go".

questions.text: Which English word means "the usual weather of a region over many years"?
questions.fun_fact: Climate goes back, through Greek, to a root meaning "to incline".

questions.text: Which English word means "a young cat"?
questions.fun_fact: Kitten is usually explained as coming from an Old French diminutive of cat.

questions.text: Which English word means "extremely hungry"?
questions.fun_fact: Ravenous has nothing to do with ravens; it comes from a root about preying.

questions.text: Which English word means "to get money by working"?
questions.fun_fact: Earn comes from Old English earnian, from a Germanic noun meaning "harvest".

questions.text: Which English word means "a person you do not know"?
questions.fun_fact: Stranger comes from Old French estrangier, "foreign", and is related to French étranger.

questions.text: Which English word means "a large amount of water covering usually dry land"?
questions.fun_fact: Flood is cognate with Dutch vloed and German Flut.

questions.text: Which English word means "to look at something very quickly"?
questions.fun_fact: Glance first described a blow that strikes at an angle.

questions.text: Which English word means "unwilling to spend money"?
questions.fun_fact: The origin of stingy is uncertain; it may come from a dialect form of sting.

questions.text: Which English word means "two things happening together by chance"?
questions.fun_fact: Coincidence reached English from French and is built from coincide plus -ence.

questions.text: Which English word means "money paid regularly to use a home you do not own"?
questions.fun_fact: Rent comes from Latin reddere, "to give back", through Old French rente.

questions.text: Which English word means "not letting light through"?
questions.fun_fact: The Latin source of opaque, opacus, is of unknown origin.

questions.text: Which English word means "a sudden strong urge to do something"?
questions.fun_fact: Impulse comes through French from Latin, from a root meaning "to drive".

questions.text: Which English word means "easy to break"?
questions.fun_fact: Fragile is a doublet of frail and is related to fracture and fraction.

questions.text: Which English word means "to make something clear to someone"?
questions.fun_fact: Explain comes from Latin explanare, from ex- plus planus, "flat".

questions.text: Which English word means "a short sleep during the day"?
questions.fun_fact: Nap comes from Old English hnappian, "to doze".

questions.text: Which English word means "the land along the side of a river"?
questions.fun_fact: The money kind of bank comes from Italian banca, a moneychanger's bench.

questions.text: Which English word means "money you must pay to the government"?
questions.fun_fact: Tax is a doublet of task.

questions.text: Which English word means "to make something smaller or less"?
questions.fun_fact: Reduce comes from Latin re- plus duco, "to lead".

questions.text: Which English word means "extremely tired"?
questions.fun_fact: Exhausted also means depleted of resources.

questions.text: Which English word means "to be present at an event"?
questions.fun_fact: Attend comes from Latin attendo, from ad-, "toward", plus tendo, "to stretch".

questions.text: Which English word means "a feeling that something good may happen"?
questions.fun_fact: Hope is cognate with Dutch hopen and Swedish hoppas.

questions.text: Which English word means "certain to happen and impossible to avoid"?
questions.fun_fact: Inevitable comes from Latin in- plus evitabilis, "avoidable".

questions.text: Which English word means "full of life and energy"?
questions.fun_fact: Lively is simply life plus -ly.

questions.text: Which English word means "to make something better"?
questions.fun_fact: Improve comes from Anglo-Norman emprouwer, from prou, "profit".

questions.text: Which English word means "a scientist who studies stars and planets"?
questions.fun_fact: Astronomer displaced the Old English word tungolcræftiga.

questions.text: Which English word means "a large flat area of land"?
questions.fun_fact: The noun plain, a flat area of land, is a doublet of plane, piano and llano.

questions.text: Which English word means "a sound that comes back after hitting a wall"?
questions.fun_fact: Echo comes from Greek, and may share a root with sough.

questions.text: Which English word means "a person who watches an event"?
questions.fun_fact: Spectator is borrowed from Latin, from a verb meaning "to watch".

questions.text: What does the English word "hesitate" mean?
questions.fun_fact: Hesitate comes from Latin haesitare, an intensive of haerere, "to stick fast".

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "This jacket is similar ___ mine."?
questions.fun_fact: Similar came from French similaire, from Latin similis, "like".

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "The harder you practice, ___ you will play."?
questions.fun_fact: Better is cognate with Dutch beter and German besser.

questions.text: What does the idiom "burn the midnight oil" mean?
questions.fun_fact: The phrase first referred to burning lamp oil for light at night.

questions.text: Which English word means "an object you keep to remember a trip"?
questions.fun_fact: Souvenir is the French word for "memory".

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "She is said ___ the best chef in town."?
questions.fun_fact: Said is say plus -ed, from Old English sǣde.

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "She speaks English very ___."?
questions.fun_fact: Well comes from Old English wel, which could mean abundantly, very or fully.

questions.text: Which English word means "a doctor who looks after your teeth"?
questions.fun_fact: Dentist was borrowed from French dentiste and is related to dental and denture.

questions.text: Which English word means "not allowed by law"?
questions.fun_fact: Illegal is il- plus legal, borrowed from French illégal.

questions.text: Which English word means "to tell someone about a danger"?
questions.fun_fact: Warn comes from Old English warnian, "to take heed", and is cognate with German warnen.

questions.text: Which English word means "a long, angry speech"?
questions.fun_fact: Tirade was borrowed from French tirade, "monologue, speech".

questions.text: English: which word fills the gap in "The window ___ by the wind last night."?
questions.fun_fact: Broken is cognate with Dutch gebroken and German gebrochen.
